The Treatise on Dramaturgy,
Chapter Eight.
The Sages said:
Through your grace, we have heard everything regarding the successive arising of the dramatic sentiments (bhāvas) and aesthetic flavors (rasas); we now desire to know them further. (1)

How many kinds of sequential modes of dramatic representation (abhinaya-krama) should be performed by experts in drama? Furthermore, how is this representation to be carried out, and into how many varieties is it said to be divided? || 2 ||
O Great Sage, explain all of this according to its true nature: who is to be employed in which dramatic representation by one desiring success? (3)
Having heard those words of the sages, the sage Bharata replied again with a statement concerning the four modes of dramatic representation.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, I shall relate to you everything concerning why this dramatic performance was indeed presented according to the prescribed rules. (5)

Regarding what was stated—that there are four modes of representation (abhinaya)—we shall now explain them. Here it is asked: why is it called "representation" (abhinaya)? To this it is replied: the prefix *abhi-* [is used]. (p. 2)

The root *ṇīñ* has the meaning of "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*). When this [root] is established as *abhi-nī*, the form *abhinaya* is derived by adding the suffix *ac* according to the rule *erac*. This should be understood through the explanation of the root's meaning. Regarding this, there are two verses: || 6 ||
The verbal root *ṇī* (to lead), preceded by the prefix *abhi*, is determined to have the sense of "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*).
Because it leads [the performer] toward the performance, it is therefore remembered as *abhinaya* (acting). || 7 ||

Because it manifests various meanings through its application, being joined with the primary branches, the subsidiary limbs, and the minor members, it is therefore known as abhinaya (gesticulation). || 8 ||
O twice-born ones, this dramatic representation (abhinaya) of drama (nāṭya) is fourfold;
within it, drama is established in its many diverse varieties.

O Brahmins, dramatic representation (abhinaya) is known to be proclaimed as fourfold: indeed, it consists of the physical (āṅgika), the vocal (vācika), the artificial (āhārya), and likewise the internal (sāttvika). || 10 ||
The *sāttvika* [abhinaya] has already been described by me along with its various states (*bhāvas*);
now, listen as I explain the *aṅga-abhinaya* (the representation through limbs) first.

(3) But bodily [acting] is to be known as threefold: that which is produced by the body, that which is born from the mouth, and likewise that which is performed through movement, joined with the major limbs, minor limbs, and sub-limbs. || 12 ||
Endowed with the head, hands, waist, chest, sides, and feet,
and joined with the major and minor limbs, the compendium of dance consists of six parts.
Its six limbs are the head, hands, chest, sides, hips, and feet;
the eyes, eyebrows, nose, lips, cheeks, and chin are the secondary limbs (upāṅgas). || 14 ||
Its branches, its dance, and likewise its sprout—these are the elements of dramatic representation that performers should understand here. (15)

The branch (śākhā) indeed consists of bodily movement, while the sprout (aṅkura) would be the indication (sūcanā). Dance (nṛtta), however, is accomplished through aṅgahāras and is based upon the karaṇas.
O Brahmins, listen as I describe first the action of the head in facial expression, which is the basis for various emotions and sentiments. (17)
It is unshaken, shaken, cleansed, and indeed thoroughly cleansed; it is carried away, tossed about, completely shaken off, and likewise bent. || 18 ||
The head-gesture (śiras) should be known as being of thirteen types: the lowered, the turned away, the raised, the directed downwards, and the shaken. (19)
(4) Slowly, after the shaking [of the head], it should be shaken upwards and downwards;
that same [action] performed rapidly and repeatedly is the "shaken" (kampita) movement of the head. || 20 ||
When [the hand] held straight is tossed upward and downward, it becomes *ākampita*;
that which is moved repeatedly is here called *kampita*. || 21 ||
In questions concerning perception and apprehension, as well as in speaking of intrinsic nature,
and likewise in explaining or summoning, the head should be moved unsteadily.
A nod of the head is prescribed in cases of anger, deliberation, cognition, assent, and threatening; as well as in questions and words of excellence. (23)
The shaking of the head slowly and properly is intended as *dhuta*;
however, from shaking it rapidly, the head becomes *vidhuta*.
The head is shaken when something is undesired, in dejection, in wonder, in conviction, likewise when looking to the side, in an empty space, and in negation. (25)
When one is seized by cold, afflicted by fear, terrified, or likewise feverish,
or when liquor has just been drunk, the head becomes reeling.
When the head is moved from side to side, it is called *parivāhita*;
when it is shaken repeatedly sideways, it is called *ādhūta*. (27)
It is employed in accomplishment, wonder, joy, remembrance, and likewise in indignation; it is used in deliberation, hesitation, playfulness, and persistence. (28)
In pride, desire, and viewing, as well as in looking upward while standing at the side,
the head should be known as "shaken" (ādhūta) in cases such as self-conceit.
That which is cast downward once and then shaken is known as *śiras*;
it is prescribed for purposes such as conveying a message, summoning, and [the ritual] called *ālopa*.
The head should be known as "bent" (añcita) when the neck is slightly tilted to one side;
it is used for one who is diseased, fainting, intoxicated, in deep thought, or when supporting the jaw.
That which has the shoulders raised, the garment clinging [to the body], and the creeper-like eyebrows slightly contracted, should be known as *nihañcita*; one should employ this among women.

In pride, arrogance, and playful grace; in coquettish affectation and amorous agitation; in affected indifference, affected languor, paralysis, and jealous anger—therein lies the *nihnuta* (the concealed). 33.
That which is called *parāvṛtta* here is so named because it imitates a turning away;
it occurs when one turns the face away, looks behind one's back, and so forth. (34)
The head should also be understood as "uplifted" (utkṣipta) when it is positioned facing upwards;
it is employed as "uplifted" in connection with lofty or divine matters. (35)
The wise have declared that being situated with the face turned downward is "downward-directed" (adhogata);
the head is directed downward in shame, in prostration, and in sorrow. (36)
From whirling in all directions, the head is said to be "shaken" (lolita);
it is prescribed for conditions such as fainting, disease, intoxication, possession by spirits, and sleep.
The natural configuration, which is straight and innate, is produced from its own nature for the sake of auspiciousness, study, meditation, and actions that lead to victory. || 38 ||
There are many other varieties besides these that rely upon worldly dramatic representation;
these should be employed by performers in accordance with the nature of the world. (39)
Indeed, these thirteen types of head-work have been declared by me;
hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the *dṛṣṭis* as well.

The erotic, the terrifying, the comic, the pathetic, and likewise the marvelous, as well as the furious, the heroic, and the loathsome— these are to be known as the perspectives on the aesthetic flavors (rasas). (41)
Glossy, joyful, dejected, angry, haughty, fearful, loathsome, and astonished—these are the glances associated with the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva). 42.
Empty and indeed soiled, weary and likewise possessed of shame; exhausted and suspicious, dejected and likewise with closed eyes. || 43 ||
The contracted, the scorched, the crooked, and likewise the graceful;
the deliberated, the half-bud, the wandering, and likewise the agitated. (44)
The ākekarā, the vikośā, the trastā, and likewise the madirā—these are indeed the thirty-six glances; upon them, dramatic performance (nāṭya) is established. || 45 ||
I shall now fully explain the characteristics of this method of visualization, which is based on the various flavors of phenomenal existence, according to the application of the ritual actions. (46)
A gaze produced by joy and clarity, exceedingly lovely and full of passion, accompanied by the movement of the eyebrows and side-long glances, is prescribed for the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra). 47.
With the corners turned upward and fixed, and the pupils quivering and rolling upward, the gaze should be known as extremely terrifying when used for the *bhayānaka* (terrible) rasa. 48.
With the eyelids gradually contracted and the pupils slightly wandering,
a smiling gaze should be directed toward one who is deceitful. (49)
With the upper lids drooping, tearful, and with pupils sluggish from grief, the gaze directed toward the tip of the nose is the "compassionate" (karuṇā) look in the pathetic sentiment (karuṇa-rasa).
That gaze which has the tips of its lashes slightly contracted, with pupils turned upward in wonder,
gentle, and with wide-open corners, is the "wonderful" (adbhutā) gaze used for the marvelous (adbhuta).
Cruel, harsh, reddish, and wide-open, with fixed eyelids and pupils, and distorted by a frown—such is the gaze known as *raudrī* (fierce) in the context of the Furious Sentiment (*raudra-rasa*). 52.
The gaze that is radiant, blossoming, agitated, profound, and even in its pupils, with its center fully opened, belongs to the Hero; it is the locus of the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa). 53.

The loathsome gaze (bībhatsā dṛṣṭi) is considered to be one where the corners of the eyes are contracted, the pupils are rolling and floating, and the eyelashes are closely pressed together and motionless. (54)
Fixed on the tip of the nose, with unblinking eyes, moving downward, and with half-closed lids—such is this tranquil gaze. (55)
For these visions born of aesthetic flavor (rasa) should be understood as endowed with their specific characteristics;
hereafter, I shall describe those based upon the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva). 56.
With its center slightly opened, sweet, longing for a steady gaze, and possessing graceful, joyful eyebrows—this affectionate glance is born of the sentiment of love (rati). (57)
Moving, containing a smile, with pupils entering and blinking,
slightly contracted, and joyful— the gaze is thus proclaimed in the context of laughter. (55)
With eight or nine folds, with pupils obstructed and turbid like water, wandering about dejectedly—this is called the gaze of grief. (56)
With the eyelids steady and raised, the pupils turned upward, and the brows slightly knit, this gaze is prescribed for the angry look when one is enraged. (57)
That gaze of hers,
which is steady and wide-open at the pupils, is exceedingly haughty and born of great resolve.
With both eyelids closed due to lack of vision and pupils trembling with fear, the gaze directed outward is filled with terror in a state of dread. (59)
In the case of disgust (*jugupsā*), the gaze is contracted, with the pupils closed, directed toward the object of focus, agitated, and filled with loathing. (60)
With eyes wide open, the two lids lost and the gaze level, she is known as "Astonished," characterized by wonder. (61)
These permanent states (*sthāyibhāva*) should indeed be understood as the [foundational] gazes by the wise;
I shall now fully explain the characteristics of the transitory gazes (*sañcāriṇī dṛṣṭi*).
(10) Equanimous, with even [upper and lower] lips, unwavering, and perceiving emptiness;
this meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) which does not grasp at external objects is proclaimed as the "view of emptiness" (*śūnyadṛṣṭi*).
The gaze is one whose eyelashes are quivering, whose lids are not excessively closed, which has darkened corners, is itself soiled, and has wandering pupils. (64)
With its lashes drooping from fatigue, its corners thin and turned upward, and its pupils sinking as it falters—the exhausted gaze is thus described. (65)

But what is the gaze possessed of shame? It is one where the tips of the lashes are slightly raised, the lids droop and turn upward out of modesty, and the pupils are cast downward with bashfulness. (66)
That gaze in which the eyelashes of the furrowed brow are withered, which is slack and slow-moving,
and in which the pupil has gradually receded, is known as the "withered" (glānā) gaze.
The gaze is considered to be slightly tremulous yet steady, partially raised and turned sideways, with pupils dull and startled, and full of apprehension. (68)
The gaze of one who is despondent should be made with eyelids wide open, the corners turned outward, blinking, and the pupil slightly fixed. (69)
With half-closed lashes quivering, the upper lids slightly curved like buds, and the pupils opening slowly with pleasure—the "bud-like" gaze (mukulā) is thus described. || 70 ||
With the tips of the eyelashes contracted and the lids likewise contracted,
with the pupil sunken and curved, such is the contracted gaze (kuñcitā) as it is described. (71)
The gaze with its pupils dulling and its lids flickering, overwhelmed by heat and scorched, is indeed pained. (72)
Drooping, with its eyelids slightly contracted, looking askance slowly, hidden, with the pupil concealed, and oblique—such is the gaze described as *jihmā*. (73)
Sweet, with curved outer corners, accompanied by a contraction of the eyebrows and a smile, and possessing the transformations of love—that gaze is known as *lalitā* (graceful). || 74 ||
With the eyelids raised by reflection and the pupils dilated, with the face turned downward—this is the gaze known as "reflected" (vitarkitā). || 75 ||
The gaze known as *ardhākuñcitā* (half-closed) has lashes that are half-unfurled, lids that are half-blossomed with joy, and pupils that are slightly rolling. (76)
With unsteady pupils and a wandering,
agitated gaze, with wide-open and dilated eyes, such a wandering vision is described.
When the two eyelids throb and then become fixed and drooping,
and the pupil is agitated and rolling, this is the "disturbed" (vipluta) gaze.
With the corners of the eyes contracted, the lids meeting and half-closed,
and the pupil repeatedly turning back and forth— such a gaze is known as *ākekarā*. (79)
With both lids uncovered, fully blossomed, and unblinking, with a pupil that does not remain fixed—
such is the gaze known as "uncovered" (vikośā).
That gaze in which the eyelids are turned upward out of fear, the pupils are trembling,
and the middle of the eye is dilated with terror, is declared to be the "terrified" (trastā) look.
With a whirling waist and eyes turned toward the corners of her emaciated face, her gaze expanded at the outer edges;
such is the intoxicating look in the first stage of youth.
With the eyelids slightly contracted and the pupils slightly rolling, the gaze that moves without fixed stability belongs to one in the state of middle passion. (83)
The gaze that is both blinking and unblinking,
with the pupils slightly visible and directed toward the lower part [of the face], is prescribed for the lowest stage of intoxication.
Thus have these thirty-six views been characterized by me;
now learn their application, whether they be innate or born of objective entities. (85)

But those born of rasa have their gaze fixed upon the stable emotions (sthāyins) within the rasas themselves; listen now to how the transitory emotions (vyabhicāriṇīs) are situated among the moving emotions (sañcāris). || 86 ||

(13) An empty view is said to be afflicted even when one is tormented by reflection; it is also established as being stained in the case of world-weariness and discolored in the case of pallor. || 87 ||
*Śrāntā* is prescribed for exhaustion, fatigue, and perspiration; likewise, *lalitā* is used for modesty.
Similarly, *glānā* is employed for epilepsy, disease, and lassitude.
In a state of doubt, the gaze is known as "doubtful"; in a state of dejection, it is "dejected.
For the purposes of sleep, dreaming, and pleasure, the gaze is desired to be "half-closed" (mukulā). || 89 ||
It is used for the states of contraction, envy, the undesirable, and painful vision; likewise for being tormented, for despondency, and for injury and affliction. (90)

The *jihmā* (sidelong) glance occurs in envy (*asūyā*), as well as in dullness (*jaḍatā*) and laziness (*ālasya*). The *salalitā* (graceful) glance is recorded for steadiness (*dhṛti*) and joy (*harṣa*), while the *vitarkitā* (speculative) glance is for reasoning (*tarke*).
The eyes are half-closed in delight at the pleasure of fragrance, touch, and so forth; they are wandering in agitation, in alarm, and likewise in confusion. (92)
The *viplutā* (distraught) occurs in states such as fickle-mindedness, insanity, suffering, affliction, and death;
the *ākekarā* (squinting) occurs when looking at things difficult to behold or during glances of separation. (93)
Vikośitā occurs in those possessing pride, indignation, ferocity, and malice;
trasta is the gaze of one who is terrified; and madirā occurs in states of intoxication. || 94 ||
(14) These thirty-six views have indeed been correctly set forth; likewise for those views born of aesthetic sentiment (rasaja) and those born of emotional states (bhāvaja). || 95 ||
Listen as I describe the movements of those whose eyebrows are like the bow of Tārā:
whirling, turning, falling, shifting, and entering. (96)
Turning back, rising up, emerging, and likewise the natural state—these, O best of the twice-born, are the nine actions of the stars. (97)
Listen now with joy to the clear definition:
the rotation of the two pupils within the circle of the lids is known as *bhramaṇa*. (98)
Turning, moving, triangular movement, falling, and likewise drooping;
trembling, shaking, and it should be known that *pra-eśa* is internal penetration. (99)
*Vivartana* is a sidelong glance; *samudvṛtta* is an upward movement;
*niṣkrāma* and *nirgama* are said to be the same; and *prākṛta* is that which arises from one's own nature.
Now, learn their application within the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and emotional states (bhāvas). || 101 ||
Whirling and turning upward are for the heroic and the furious sentiments;
indeed, in the fearful sentiment, a departure accompanied by movement should be performed.
The entrance [of the hero] is desired here even for the comic (hāsya) and the loathsome (bībhatsa);
the exit should be performed in the pathetic (karuṇa), and likewise the departure in the marvelous (adbhuta). 103.
The Prākṛta language is used for the remaining [sentiments] and for the erotic (śṛṅgāra) when it is transformed;
this action, which rests upon worldly activity, is indeed established by its very nature. (104)
In this manner, one should employ the actions of the stars regarding tastes and dispositions;
now, in this very context, I shall explain the various methods of observation. 105.
Gazing straight ahead and looking around should be performed with evenness;
likewise for looking far off, looking upward, looking downward, and looking about.
That which is seen as level and gentle is known as "equal" (sama);
that which has the pupil positioned between the lashes, being triangular and turned askance, is called "sidelong" (sācīkṛta).
That which is joined with the detailed description of form is known as *anuvṛtta*;
that which is a sudden glance is called *ālokita*. (108)
Looking behind is *vilokita*, while looking from both sides is *pralokita*; looking upward should be known as *ullokita*, and looking downward as *avalokita*.
Thus is this procedure for visualization, which is the locus of the essence of all phenomena; now learn the ritual of the *puṭa* that follows it, pertaining to Tārā. 110.
Opening, closing, extended, contracted, even, turned away, throbbing, covered, and struck. (111)
The separation of the two lids is proclaimed as *unmeṣa* (opening);
their coming together is *nimeṣa* (closing), and the expansion is *prasṛta*.
Contracted (*ākuñcita*) is that which is bent (*kuñcita*); even (*sama*) is known as natural (*svābhāvika*).
Likewise, there are the turned-over (*vivartita*), the raised-up (*samudvṛtta*), the quivering (*sphurita*), and the throbbing (*spandita*). (113)
*Sthagita* is said to be *pihita*, while *āhata* is *vitālita*.
Now, learn the application of these in the context of *rasa* and *bhāva*.
In anger, the action is described as being turned away along with the closing and opening of the eyes;
in wonder, joy, and heroism, it is known as being extended forward.
In the perception of the undesirable, as well as in smell, taste, and touch, the gaze should be contracted;
in the erotic sentiment it should be level, and likewise quivering in cases of jealousy.
It should be covered during sleep, fainting, wind, heat, smoke, rain, and affliction by collyrium;
and it should be fanned away in cases of eye disease and injury.
Thus, regarding these sentiments (rasas) and emotional states (bhāvas), the procedure for the pupils of the eyes has been explained;
now learn the movement of the eyebrows which follows from this very [procedure]. 118.
Throwing upwards, throwing downwards, the frown, the clever, the contracted, the released, and the natural—thus it is sevenfold. (119)
The raising of the eyebrows is their upward movement, either simultaneously or one by one; by this very same sequence, their downward movement constitutes the downward-facing [expression]. (120)
The knitting of the eyebrows by raising their roots is known as *bhrukuṭī*.
When the eyebrows are slightly raised with a graceful, sweet, and elongated movement, it is called *catura* (the clever). (121)
When one or both eyebrows are slightly bent and curved, it is *kuñcita*; when one eyebrow is raised gracefully, it is *recita*. (122)
But that which is born together is known as the innate action, the inherent nature;
now I shall fully explain the purpose of their aesthetic flavors and emotional states.
In anger, in deliberation, in sportiveness, in playfulness and the like, as well as in naturalness, and likewise in seeing and hearing, one should raise a single eyebrow. (124)
The *utkṣepa* (upward movement) is used for astonishment, joy, and anger—indeed, for both [the male and female characters];
the *pātana* (downward movement) is used for envy, disgust, laughter, and smelling. 125.
In places of anger that are inflamed, the wise man should employ a frown;
[he should employ it] in the erotic, the graceful, the gentle, pleasant touch, and awakening. (126)
In such circumstances,
one should employ wit when there is conversation between a man and a woman consisting of various changing states.
In the *moṭṭāyita*, *kuṭṭamita*, and likewise in the *kilikiñcita* [sentiments], the *nikuñcita* should be employed; however, the *recita* is to be applied in dance (*nṛtta*).
One should likewise perform the natural [expression] when the states are not pierced;
thus has the action of the eyebrows been explained—now learn the action of the nose. (129)
The wise have declared that the nose is of six kinds: the natural, the bent, the drawn-out, the with-sigh, the contracted, and the distorted.
The *natā* (bent) is characterized by the lids being repeatedly closed; the *mandā* (slow) is known as that which is relaxed;
the *vikṛṣṭā* (drawn-out) has its lids fully opened and draws in the breath with an upward exhalation. || 131 ||
The nose that is contracted, slightly bent, and even is known as its natural state;
this is indeed the characteristic of the nose—now learn its application. (132)
When women are overcome by the tremors of passion or when they are sighing,
the nose should be bent downward by those who perform the art of drama.

One should employ it softly in states of world-weariness, longing, and anxiety, as well as in grief; one should employ it intensely in the sentiments of the Frightful and the Heroic, and likewise in cases of strong odor and distance.
Likewise, when smelling something desirable or when exhaling, one should employ a long exhalation;
and a contraction of the face should be made in cases of disgust, envy, and the like. (135)
In the remaining [remaining] states, experts should likewise recognize the natural [expressions]:
the emaciated, the blooming, the rolling, the trembling, the contracted, and the even.
Six types of swellings have been indicated; their characteristics are now described:
it should be known as *kṣāma* (emaciated) when depressed, and *phulla* (full-blown) when expanded. (137)

That which is extended is called *ghūrṇamātra*; it may be trembling (*kampita*) or quivering (*sphurita*). It may be contracted (*kuñcita*) or shriveled (*saṃkucita*); that which is even (*sama*) is said to be natural (*prākṛta*). || 138 ||
The characteristics of the cheeks have been declared; now learn their application:
they should be emaciated during states of suffering, and blossoming indeed during great joy. (139)
The *ghūrṇa* (rolling) movement occurs in enthusiasm and pride; the *kampita* (trembling) in anger and joy;
and the *kuñcita* (contracted) movement, accompanied by horripilation, occurs upon touch, in cold, fear, and fever. (140)
In the remaining states, the natural function (gaṇḍakarma) occurs;
these are turning, trembling, emission, and concealment. (141)

The six qualities of the lower lip are: *saṃdaṣṭaka* (biting), *samudga* (closing together), *vikūṇana* (contracting), *vivarta* (turning away), *vepana* (trembling), and *kampana* (shaking). || 142 ||
Departure is emission, while entry is concealment;
that which is bitten by the twice-born is *saṃdaṣṭaka*, and natural elevation is *samudga*. (143)
Thus the characteristics of the lips have been declared; now learn their application:
they are employed in expressions such as envy, pain, contempt, and laughter. (144)
*Kampana* (trembling) occurs in feelings of cold, fear, anger, and haste;
likewise, *visarga* (emission) occurs in the amorous play of women, in a side-long glance, and in the act of coloring [the lips].

The *vinigūhana* (concealment) gesture is employed in acts of deception; the *sandaṣṭa* (biting) gesture is used in acts of anger; the *samudga* (clasping) gesture is for compassion; and the *cumbana* (kissing) gesture is for rejoicing.
Thus the actions of the lips have been described; now learn those of the chin:
*kuṭṭana* (crushing), *khaṇḍana* (biting), *chinna* (cutting), *cukkita* (champing), *lehita* (licking), and *sama* (even).
And here, the chin is marked by the act of biting;
gnashing is the friction of the teeth, while clashing is their repeated breaking apart. (148)
*Chinna* (cut) is a firm embrace; *cukkita* is a sudden release from a distance. *Lehana* is licking with the tongue; *leha* is a slight contact that becomes equal [to the previous]. || 149 ||
When the lower lip is bitten by the teeth, the application of these [mantras] is "it is bitten";
for those seized by fear, cold, fever, or anger, there shall be a crushing [of the affliction]. (150)
There is an interruption during recitation, Vedic study, conversation, or while eating;
and it is interrupted by a cut, illness, fear, cold, physical exertion, weeping, or death. (151)
In yawning, the action is "slipped" (cukkita); likewise, in longing, it is "licking" (lehana). In natural states, it is "even" (sama); in acts of anger, it is "bitten" (sandaṣṭa). || 152 ||
Thus, regarding the action of the teeth, lips, and tongue, there is the operation of the chin;
and [the movements] are the withdrawn, the shaken, the bent, and the curved. (153)

Likewise, the *udvāhi* (upward-moving) [gaze] is open; however, the actions born therein are turned away (*vyāvṛtta*) and withdrawn (*vinivṛtta*). The *vidhuta* (shaken) [gaze] is extended obliquely. || 154 ||
Downward-facing, bent back, bent forward, slightly extended, with parted lips, opened wide, raised upward, and cast aside. (155)
Performers should employ [these gestures] for women when they have turned away from malice, or when they are affected by envy and anger, or during acts such as contemptuous sport. (156)

The *vidhuta* (shaken) gesture is used in warding off, as well as in expressions such as "it is not so," and the like; the *nirbhugna* (bent) gesture is also to be understood for deep gazes and similar actions. || 157 ||

Commentators explain the "acceptance" [of the object] through the application of *rocanā* and sandalwood paste for auspicious *tilaka* marks and the like. By *rocanā*, a reddish luster is indicated.
In that case, the gesture is performed by joining the two ring fingers. As it is said:
"Upon seeing an ascetic, the two [hands] should be raised and turned away. (p. 34)
And they should be made facing each other at the sight of the doorway. || 35 ||
They should be made facing upwards and downwards, positioned at the front of the mouth, during the battle with the submarine fire (vaḍabānala) and upon seeing the sea-monsters (makara). 36.
By this very [method], the waves of monkeys leaping, as well as the wind and women, are to be enacted in drama by those skilled in dramatic art. (37)
When gazing at the crescent moon, the thumb should be extended forward;
however, when men are traveling, it should be turned away from them by those who employ it. (38)
When the hand is in the tripatāka position and turned backward,
with the index finger and middle finger [extended], it is then called kartarīmukha.
On the path, with face cast downward, he performs the acts that delight the stage of his footwork;
thus, who is the one who uproots [obstacles], and by whom is Indra brought under control?
Both pleasure and pain are easily endured.
*Ālambhana* means touching the body; *drohikācamana* refers to the sipping of water by a malicious person. Therefore, the suffix *kan* is applied even when it is a name (*saṃjñā*).
This is indeed a name, as it cannot be derived from the root *labh* (to obtain). It is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) because [the object] is very small.
Here, due to lack of respect or excessive affection, one touches with the ring finger itself; thus, one goes upward.

"Amīha-utara-u (? refers to the moving of a decorative mark (*alaka*) from one place to another for the purpose of arranging it, as when Udayana moved Susaṅgatā’s mark in the *Ratnāvalī*. Others maintain that it refers to the showing of the forehead (*alika*), such as in the phrase "the breaking of high locks of hair" (*uttālālakabhañjanāni*) through the breaking of the decorative mark (*alakabhañjana*).

He defines the *kartarīmukha* (scissors-mouth) gesture: by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "tripatāka and," the subsequent [definition] is brought forward. "With edges not joined" (*avolikinī*) means, that is to say, unconnected. Such a form is produced for the *kartarī* and is likewise performed in expression (*abhinīyate*).
The word "on the path" (*pathi*) is a separate term; in cases such as "here and there," it indicates the way. Therefore, in this context, it is with the face turned downwards.
It is connected [to the following]: *caraṇa-racanā* is the decoration of the feet with musk and the like, such as the drawing of leaf-patterns;

*rañjana* is the coloring with lac-dye. A *raṅga* is that in which the heart is colored—namely, a square design made with saffron and the like, such as a *catuṣkoṣṭha* or a *tilaka*; one who creates that is called *raṅgayati*.
But with the face turned upwards, one should fashion the fang, the horn, and the line. (40)

One should perform [the ritual] with the "fallen," "death," "transgression," and "reversed" movements, as well as the "placed" [movement], using the scissors-like gesture with the tips of the fingers in a split and curled manner.
Whether joined together or separate, it is employed by those who know it upon the backs of deer, yaks, buffaloes, celestial elephants, and bulls, as well as on city gates and mountain peaks. (42)
That hand whose fingers, together with the thumb, are bent like a bow is known as the *ardhacandra* (half-moon); its application in ritual acts will now be described.

By the word *eva* (only/just), he describes the movement: immediately after the face characterized by the index finger has gone downward, there is looking back, then again going downward, and then again looking back.
"Bitten" (*daṣṭam*) refers to the act of biting and similar actions such as tearing, [extending] from the region of the nose to the end of the ear.
While walking, [one should avoid] touching a horn with one's own limbs within the range of two cubits; the reading of a document placed upon a leaf is [to be avoided].
Transgression is an offense. "Parivṛtta" means turned away or reversed.
"Vitarkita" means conjecture or deliberation. "Nyasta" means depositing. "Bhedana" means inversion.
The middle two [fingers] reaching the back of the index fingers, and then their movement, followed by their return to their original form—this is a *dvandva* compound denoting a collective.

By this, one should infer the application of the term as a compound, a non-compound, or in reverse order, such as "twice," "thrice," and so forth. This refers to the form of the fingers belonging to the "scissors-mouth" (*kartarīmukha*) [mudrā].
The face is the primary part; thus, the connection is that it is "accompanied by bending and turning.

Regarding the half-moon (ardhacandra), he says "together with the thumb"; since the thumb is also bent like a bow, this precludes the interpretation of it being merely a curved [finger]. It is "well-known," meaning its form is established by its very name.
And by those [rays] moving upward, young trees are scorched above;
by this [process], young trees, crescent moons, conch shells, jars, and bracelets [are produced].
It is characterized by expulsion, exertion, a middle comparison, and fullness. || 44 ||
The expressive application (abhinaya-yoga) for women's waist-bands, girdles, hips, faces, forehead-ornaments, earrings, and so forth, should be performed with the half-moon (ardhacandra) [mudrā]. 45.
In the Arāla mudrā, the first finger (the index finger) should be bent like a bow, the thumb likewise contracted,
and the remaining fingers separated, turned upward, and curled at the hand.
By this [gesture], the qualities of courage, audacity, heroism, beauty, fortitude, and divine profundity are indicated.

From the literal meaning of the term "half-moon" (*ardhendu*), it is understood that by the expression "moon-streak" (*śaśilekhā*), only a mere crescent is to be represented; this is stated to be performed with the index finger slightly extended. As for "conch" (*kambu*)... [text fragment].
Thus it is to be enacted by him; however, its specific grasping will be explained in the section on *karkaṭa*. A bracelet is [held] facing the interior of the forearm.

"Driving out" (*nirghāṭana*) means expulsion by force. Regarding the phrase "the sounding of an iron forest," that is incorrect; rather, one should enact "exertion" (*āyasta*), which is fatigue, by turning away and displaying the playfulness of the cheeks and eyebrows. In the middle—

That which is compared to the belly and so forth is called an *upamā* (simile); from that, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied. Thus, the meaning is this: one should represent the leanness (*kārśya*) of the waist by means of that [comparison]. And "pīna" means stout; [the word] "ardha" refers specifically to the middle part. Because of the word "ca" (and), one should represent it with two half-moons (*ardhacandra*). Others, however, [read] "pānaṃ."

They explain *capaka* and so forth as "drinking," reading [the text] accordingly. *Jaghana* is the front part of the buttocks and the region of the hips. On the surface of the face, the *patrāṇi* are decorative designs (*bhaṅgāḥ*).
A *talapatra* is a specific type of ornament. A *patra* is either a tooth-design or a lotus petal.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), lotus stalks and so forth are meant. This [gesture] should be performed by one born in each respective field (*kṣetra*) according to the requirements: the union of both sides, or the two ends of the sides being turned downward, either individually or together with another.

Regarding the *arāla* [hand], he says: "The first is bent at the joint. The "first" is the index finger (*tarjanī*); the others are the middle finger (*madhyamā*) and so on, ending with the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*).
"They stand not far from the backs of those in the east. This hand is *arāla* because of its curvature.

In such expressions as *arālapakṣman*, the word *arāla* has the meaning of "crooked. *Sattva* is steadfastness; *śauṇḍīrya* is pride; *vīrya* is energy; *kānti* is beauty; *divya* refers to that which is situated in the sky; and *gāmbhīrya* is depth.
Likewise, benedictions and states of being designated as beneficial should be performed. (47)
Furthermore, by this [means], the gathering of women's hair as well as its elevation, and likewise the description of one's own entire body, should be performed. 48.
The yoga of the marriage of curiosity is performed by circumambulation alone;
and the union [is formed] by the joining of the tips of the fingers in a svastika shape, indeed in a circular manner. (49)
One should perform circumambulation and the circular movement, as well as the great assembly; and whatever substance is fashioned from the earth and wood, that too should be represented. || 50 ||

That by whose power facial expressions are not perceived during states such as anger, joy, or fear is known as "depth" (gāmbhīrya). Benedictions such as "svasti," "bhadram," and "puṇyāham" are designated as "beneficial" (hita).

These are the states of happiness. In that regard, in the heart, at the side, and in front, there is movement—whether by remaining steady or by moving—and the performance [of gestures] according to what is appropriate. Even in these parts, it should be performed with a face that is not distorted (*arāla*). "Seizing" (*sa-graha*) refers to the binding of the hair; "drawing out" (*utkarṣa*) is the act of making it disheveled. Because of the repeated seizing, there is an interval [between actions] two or three times.

"Going, wandering, and so forth are obtained. "In that very manner" means it should be performed in such a way that there is a description of all the limbs. By this, moving from the second side to one's own side is obtained. *Kautuka* refers to the customary practice of the bride and groom prior to the wedding; it is well known as the "inner wedding" (*antarvivāha*).

The marriage ceremony takes place with the fire as witness. The union of the tips of the fingers of both hands in the form of a *svastika*, characterized by that [gesture], should be enacted as the ritual of the wedding-festival (*kautuka-vivāha-yoga*), moving in a circular manner toward the right (clockwise) direction.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the word "tu" (but/rather). The particle "eva" (only/just) is to be construed out of its natural order.
Conjunction (*samprayoga*), however, consists merely of close contact, arising solely from the joining of the tips of the fingers in the *svastika* gesture;
this pertains to the deities and involves circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*).
It is used for summoning, warding off, and creating various forms;
it is auspicious for removing sweat, smelling fragrances, and for all that is auspicious.
However, those rites previously described as being performed with the *trapuṭaka* hand should be properly employed by women through the application of haste.
When the ring finger of the *arāla* hand is curved, that hand is called the *śukatuṇḍa*; now learn its function. (53)

A circular arrangement is round; it represents a great crowd or a multitude of people. One should perform the gesture by moving from one side to the other along this very circle. In summoning, the fingers fall [toward the body]; in warding off, the fingers are cast outward. This is the formation.
"An unprecedented rising has arisen; O Lord, I am your ornament," and so forth. "Nishsheṣeṇa" means completely, or measurement, or delimitation, or existence, as in "jalaṇihi-alaṃvemā.
Others say "nirdāna" means the uprooting of grass and the like. Others say it means a non-existent creation, repetition, or uprooting. [The word] "aneka" [is used].

Where "separated" (pṛthagbhūtam) is said to mean the absence of connection, there the application of the word *vahiḥ* (outside) is used with the fingers extended, as in examples such as *kahiṃ ha kahiṃ ha*. Regarding the fragrance of a scent, there is the act of smelling. The reading is *śubhaḥ śubhe caiṣa*; the meaning is that this [gesture] pertains to the hand.

Others read "caiva" (and indeed), supplying an ellipsis; by means of the particle "eva," they state that the quality of being directed toward that field belongs specifically to the hand. Whatever actions of the *tripatāka* hand—such as invocation (*āvāhana*) and descent (*avataraṇa*)—are to be represented through dramatic performance, those same actions should also be employed by women through the application of the proper technique for the *arāla* hand.
However, the *tripatāka* [gesture] is not prohibited for them; rather, in place of the *tripatāka* used by men, the *arāla* is prohibited.

Regarding the phrase "parrot-beak" (*śukatuṇḍa*) for eating and idleness: the particle *tu* indicates a distinction from what precedes it. The second occurrence of the word *api* has the sense of "also," permitting a curvature of the index finger as well, because of its similar shape. By the term "parrot-beak,"...

By this [term], however, one expresses the meaning: "I am not," "you are not," or "there is no task to be done"; and it is used with contempt in the context of summoning, dismissal, or saying "shame! (dhik). (54)
That hand whose fingers are positioned with their tips toward the center of the palm, and over which the thumb is placed, is designated as the *muṣṭi* (fist). || 55 ||
This [knowledge] applies to striking, exertion, advancing, and likewise to pressing; as well as to massaging, and to the grasping of swords, clubs, staffs, and spears. || 56 ||

For in each case, this meaning of the sentence is indeed singular: "neither I, nor you, nor the task. This is not a gesture of total negation; rather, it refers to the state of *artha*—that is, when there is a purpose (*arthanā*) such as in a quarrel born of jealousy and affection. The word *artha* here means "purpose" (*erac*, Pāṇini 3.3.56).

When there is a contemptuous summons and a dismissal by the casting of five fingers, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consists of touching [the object] once, twice, or thrice according to the method of application. By the word "fie" (*dhik*), which carries the sense of censure, that which is unworthy of acceptance is indicated; for what is the use of one defiled by the sin of killing a child?
In such passages, the meaning is "this is the gesture" (*bhinaya*).
Regarding the fist, he says "that of which the fingers... [and so on]. By saying "in the middle of the palm," he dispels the doubt that it refers to the base of the thumb.
By saying "properly situated at the tips," he avoids the faults of being hidden or sparse at the ends. By saying "above,"...

The meaning is that one presses the region of the middle fingers. "Designated" means that in common worldly usage, the word *muṣṭi* (fist) is well-known in this very sense. "Exertion" (*vyāyāma*) refers to seizing the forearm of an opponent in combat, in sword-fighting, and so forth; by the inclusion of the term *sakala* [sword], it includes dagger-fighting, wielding a staff, and the like.

It should be applied. Regarding "nirgama" (emission), it refers to [the application of] ginger, *surasā*, and so forth. Regarding "pīḍana" (pressing), it refers to the pressing of the breasts or the milking of buffaloes and other animals.
Regarding "saṃvāhana" (massaging), it refers to the kneading of clay. Regarding "asi-yaṣṭīnām," likewise, it refers to massaging, warding off, or wiping.
And when the thumb is raised from this very fist, that hand is to be known by practitioners as the *śikhara* (peak) mudrā. || 57 ||

[The application of this art] is for the discharge of arrows, goads, hooks, and bows, as well as for the throwing of lances and spears, and for the coloring of the lower lip and feet, and for the removal of impurities. || 58 ||
When the index finger of this very same mudrā called Śikhara is bent and pressed down by the two thumbs, it is then known as the Kapittha. || 59 ||

The groups of weapons—the sword, bow, discus, tomara-club, spear, mace, javelin, and thunderbolt—are to be represented through gesture; however, one must also act in a manner that is wholesome and truthful.

When the ring finger and the little finger are raised and curved, he says that this is the *śikhara* [mudrā]. The repetition of the term "fist" (*muṣṭi*) is for the purpose of indicating that, within the scope of those who employ the fist, when there is something to be represented by the *śikhara*, or when there are two [objects], or in actions such as firm pressing and so forth, one should employ the fist; therefore [he says it again].
Thus it has been stated by the practitioners. "Raśmi" means a rein, a tether, or a ray;

the connection [of the term] is with their "saṃvāhana," which means grasping. And here, there is the application of either both or one [of these], in positions such as supine, face-down, lateral, upward, and so forth. According to the method of application, there is the raising of the *ālaka* (eyebrow).
Or, there is the pressing of the cheeks and so forth for the purpose of bending [the limbs].

He speaks of the *kapittha* (wood-apple) seal; the mention of its name is as before, and its purpose is as follows: in this seal shaped like a wood-apple, the thumb and index finger are the two fingers. "Weapons" means arrows and the like used for drawing them back. This is the task to be performed.

In this context, a snap of the fingers (*choṭikā*) is the proper application. Now, he describes the *khaṭakāmukha* [hand gesture] as "with the upraised and curved [fingers]. Here, the ring finger and the little finger are upraised and curved. Furthermore, because of the repetition of its name, its application is in such matters as drawing a bow, performing a task, speaking the truth, or taking wholesome food.
But at that time, this very same *kapittha* [mudrā] becomes the *khaṭakāmukha*. (60)

The offering of oblations, the offering of sacrificial food, the parasol, the carrying of the staff and the dragging of the rope, the waving of the fan, the holding of the mirror, as well as the breaking and the grinding; || 61 ||
Holding onto long staffs and grasping at pearl necklaces, as well as hanging onto flower garlands, wreaths, and the ends of garments. (62)
The tasks are churning, pulling at the ladle, gathering flowers, and pricking with a goad;
and the tasks are likewise drawing with a hook and a rope, and gazing upon women. 63.
When the index finger is extended in the hand known as *khaṭaka*, it should then be recognized by practitioners as the hand called *sūcīmukha*. (64)

The word *turu* is a suffix indicating distinction from the preceding; the second *tu* is for emphasis. "Slight separation" (*viralatvam manāk*) occurs between the ring finger and the little finger; by the use of the word *saha*, there should be no apprehension of a complete disjunction. Regarding the term *khaṭakāṅkṣāyām*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied to form *khaṭaka* in the sense of "one afflicted by hunger, thirst, and thirst" (*kṣuttṛṭpipāsārtayoḥ*). Thus, it is *khaṭaka*.

Because this [hand] is described as being at the mouth of the *viṭabhogra* (?), it is therefore called the *khaṭakāmukha*. The *hotra*—the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and so forth—is held with the palm facing upward (*uttānena*). The *havya*—the clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth—is offered with the palm facing forward (*āmukhena*). The drawing of the reins (*valgā*) and so forth of the sacrificial animal (*pragraha*) for the purpose of restraining its movement is performed with a moving fan (*vyajana*), such as a palm-leaf fan (*tālavṛnta*) and the like.
Holding up a mirror means that one has recognized the mirror face-to-face;

by this very act, they perform the dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*) of the invocation to Gaurī. "Breaking" refers to the activity of fanning with a palm-leaf fan or the like. "Grinding" refers to [the preparation] of saffron, musk, camphor, and so forth.

In the passage beginning with "with two hands, on two sides, by means of long, circular wheels, and pivots, the feet revolve," the mention of long staffs, wooden poles, and so forth refers to pearl necklaces and the like;
at the beginning, the two arms indicate the grasping of both ends. The hanging down of the edge of the garment—
(42) I shall now describe in brief its various applications regarding the forefinger (*pradeśinī*):
when it is turned upward, moved, shaken, expanded, raised, or made to tremble.
The discus, lightning, banners, clusters of blossoms, earrings, and even those with crooked gait—all these are to be designated as "well-spoken" (sādhuvāda). || 66 ||
The young snakes, the hoods of the serpents, the wives, the lamps, the creepers, and the sprouts—
these were all led upward by her as she moved in a circular flight-path with her body tossed aloft.
Furthermore,

this is the mimetic representation (*abhinaya*) of pulling hair and so forth for the sake of sport— performed by women during marriage ceremonies, during lovers' feigned anger (*praṇayakopa*), and while following a path— using stars arranged above as targets and the noses as single-staff poles; it is not possible for it to have the nature of clinging to an upper garment (*uttarīya*).
In the demonstration of women, this gesture (*abhinaya*) is for the sake of forming a square on one's own side; they place the second hand up to the elbow (*kūrpara*).
Regarding the *sūcīmukha*, it is called *khaṭaka*; its face is indeed shaped like a needle (*sūcī*).

Bent with the face downward, restless, moving from side to side, trembling, vibrating right there, yawning, contracted, extended, raised upward, going up, moving, and proceeding as a gesture (*abhinaya*).
(The word *cakra* [wheel] refers to) a weapon, an instrument for action, a chariot wheel, and the subjects of a kingdom. In the sense of a wheel (*cakre*).
One should fashion [the designs] with faces turned upward, situated on the sides, or moving toward the other side;
the lightning should be depicted as moving up and down with its face turned upward. In this manner, other [motifs] are to be visualized.
These include flower-clusters, creepers, ear-ornaments, ear-filling flowers, curved gavaya-deer, fish, and so forth—auspicious signs that are like words of praise. Bhadra!

The separate mention of "the beautiful ones" (*śobhana*) and so forth refers to young snakes, because their mode of movement differs from that of fish. One should discern the internal distinctions among creepers (*vallī*), vines (*latā*), and flower-clusters (*mañjarī*);
for example: gourds and the like are creepers; grapes and the like are vines; and mangoes and the like—[are flower-clusters].
*Mañjaryas*: A *śikhaṇḍa* is the tuft of hair on the heads of young boys; it refers to the side-locks (*kākapakṣa*). *Paripatana* means falling;

*vakra* is curvature, and *maṇḍala* is circularity. These form a *dvandva* compound in their collective sense. Furthermore, the particle *api* is used here in the sense of "more" or "excessively. The mention of being "upwardly curved" is according to its technical application (*prayoga-vṛtti*).
It is to be divided according to its variety: the stars are the constellations; *ghoṇā* is the nose. (One) [is explained] by means of the two terms *eka* and *tva*. The staff.
And Vinatā should likewise be fashioned among the fanged creatures by means of such a configuration of the mouth.
Furthermore, the seizing of all [planets] situated within the mandala is likewise for the world;
indeed, it applies to matters of bowing and rising, as well as to the first, the long, and the day.
Near the mouth, it should be contracted during a yawn; when forming a sentence, it should be curved near the ears during a yawn or at the occasion of forming a sentence.
Furthermore, it should be extended, trembling, and turned upward while saying "no" or "say."
A threatening gesture toward another; a staff, a club, or a broad [object]; when [pointing at] a constellation, the index finger is raised.

Regarding "among fanged creatures" (*daṃṣṭriṣu*), by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), this also includes those not commonly known as fanged, such as *rākṣasas* and the like. The "application" (*yoga*) in the mouth refers to the part characterized by its protrusion;
being bent and connected with that, it is thus [shaped] in the form of a fang.
The meaning is that it should be made with the palms facing each other.

Furthermore, by the word "again," it is understood that [the hands] are extended while facing upward and downward. The word "grahaṇam" (seizing/grasping) is a term where the abstract state is primary; thus, the meaning is "seizing in its entirety. Of the world...

Whether it be an object being perceived directly or one being remembered, the representation (*abhinaya*) consists of the act of grasping it as "this" through a direct indication toward what is in front, and as "that" through a reference back to the field of the ears; this is the nature of recollection according to worldly convention. Because it is the first due to its singular nature, it is the primary and the short.
In relation to the repetition [of the movement], when bent down here and there it moves upward; when elongated, it is raised; and the opposite occurs during the day.
When bent downward on one side and raised upward on the other, with the surfaces joined together and side by side due to their mutual contact, it indicates rising and setting.
First contracted, then expanded and extended near the edge of the face, it is employed when deliberating on a matter;
or, as some read, when it is performed as a gesture of dismissal (*utsārita*). When it is expanded near the ears, it is curved and superior;
or, according to another reading, it serves for the expression of speech (*vākya-rūpaṇa*). The word *mā* is used in the sense of prohibition, while *vada* is used for speaking.

In this context, "trembling and upturned" means excessively contracted and extended. Upon seeing anger, or during the wiping away of sweat, [the brows] are extended over the forehead and so forth, removing the perspiration. "Kuntalas" refers to the hair; regarding the performance (*abhinaya*) concerning those [features] such as decorative leaf-patterns (*patrabhaṅga*) resting on the cheeks.
It should be performed when there is a display of anger and when perspiration appears. || 71 ||
In the dramatic representation of [the hero's] hair, earrings, armlets, and the cheeks;
likewise in pride, in the thought "I am," on the forehead, and similarly in anger when pointing out the enemy. || 72 ||

And when it is specified as "who is this?", [the mudrā] should be applied with the fingers joined together when there is conjunction, and separated when there is disjunction, just like the scratching of an itch on the ear. (73)
In a quarrel, they are joined with the *svastika* and mutually pressing;
in a binding, they are on both sides, on the left and the right, at the end of day and night.

One should employ [the mudrās] with the two hands facing each other and then turned away from each other, and with them separated; one should always display the full orb of the moon with both hands. (75)

The *śliṣṭā* [mudrā] should be placed on the forehead of Śakra, resting supinely; it should be applied to whatever pertains to that field. In the dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) of pride, it is directed toward the forehead. When indicating an enemy who is present, it is directed forward; when indicating one who is absent, the specific distinction is the prior intensity of battle.

In the investigation, it consists of three aspects: "this one is a wicked soul," "anger" being a fury preceded by agitation, and "previously committed" referring to the purpose of the inquiry; and "there he is" is used in pointing out an object situated at a distance. Scratching the ear is well known, as is harsh speech; "joined" refers to the two lower parts.

The meaning is "due to lateral continuity. However, by separating those two on the ground and moving toward the left side—either facing each other or with backs turned—the conclusion of the day should be indicated by the two [hands] moving to the left side; for the left belongs to Soma, while the right belongs to the Sun.
The foremost part of the sun [is perceived] by the two [hands] moving toward the right side, indicating the end of night;
"by the two separated" means by those [hands] at a distance of one *tāla*, which, due to their long and short proportions, are used figuratively; "by the two, however," refers to the thumbs—
By rotating it in a circular manner, one should display the mandala of the moon as perfectly round. (76)
And on the forehead of the one with the lion-like eyes, it was turned sideways and upwards for Śakra;
and again, its tip was whirled around upon mountains that were like mechanical devices for turning forms and stones.
Likewise, during the serving [of food], she should always be depicted with her face turned downwards;
when representing Śambhu, she should be joined to his forehead-paṭṭa with her face turned downwards.
Even for Śakra, that [mudrā] should be made facing upward by those who know it;
however, it should be placed crosswise when the fingers, together with the thumb, are spread apart and bent. || 79 ||
For it should be upright, with its tip unattached, and shaped like the calyx of a lotus;
likewise, the grasping of bilva or kapittha fruits and the sight of women's breasts [are auspicious signs].
For when seizing the acquisition of meat, those [fingers] have their tips bent;
one should point out many types of citron and pieces of meat. (81)

The meaning is that when there is extension, it follows from contraction. "Circular" means one should display a circle by whirling, as in the case of the moon; the word *ca* (and) has the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*). When the third eye of the Blessed Lord Hara has been displayed, regarding the performance of the corresponding dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*) to be executed there, [the movement] is on the forehead.

Or it may be directed upwards. Thus, in the dramatic representation (*abhinayana*) of Śakra, the hand should be placed flat on the forehead and turned sideways, because here the index finger alone is predominant. As for the representation of Maheśvara and Śakra seen in the world using the middle finger in the *khaṭakāmukha* gesture, that should be understood as non-canonical (*alākṣaṇika*).

Now he defines the *padmakośa* (lotus-bud) hand gesture with the words: "whose fingers are spread apart" (*viralāḥ*) and "upward" (*ūrdhvāḥ*), meaning according to the statement of the *Caturveda*. It is so called because its interior is curved inward like the bud (*kośa*) of a lotus.
"Grasping" (*grahaṇam*) means that by which something is grasped; the meaning is "gesticulation" (*abhinaya*). Thus, the breasts are shown.

"By this" refers to the sight of the breasts; "like a lotus bud" is connected with what precedes it. However, in the case of grasping the *bilva* fruit and so forth, it is those very fingers [that perform the action].
In the worship of the deities, the offering of bali-oblations, the presentation of the full vessel, and the giving of the sacrificial cakes (piṇḍas),
one should perform the scattering of flowers with the hand shaped like a lotus bud.
With both hands— the fingers of which are separated, slightly apart, and moving, released from the wrist—
this gesture should be performed by turning them outward to represent a blossoming lotus and water-lily.
When all the fingers, together with the thumb, are joined,
and likewise the palm is concave, that is the *sarpaśiras* (serpent-head) hand gesture.
This [mudrā] is to be employed for the offering of water, when moving like a serpent, for sprinkling water, for clapping, and for such acts as striking the frontal globes of an elephant. (85)
The joining together of all the fingers with their tips pointing downwards, while the little finger and the thumb are turned upwards—that shall be the *mṛgaśīrṣaka* [mudrā]. || 86 ||
At the joints (*parvan*), they become excessively contracted. Regarding the phrase "the acquisition of meat by carnivorous creatures" (*kravyādānām āmiṣalābham*):

here, *labhi* means seizing (*grahaṇe*). Some say that it refers to the seizing that occurs when there is the acquisition of meat. "The taking away of strength" (*baler haraṇam*) means either its removal or the induction of various states [of weakness]. "The first morsel" (*agrapiṇḍaḥ*) refers to the food for cows and other animals, or where it is for one who has died.

In rites such as festivals or the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha, the practice of wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*) should not be performed; this applies up until the offering of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*). The "scattering of flowers" (*puṣpaprakara*) is done by scattering them twice or thrice with the fingertips.
Regarding the "serpent-head" (*sarpaśiras*), it is said that the fingers are joined together; that is, they are closely pressed together along with the thumb.

The meaning is that the thumb is contracted. Its name is derived from the fact that its palm is concave when facing the center, or because it is equal to the head of the serpent (sarpa-śiras). It is used for the offering of water to the gods and for receiving water when it is being offered.

In this context, at the present time, today, and upon the arousal of power (*śakti*), as well as when it has fallen, during the wiping away of sweat, and during the *kuṭṭamita* movement, one should be in motion. (87)
When the middle, ring, and thumb fingers are positioned upon the three sacred fires, the index finger is bent at the first joint,
and the little finger is likewise held upwards.

By this [method], various light representations of young fruits are produced, by which the actor (*gṛhītṛ*) performs his mimetic gestures (*abhinaya*). When moving like a serpent, he keeps his face downward. The preparation of water [is indicated] by means of saffron, sandalwood, and so forth. Slapping with the thighs, arms, and other limbs occurs in the context of wrestling (*mallayuddha*).

Regarding *mṛgaśīrṣaka*: it is that which has a horn situated on its head like that of a deer (*mṛga*). The word *śīrṣa* is another form [of *śiras*]. "Here" (*iha*) is used to indicate a perceptible locus. "Now" (*sāmpratam*) is used to indicate the present time.
"There is" (*asti*) is used both as a gesture of acceptance and as a gesture of possibility. "Today" (*adya*)...

Although the meaning was already conveyed by the description of the present state, it is mentioned again with a specific gesture so that there may be no contradiction with the *sūcīmukha* (needle-mouthed) gesture. In this much [of the action], he faces downward; when exerting power or when the hand falls, he faces upward; and when wiping sweat from the cheeks and such, the palm facing them, he faces upward.

*Kuṭṭamita* is an ornament of feminine gesture consisting of an affectation of distress due to the influence of joy; in this regard, it is said that the palms face outward with fingers spread, and that the fires are situated in the form of the *tretā*. The fires in the form of *tretā* are the *āhavanīya* and the others.

"Likewise, their configuration is such that the thumb is joined at the tip of the [other fingers] while they are spread apart"—this is the meaning. *Kaṅgu* is *priyaṅgu*; "it takes (*lāti*) that" is the derivation. What kind of hand is used for gathering *kaṅgu*? Some say it is the "scorpion" (*vṛścika*) hand, which is like a *kāṅgula*. By this, young fruits are [gathered]; in their illumination...
"Like pearls and jujube fruits" means they are small in size due to their lightness; that is to say, they are morsels of clay balls.
"The fingers" refers to the thumb, the index finger, and the middle finger; their outward projection [constitutes the gesture].
Deeds born of anger [are accomplished] by the words of women and the snapping of fingers. || 89 ||
One should display emeralds, lapis lazuli, and the like, as well as flowers;
those who know [the ritual] should grasp it like a "cat's footprint" during such applications. (90)
Indeed, he whose fingers, when turned upon the palm, remain curved at the sides and scattered, is one who possesses the *alapa* hand-mark.
In the statements regarding emptiness, such as "there is no 'belonging-to-anything' (kasyatva) for the agent of negation," women must again be introduced by means of this [very same argument]. (92)
Where three fingers are extended and likewise the little finger is turned upward,
with the thumb situated in the middle of them— that hand is known as the *catura*.

He describes the *alapallava* as "āvartitā" and so forth. Those who perform a turning or a revolving in the sequence beginning with the little finger; it moves, thus it is *ara*, meaning moving. Because it has the form of a moving leaf, it is the *pādalapallava*. Its name is also *alapadmaka*. It is for the purpose of making a gesture (*abhinaya*) to express negation, such as "whose skin? or "there is none."
And the words beginning with "that which is employed according to the rules of that treatise" (*tacchāstraprasatprayuktam*) are for the purpose of false censure.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "I" (*ahamartha*), in the context of an introduction (*upanyāsa*), a gesture (*abhinaya*) is presented by women; it is introduced again and again because it produces wonder, and thus it is called an "introduction."
"Catura" refers to that [hand gesture] where three [fingers] are extended. Regarding "in the middle": it is precisely in the middle of the middle finger (*madhyamā*).

The word *catura* ends in the vowel *ā*, being formed with the suffix *ac* because four fingers exist therein due to their being joined with the thumb; or, it is called *catura* because it performs four types of expressive gestures (*abhinaya*).
In the case of sincerity, deceit, and so forth, there is a distinction based on the change in the color of the face. The manner [of expression] is revealed by one [eye] when there is no penetration;
however, when there is penetration, it is by both eyes of those who are to be represented, in the relationship of the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, such as "lotus petals" (p.

One should employ [the teacher] in matters concerning policy, discipline, and rules; in being highly skillful with children, the sick, and sentient beings; and in the use of speech that is appropriate, beneficial, truthful, and conducive to tranquility. (94)
With one or two hands, having formed some kind of mudrā, he reveals his conduct after it has been examined and scrutinized; it is both deliberated upon and felt with shame. (95)
The comparison of the eyes, the depiction of the lotus-petal form, and the description of the deer’s ears—one should execute these only with skillful application of the combined techniques. || 96 ||
Playfulness, passion, and desire; memory, intellect, and discernment; forbearance, nourishment, and mere consciousness; affection, deliberation, association, and purity. (97)
Cleverness, sweetness, courtesy, gentleness, happiness, and good character;
inquiry, the logic of conversation, dress, softness, grassy meadows, and moderation. (98)
The particle *eva* is used here to exclude solitude on the bank. By this, the playful gestures (*līlā*) and so forth belonging to another are being enacted.

*Ruci* means brilliance or luster; or it refers to *vibhāvanā*, which consists of deliberation and exclusion, or excellence. In the operation of vision, however, it is specifically the *kartarīmukha* (the scissors-like gaze). *Saṅgata* means friendship due to mutual contact at the tips; *mādhurya* means heart-pleasing.

One should observe his courtesy (*dākṣiṇya*), kindness (*ānukūlya*), gentleness (*mārdava*), and mildness (*mṛdutva*) through his speech beginning with the letter *śa* and so forth; as well as his character (*śīla*), disposition (*svabhāva*), dress (*veṣa*), attire (*nepathya*), or residence (*veśa*),
his status as a courtesan’s associate (*gaṇikāsthāna*), and his wealth (*vibhava*) by moving from side to side and observing his majesty (*abhibhava*).
(50) Prosperity and adversity, sexual pleasure, virtues and vices, youth, home, wife, and likewise various castes— a clever man should employ these in this manner. (99)
One should produce white with the thumb, red and yellow with the ring finger, and blue with the little finger; thus one should apply the colors with a well-groomed hand. || 100 ||
In the *bhramara* hand gesture, the middle finger and thumb form a pincer, the index finger is bent, and the other two fingers are raised and spread apart. 101.
The procedure for gathering flowers—such as the lotus, the blue lotus, the white water lily, and others with long stalks—and making them into ear-ornaments (karṇapūra) must be performed. 102.
In cases such as threats and the like, the action should be performed with a falling away [of the hand] and accompanied by sound;
likewise in forceful speech, in haste, and in the *viśvāsana* (concluding) *tāla*. (103)

The index, middle, and thumb fingers, positioned like the triple fire (tretāgni) and held without gaps, should be used to mime the act of walking; in this manner, other gestures are to be inferred. One should indicate "wives" with two joined hands in the form of a facing svastika. Thus, the specific areas of the body from the chest up to the head are defined.

One should perform specific gestures (abhinaya) by imagining, as appropriate, the states of being joined or unjoined, mobility or stability, facing forward or turned away, upward or downward, triangularity, and so forth.
He shows the *bhramara* (bee) mudrā with the middle finger and the thumb; the *sandaṃśa* (tongs) is the joining of the tips. Because it has that shape, the hand is called *bhramara*.
He describes the *haṃsavaktra* (swan-beak) as being formed by the index, middle, and thumb fingers; "without intervals" means they are not spaced apart.
It negates [the objection]. Terms such as "smooth" (*ślakṣṇa*) and so forth function in the sense of smoothness and so on.
Forms such as quivering, rubbing, churning, shaking, throwing, revolving, moving away, and so forth, should be applied according to their respective fitness through logical reasoning.
In the *haṃsavaktra* [mudrā], the remaining two [fingers] should be extended straight. || 104 ||

A specific mode of representation should be employed for the meanings of "smooth," "slight," "loose," "light," and "insubstantial," as well as in connection with "softness," by means of the fingertips being slightly vibrated. || 105 ||
When three fingers are extended evenly and likewise the little finger is raised, while the thumb is bent, it is known as the *haṃsapakṣa* (swan-wing) mudrā. || 106 ||
And this [water] should be offered into the water for the funeral libation (nivāpa), as well as upon the cheek;
it should be used by the Brahmins for the purposes of receiving gifts, sipping water (ācamana), and eating. || 107 ||
It is to be employed in embracing, in the manifestation of great paralysis, in causing horripilation, in touching for the purpose of anointing, and likewise in massage. (108)

Furthermore, specific variations of the tremulous glance (vibhrama) should be performed by women with their hands placed between the breasts, according to the sentiment (rasa), as well as during sorrow and when holding the chin. 109.

He describes the *haṃsapakṣa* (swan-wing) hand gesture as the fingers being spread evenly above the little finger. "In that manner" means they should be closely joined at the base and slightly curved. Regarding the water for the funeral offering (*nivāpa*), it is to be given into its water for the sake of merit during the ritual pouring of water; some say it is used when resting the cheek in thought with the back of the fingers turned away.
That is incorrect, for this is merely the holding of the jaw; why then would leaf-patterns (patrabhaṅga) and the like be applied to the cheek?

When embracing or when great paralysis (mahāstambha) is to be represented through performance, the state of "joined hands" (saṃyutakaraṇatva) should be understood as occurring from the second shoulder by means of the circular movement (maṇḍalīkaraṇa) of both arms, due to the bristling of the hair (romaharṣaṇa).

The transition to another emotional state occurs through the touch of a beloved person while one is out of sight, by means of the "crossing of hands" gesture; likewise, during the application of ointments or the rubbing of the limbs. Regarding the phrase "according to the sentiment" (*yathārasam*): this [transition] is indeed possible in the cases of love, humor, wonder, and even in sorrow, due to the association with specific transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*). And when there is suffering...
When the ring finger and the thumb form a pincer-like grip, with the middle of the palm slightly curved inward, that is known as the *daṇḍaṃśa* (the "sting") gesture. || 110 ||

The *sandaṃśa* (tongs) is to be known as threefold: namely, the *agraja* (arising from the tip), the *mukhaja* (arising from the mouth), and likewise the *pārśvagata* (situated on the side); it is further augmented by rasa and bhāva. || 111 ||
The tip-pincer (agrasandamśa) is used for gathering and stringing flowers, for grasping grass, leaves, hair, and thread,
and for extracting splinters or their fragments.
Plucking a flower from its stalk, filling a wick or a probe with [substances],
and the utterance of "fie" in anger— these are the functions of the *mukhasandaṃśa* (the mouth-tongs).

In the wearing of the sacred thread, in piercing, in qualities, in subtle targets, in yoga, and in meditation—even when [the effort] is slight—the application of the senses must be performed with focused coordination. 114.
That which is the "holding of the jaw" (*hanudhāraṇa*)— here, those states (*bhāva*) among the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) which are the "consequent expressions" (*anubhāva*),
such as specific glances, horripilation, and so forth— is augmented and clarified by them (as stated in verse 111).
This should be understood as referring to all specific hand gestures (*hasta-viśeṣa*), because it is defined in the middle [of the section].

Regarding the *sandaṃśa* (tongs): "the tongs formed by the index finger and thumb" is its clear meaning. For the plucking of delicate flowers, there is the "fore-tongs"; for grasping thorns, splinters, and the like.
When one extracts a flower by pulling it from its stalk—such as a saffron flower and others—it is done with a wick-stick (*varti-śalākā*).

The filling of deficiencies and so forth is done with a tube of collyrium and a wick. Regarding the quality of pearls and other gems in piercing, when they are shaped like a bow, there is the application of a joining method;
this is not merely for the purpose of gluing, but rather for the support of both hands. And that [support] exists by being situated on both sides.
(53) And in the expression of words that are soft, contemptuous, envious, or faulty, the *pārśvasaṃdaṃśa* [gesture] is employed with the left hand,
its tip slightly turned away. || 115 ||
Women should perform the painting of eyes, the application of collyrium, the arrangement of decorative stalks and sprouts, as well as the pressing out of lac-dye. 116.
When the fingers are brought together and joined, with their tips meeting and pointing upwards like the beak of a swan, that indeed becomes the *mukula* (bud) hand gesture. || 117 ||

In the worship of the gods and the offering of oblations, as well as in the form of lotuses, blue lotuses, and buds, and even in the kissing of a paramour, it should be performed in a contemptuous and scattered manner. 118.

It should be visualized as being of a delicate and unsubstantial nature. "The crafting of coral" (pravālaracana) means the fashioning of leaf-designs on the surface of the cheeks, the tops of the arms, and so forth; or else, it refers to the application of a sprout itself—adorned with cut-out leaf-patterns and placed upon the forehead and other areas—for the purpose of joining it there.

The application of the hand: by the phrase "by women," he indicates the pressing with a limited amount of lac-dye. He describes the *mukula* (bud) as "having the tips joined together"; it is called a *mukula* because of its bud-like shape.

However, regarding the engagement in the activity of the *mukula* at the commencement of the worship of the gods and so forth, those who read [the text] as "like the calyx of a lotus" [are referring to that].
Some say it is "the kissing of the basket" (*piṭaka*). There is a reading *śapiṭeti* (or *viṭeti*). To reveal his own intention, he says:

"In the presence of women, rogues (*viṭas*) kiss their own hands thus folded"—this is "the kissing by the rogue. Alternatively, it refers to when rogues, with all five fingers, make a sound against the breasts, chin, and other parts of women.
In the *Kāmasūtras*, it is stated that [the penis becomes erect] upon the touch of the nails, during eating, counting money, frowning, giving gifts, and in haste. (p. 54)
Likewise, this should be employed by those who know it among blossoming flowers. || 119 ||
When the fingers of the lotus-bud hand are contracted, it should be known as the Ūrṇanāsa mudrā, used for seizing thieves of hair and the like. 120.
Likewise, there is the representation of scratching the head, diagnosing a fistula disease, lions and tigers, as well as the grasping of a stone. 121.
The middle finger and the thumb should form a pincer, the index finger should be bent, and the remaining fingers of the *tāmracūlaka* hand should be placed flat upon the palm. 122.
The *vicyuta* (separated) and *saśabda* (with sound) [movements] are to be employed in cases such as rebuking;
likewise, in the *tāla* (tempo), in *viśvāsana* (consoling), and in those designated for the purpose of speed.

*Churitaka* refers to the kissing of that [the woman] by the lover (*viṭa*). *Hiraṇya* (gold) is indicated by means of a bracelet (*kaṅkaṇa*), while [the giving of] rings and so forth is indicated by their removal. *Gaṇanā* (counting) refers to the number five. By the phrase "by those who know it," he causes one to keep in mind the appropriate course of action.
Regarding the phrase "the spider's lotus-bud": a spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) is a web-weaving insect.

Since it possesses such an arrangement of organs for capturing flies and other insects, the suffix *ac* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). This is also the case when capturing hair, due to the suspicion of being seen by others through theft.
The *lāghā* and so forth are the graspings. Where one should represent lions, tigers, and the like by means of the *svastika* gesture applied to the region of the chin;
for they stand with the *svastika* and possess claws on their seats. *Prastara* is a stone;
