others say it is a touchstone. Some say it is a bundle of *darbha* grass.
He says that the *tāmracūḍa* [mudrā] consists of the joining of the middle finger and the thumb.

It is called *tāmracūḍa* because its shape resembles a cock with its crest unbound (*cūḍāmukta*). Regarding the term "in the *tālas*" (or "the *tāla*"), it refers to the measurement of time, as in the expression *sahijju* and so forth in certain *tālabhūmi* passages.
Likewise, for the invitation to converse with children, this very hand-gesture should be employed during the divisions of time known as *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, *nimeṣas*, and *kṣaṇas*. (124)
Alternatively:
the fingers joined and curved, with the thumbs pressing upon them from above, and the little finger extended—this is known as the *tāmracūḍa* hand gesture. || 125 ||
"One should display a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand pieces of gold,
as well as sparks and droplets, with fingers quickly released.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, these hands have been described by me as being unjoined.
(Now, regarding the joined hands:
Therefore, listen as I describe the joined hands. 127.

*Saṃjñitam* refers to the calling out by means of hair and so forth. Others, however, recite another definition for this: "the fingers joined together," and so on; the meaning is that it is simply a fist with the little finger extended. This is done quickly, with the fingers released.

Regarding the term "uncombined" (*asaṃyutā*): first of all, these [syllables] are uncombined; however, they are not exclusively uncombined, for we see others [such as *ko-hala*] produced by them as well. Therefore: from these very uncombined [syllables], when there is a further conjunction with others, those which are combined arise; learn from me those [combinations] myself.
Disregarding these words, consider this: for instance, the representation of women is performed with the *tripatāka* hand placed upon the elbow and the *khaṭakāmukha* at the side;

furthermore, the discharge of an arrow is indicated by the left hand moving toward the ear in the *khaṭaka* position, or by either the *kapittha* or the *muṣṭi* hand. We shall attend to this in the context of the *citrābhinaya*.
Let this suffice for now. The connection is as follows: "By the word 'ca' (and), understand that there are other [mudrās] which will be described.
Furthermore, the *añjali* is traditionally defined as the joining together of the two hands, which are like two banners.
In saluting deities, teachers, and friends. || 128 ||
Furthermore, its three locations are the chest, the face, and likewise the head.
It resides in the head of the deities, but for the gurus, it is situated in the mouth. (129)
And when resting upon the chest of his friends, it becomes unrestrained for women;
by grasping each other’s sides with both hands, they are joined together.

The hand is called *kapotaka*; learn now its function. It indicates the *añjali* (the hollowed palms) by means of the two *patākā* hands. Even when joined with another [hand], it does not receive a different name; just as the connection between the two *sūcīmukha* hands is used to represent various gestures (*abhinaya*). But in this case—

The word "tu" (but/however) indicates that this is another name [for the same thing]. The phrase "is remembered" means that it is well-known even in common worldly usage, as in such passages as *loke 'pi prāñjaliḥ puṣpaketuḥ* (Kumārasambhava 2.63). By the inclusion of the prefix *sam-* (properly/together), this joining of all the fingers facing one another is indicated. He now analyzes the application (*viniyoga*) already stated.

In the phrase "of the deities" (*devatānām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*) with respect to the act of salutation; in "of women" (*strīṇām*), it is the genitive case used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
Regarding the pigeon, the mention of the numeral "by both" (*ubhābhyām*) is according to preference.
This is for the purpose of establishing the relationship between the substratum and the superstratum. It trembles, thus it is a *kapota*, a timid bird;
another [creature] of that nature is also a *kapota*. Since this [particular one] shines forth from that [source], its state of being an object of fear is indicated by its very name.
For instance, in the first act of the *Rāmābhyudaya*, in the mime of the breasts, this very [gesture] is the primary one.
The phrase "situated on the chest" (*vakṣasstha*) is to be connected with every instance. In the representation of fear (*bhītābhinaya*), however, it is also [performed] when trembling.

The mention of "by women" (*strībhiḥ*) is an indication of the inferior [type of character]; for in cases such as the assumption of modesty (*vinayagrahaṇa*), there may also be the *kuṭṭana* (striking) and so forth. And this very gesture is well-known in the world as the *kūrmaka* (tortoise-like) because of its tortoise-shaped form.

Because his limbs are rubbed by the fingers, he is called "one whose face is rubbed by the fingers. Fatigue and anxiety (occur) upon accepting the discipline, when performing prostrations, and when conversing with the teacher. (p. 57)
In cases of cold or fear, women should place it upon their chests while trembling;
this very same gesture, when released after being rubbed with the fingers, is used for expressions of distress.
The word *etāvat* is used in the sense of "this much" and in the sense of "there is nothing more to be done now. For example: "That hand whose fingers are not interlaced with one another... (133)
That hand should be known as the *karkaṭa*; its application (*karman*) will now be described.
It is used for crushing the limbs of one intoxicated, upon waking from sleep, yawning, or when the body is large. (134)
It should be employed by those who know the true nature of things for supporting the jaw and grasping a conch shell.
Regarding the *karkaṭaka* (crab-hand), it is that in which the fingers are joined such that their intervals—the spaces between them—are drawn out;
this is because the fingers are positioned here in the form of a pair of crab pincers facing one another.

The *karkaṭa* (crab-hand gesture): When performing the act of yawning (*madana*), which involves stretching the limbs, the fingers of both arms are turned away from the body—whether forward, to the side, or upward. The term "the posture of one who has just risen from sleep" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*); for this gesture is employed at all times during yawning. However, in the representation of a large body, the palm of this hand should face forward toward the region of the abdomen.

The *hasta* [gesture]: for supporting the jaw, the fingers are placed with their backs against the region of the jaw; for grasping a conch, the fingers are slightly contracted and directed toward one another. This very point is stated by the word "artha" (*artheti*):
that which is the *tattva*, the ultimate reality, of the object to be represented (*abhineya*), those who know it in order to pursue it in performance—
With those [hands], when the *avarāla* positions are placed at the wrists and employed by women, they are effective. (135)
With both hands turned upward and resting on the left side, it is proclaimed as the Svastika mudrā.
By performing the *svastika-vicyuti* (the swastika-release), one may represent the quarters, the clouds, the sky, the forest, the oceans, the seasons, the earth, and likewise a vast flood.
A *khaṭaka* placed upon a *khaṭaka* becomes a *khaṭakāvardhamānaka*. || 137 ||
It should be employed for the sake of the erotic sentiment, as well as in the act of prostration.

Now, regarding the *svastika* [hand gesture], he says: "placed upon the wrist. Wherever the term *svastika* is employed in its pure sense, such an arrangement should be understood to apply to those specific locations;
however, depending on the context of the meaning, it may also be applied elsewhere, as in the case of dramatic representation (*citrābhinaya*) and so forth. For example:

In passages such as "because of causing the removal of the svastika" (9-20), although there is also the application of the *patākā* [hand-gesture], nevertheless, the state of being placed upon the wrist (*maṇibandhana*) is indeed the form that conforms to its name. For this very reason, some have understood that its definition is complete with just this much, while the remainder is for the purpose of indicating the direction of examples. [The phrase] "employed by women" refers to this.
The meaning is that the actions of the *patāka* and *svastika* [hands] are to be performed by women with this very [hand].
It is called *svastika* because its shape is identical to the characteristic form of the *svastika* object.
Regarding the *khaṭakāvardhamāna*, it is understood as "the *khaṭakā*. Others, however, [describe it as] facing each other.

They say its form consists of two *khaṭaka* [hand gestures]. It receives this name because the *khaṭaka* is joined externally on all sides (*ā samantāt*). This applies to matters of *śṛṅgāra*, that is, for the purposes of *śṛṅgāra*, such as taking betel and so forth. For it will be stated as follows:
"Having performed the *khaṭakāvardhamāna* gesture, one should proceed with the *viṭagati* (the gait of a libertine). (A 12-110).
"Likewise" means that, for the most part, in the very performance [of the rite], such as the propitiation of the Goddess (*īśvarī*), there is prostration.
This [gesture] should be employed in holding a conch shell, as well as among white, blue, and jasmine lotuses.
Or rather, this is the reading: (p. 59) (others—)
It should be employed for holding the stalks of white and blue lotuses when acting as a parasol-bearer. (Thus.
When the two *arāla* hands are reversed and turned upward, they are known as the *vardhamānaka*;
this hand gesture is to be understood as the *utsaṅga*, used for grasping a touch. 139.
It arises from crushing, as well as from anger and resentment;
furthermore, it occurs when women are squeezed or out of jealousy. (140)

He describes the *utsaṅga* [mudrā] with the words "but the *arāla*s... The phrase "crossed" (*vyatyasta*) means in the form of a *svastika*. "Upright" (*uttāna*) means facing oneself. "Vardhamānaka" means bent; by this, it is meant that the right [hand] is in the region of the left shoulder. For this very reason, the *svastika* nature of the forearms (*prakoṣṭha*) is indicated. Thus, the *svastika* itself is situated on the right side.

Some say it is "inversion" (*viparyastatva*); others say it is "facing downwards" (*adhonakhatva*). However, the more logical view is that when one forms the elbows into the shape of a *svastika*, and the fingers are outside the space between the armpits as they enter from within, while the backs of the hands face outward, then it is "inversion."

It is called *utsaṅga* because it renders [the object] fit for being taken onto one’s lap. It refers to the representation (*abhinaya*) of the perception of a touch that is otherwise beyond the senses. *Niṣpeṣa* means pressing; whatever is performed with it, it signifies that which is to be accomplished with extreme effort. As in the expression of anger: "Here I am, in the machine of your arms that firmly crushes me," and so forth.

Regarding the expression of indignation (*amarṣakaraṇa*): as in the case of a Vidūṣaka or similar character expressing jealousy, refusing to be appeased, and [repeating the action] either successively or at once. Others read this as *siṃhāvalokita* (the lion’s glance). They explain that the genitive case is used here either in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) or the object (*karmaṇi*).
When the *kapittha* hand encircles the fist,
that hand should then be considered by name as the *niṣadha*. (141)
Gathering, grasping, and retention; the pledge, and truthful speech;
brevity and the concise—these should be indicated by one who is pressed. 142.
When the hand is pressed by Mṛgaśīrṣa at its peak, it should be known as Niṣadha; it is produced when one is afflicted by fear.
Having taken the right arm with the left hand inside the elbow,
one should likewise place the left [hand] inside the elbow of the right.
And that right hand should be formed into a perfect fist;
this is the Niṣadha hand—now learn its ritual application.

By this [same method], firmness, intoxication with pride, elegance, eagerness, the arrogance of valor, self-importance, steadfastness, the pillar-like stability [of character], and so forth are to be portrayed. (146)
Alternatively—
those known as the *niṣadha* and the two *haṃsapakṣa* [fingers], turned away from one another,
should be employed for striking against lattice windows and the like. (147)

He states the prohibition with the words "mukulantu" and so forth. Since the bud, being encircled by the hand [shaped like] a wood-apple (*kapittha*), remains seated within it, this is the prohibition. (The summary: "Proper grasping" (*samyaggrahaṇam*) is the acquisition and acceptance of the meaning of the scriptures and so forth; "retention" (*dhāraṇam*) is non-abandonment; "observance" (*samayaḥ*) is a rule.

"Truthful speech" means "that which is real"; this is the summary, the essential meaning, even when the whole is being condensed by this alone. For it has been stated that "acting" (abhinaya) refers to the representation of a substance possessing those qualities through accepted acting.
"Condensed," however, means properly cast together or placed in a certain position.
When the two shoulders are relaxed and released, and the two *patāka* hands hang down loosely in the performance, that is designated as the *dola* (swinging) gesture. (148)

The application of dramatic representation (abhinaya-yoga) should be employed in cases of agitation, despair, fainting, and the onset of intoxication; likewise in sudden onset, as well as when overwhelmed by disease or wounded by a weapon.
That which is called *sarpaśiras* (serpent-head) has its fingers held close together;
when the second [hand] is joined to its side, it is known as *puṣpapuṭa* (flower-bud).
By means of this, various kinds of things resembling grain, fruit, and flowers are joined;
they are to be taken up and brought forward, as well as for the bringing in and taking away of water.
He defines *dola* with the words "the shoulders" (*aṃsau*). Because the hands hang down prominently, looseness—that is, a lack of firmness—occurs in the shoulders.
This means that when there is looseness of the fingers, characterized by their lack of support or their being withdrawn during the performance of a manual action.
It is called *dolā* because of its swing-like form. This hand is of such a nature that it possesses a connection (*yoga*) with the activity of mimetic representation (*abhinaya*).

By the word "to be performed" (*kārya*), he indicates the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) involved therein, such as moving from side to side in various representations, falling down, or becoming rigid. [The phrase] "on all sides arising from calamities such as fire" refers to...
The fault is [the injury known as] *abhighāta*.

Regarding the "flower-bud" (*puṣpapuṭa*), he says it is the "serpent-head" (*sarpaśiras*). Even though it is firmly placed upon the finger without any gap, he says "on the side" (*pārśve*) so that it does not face directly forward. The second [term] refers to both the serpent-head and the hand.

"Grasping flowers with such a hollowed palm" refers to the *puṣpapuṭa* (flower-cup) mudrā. As for the *patāka* (banner) mudrās, they occur when both hands have the thumbs pointing upward and the palms facing downward.
When these two are placed one above the other, that is then known as the *makara*. || 152 ||

The depiction of lions, pythons, and leopards, as well as crocodiles, sea-monsters, and fish—whatever other carnivorous creatures are to be represented, they should be portrayed according to the requirements of the context. (153)
When the two hands, resembling the heads of serpents, rest upon the elbows, that hand is called Gajadanta; now learn its function. (154)
And this [is used] during the wedding of brides and grooms, in cases of excessive physical strain, when seizing a pillar, and likewise when uprooting mountain rocks. || 155 ||
Regarding the statement "the two flags are [shaped like] makaras": it is called a *makara* because the two thumbs are positioned like the two ears of a makara.
"Of leopards" means those with variegated bodies. The connection is that this is an illustration of "fishes" and so forth.
"By way of the application of meaning" means that it should be employed according to the requirements of the situation, such as by moving while stationed at the front, the sides, and so on.

Regarding the "elephant-tusk" [hand position], it is said that the elbows and shoulders are "appropriately positioned. By the terms "elbow" (*kūrpara*) and "shoulder" (*aṃsa*), the space between them—the proximity of both—is understood.
However, as for the "eastern-southern" [positions], they are bent there and directed toward the wrapping of that location; namely, the right [hand] on the left arm, and the left hand on the right.

Due to its connection with the form of a pillar, the shape of tusks, and the application [of these features], it is called "elephant-tusk" (gajadanta). When leading brides and bridegrooms to the wedding site or when uprooting stones, the movement back and forth (gatāgata) is to be understood as occurring.
Having placed the two hands like parrot-beaks against the chest and slightly bent toward each other, then slowly turned downward and twisted, this is known as the avahittha [hand-gesture]. || 156 ||
When there is weakness, sighing, the appearance of emaciation in the limbs, and longing, those who know [the art] should employ the appropriate application of dramatic representation. || 157 ||
The *vardhamāna* should indeed be known as having two swan-wings turned outward;
it is to be employed for opening lattice windows and the like. (158)
Gathering, grasping, and extracting; the convention and the word of truth; the concise and the condensed—these should be indicated by means of compression when pressed.
For these have been stated as being of two kinds: uncombined and combined, in brief.
However, those who are performers of dramatic gestures here must also be accomplished through their meaning elsewhere.
He describes the *avahitthaka* (the concealed gesture) with the words "parrot-beak" (*śukatuṇḍa*) and so forth. Facing forward and previously turned upward, they are bent downward by their movement;
being cast down, they are directed downwards. It is called *avahittha* because it indicates concealment (*avahittha*). For by acting in this way, one does not reveal one's own inner intention.
Regarding the *vardhamāna* [hand-gesture], he says: "The *vardhamāna* is indeed to be known as having two swan-wings turned away from each other.
Although they are situated like a *svastika* relative to one another, they appear close to one another at the target point;
they are merely turned away from each other without the *svastika* configuration, through their mutual movement.
"Expansion through yoga" refers to the state of increasing. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the chest, door-panels, and so forth are included.
Concluding, he indicates: "For these have been stated. For these have indeed been stated;

since they have been described in the context of dramatic performance (*abhineya*) by resorting to a summary. The particle *tu* ("for") implies that this is because they have been stated elsewhere as well.
From the meaning [expressed by] the performance (*abhineya*), further meanings (*arthāntara*) can be established and are worthy of being so;
for, by way of direct orientation (*ābhimukhyatayā*), the meaning is not [limited to] a single mode, but rather the unseen meaning is [revealed] within the meaning through the meaning itself.
Others have also said:
"Having understood the reality through form, gesture, signs, and birth,
the wise should perform hand gestures after reflecting for themselves."
In drama, there is no object whatsoever that does not require representation;
whatever form is observed [in reality], it has been declared as being manifoldly expressed through that very form. (162)
Furthermore, whatever other worldly gestures (karas) exist here that are connected with specific meanings, they should be employed at will according to the movements of rasa and bhāva. || 163 ||
Having considered the place, the time, the application, and the appropriateness of the meaning,
these hand gestures (hasta) should indeed be employed, especially by men and women.
Having thus stated this mode of representation (*abhinaya*), he shows that there is yet another mode by saying, "There is nothing whatsoever.
Here, "drama" (*nāṭya*) refers to the divisions and other elements conducive to it. The reason for this is given as: "of whatever [element], whatever is seen.
Having thus permitted the application of the aforementioned modes of representation even through their intermixture, [he now addresses] that which was not mentioned.
To include these, he says, "and others as well. "Meaning" (artha) refers to the capacity for expressive gesture (*abhinaya*) and an excellence of beauty.

"According to desire" (*chandataḥ*) means following the flow of the dramatic teacher’s (*nāṭyācārya*) will. "Flavors" (*rasa*) are the permanent emotions (*sthāyin*); "states" (*bhāva*) are the transitory ones (*sañcārin*). Those various movements that indicate them are the *sāttvika* and *upāṅga* [expressions].

Together with these: thus, in demonstrating the worldly conditions (*lokadharma*), it should be understood that this enumeration of dramatic performances (*abhinaya*) is merely by way of well-known examples. *Deśa* refers to a specific location; *prayoga* refers to the specific nature of the performance, whether gentle or vehement; and *artha-yukti* refers to the logical justification of the matter.
"By way of the distinctions of primary, secondary, indicative, and suggested meanings. "Having considered" means having reflected.
"Should be employed" (p.
I shall now fully describe all the actions performed by every hand, which are indeed produced through rasa and bhāva.
Elevation, drawing away, and likewise attraction; as well as grasping, restraint, summoning, and even piercing. (166)
Union and separation, as well as protection and liberation;
likewise, distraction and shaking, as well as emission and threatening. || 167 ||
Cutting, splitting, bursting, crushing, and likewise beating—these are to be understood by those who know them as the actions to be performed against the laborers. 168.
The upward-facing, the lateral, and likewise the downward-facing—these are the three types of hand movements based on the principles of dramatic art (nāṭyatattva). (169)

The *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of possibility (*śakyārtha*). "Specifically" means that for persons, there are general modes of conduct based on their respective [status]. For this very reason, the hand-gesture (*hastābhinaya*) has extremely limited usage among the most excellent [persons]. "Produced by rasa and bhāva" refers to the distinction between the permanent (*sthāyin*) and the transitory (*sañcārin*) emotions.

The meaning is: "by virtue of the various distinctions among those respective excitants" (*vibhāva*). For instance, the pulling of the hair toward Vidūṣaka [is imagined] by means of the *khaṭakāmukha* [hand-gesture], toward the beloved by means of the *arāla* [gesture], and during play or in a quarrel by means of a fist, and so forth—thus it should be inferred.

Moving upward, downward, or to a distance; making otherwise; drawing up, and so forth—these constitute *utkarṣaṇa* (elevation) and the like. *Parigraha* is grasping with a circle [of limbs]. *Nigraha* is destruction. *Todana* is striking. *Vikṣepa* is casting away; it is a discarding that involves a contemptuous shaking or trembling. *Visarga* is a respectful abandonment. *Sphoṭana* is expansion.

"Twisting" (*moṭana*) and "contracting" (*saṅkocana*) are among the types [of gestures]. There are other such types as well. To clarify what was stated—that these are produced by rasa and bhāva—it is said: "All [gestures] should be manifested through the eyes, eyebrows, facial coloration, and so forth. "Movement" (*pracāra*) refers to upward turning, moving sideways, facing downward, and so on. This applies to the representation of things that are out of sight (*parokṣābhinayane*).
The gaze and other [elements] follow the hands, but in direct perception (pratyakṣa), it is the reverse.
All movements of the hands in ritual applications (prayoga) should be performed according to the rules. (p. 66)
It should be manifested by the wise through the expressions of the eyes, eyebrows, face, color, and so forth. || 170 ||

Having carefully observed the instrument, the action, the position, the method of movement, and the performance, the gestures of the hands should be executed by those skilled in them according to worldly convention. (171)
The hands of the superior [practitioners] should move across the region of the forehead;
those of the middling should rest upon the chest; and those of the inferior should go downward. (172)

He summarizes all of this with the word "instrument" (*karaṇam*). The instrument consists of the wrapping and so forth; the action (*karman*) is that which is to be performed; the location (*sthāna*) is the field such as the forehead and so forth; the disposition (*sanniveśa*) is the state of being supine and so forth; the movement (*pracāra*) is the small amount and so forth; and the reasoning (*yukti*) is the logical justification for primary, secondary, and other meanings—for instance, in the expression "this Brāhmaṇa is a bull," the meaning is not that of a wild animal.

The *kartarīmukha* and *mṛgaśīrṣaka* [hand gestures] are generally employed in the representation of Hari; however, in the representation of folly, they are primarily used in the manner of the *caturaśuka* and the tip of the *tuṇḍa* [hand gestures]. Furthermore, "reasoning" (*yukti*) refers to the investigation of the relationship between qualifiers and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), and so forth. For example, as in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities themselves are included in the cognition (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).

The meanings of the *vṛtti* (verbal forms) and the meanings of other words (*anyapadārtha*) are to be represented through horripilation, the breaking out of perspiration, and trembling—this is [stated in] the *Ratnāvalī* (1.1).

However, in cases free from such indicative marks (*upalakṣaṇa*), only the meaning of the other word is [to be represented]; yet even there, for the sake of conveying the state of being indicated, the meaning of the *vṛtti* must also be represented. But the teachers say that this [latter case] lacks true immersion (*anāveśa*). Action (*kriyā*) is threefold.

It takes the form of an injunction, a prohibition, or neither. For in cases such as "Go" (*gaccha*) or "Do not come" (*māgaccha*), [respectively] the meaning of the suffix alone is enjoined, while in the case of prohibition, the meaning of the root alone is negated.

In the form of neither, as in "Let the noble one descend" (*avataratv āryaḥ*), there is no injunction; rather, only the meaning of the root is to be indicated. By the imperative suffix (*loṭ*), however, only one's own intention is expressed.
Since that which is being manifested is subordinate, it is the meaning of the root itself that must be represented. Here, he states the pervasive reason: "by means of worldly convention.
Regarding the phrase "having made [it] the instrument" (or "the object"), the locus has been stated. He analyzes that [locus] with the words "of the highest," and so forth. Among the highest...
In the case of substances such as gold, those [lines] that are close are superior, those in the middle are middling, and those that are distant are inferior.
Some maintain that this is because terms such as "forehead" (*lalāṭa*) are intended as mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*). In these fields, having first performed the drawing and placement, the superior—
In the *jyeṣṭha* [mudrās], the movements should be very slight; in the *madhya* [mudrās], one should employ them with moderate [movements];
and in the *adhama* [mudrās], the hands should be employed by the performers in a scattered manner.
Dayas— such as kings, ministers, jesters, and so forth— should perform their abhinayas in the appropriate place for abhinaya;
by this, when superior beings such as deities, gurus, and kings are indicated,
they should be represented with hands such as the añjali held at the level of the forehead-region, whereas middling beings...

The lowest [signs] are those moving in the chest-field (*vakṣaḥkṣetra*) by means of four fingers and so forth; those moving in the lower field (*adhaḥkṣetra*) are by means of the parrot-beak (*śukatuṇḍa*) and so forth.

Therefore, when seeing the moon, stars, and so on, it is not contradictory that even for the lowest [sign], the hands move in the forehead-field (*lalāṭakṣetra*), and so forth. And this is more logical, according to the Upādhyāya: "Those who [use] four fingers and so forth..."
These [gestures] have been described as having mutually contradictory objects, such as truth, falsehood, profundity, and audacity;

this statement is for the purpose of distinguishing them. Regarding those excellent objects such as grain and the like, their representation in performance follows the sequence beginning with "being located in the region of the forehead" and so forth.

He also states another distinction regarding the application of gestures (abhinaya) in the verse beginning with "In the *jyeṣṭha* [type of performance], there should be very little movement," and so forth. In a *prayoga* of the *jyeṣṭha* type—such as a *nāṭaka* which teaches the means to attain the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*)—the hand-gestures (*hastābhinaya*) are few because of the predominance of direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*). However, in the *madhyama* type—such as a *bhāṇa* whose fruit is mere entertainment—the gestures are moderate, for in such cases, direct perception is indeed primary.

In that regard, some maintain that because of the predominance of what is spoken by the *ākāśabhāṣita* (off-stage speech), the term "time" (*kāla*) applies to low-quality dramatic poetry (*nṛttakāvya*) and to the *piṅgaka* and similar forms. However, this is incorrect because it is not consistently established; for even in the *nāṭaka*, this [off-stage speech] is frequent.
Furthermore, when an event occurring elsewhere is to be represented through performance, the primary representation must be carried out by the principal character (*uttamapātra*), and not otherwise.

Because of this qualification, others—considering that in this drama the cognition of a particular is one that has grasped its qualifier—and not accepting this [previous view], say: "Wherein a collection of word-meanings can be understood through a single gesture or through many, because of their mobility; for example: 'That which is the first creation of the Creator' (*Śākuntala*...)."

In this regard [1-1], only a single gesture (*abhinaya*) of water and fire should be employed by the *uttama* (superior) actor; however, by the *adhama* (inferior) actor, many may be used due to his restless nature. By the *madhyama* (middling) actor, a moderate number is used. This is the established practice (*pracāra*), or rather, the *vartanā* (mode of execution), which is "small" when applied to the *uttama*. But this [latter case] results in a loss of aesthetic beauty (*śobhā-vicyuti*). Now, that which arises from the eyes... (Raghu 2.75).

In such cases, because there would be the undesirable consequence of following the performance of a "boldness" (*prauḍhatva*)—consisting of a sentence-statement regarding a referent object (*padārtha*) [derived] from two metaphors brought forth by effort—one does not pay heed to it. Those which convey a limited performable [meaning] are clearly the indicators of the sense; for therein, the meaning, context, and so forth, are easily understood.

Because of its assistance: for affliction (*kleśa*) consists in the obstruction of an infinite variety of meanings; such [obstructions] are like hands upon those of superior nature. But the inferior ones speak with verbal entanglement as it is stated.
Thus, in a performance (*abhinaya*), the enhancement of that which is being doubted—due to an abundance of scattered [elements]—is dependent upon the acting itself.
The hands, characterized by the gesture of drawing away (*vikarṣaṇa*), should be executed by those of superior and middling [ability].
Even when based on lowly objects, they possess the nature of worldly activity. || 174 ||
Alternatively, having encountered a different application or a different time, the wise should either employ the hands in a reversed manner or not at all. (175)
When one is despondent, fainted, ashamed, afflicted by loathing or grief, languid, dreaming, agitated, motionless, drowsy, or dull-witted; || 176 ||
"Thus say some. Others, however, say: 'The movement (pracāra) will be described as threefold and fivefold.

Among these, because it is the fruit for the superior [actor], the movement such as *uttāna* and so forth is of a single flavor; but for the inferior, it is extremely complex. However, this is most appropriate here regarding the supreme performance (*abhinaya*)."

In cases where the object is the self, present, and perceptible, the application of the hand is minimal—as in *hi-a-a samassasa* (*Śākuntala* Act 7), and likewise in *tanvī meghajalārdravalkalatayā* (*Vikramorvaśīya* 4.38).
For here, due to the predominance of *sāttvika* [emotions], there is a state of seniority (*jyeṣṭhatva*). However, when the form pertains to another who is imperceptible, future, or past—

Because there is no opportunity for *sattva* due to lack of mastery, the lowest form of representation (*abhinaya*) is considered "devoid of *sattva*" according to the statement: "The lowest is remembered as being devoid of *sattva*" (22.2). In that [lowest] case, the hands are scattered, distracted, and most numerous, as in the description of battles involving external movements by characters such as Kuñjaraka and Sundaraka. However, in cases other than these...
The middle application of the hand is as follows: for example, when the Vidūṣaka, being visibly present, describes a garden or similar setting that evokes a particular state of being;
therein, the characteristic of excellence (*sauṣṭhava*) is perceived.
"Excellence (*sauṣṭhava*) is said to be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), when it is applied according to the sequence of execution" (10.77).
Those [gestures] lacking that are for the inferior [actors]. (Regarding the words "Alternatively," etc. Others, however, say:
"In whatever manner their defining characteristics have been described, those who possess forms that are otherwise incomplete or unjoined are [considered] deficient in performance (*abhinaya*)."

"Like the pronunciation of conjoined phonemes. (Regarding "the reverse"): this refers to the opposite, such as clarity (*sauṣṭhava*) occurring in the expression of fear, disgust, and so forth, or during the onset of cold weather and the like; or the lack of clear form (*asphuṭākṛtitva*) occurring in feigned indifference (*avahittha*) and the like; or even clarity (*sauṣṭhava*) occurring despite the presence of a lack of clarity (*asauṣṭhava*). "Distressed" (*vihasta*) means the impairment of the hands; "intoxicated" (*matta*) means by liquor.

One who is intoxicated is so due to intoxicants, and one who is insane suffers from epilepsy. Anticipating the question, "Is every [state] here expressed through hand-gestures? he speaks for the purpose of providing an exception (p.
When one is seized by disease, afflicted by old age, tormented by fear, overwhelmed by cold, intoxicated, heedless, insane, or established in meditation and austerity; (177)
When struck by a shower of snow, when bound, when floating upon water, when feigning sleep, when agitated, and likewise when the nose is being pinched; (178)
One should not employ mere hand gestures; rather, one should rely upon the inner being (*sattva*).
Likewise, one should employ specific modulations of the voice (*kākubheda*), which manifest various meanings, aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), and emotional states (*bhāva*). (179)
Where both hands are separated,
one should perform vocal expression (vācikābhinaya) through various glances and looks, using pauses that reveal the meaning.
The movement of the limbs is threefold—upward, lateral, and downward—and it serves as the basis for both dramatic dance (nāṭya) and pure dance (nṛtta). || 181 ||

Regarding the term "kārya" (to be performed): those hands which indicate an internal mental state—such as a pigeon indicating fear, a crab indicating the manifestation of passion, a drum indicating grief, or a parrot’s beak indicating envy—must indeed be performed. This is because they are *anubhāvas* (consequent expressions) of the *sāttvika* [emotions], and since these are of the nature of *bhāva* (emotional states), the *sāttvika* [expressions] must also be performed; this is understood through repetition (*āvṛttyā*). However, those which...

Those [external objects] which indicate the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth of external substances should not be made [the focus]. However, he states that specific case where none at all should be made [the focus]:
"where they are distracted" (*vyagrau*), as for example when the hands of a charioteer are occupied with the goad and the reins.

Regarding "by glances" (*vilokanaiḥ*): it means that by this [glance], the movement of the mind (*cittavṛtti*) is observed; thus, one should manifest [it] through changes in facial color and so forth. This is the meaning.
"By those who reveal the meaning" means by those who effect the obstruction of the characteristics of recurrence (*anuvṛtti*).
Others, however—
"Upright, circular, triangular, stationary, and downward-facing—
these are the five movements of the hand based on dramatic dance (*nāṭya* and *nṛtta*).
Thus, these hands should be understood as the basis for various types of expressive gestures (*abhinaya*)."
Henceforth, I shall describe the hand gestures based on dance. (183)

He describes the movement of the hands as determined by their positioning in different directions, beginning with "upturned" (*uttāna*) and so forth. For example, the *patāka* hand is used in the mimetic representation (*abhinaya*) of "placed upon the earth" (9.22);
or, in the mime of the tongue, the *tripatāka* hand is positioned at the front of the field of the mouth. The *muṣṭi* hand is used when positioned at the side, as in the mime of a bow.

As in the gesture for the ocean, it is downward-facing and placed in the region of the forehead; as in the *svastika-patāka*, it is contracted and revolved—here, in the case of the *tripatāka*, it is upward-facing, downward-facing, triangular, with the tip forward, and indeed downward-facing: these are the five movements of the hand.

Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa recites: "In that regard, when [the hand] is on the lower surface, it is face-down and internal; when on the upper surface, it is forward-facing; and when triangular, it extends along three sides. Even here, however, there are further sub-divisions of the even, uneven, and triangular types, as well as those beginning with the upward-facing (uttāna) and so forth. Thus, a threefold classification alone is appropriate. In that context, the production of rasa depends upon the enactment (abhinaya).

That which was called "vastu" consists of *karaṇas* and *anubhāvas*. Among these, *aṅgahāras* are collections of *karaṇas*, and the definition of a *karaṇa* has been stated [in the passage beginning]: "Those *sthānas*, those *cāryas*, and the dance-hands... (4.59), and so forth. Therein, the *sthānakas* and *cāryas* will be defined in their own section (1.13).
Following the discussion on the hands (*hasta*), the dance-hands (*nṛttahasta*) must now be described. Furthermore, some of these may also be employed for dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*);

for instance, the two *latāhasta* hands are applied toward the performance of dance-gesture (*nṛttābhinayana*), just as the *karihasta* is used for the gesture of an elephant. The same applies to the *caturaśra* and other hands according to their specific application.

With the intention that it should be seen, he says, "henceforth" (*ata ūrdhvam*). The status of being a cause arises from its being the substratum of the *nṛtta* consisting of *karaṇas*. The meaning of "henceforth from these *abhinaya* hands" is that they are also worthy of being counted as *abhinaya* hands on the back. In that regard:

Situated eight finger-breadths from the chest, facing forward, and with palms turned upward like a *khaṭakāmukha*, the two hands, with elbows and shoulders level, are proclaimed as the *caturaśra* (square) mudrā. (184)
The two hands, formed like the wings of a swan and turned outward like fans, are to be known as *udvṛtta*; alternatively, they may be called *tālavṛntaka*. (185)
When the two hands are positioned square and formed like the wings of a swan,
they should be known as *talasūkha* when placed obliquely and facing one another.

Since the squareness of the limbs is the very life of dance, he first describes the two shoulders as being square, which arise from that [squareness]. They are situated at a distance of eight finger-breadths beyond the chest; however, because they are separated by eight finger-breadths from each other, it is merely to be imagined that, on the contrary, squareness is produced.

Regarding the phrase "facing eastward" (*prāṅmukhau*): they face the same direction as the performer, not necessarily facing the performer himself. The equality or lack of disparity between the two elbows and the two shoulders is like that of a balance scale (*tulā*). They are called "square" (*caturaśrau*) because they provide a four-cornered symmetry of the limbs. This is indeed a specific type of drawing-in (*ākarṣaṇa*), which is itself a form of dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*).

From the dual number, when free from exceptions, the application of the two alone must be established as the reason; even though the other hand possesses a second type [of movement], it is designated as merely "square" (*caturaśra*) because its form is identical, and thus there is no contradiction regarding the number sixty-four. This applies everywhere in the same way.

Now, regarding the *udvṛtti* [movement], it says: "formed with the wings of a swan. First, they are square; then, by means of a winding movement (*udveṣṭhita-vartanā*), they become like the wings of a swan—the word "formed" (*kṛta*) indicates this procedure. One [hand] turns upward, while the other, facing downward, revolves toward the region of the chest; this is what he states.

"Like a palm-leaf fan" (*tālavṛntavat*): because it is turned upwards at the time of rotation, it is "raised. By this other name, he expresses that its object is the palm-leaf fan and that it is to be performed. Now, regarding "the palms facing upward" (*talasaukhyau*)—meaning "situated in a square"—he states by the word "likewise" (*tathā*) that this [movement] is preceded by the "turned-away" (*vyāvṛtta*) and "raised" (*udvṛtta*) positions.
At the conclusion of that [performance], his two arms, positioned at his sides, are like the wings of a swan, standing in a triangular formation;

because their palms face one another, they are "palms-to-mouth" (*talamukha*). This same gesture is also employed in contexts such as "he plays the mṛdaṅga drum sweetly" (*maṇḍalamahurijima vajja-i*).
Those same two [hands], positioned at the ends of the wrists in the form of a *svastika*,
are renowned as the *svastika* [mudrās]; when they are displaced and scattered apart, they are the *viprakīrṇaka* [mudrās].
The *alapallava* and *saṃsthāna* are called "upward"; the *padmakośa* and *arāla* are called "khaṭaka," as well as *arālakhaṭakāmukha*. (188)
Others, however, say:
"In that same manner, when both hands are curved and extended as far as the wrists, they should always be known by practitioners as the *arāla-khaṭaka* [hand gestures]. Thus it is said.
When the arms and forearms are bent and the hands are turned away with their palms thrust inward, they should be known as the *āviddhavakra* (twisted-curved) hands.
Now, regarding the *svastika* and *viprakīrṇa*: these are those very same [hands]. The meaning is that they are indeed the *talasūkha* hands. "Internal" means near.
*Svastika* is a specific technical name for a particular configuration. (Regarding the term) *vicyutau*, it means having fallen away suddenly and specifically.
Thus, the *svastika* and *viprakīrṇa* subsist upon the nature of the four hands previously described in the context of *nṛtta*.
Regarding the *arāla-khaṭakāmukha* hands: he says that they have the configuration of *alapallava*.

Having formed the *patāka* hands like a *svastika*, and having made those same two hands face upward as *padmakośa* with the *vyāvartitakaraṇa-vartanā* characterized by *alapallava* ending in a rotation, immediately thereafter—

With the two hands in the form of the buds of a lotus (*bhāvinalinīpadmakośa*), one should form one hand as a *arāla* and the second as a *khaṭakāmukha*, arranged in a square formation (*cāturaśryasaṃsthāna*). Others say it is done with the *svastika* gesture. Still others say that from those [positions], the two hands become *arāla* and *khaṭaka*.
When both hands have the middle fingers and thumbs shaped like the heads of serpents and are known as being extended obliquely, they are then called *sūcīmukha* (needle-mouthed). 191.
Others say:

when the two hands are in the form of snake-heads and positioned as a svastika, with the thumbs extended toward the middle, they are then to be known as the *sūcīmukha* (needle-mouth) mudrās. || 192 ||
The *recita* hands should also be understood as having the wings of a swan and moving rapidly; when the palms are extended and turned upward, they are designated as *recita*. (193)
Now, regarding "the uncrossed and curved" (*athāviddhavakrau*)—as in the phrase "by means of the arms, shoulders, and tips of the elbows"—this is read thus for the sake of metrical requirements.

However, the actual meaning is as follows: having performed a rotation (*āvartana*) characterized by the sequence of the two shoulders, the tips of the two elbows, and the tips of the two arms, while making the *patāka* hands curved and graceful (*savilāsa*).

When the hands, beginning with the little finger, have their fingers turned away [from each other] and are joined in that manner, and when the two Haladhārin (plow-bearers) have their palms facing downwards, it is called by this name.

Next, regarding the *sūcīmukha* (needle-mouthed): "the hands are like the heads of serpents," meaning they are positioned in the square stance (*caturaśrasthāna*) with the hands shaped like serpent heads.

When the thumbs are placed upon the middle fingers, and the tips of the index fingers are extended sideways and opened by moving toward the sides, and such a pair of arms is alternately extended outward, then they are called *sūcīmukha*, being like needles (*sūcī*) in their outward extension.

Because of their extension. In that context, the word "tu" (but/however) indicates an alternative reading. Some read: "The *sūcīmukha* [hand-gesture] has the thumbs extended in the middle; the *svastika* and *sarpaśīrṣaka* [gestures are formed].
This is the reading of some.

Now, regarding the statement "the *recita* and also the half-*recita*": some, wishing to avoid the redundancy of the term *recita*, say that there are two definitions. According to them, the *haṃsapakṣa* [hand gestures] are *recita* when they are swift, moving, and unaltered.
When the left [hand] is square and the right hand is extended,
these should be known by those who know the principles of dance as being designated "half-extended" (ardharecita).
When the elbows and shoulders are bent and the hands are formed into *tripatāka* gestures, these two, when turned slightly sideways, are known as *uttānavañcita*.
When released from the wrist-binding, they are known as *patāka* and *pallava*;
when emerging from the top of the arm, they are proclaimed as *nitamba*.
Likewise, even when performed with the palms extended upward and spread out, they are called *recita*. Others, however, say that this is a single sentence:
"The two which, being *recita*, constitute a rapid whirling, are designated by the name *recita*. There is no tautology;
for although the *ardharecita* is already understood through the name itself, the repetition serves to establish the position of the fourfold symmetry without distinction.
Indicating [the movement] even within the intervals of dancing hand gestures, he indicates the application through the succession of body parts.

Now, regarding "upturned and bent" (*uttānāvañcitau*): "bent" (*añcitau*) means that the two *trapatāka* hands, having been placed in any one of the fields of the shoulder, cheek, or forehead, are joined with the action of bending.
Facing each other and slightly oblique, there is a slight bending and shifting at the shoulders and elbows. At the time of this bending, because they attain an upward orientation,
and through further bending they engage in the action of rising, they are described as "softly raised and bent."

Now, regarding the *pallava* [hand gestures]: "when released from the wrist-connection," etc. By extending the arms with the hands turned upward and performing a revolving motion, the two *patāka* [hands] take the form of a *svastika*. They are so called because of their *pallava*-like (sprout-like) shape.
Others, reading "the *pallavas* are relaxed," maintain that the term "*tripatāka*" [from the previous verse] is to be supplied here.

Now, regarding the *nitamba* (hips): [the rule] "from the region of the arms and the head" applies. The term *patāka* (flag-hand) is understood to carry over. From the region of the shoulders, the two *patākas* emerge alternately—upward-facing and downward-facing—in a variegated manner;
because the region is implied by the name, when they occur in that same alternating fashion in the region of the hips, they are called *nitamba*.
Emerging from the region of the hair and likewise rising up at the sides,
these two hands are to be known as the *keśabandha* (hair-binding) mudrās, according to the consensus of the teachers. (197)
When the two hands are extended horizontally and likewise positioned at the sides,
they are to be known as the *latā* (creeper) hands for the purpose of dramatic gesture (*nṛttabhinayana*).
The *latāhasta* (creeper-hand) is raised high and shaken from side to side;
another, the *tripatāka* (three-fold banner), is placed at the ear—this is proclaimed as the *karihasta* (elephant-trunk hand). || 199 ||

Now, regarding the *keśabandha* (hair-binding) [mudrās]—starting from "from the region of the hair": first, having risen from the lateral field (*pārśvakṣetra*) by means of a rotation of those sides, they reach the cranial field (*śiraḥkṣetra*);
therefore, just as was stated for the *nitambahasta*, they emerge from the region of the hair with various hand gestures (*vicitrahasta*), and likewise in that very manner.
Furthermore, by way of variation, these two hands move back and forth individually only at the region of the hair;

they are called "hair-binding" (*keśabandha*) because of their connection with the hair, and they are approved by the teachers because they produce an excellence of beauty. Now, regarding the "creeping-vine hands" (*latāhasta*): it is said that they are extended obliquely. The term "flag-hands" (*patāka*) carries over [from the previous definition]. Others, however, [apply them] to the hips and other parts.
The term *tripatāka* is understood to carry over into the descriptions of the *latāhasta* (creeper-hand) and other gestures.

Now, regarding the *karihasta* (elephant-trunk hand): "elevated," and so forth. It is that which is raised in the process of joining [the hands]. "Swinging" (*vilolita*) means moved back and forth like a swing. According to some, because of the mention of the "other" [hand], the *tripatāka* itself is called the *lalāṭa* (forehead-hand).

Others read "another called *khaṭaka*. Because of its similarity [to the preceding], there is no commencement of this [movement] as with the *caturaśra*; yet, even though it is commenced by a dissimilar [element], it receives the designation of *nṛtta* (dance) due to its practice, like the *ārāla-khaṭakāmukha*. Therefore, [it is not a *tāla*].
When both hands, formed as triple-folds (tripatāka), are placed upon the hips, they should then be known by practitioners as the "wings-turned-away" (pakṣavañcita) hands. || 200 ||
When those same two are turned over, they are known as the "illuminators of the wings";
when their palms face downward and are thrust upward, they are to be understood as the "wings of Garuḍa. (201)
The two hands formed into swan-wings, when turned outward and then rotated, with the arms likewise extended, are known as the "staff-wing" (daṇḍapakṣa) gestures. || 202 ||
The dual number [is used] because there is no "elephant-trunk" (*karihasta*) formation when each [hand] is employed separately; therefore, it is indeed in the singular.
And this name [is given] because it has that form.
Now, regarding *pakṣavañcita* and *pakṣapradyota*—the reading is *kaṭiśīrṣa*. In the *Vṛtti*:

The two wings, having moved so as to be deceptive and facing him, illuminate him; thus they are so described. By the use of the particle *eva*, he indicates that there is a beauty in the application of these two in a mixed manner. Now, regarding the two wings of Garuḍa—“with faces turned downward”: having become with faces turned downward upon the region of the hips (*nitamba-kṣetra*).
Propelled by the *tala* [hand], moving swiftly upward, and through the projection resembling the wings of Garuḍa (*tārkṣyabhujākāra*),
the two *patāka* [hands] are perceived according to the authority of the *liṅga* and *vākya*, having easily attained the state of being struck by the *tripatāka*.

Now, regarding the *daṇḍapakṣau* (staff-wing gestures): these are performed with the wings of a swan (*haṃsapakṣa*). Upon the turning away of one swan-wing, there is a graceful movement from the side toward the region of the chest; simultaneously, the second [wing] is moved by the rotation of the body, extending as far as the full stretch of the arm.

Regarding the phrase "again by another limb," both arms are extended and then turned away and turned back; thus, when the arm is like a staff at the side, they are called *daṇḍapakṣau* (staff-wings). According to others, the extension of both occurs simultaneously, whereas the turning away and turning back occur sequentially.
The *ūrdhvamaṇḍalina* hands are so called because they are turned toward the upper region; those same two hands, when placed at the sides, are known as *pārśvamaṇḍalina*. || 203 ||
One should be wrapped forward (udveṣṭita) and the second wrapped backward (apaveṣṭita);
when whirled at the position of the chest, they are known as the "chest-circling" (uromaṇḍalina) gestures.
The chest, made formidable by the movement of the forearms like sprouts, proceeds with the sequence of a half-rotation (*ardhabhramaṇa*).

Then, regarding the two "upward-circular" movements (*ūrdhvamaṇḍalī*): by means of a maneuver that turns away from the region of the chest, one effects a lateral movement across the field of the forehead; from there, one performs a rotation like a full circle (*maṇḍala*).
The *prasāritau* (extended) and *ūrdhvamaṇḍalinau* (upward-circular) [hands] are mentioned; the phrase "with arms extended" (*prasāritabhujau*) continues to apply here.
Some maintain that the definition of these two extends only as far as reaching the forehead, while the remainder belongs to the *pārśvamaṇḍalinau* (side-circular) hands.
According to the statement "those same two placed at the sides," they are well-known in dance (*nṛttaprasiddha*).
Others say that the two upper circles consist of the nature of movement (*vartanā*). Now, regarding the two side circles—those same two [upper circles] are the side circles;

they are the very two upper circles, moving to the sides, shaped like banners (*patākā*), and facing one another. Others, however, with the intention of providing an etymological justification, [place them] on their own sides...
They say that the nature of these two consists of the whirling and turning of the arms in an unextended manner.

Now, regarding the *uromaṇḍalinau* (the two [hands] revolving around the chest): the term "udveṣṭita" (twisted) indicates simultaneity through its conjunction with the word "ca" (and). The word "urasaḥ" (from the chest) is in the ablative case; starting from there, they are whirled within the lateral space (*pārśvakṣetra*), such that one arrives at the place of the other.
"Gait" refers to the movement [of the feet]. Others, asserting that it is the sixth [mudrā], say that "abiding" occurs in that very state.

Others describe the *haṃsapakṣa* (swan-wing) mudrā as being formed by the fingers of the upper side of the hands. Now, the *alapallava* (sprout-like) and *kārāla* (fearful) mudrās are formed by the half-circles of the chest and sides; these are hands turned upward from the region of the chest.
The *saṃstambha* (stiffening) is extracted by means of a movement that turns the limbs away, causing the hands to assume the position of young shoots.
Furthermore, the *pārśvāvarta* (side-turning) and the *uraḥpārśvārdhamaṇḍala* (half-circle of the chest and side) are to be understood [as distinct movements]. (205)
When the two hands, from the wrists down, are bent and then extended,
and are formed into the gestures known as *khaṭaka*, they are then called *muṣṭika-svastika*.
When the two hands are turned outward and then rotated inward like the sheaths of a lotus, they should be known by practitioners as the *nalinī-padma-kośa* (lotus-bud) gestures. || 207 ||

Simultaneously with that, the second hand, with its arm extended along the side, is brought to the region of the chest by means of a curved configuration formed by the curling of the index finger and other fingers. Again, it is thus: one hand is on the chest and the second is at the side.

"Perform the movement of coming and going as in a maṇḍala"—thus it was said. Now, regarding the *muṣṭika-svastika* (the fist-cross): "The two hands [should extend] to the wrists. One hand is bent by means of the *arāla-vartanā*, while the other is extended by means of the *alapallava-vartanā*; then follows the rotation of the limbs (*aṅga-paryāya*). Thus, after this sequence of *vartanās*:
The experts [in this field] maintain that because it originates from the *muṣṭi* (fist) through the sequence of the two *khaṭakāmukha* (scissor-mouth) gestures,
it is designated as the *muṣṭikasvastika*; this is for the purpose of permitting the employment of any one of the *muṣṭi*, *śikhara*, *kapittha*, or *khaṭakā* gestures.

Now, regarding the two lotus-bud gestures (*padmakośau*) called *nalini*: "the two lotus-buds" means that the two lotus-buds face each other with their wrists joined. According to some, one thumb is placed facing the little finger of the other, and there is a turning of the faces through movement. However, this is the correct interpretation here: they are turned by means of a rotation.
When there is the union known as "the two lotus-buds" (*padmakośa*): having placed both hands within this very fist in the *svastika* field,

when there is a rotation by means of the *vyāvartita* movement starting from the little fingers, such that they are turned away from one another, and immediately thereafter the two [hands] become like lotus-buds— then [that occurs].
This name is derived from the fact that many lotuses arise within a *nalinī* (lotus pond).
Then, having formed the two hands with their tips entwined like tender sprouts...
The two [hands] should be raised upward, extended, and thrust forward, made prominent. || 208 ||
The two graceful hands reaching toward the region of the head are known as *pallava*;
when they reach the elbows in a crosswise position, they are called *latā* and *valita*.

However, in the case of instrumental action (*karaṇa*), the dance-hands (*nṛttahasta*) should be employed specifically; likewise, in the dramatic representation of meaning (*arthābhinaya*), performers should employ the *patāka* and other hand gestures. (210)
Furthermore, there may be a confusion among them due to their application according to the requirements of the meaning;
however, in this context of drama and dance, the designations are used according to the predominance [of the specific hand gestures].

Now, the *ulbaṇa* (excessive) and *lalita* (graceful) [hand gestures]: "The hands with their tips turned away" means that having positioned the two hands primarily by turning them away from the region of the chest, they are extended into the region of the upper shoulders and become *āviddha* (twisted), with the rows of fingers moving toward the shoulders like sprouting leaves; at that time, they are *ulbaṇa*.
These two are called *ulvaṇau* (excessive) because they indicate a state of mind overcome by joy.

Now, the *lalitau* (graceful): when the two hands, like young sprouts, reach the region of the head and move with grace, they are called *lalitau*, because they produce a charm of the limbs through their circularity.

Now, regarding the *valita* (twisted) hands: "placed in a cross-pattern at the elbows. Because the two vine-like hands (*latāhasta*) form a cross-pattern (*svastika*) at the position of the elbows due to the twisting of the arms, they are called *valita*. The word [“twisted”] itself indicates other such modes of movement.
Since I shall describe the hands as they depend upon the *karaṇas*, the qualifying portion [of the definition] is used precisely because of their connection to the *karaṇas*.

The mention of the instrument (*karaṇa*) being employed is for the sake of the result. Just as from another statement, "The priests proceed wearing red turbans," the activity of the priests is obtained, so too the case ending in "two" (*dvau*) is intended to enjoin the meaning of the subordinate word (*upapada*); thus the reading "the instrument" or "the instruments" (*karaṇam* / *karaṇāni*) is used in the sense of "indeed" (*hi*).

*Karaṇa* (the instrument): that by which a specific gesture (*abhinaya-viśeṣa*) is produced or accomplished through the force [of movement], specifically by a particular action of balancing the fingers, such that at its own completion it becomes free of further expectancy—that is *karaṇa*.
For example, the *alapaṭṭava* [gesture] is formed by the rotation of the little finger and so on; however, in the case of a reverse rotation...
In the absence of completion, there arises a requirement for another action regarding the process;
this is precisely what those who know the true nature of the auxiliary (*aṅga*) call the "breaking" of the auxiliary (p.
Dissociated and associated hand gestures are thus proclaimed as *nṛttahastas*.
Hereafter, I shall describe the hands based on their application in *karaṇas*. (212)
Those who instruct on dramatic hand gestures (nāṭyahasta) must diligently understand that the fourfold *karaṇa* applies to all hands alike. (213)
Now, one is the *āveṣṭita* (encircled), another is the *udveṣṭita* (unwound), the third is the *vyāvartita* (turned away), and the fourth is the *parivartita* (revolved). || 214 ||
When the fingers, beginning with the index finger, are wrapped around in their proper order by the interior [of the hand],
that is called the *āveṣṭita* (encircled) formation.
O Brahmins, when the fingers beginning with the index finger are uncoiled outwardly in succession, that mudrā is called Udveṣṭita.
When the fingers, beginning with the little finger, are rotated inwardly in their proper sequence,
that mudrā is called Vyāvartita.

They employ [these gestures]. Therefore, those hands in which the index finger and so forth are contracted perform actions like an *ālava* (hand gesture), as in the cases of the parrot-beak (*śukatuṇḍa*), the clever deer-head (*mṛgaśīrṣaka*), and others; other examples should be inferred in this manner. As for the *patāka* (flag) hand, however, its universality consists in its being the common source (*sarvaprakṛti*) because it performs the function in all variations (*vartanā*). For that very reason—

The designation "banner" (patākā) is used because of its predominance. By the word *nāṭya*, the expressive hands (*abhinaya-hasta*) are indicated; by the word *nṛtta*, the dance hands (*nṛtta-hasta*) are indicated. Internally...
O Brahmins, when the fingers, beginning with the little finger, are rotated outward in successive order, that mudrā is called Parivartita.
In dance and the application of dramatic gesture, one should employ the *karaṇas*—which involve the face, eyebrows, and eyes—along with the hands resting upon the various *vartanās*. || 219 ||
For it may be positioned horizontally, upwards, or downwards; it may be bent, cast away, moving in a circular motion, in the svastika posture, or following behind. || 220 ||
By being directed toward the palm, [the fingers] reach as far as the region of the chest from the outer side toward the body;
therefore, by the opposite process, the state of being outward-facing (bahirmukhatva) revolves starting from the little finger.
Thus, being inward-facing (abhyantaratva) consists precisely in facing the palm, while the emergence outward occurs from the region of the chest.
The opposite of this constitutes the external [mudrās].

Anticipating the objection, "But what is the use of these [mudrās] such as the āveṣṭita and others?", he demonstrates their status as the most effective means of accomplishment by stating, "In dance and in the application of dramatic gesture. In dance and in drama, one should employ the *karaṇas* with excellence. By what?

He says "by means of the cause" [referring to] "with the hands," because the *vartanās* (turnings) have arisen from them, and the produced and the producer exist in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior. "Hands" refers to the hands used in dance (*nṛtta*) and dramatic gesture (*nāṭya*). To the question "How should one employ them? he replies:
"joined with the face, eyebrows, and eyes. For it is from that very place where the *vartanās* proceed that the face and so forth follow.

The intended meaning is as follows: the phrase "those by which the colors of the eyes, eyebrows, and face are manifested" is a grammatical construction used for the purpose of filling out the verse regarding the *abhineyas* (objects of representation). However, since this [manifestation] pertains to the *vartanās* (movements), there is no tautology.
Because the movement of the fingers occurs in connection with the arms, he describes their various distinctions starting with "placed obliquely," "upwards," and so forth.

*Tiyaṅ* means moving sideways; *ūrdhvaḥ* means going even above the head; *adhomukhaḥ* means facing downward while touching the ground; *añcitaḥ* means having emerged from the region of the chest and returned to the very region of the head—this is the *apaviddha* maṇḍala.
(82) "Twisted" and "extended"—these are indeed remembered as the varieties;
they should always be understood by dancers as pertaining to the arms in their execution. 221.
O brahmins, the procedure for the hands has been described by me in brief;
hereafter, I shall explain the operations of the heart, the abdomen, and the sides.
The chest is said to be of five kinds: bent, straightened, trembling, raised up, and even. (223)
With a depressed back and elevated spine, with drooping shoulders and being slack in some places, that chest should be known as "contracted" (ābhugna); now learn its application. || 224 ||

Moving in every direction, it wanders; because it follows the back of its own body, it is called "following the back" (*pṛṣṭhānusārī*). When it is unwound by the turning of the wrist, it clearly pursues the tip of the [hand] as it is extended for the purpose of exiting.
In these four *karaṇas*, there is variety through the fast, medium, and slow tempos, and so forth, as well as through the alternating succession of the arms.

When all [the operations] are applied through their combination (*yojanā*), then hundreds of thousands of operations such as *ghāta* and *vartanā* are included within this very [system]; thus, what some call forty and others call one hundred is indeed false. Therefore it is said: "The specific details contained within the *karaṇa* must necessarily be known."

This is constant, because there is no purpose other than this. Now he describes the actions of the chest with the words "bent" (*ābhugna*) and so forth. "Sunk" (*nimna*) means contracted. "In some places" means having made it slack, loose, and unsupported here and there in the middle, [the chest] is bent down and falls downward.

(83) In cases of agitation, despair, fainting, grief, fear, disease, or a heart-thorn; in cold touch, rain, or when one is possessed by shame, [the *kampa*] is employed according to the requirements of the situation. (225)
It is stiff, with a sunken back, drooping shoulders, and a protruding chest; indeed, understand now its function as well. (226)
It should be employed against arrogance, pride, and astonishment, as well as toward truthful speech,
the utterance of "I" out of vanity, and excessive haughtiness.
(Regarding this, some [commentators] say—this is an interpolation:
"It should be understood by practitioners that this [gesture] is used for women during long sighs, yawning, stretching, and likewise in *bibboka*. )
When the chest is made continuous by upward throws and is caused to tremble,
that is to be known as the *ura* (chest) gesture by practitioners of drama.
Those skilled in drama should employ [the breath] in laughter and weeping, in exertion and fear, as well as in panting and coughing, in hiccups and pain, according to the requirements of the meaning.

*Vivāṃsau*: where, even without cold, there is wandering on the path just as on a foul day; thus it is called *varṣa*. Having raised [the shoulders] properly, they have emerged with shoulders that are straight (*śuddha*) or curved (*bhugna*).
*Hikkā* is clear.
(84) Performers should know that the *udvāhita* (raised) posture consists of the chest being lifted upward;
it is employed in long sighs, looking upward, yawning, and similar actions. || 231 ||
When all the placements of the limbs are arranged in a square formation, the chest should be known as even, well-poised, and endowed with aesthetic grace (sauṣṭhava). || 232 ||
This correct analysis of the chest has been fully explained by me;
hereafter, I shall describe the characteristics of the two sides.
Bent, raised, extended, and turned, as well as drawn back—thus the action of the sides is fivefold. (234)
The hips should be bent outward and the side likewise bent;
similarly, with the shoulders drawn back, it is known as the slightly inclined side [posture]. || 235 ||
The other side of the dancer, however, is reversed according to the rules;
it becomes elevated by the hips, sides, arms, and shoulders being raised high. (236)
It should be extended by stretching both sides;
here, it is intended that the *vivartita* (twisted) position is achieved through the turning of the three [parts] as well. (237)
Through the withdrawal and removal [of the limbs], it becomes *apasṛta* (withdrawn); this is called the characteristic of the side (*pārśva*). Now, learn its application.
The *upasarpa* (approaching) gesture is used for what is bent; the *apasarpaṇa* (withdrawing) for what is raised;
the *prasārita* (extended) for joy and similar states; and the *vivartita* (revolved) for turning around. (239)
But when it has turned away, it becomes withdrawn to the side by the force of its purpose;
understand these actions of the sides of the belly. (240)

The abdomen is said to be of three types: emaciated (kṣāma), sunken (khālva), and full (pūrṇa). That which is thin and sunken is called khālva, while that which is distended is called pūrṇa. || 241 ||
A thin smile occurs during laughter, while it may appear during weeping, sighing, yawning, illness, asceticism, exhaustion, or when afflicted by hunger; indeed, it is desired in these states. (242)
The abdomen is full when one is breathing heavily, when it is distended, or in cases of disease, overeating, and so forth.
Others, however, say:
"The abdomen may be of four kinds: emaciated, sunken, normal, or full. (243)
86) Thus has the function of the abdomen been described; now learn that of the hips:
it is severed, withdrawn, emitted, and likewise shaken. || 244 ||
The *udvāhitā* (raised) hip is thus; in both dance (*nāṭya*) and rhythmic movement (*nṛtta*), the hip is said to be of five kinds.
The *chinnā* (severed) hip is defined by the twisting of the waist. || 245 ||
When facing forward while the other side is turned away, it is called *nivṛttā*; when turned back, it is *nivartitā*; and from revolving all around, the hip movement is to be known as *recitā*.
When the hips move rapidly in a horizontal direction, they should be known as "trembling";
when the hips are raised slowly by lifting the sides of the buttocks, they are "raised. (247)
Furthermore, I shall explain their application and purpose:
they are used in cases such as being cut off, agitation from exertion, turning away, and gazing. (248)
The *nivṛttā* [gait] is used for walking on the path, while the *recitā* is used for whirling and similar movements;
the *prakampitā* should be employed for the gait of those who are hunchbacked, dwarfish, or short of stature. (249)
It should be applied when the [breasts] are large, or when women are engaged in amorous play;
likewise, it involves trembling, twisting, stiffening, and turning over. (250)
One should perform these five movements of the thighs (*ūru-karma*): turning, as well as repeated bending and raising of the side of the hip, which results in the shaking of the thigh. (251)
When the knee moves inward, that is known as *valana*;
here, it should be understood as *stambhana*, consisting of the action of *apaviddha*.
That which arises from the *valita* (twisted) and *āviddha* (thrust) movements is called *udvartana* (turning upward);
where the heel moves inward, that is *nivartana* (turning back). || 253 ||
For those who are unworthy recipients, there should be trembling in the various states of existence and even in times of fear;
likewise, women should perform a turning movement during their independent movements.
One should employ *stambhana* (stiffening) for both exertion and dejection; likewise, the wise should apply *udvartana* (massage with unguents) during physical exercise and the *tāṇḍava* dance. (255)
And a turning back (vivartana) should be performed during the sequence of hurried movements and so forth;
these include the actions of the hips, the triple-joint region, and the shoulders, as well as the actions of the sides.
Regarding the gaits, it has been stated that they consist of the action of the apaviddha; this means, in effect, a state of non-action.
Furthermore, other things should be adopted by practitioners according to what is observed in the world. (256)
Thus the characteristics of the thighs have been declared; now learn those of the shanks:
they may be rotated, bent, cast forward, or even raised upward. (257)
Likewise, the turning [of the body] and the movements of the shanks are fivefold:
from the left side to the right, and from the right to the left. || 258 ||
O Brahmins, wherever the foot moves, that is called *āvartita*;
one should lead it into *āvartita* in sequence by means of the *jaṅghā-svastika* (crossed shanks) yoga. (259)
The *nata* (bent) posture is to be understood by practitioners from the contraction of the knee;
furthermore, the *kṣipta* (thrown) posture is designated from the throwing out of the shank. || 260 ||
It is *nata* (bent) from the bending of the knee; it is *kṣipta* (thrown) from being cast outward;
and *udvāhita* (raised) is to be understood here as that which is raised upward. (261)
That which involves leading back [the gaze] is called *parivṛtta* (turned back);
it should be employed as *āvartita* (revolved) during the movements of the *vidūṣaka*.
The *nata* (bent) gesture should indeed be employed in standing, sitting, walking, and so forth;
the *kṣipta* (thrown) gesture is used in connection with physical exercises and in the *tāṇḍava* dance. 263.
Likewise, the *udvāhita* movement should be employed for actions such as leaping;
however, in the *tāṇḍava* and similar dances, it should be performed by the practitioners in a *parivṛtta* (rotated) manner.
Thus has been described the action of the shanks; now learn that of the feet:
the *udghaṭṭita* (the raised), the *sama* (the level), and likewise the *agratalasañcara* (the gliding on the tips). || 265 ||
The foot is known to be of five types: *añcita* (bent) and *kuñcita* (contracted).
Standing on the tips of the toes, the heel is brought down to the ground. (266)
That foot by which [the movement] is performed is called *udghaṭṭita*.
Having employed this application for the purpose of imitation within the *udveṣṭita* movements,
it should be performed either once or repeatedly with a fast or medium tempo.
That which is naturally formed on the ground and remains perfectly level,
with feet even, should be known as the *samapāda* (even-footed) stance, which serves as the basis for natural gestures.
He is steadfast in the enactment of natural dispositions and in the employment of various dramatic techniques. || 269 ||
Furthermore, when the foot-measure has been recited, those who know the ritual procedure must perform the *calita* again.
From the outward casting of the heel, there is a falling [of the foot] with the thighs drawn in; this is the *vartanā* (turning) *karaṇa*.
By the phrase "when such an action exists," he shows that one must repeatedly perform the movement from the tips of the soles of the feet and return to the original position.
When the upwardly distorted [foot] is rubbed, it is the *anudghaṭṭita*; that *karaṇa* which takes the form of an unwinding is called *udveṣṭita*.

The passage beginning with "yadāṅgulya" (when [the movement] of the fingers... refers to that very same [action], which is manifold due to the various distinctions of arm-movements (*bāhukarman*). In this context, its "application" (*prayoga*) is its employment based on the mode of execution (*vartanā*). Some, however, have stated that its application also serves for the purpose of imitation (*anukaraṇa*) once the actual performance has been reached, as in the case of Purūravas and others in works such as the *Vikramorvaśī*. By this, the scope of drama (*nāṭya*) is addressed.
The application has been stated.
90) When the heel of the foot itself is positioned on the inner side of the [other] foot, [it is the *samapāda* stance]. || 270 ||
When the big toe is positioned on the outer side, that is known as the tryaśrapāda (triangular-foot) posture.
