Having abandoned (or: having made) the position of equal feet, and likewise at the *aśvakrānta* [step], one should form a triangular foot in the prescribed manner for purposes such as when one is distressed.
When the heel of this very same even-footed stance is brought toward the inside,
it should be known as the "triangular foot" (*tryaśrapāda*), which is employed in various standing positions (*sthānaka*) and the like. When the rear heel is raised, the big toe is likewise extended.
When all the toes are slightly bent during the movement of the forepart of the foot, it is called *alya*.
By this [method], there occurs striking, pounding, standing, thrusting,
trampling the ground, whirling, tossing about, various breath-exhalations (recakas), and the movement of the heels.
He whose heel remains on the ground and likewise the forepart of his foot [is raised]. || 275 ||

"Neither with the front nor by bending, yet not hurrying"—thus is the urging and the impelling; "nikuṭṭana" is the restraining of that [movement]; "sthita" refers to standing postures and the like; "śubhana" is pressing (*pīḍana*); "hanana" is striking;
"vikṣepa" is the removal of a living being.
When all the toes are contracted, that foot is called "contracted" (añcita).
Likewise, in the movements of standing on the tips of the feet, and in turning forward and turning back; || 276 ||
This [stance] should be employed when struck by the foot and in various *bhramaraka* movements.
That foot whose heel is raised, whose toes are likewise contracted,
and whose middle part is also contracted, is known as the *kuñcita* (contracted) foot.
And likewise, in the *udāttagamana*, as well as in the *vartita* and *udvartita*. || 278 ||
And one should apply this quarter-verse even when the sequence has been transgressed.
The heel should be raised, while the big toe remains firmly planted on the ground. || 279 ||
And the left [leg], remaining in its natural position, is proclaimed as the "needle-foot" (sūcīpāda).
The application of that [nūpura] in the execution of dance movements has been proclaimed. (280)
The execution of the foot, the shank, and the thigh must be performed equally by the practitioners;
for in the execution of the foot, everything is held to be accomplished by means of the shank and the thigh. (281)
*Bhrāntaka* (the whirling) is a various *recaka* (extension) of the mind; *karapādarecaka* (extension of hands and feet). *Añcitā* refers to those [steps] that are extended;

*añcita* means raised up, used in the gait of the *vidūṣaka* and others. Those performances (*prayoga*) in which the *bhramarī* *cārī* occurs are called *bhramarakas*. Others recite "sūcī" as the sixth foot. Of the *nūpura*...
In the performance and binding of foot ornaments, the actions of the waist, thighs, calves, and feet—
employed in combination through a variety of intermingling with other movements— are called *cārī*.

Since the movement of that entire collection is accomplished through the differentiation of circular formations (*maṇḍala*), it is by means of the actions starting from the waist and ending with the feet that [the dance is formed].
The Ācāryas have already stated this; for that very reason, their specific application has not been mentioned separately.
However, immediately following [that], these two chapters were taught for the purpose of demonstrating examples of their various manifestations. Having kept all of this in mind, he says:

"Performing the feet, shanks, and thighs," and so forth. "Together" (*samam*) means simultaneously. The reason for this is stated as "of the foot," meaning that among the actions such as performing the navel, shanks, and thighs, the action of one foot [is simultaneous with] the other.
Just as the foot moves, so too does the thigh move;
because their action is identical, one should employ the *pādacārī* gait. || 282 ||
Thus has been declared the definition and the function of that which is born of the limbs (aṅgaja). Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the *cārīs* and *vyāyāmas*.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Representation of Gestures," in the illustrious *Nāṭyaśāstra* of Bharata.
He clarifies this very point with the words "just as the foot. By the phrase "of those two," the *jaṅghā* (shank) is also included in between.

He shows that everything pertaining to the limbs (*āṅgika*) is stated here by saying "this is what [has been] said. With the words "thereafter," he provides a thematic outline (*sūtra*) for what is to be discussed immediately following. The term *cārī-vyāyāma* refers to that by which the various movements are characterized and illustrated by way of examples.
Auspiciousness.
Abhinavagupta, whose distress was shattered by the grace of the ornament of the bud-like rays of the coldest moon,
dispelled the heat of doubt in the ninth chapter.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on the Physical Expressions (Āṅgika), in the Abhinavabhāratī, a commentary on the Nāṭya-veda composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara Abhinavagupta.
The Nāṭyaśāstra by Śrī [Bharata]:
Chapter Ten.
(Thus, the movement of the foot, the calf, the thigh, and likewise the hip, when performed with equal action, is proclaimed as *cārī*. || 1 ||)
The noble ones, having entered upon the method, exert themselves toward one another;
because they are endowed with the constituent factors, it is therefore called "exertion. (2)

May Lord Śambhu be victorious— he who is motionless, whose nature is existence, who moves within the sky and the earth, who bestows the supreme goal, and who is at all times the essence of mere sound.
It has been stated that [the term] *cārī* has the characteristic of physical exertion (*vyāyāma*). Regarding this, there is a doubt concerning the compound and the meaning of the word *vyāyāma*.

With the intention of removing these two doubts—namely, whether the suffix *iñ* after the root *car-* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the abstract state (*bhāva*), and whether the word *cārī* is well-known in its conventional sense by virtue of the rule "after a *kṛt*-suffix ending in a vowel other than *ktin*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied"—he says:

"Accordant with the method" (*vidhānopagata*) means that falling into mutual conjunction is the intended meaning of the term "exertion" (*vyāyāma*). The sense is that it is a *karmadhāraya* compound, namely, "exertion which is itself the conjunction. As for the etymological meaning:
they "exert themselves" (*vyāyacchante*), meaning they fall into mutual [conjunction]. To the question "In what [order] is there a rule?", he says: "Mutually, the preceding..."
The movement is restricted to the subsequent [action] and not to the preceding one; therefore, because it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the *ātmanepada* affix applies.

By the rule "from a compound with *paraspara*," he prohibits the *ātmanepada* arising from the reciprocal exchange of action (*karmavyatihāra*), but not that prescribed by the rule "after *āṅ*, with *yam* and *han*. Now, what is that restriction? He says: "those that have come under the heading of a specific injunction" (*vidhānopagatāḥ*).
Since one [act] has been undertaken by the principal [agent], another follows by force;
is it not then a case of mutual dependence? No, for they are properly joined, employed, and set in motion by some member that serves as the principal.
That which is the movement of a single foot is designated as *cārī*; whereas the stepping with both feet together is what is called a *karaṇa*. (3)
The combination of the constituent parts (karaṇas) is called a "segment" (khaṇḍa). When three or four such segments are joined together, they form a "mandala. || 4 ||
Dance is extended through *cārīs*, and likewise movement is performed with *cārīs*;
the discharge of weapons is also by means of *cārīs*, for *cārīs* are proclaimed as essential in combat.

The plural number is used here in view of whatever [limbs] may be required. This is what is meant: when a certain limb becomes primary—such as the hand in a gesture (*abhinaya*) or the foot in walking (*gati*)—then the *cārī* (foot-position) useful for that is primary;
and the preceding *cārī*, which is appropriate for the accomplishment of that [primary] *cārī*, is relied upon by the subsequent one.

"Exertion (*vyāyāma*) consists of mutual restriction. In this regard, he defines the divisions of exertion according to its being concise, intermediate, or extensive. "Single-foot movement" (*ekapādapracāra*) refers to the movement of the hips and so forth with one foot alone; it is "distracted" (*vyākṣipta*). "With two feet"—by the word "foot" (*pāda*), [the meaning is as follows:]...

Its application: the word "name" (*nāma*) means that this [term] is now being prescribed as a designation (*saṃjñā*), which is indeed different from what is already well-known through its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). This is the concise explanation regarding the beginning of other gestures (*abhinaya*) and so forth. Because of the plural number in the word "of the *karaṇas*" (*karaṇānām*), [it is like the rule]: "One should sacrifice three *kapiñjala* birds."
For example: otherwise, if there were no fixed rule regarding multiplicity, where would the distinction between *khaṇḍas* and *maṇḍalas* lie?

This is the intermediate effort; [the phrase] "increasing by means of the *upavṛtti*" refers to three *auras*. Furthermore, because the word "or" (*vā*) is used with reference to the square *tāla*, there is also a mixing [of types].

By indicating this, he also adopts another enumeration. For instance, in the fourth maṇḍala called *sūcīviddha* (11–12), he will describe the *cārīs* [starting with]: "One should place the *sūcī* as the first step," and so forth.
However, in the seventh, named *alātā*—having whirled around the maṇḍala in succession by means of these *cārīs*.

"Sixfold or sevenfold" (11-22), and "in the twelfth [chapter], with one and a half [verses]"—it is the same elsewhere. There, he first demonstrates the worldly nature of the *cārīs* by saying "by means of the *cārīs*"; [he shows] that dance (*nṛtta*) consists of *aṅgahāras*, and that it is extended and pervaded by those *cārīs* respectively.
"Movement" refers to gait. "The discharge of weapons" refers to combat with discuses, spears, and the like;
"combat" (*yudha*) refers to fighting with swords, striking, and so forth, as well as wrestling (*niyuddha*). He applies this even to the present context:
This drama that has been introduced is established entirely within the *cārīs*;
indeed, without the *cārīs*, no part of the drama can proceed. (6)
Therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the prescription for *cārīs*, as to which [cārī] is to be employed in what [situation], whether in dance, combat, or movement. (7)
Samapādā, sthitāvartā, and likewise śakaṭākhyā; adhyardhikā, cāṣagati, and another, vicyavā. (8)
The *eḍakākrīḍitā*, the *baddhā*, the *ūrūdvṛttā*, and likewise the *āḍḍitā*;
the *utspanditā*, the *janitā*, the *syanditā*, and the *cāpaspanditā*. (9)

Regarding the phrase "that which is this": by the word *yat* (which), the connection with the dharmas already explained is referred to; by the word *etat* (this), the connection with the dharmas yet to be explained is indicated. Thus, he declares the extensiveness of the drama (*nāṭya*).
"Some limb" refers to the head, hands, and so forth—some together with the movements (*cārī*), and some through their sequential relationship as preceding or following.

Regarding the term *saṃpravartate*, it functions as *saṃvartate* in the sense of proceeding with wickedness, or it proceeds correctly through action, or it proceeds by means of the impermanent; thus, the application of the meaning of the prefix (*upasarga*) is optional. Likewise, the Master Bhartṛmitra maintains that even in the case of a limb (*aṅga*), the reality of acceptance (*svīkāratattva*) is being examined.
Furthermore, because it would entail excessive labor regarding the subject at hand, the mind—being weary of the mere desire to manifest proficiency in words and sentences—desists (is restrained).
"Definition" refers to the illustration. "In dance" means in the context of *karaṇas*, *aṅgahāras*, and so forth. "In which... [refers to the following].
The term *napuṃsaka* is a singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). Likewise, [the phrase] "as stated and as will be stated" (p.
96) refers to the sixteen [syllables] beginning with *samotsārita*, *mattalla*, and *mattalī*.
These noble women are remembered as being of the earth; now listen again to those of the sky.
For indeed, there are the *atikrāntā*, the *apakrāntā*, and likewise the *pārśvakrāntā*;
as well as the *ūrdhvajānu*, the *sūcī*, and the *nūpurapādikā*. (11)
The swinging-footed, the cast-off, and those known as the whirled and the upturned;
likewise the lightning-twirling, the fire-brand circle, and the snake-frightening. (12)
The Mṛgaplutā, the Daṇḍā, and the Bhramarī—these are known as the sixteen Ākāśikyas; learn now their characteristics.
The remainder [is as follows]: "by means of steps made without intervals, and likewise even with the nails.

In that regard, what was stated concerning dance (*nṛtta*) will be explained in the context of combat (*yuddha*); the remainder is that this principle is to be inferred [for other cases]. And regarding movement (*gati*), it will be explained in the twelfth chapter. Thus, the meaning of these three chapters has been indicated here.
Regarding this, he states the summary: "Those belonging to the earth" (*bhaumya*) means those who exist on the earth;

likewise, "those belonging to the sky" (*ākāśikya*) refers to those who move above. "Are recorded" (*smṛtāḥ*) means that for the purpose of exposition here, as much as is remembered from the Vedic citations is provided, while the remaining [details] are to be stated by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Therefore, this should not be doubted. If...
It is not clear from that [text] by how many distinctions this enumeration was stated;
therefore, those definitions which are not etymologically meaningful are now being explained.
But that movement, based on a stationary position, should be known as the *samapādā* posture. || 14 ||
Having made an inner circle with the foot dragged along the ground, one should then move the other [foot] away; that is known as the *sthitāvarta* (the standing-turn). || 15 ||
Seated with the limbs relaxed, having extended the foot so that the sole moves along the ground,
and having raised the chest, one should employ the Śakaṭāsya (cart-mouth) posture.
When the left foot is behind the right,
that movement of withdrawal should be known by the wise as *sādhyardhikā*.
Now, regarding the *samapāda* [stance]: one might ask, "How can there be a *cārī* (movement) when one is in the *samapāda*? He replies: "By resorting to a position" (*sthāna-saṃśraya*).

The meaning is that when one who is indeed in the *samapāda* moves to another location, it is precisely then that it becomes a *caraṇa-cārī* (a movement of the feet), because it is designated as such by virtue of its functional suitability.

Now, regarding *sthitāvarta*: "by rubbing the ground" means by moving on the tips of the feet toward the inner circle; "up to the *svastika* of the second knee" indicates the specific manner of placement (*sanniveśayoga*), the word "again" (*punaḥ*) highlighting this distinction. Thus, if that [first knee] is joined in the form of a *svastika*, then one should extend the second [knee].
One should draw one's own side toward oneself, such that the position of one becomes the position of the other.
Now, regarding *śakaṭāsyā*: "with limbs settled" means with the upper body held steady through effort.

It is so called because by it the cart (*śakaṭa*) is to be thrown or cast away. When one foot is on level ground, having made the other leg—with its toes tucked in—bend at the knee, extend the shank, and place it against one's own side...
Some say that the placement of the foot moving along the surface of the three [points] is like "nirodhana" (or "recana").
However, this definition is indeed inconsistent with the meaning of the term being defined.
Now, regarding the *adhyardhikā*: "of the left" means of the right; "behind" means at the region of the heel; "of that" refers to...

In the movement toward the right, the position is such that one occupies three-quarters of one's own side. Regarding "non-separation," it should be understood as referring to intervals of one and a half *tālas* and so forth. Others say that while one foot has a full gait, the other has a gait of half a *pāda*. This is stated thus because of the predominance of the specific technique (*karaṇa*), and this applies to the left foot as well.
It is indeed joined with the back.
98) The left foot is extended and then likewise drawn back.
Or, in the case of a retreat, it is prescribed that one should move to the left or slip away to the right. || 18 ||
From the *vicyavā* stance with feet together, one should perform the *vicyavā*;
striking the surface of the earth with the tip of the palm of the foot. (19)
When one leaps up with both feet moving on the surface and then descends,
performing this alternately, that is called *eḍakākrīḍitā*.
Now, as for the movement of the blue jay (*cāṣagati*): "to the left" means behind the right [foot]; thus, the left foot always steps aside.
"Extended" means [the leg] is stretched forward to the distance of one *tāla*; then that same [leg], having stepped aside, is drawn back to a distance of two *tālas*.
The left [foot] steps aside together with the right. Having leaped slightly—

The term *cāpagati* refers to the movement of a bow, characterized by its simultaneous drawing apart and contracting together, as well as its recoiling with a sudden jerk. Others read the term as *savyopasarpī*; in that case, "clinging" (*śliṣṭatva*) is the literal sense, while "recoiling" (*apasarpaṇa*) is the intended meaning.
Now, *vicyavā*: the term "of the foot" means "of both feet.

Now, *ailakākrīḍitā*: having leaped slightly from one thigh and ankle region, there is a further leap with another limb; that *cārī* in which there is such a falling [to the ground] by turns is [called] *ailakākrīḍitā*.
Because it is similar to the gait of a goat, it is called the "Goat’s Play" (eḍakākrīḍitā).
Having formed the *svastika* by interlocking the shanks of one another,
and because there is a twisting (*valana*) with the thighs, this is declared to be the *baddha* gait. (21)
When the heel of the foot moving on the surface is turned outward,
and the shank is likewise arched and the thigh is rotated, that is known as *ūrūdvṛttā*.
When one foot moves on its toes either in front or behind,
rubbed by the second foot, that [gait] is called *aḍḍitā*.

Now, regarding the *baddhā*: some say that when there is merely the twisting of the two shanks while the legs remain in the *jaṅghā-svastika* position, it is the *baddhā*. Others, however, maintain that it consists of the two feet moving toward their respective sides, preceded by a circular rotation of the tips of the soles through the shifting of the *svastika*.
That which they call the "thigh-binding" is so called because it is bound along the connection between the two shanks.

Now, regarding the *urvṛttā* (upward-turned) posture: when the heel associated with the foot moving on its forepart is turned upward toward the back of the second foot, and the shank is bent by the bending of the knee, it is called *urvṛttā* because the second shank is turned toward it through a rotation.

The *ūruddhṛttā* arises from the upward turning of the thigh and has as its objects shame, jealousy, and the like; others, however, say it is that which, with the heel as its second [support], moves across the sole and is directed outward.

Now, regarding *aḍḍitā*: "in front" (*agratas*). The particle *api* denotes either conjunction (*samuccaya*) or an alternative (*paryāya*). Therefore, when one [foot] is standing firmly, the second foot should be moved across the sole (*talasañcara*), rubbed and joined in succession in front and behind; this is *aḍḍitā*.
The foot should be withdrawn slowly, both externally and internally;
when this occurs in accordance with the exhalation (*recaka*), it is known as the *āryutspanditā* [movement]. (24)
With one hand in the fist-position at the chest and the other hand extended,
with the feet performing the *talasañcara* movement, this is declared to be the *janitā* ācārya.
Having extended the foot five tālas apart, one should place it in the *syandita* position;
likewise, with the second foot, one should place it in the *apasyandita* position.

Because it involves the foot's transgression of its own place; they cite the root *aḍḍu* in the sense of "transgressing" and "injuring," and the form [of the word] occurs when there is a sentient being (*sattva*).

Then, the *utspanditā* [is performed]: if it returns by means of the outer part of the little fingers and the inner part of the thumbs, it performs the coming and going of both feet. To what extent? It says: it has risen above the removal of the *pādarecita* out of regard for its beauty. That which belongs to the river—
Because it is produced by a vibration in the form of a turning back, this is called *utspanditā*; some authorities call this the *recaka* dance-hand (*nṛttahasta*).
Now, as for the *janitā*: it is so called because the feet move upon the surface [of the ground]. This alone is its essential nature (*svarūpa*):
the movement of the fist toward the chest and the movement of the other hand; this is merely its procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
It is called *janitā* because it brings about the "birth" (*janana*) of all movements, since it constitutes their inception.

Now, regarding *syanditā* and *apasyanditā*: when the thighs are seated in a manner equal to the *krama* [step], the right foot is extended five *tālas*; this is known as a *tāla* measured by the middle finger. That is called *syanditā* because its nature is extension (*prasāraṇa*).
By the reverse of this, it is also [called] *syanditā* by means of the left [foot]; this is also obtained from the synonym *aṅga*.
It has been defined again for the purpose of making known the rule of concomitance in practice.

However, in the cases of *ālīḍha* and *pratyālīḍha*, both feet have a triangular configuration; that which will be described as the life-force (*jīvitva*) from the mandala-position is specifically the right [foot].
When the feet move with a rolling gait as they step along the floor,
it is described as the *samotsaritamattalli* in its full extension. (27)
With whirling approaches on both feet,
and with hands that are entwined and cast aside, this is declared to be the *mattallī* [dance].
These noble steps (cārīs) are known as terrestrial and are based on wrestling and compassion;
now I shall fully describe the characteristics of the aerial steps (ākāśikī-cārīs). || 29 ||
The phrase "the foot [should be] five *tālas*," and so forth, applies to the *syanditā* [gait], but not so for others; this is the remainder [of the rule].
Furthermore, another distinction is that in the *sthāna* (stationary posture) stability is predominant, whereas in the *cārī* (movement) motion is predominant.
Now, when one performs the *samotsarita*, *mattalli*, *talasañcara*, *jaṅghāsvastika*, or *abhyantara* [steps] with the other [foot], that very same [rule applies].
And he performs the *dvitīyatalasañcara* (movement on the second level); then, according to others, there is the *upasarpaṇa* (approach) of those two as they whirl.

*Sama* means unimpaired; *avana* means protection; for that purpose, *sarita* means possessing movement; *madana* means intoxication; *matta* means one who extends that intoxication; and *laya* means the going [of it]—thus, it is called *samotsaritamattalli*.

The word *sarita* is derived from the root *ri*, meaning "to go," combined with the prefix *sa-* in a compound and the suffix *-ana*. *Madana* means "intoxication" (*mutkṣipaḥ*). *Layana* means "dissolution" (*līḥ*).

From the nominal stem *sari*, the form *sarita* is formed by adding the suffix *-tṛc* (or alternatively, others read it as *saṃ ā ut sarita*). For one who is not rendered disoriented by intoxication and does not flee elsewhere for the sake of protection, [the result] is indeed twofold.

This *cārī* (step) known as *mattalī* is accomplished through the "gait" (*gati*), which pertains to the domain of moderate intoxication; it is performed with both feet such that the entire surface of the soles is in contact with the ground,
by means of the *jaṅghā-svastika* (crossing of the shanks) and the two halves of a triangle.
Because of swaying or because of moving away, the *mattallī* is that which pertains to a state of intoxication that is not intense.

"Based on the performance of wrestling (*niyuddha*)" means that these [techniques] are established in wrestling from time immemorial; they exist first in the *karaṇas* and *aṅgahāras*, and from there they enter into drama (*nāṭya*). By the statement "they are remembered," it is shown that the Veda is the authority here, as they are connected to an Upaveda.
And this demonstration of separation and so forth should be understood as follows:
102) Having lifted the contracted foot, one should extend it forward.
Having lifted it up, one should let it fall; that [action] is known as *atikrāntā*. || 30 ||
Having performed a twist with the thighs, one should lift the bent foot and cast it to the side; this is known as the apakrāntā posture.
Raising the contracted foot and placing it level with the knee or the breast,
while the other foot is extended, the *pārśvakrāntā* (side-step) posture is performed.
Lifting the contracted foot, one should place it level with the knee or breast;
the second [foot] is kept steady on the ground—this is proclaimed as Ūrdhvajānu (Raised Knee).

Now, regarding "the heel is raised and passed beyond" (1-277): having placed the [foot] bent at the second ankle-region, extending it slightly forward, and raising it by four *tālas* or more according to the natural variation of the movement, it is lowered to the ground with the front part [of the foot].
She is "one who has transgressed" because she has overstepped the boundary of what should be traversed.

Now, regarding "one who has departed": having first placed her thighs and breasts together (as they were bound), and then lifting her foot and casting it aside, she is "one who has departed" because of this act of departing.
Now, regarding *pārśvakrāntā*: having raised the bent foot toward one's own side, one should drop it to the ground on its heel;

because it was previously bent, it becomes extended with force. Its definition is as follows: "Having stood [in *sthirāsanam*], the ball of the foot is placed on the ground and the heel is dropped. (9-266)
This very [practice] is known as *pārṣṇicaṇḍadhātā*. Others, however, say that one should lift [the victim] up to the second thigh-joint and then drop him by opening [the mouth].
Then, with the knee raised— meaning that its rigidity is such that its upward lifting is like [the movement] of that [other leg].
Having lifted the bent foot, one should extend the knee upward.
And she who causes [the enemy] to fall by means of the foremost yoga is proclaimed as Sūcī. || 34 ||
Having bent the foot back, one should quickly strike it down upon the ground with the sole; this is the *nūpurapādikā* stance (*cārī*). (35)
Lifting the contracted foot and swinging it from side to side, one should let it fall while bent;
this is proclaimed as the *dolapādā* [stance].
Having lifted the contracted foot and drawn it back, one should place it with the ankles crossed;
that is known as the *ākṣiptā* [posture]. || 37 ||

Now, regarding the *sūcī* (needle): one should extend the entire leg from the knee down to the knee, or from above the knee up to the thigh; having extended it, one should cause it to fall by means of its tip. It is called *sūcī* because of its needle-like shape.

Now, regarding *nūpurapādikā*: having placed the heel on the ground behind [the other leg] in a bent position (9-275), one should lead that [bent leg] behind [the body] as far as the contact of the buttock and the heel, and then cast the shank down upon one's own side with the sole facing forward in a bent manner. This produces the "jingling" (*jhaṇajjhaṇiti*) sound of anklets.

Because it produces sound and serves the purpose of the *svarita* accent, as well as being joined with anklets, it is so described. Now, regarding the *ḍolapāda*: "having lifted" means having led [the foot] toward its own side to the end of the right field (*dakṣiṇakṣetra*), and from there, one should swing it back toward its own side; thus one should lead it in the form of a swing (*dolā*). Then, one should let it fall onto the heel (*pārṣṇi*) on its own side.

Now, regarding "thrown" (*ākṣiptā*)—it means having "thrown" (*ākṣipya*). Having moved to the other side from the front by lifting the three parts [of the foot] as if in a half-moon (*ardhamaṇḍala*), one should strike the ground with the heel in a swastika (*svastika*) motion.
When, from the svastika position, one foot is bent and extended while the other falls in añcita, it is known as the āviddhā [stance]. || 38 ||
Having struck the foot and encircled it, one should leap up and bring it down;
having turned around for the second time, this is declared the *udvṛttā* movement.
One should extend the foot, turned backward and rubbed against the head, while whirling in a circle in all directions; that is known as the *vidyudbhrāntā*. || 40 ||
With the foot extended behind, turned inward, and its heel brought down, it is proclaimed as the *alātā* posture. || 41 ||

Now, regarding *āviddha*: the bent foot belonging to the *svastika* stance, whose shanks are separated, is extended; then, being *āviddha*, it should be cast with its heel onto the area of the heel of the second [foot] on one's own side.

Now, regarding *udvṛttā*: by the term *āviddha* (twisted), which relates to the *āviddha-cārī*, and by the word *kuñcita* (contracted), he shows that this [foot] has its entire mass twisted. *Āveṣṭana* (wrapping) consists in the heel being placed upon the region of the second thigh.
Having leaped up with that very foot and performed a *bhramaraka* (swirling movement), one should let it fall. Then, the second [foot] is likewise directed upwards.
Because it is present, it is "upraised" (*udvṛtta*).

Now, regarding "whirling like lightning" (*vidyudbhrāntā*): some say it is from the base of the thigh behind; however, the Teacher [states] that having turned the head from behind, from the side, and from the rear part, by means of its contact with the head, it extends everywhere.
"One should extend [the foot] while rotating it like a circle above, below, and to the sides; this is the *vidyudbhrāntā*.

Now, the *ālātā*: first it is extended behind the back part, then by a twisting motion it is brought inside, then led toward the surface facing the second thigh, and finally dropped with the heel on one's own side.
The firebrand is shaped like a whirling circle of fire.
105) Having lifted the bent foot, one should rotate the thighs in a triangular fashion.
And from the hip and knee, it becomes the "terrifying serpent" (bhujaṅgatrāsitā). || 42 ||
Having performed the *atikrāntakrama* and having leaped up, one should let it fall;
with the calves drawn up and encircled, that is to be known as the *hariṇaplutā*.
Having placed the foot with the anklet forward and extending it, one quickly performs the *āviddha* movement; that is known as the *daṇḍapādā*.

Then, for the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* [movement]: having bent and raised the second leg up to the limit of the root of the thigh, one should rotate the hip toward the buttocks by turning the knee and ankle;
one should place the knee on one's own side with the sole of the foot turned upward.
The *Bhujaṅgatrāsitā* (Terrified by a Serpent) resembles the gait of one overcome by fear of a serpent at one’s feet;
it is performed by lifting and leaping with one foot in a *kuñcita* (contracted) position as prescribed in the *Hariṇaplutā* movement,
and then immediately bringing that same foot down, while the second leg, with its foot bent (*añcita*), remains behind.
It should be cast behind; this is like the "leap of a deer" (mṛgaplutita) and is seen in the case of the Vidūṣaka and others in expressions such as "let it be so.
Now, regarding the Daṇḍapāda and Nūpurapāda [gestures]: the bent foot is placed upon the second heel.

Having placed it in front, one should extend it; likewise, having performed the *āviddhakarana* (the "twisted" movement), the action is that in which the tips of the knees are brought forward toward one's own body-field. Because the thighs, knees, and shanks are held rigidly straight like a staff, it is called *daṇḍapāda* ("staff-foot").
Having performed the *atikrāntakrama*, one should rotate the three [limbs].
From the circling of the second foot with the sole of the foot, it is known as the *bhramarī*. (45)
These are indeed known as aerial movements, consisting of graceful bodily actions;
they are to be employed for the discharging of weapons such as the bow, the thunderbolt, and the sword. (46)
Whether positioned in front, behind, or even at the sides, according to the requirements of the yoga, the hands must be placed at the feet by the practitioners of dance, O twice-born ones. (47)

Now, regarding the *bhramarī*: having raised the bent foot as prescribed in the *atikrānta-cārī*, and having rotated the thigh in a triangular manner like one frightened by a serpent, one should rotate the sacrum during the circumambulation of the sole of the second foot; it is called *bhramarī* because of this wheel-like rotation (*nemibhramaṇa*) by means of the turning of the entire body.

He demonstrates their remaining duties, such as application (*viniyoga*) and so forth, by stating "consisting of graceful bodily movements" and "the bow, the thunderbolt," and so on. Now, while defining the beauty of the body, he shows the pervasive application of the *cārīs* by stating "those in front," and so on. The intended meaning here is that, in this context, sometimes movement is predominant.
Sometimes there is the operation of the hands alone, sometimes of both; in the first case, the two hands follow and subsequently accompany the movement of the feet;
in the second, the feet follow and subsequently accompany the operation of the hands;
and in the third, both [hands and feet] [act simultaneously], through their dependence on the application [of effort] at the same time.
Engagement; yoga is appropriateness. Here, for the purpose of joining with physical beauty, the Āryas are introduced at the beginning of this chapter and also on page 107.
Where the foot is, there the hand is; where the hand is, there the *trika* (the three upper parts) is.
Having performed the emergence of the foot, one should likewise join the secondary limbs (*upāṅgas*).
Just as the foot moves along the ground during walking, so too the hand, having moved, should come to rest against the region of the waist. (49)
These noble ones, whose nature consists of graceful bodily movements, have been described by me;
I shall now declare their positions for the discharge of all weapons. (50)
The Vaiṣṇava, the Samapāda, the Vaiśākha, the Maṇḍala, the Pratyālīḍha, and likewise the Ālīḍha—these are the six standing postures (sthāna). || 51 ||

(10-73) Thus, when that predominance occurs, he says "since the hand" (*yato hasta*) in order to clarify what kind of activity the *prayojikā* (the instigator) is: "in that same manner" (*tathā*) refers to the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*), such as the eyebrows, eyes, and so forth. Now, if the hand performs the act of movement during the action of the foot, then [what happens] upon its cessation?
Anticipating the question, "What is the status of the hand?", he says: "When the foot-movement is completed"—the word "completed" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

The particle *eva* (only/just) also serves to dispel any doubt regarding its impossibility. Regarding "the hand": in dance (*nṛtta*) and dramatic performance (*nāṭya*), there are the *ardhacandra*, the *pakṣapradyota*, and the *pakṣavañcita*. Now, when the foot has reached the ground, what is the configuration of the body?

With this intention, wishing to describe the *sthānakas*, he makes his formal promise (*pratijñā*) preceded by a summary of what has gone before: "And these, O Noble One... The gracefulness of the body (*aṅga-lalitatva*) is such that by means of just these many [movements], even in the case of a simple extension (*uttānatve*), there is precisely that much variety of gait (*gatiprakāra*). The term *sthānāni* is derived through grammatical analysis (*vyutpatti*) in the sense of state (*bhāve*), instrument (*karaṇe*), or location (*adhikaraṇe*).

Regarding those which are called bodily postures (*kāyasanniveśa*), the general application (*viniyoga*) stated is "the release from all weapons. Furthermore, the meaning is that these *cārīs* have the nature of movement (*gati-rūpatva*), and that for movement, there is first the preceding state and then the subsequent state. "Of men" refers to the standing positions (*sthānaka*).
The distance between the two feet should be two *tālas* and a half-*tāla*.
Of these two [arms], one is raised and is triangular in shape, while the other is positioned at the side.
With the shanks slightly bent and the limbs held with graceful poise, this is indeed the Vaiṣṇava posture; Viṣṇu is the presiding deity here.
In this situation, conversation arising from one's own nature should be carried out with men of superior or middling rank who are engaged in various other affairs. (54)
One should employ it in the releasing of the discus as well as in the drawing of the bow,
in gestures of courageous and noble playfulness, and likewise in the display of wrath.

The meaning is that they will be defined [later]. "Situated on the side" (pakṣasthita) means with the fingers directed toward the flank. "Triangular" (tryaśra) means slightly facing forward without touching [the ground]. "Bent" (añcita) means crooked due to the bending of the knees and a certain stiffness.
That which is honored or esteemed by the "grace" (sauṣṭhava) which will be described as a limb—[this refers to] grace, or [grace] in a secondary sense.
"Foremost" (*aṅgapuraskṛtam*) means principal. Indeed, because Viṣṇu is the presiding deity (*adhidaivatam*) here, it is "Vaiṣṇava.

Therefore, this is the *sthānaka* (stage-setting) for the employment of such a person as the *sūtradhāra* (stage-manager), who is primarily male. This should be understood in the same way in subsequent instances. This—
This very same [state], when inverted, is considered to be "anger born of affection" (*praṇayakrodha*),
as well as in cases of reproach and likewise in the agitation of affection. (56)
Indeed, [these qualities] reside in doubt, envy, ferocity, thought, intellect, and memory; as well as in dejection, fickleness, pride, and the powers desired. (57)
It is characterized by the predominance of the erotic, the marvelous, the loathsome, and the heroic sentiments.
When the feet are equal, both feet remain at the same level, separated by the measure of a *tāla*. (58)
Endowed with natural excellence, Brahmā is the presiding deity here;
by means of this place, one should perform the auspicious rite for the Brahmins.
He also performed the painting of birds, as well as excellent decorative art for those dwelling in the sky,
those in chariots, and even those residing in celestial palaces (vimānas).
One should construct this location for those established in the liṅga and those established in their vows;
the distance between the two feet should be three tālas and a half-tāla.

"By this position"—this refers to that which is innate (*svabhāvaja*) and not induced by external influence (*anāveśita*). (Regarding "by the Brahmins"): he desires to receive that which is performed by the Brahmins, such as auspicious benedictions and the like. This is the station (*sthānaka*) for those situated in the sky and so forth. Those situated in the *liṅga* are the Śaivas and others who abide in their vows (*vratasthā*).

The limbs of wisdom, such as the upper body and so forth, are seated immovably and at rest where the thighs [are positioned] relative to the needle. As for how much space in the sky [is occupied], he says: three *tāla*s and a half-*tāla*.
One should fashion the seated thighs at three tālas and one and a half tālas; there, one should apply the two feet, which are triangular and situated on the sides.
For this is indeed the station of Vaiśākha, and Skanda is the presiding deity here;
by means of this station, the wise should perform the mounting of horses.
Physical exercise, the discharge [of arrows], the examination of land-birds, and the excellence achieved through physical training in the handling of the bow. (64)
And this very same [procedure] must be performed by practitioners during the *recakas*;
however, in the *aindra* mandala, the two feet should be positioned at a distance of four *tālas* apart.
With the two shoulders positioned in a triangle and the hips and knees held level,
one should employ weapons such as the mace and the thunderbolt with circular movements.
The vehicle of the elephants is the description of the "thick-winged" (sthūlapakṣin). The meaning is that the region of the sky is below three and a half tālas. Viśākha is Skanda.
Because they alone emerge for battle and other such activities from the limbs that have been pervaded, it is they [who are meant].

By means of the sequence of taking up speed and urging from the rear; the word "in the Aindra [stance]" is the ellipsis, indicating that here too one should suggest the state of having thighs seated in the space of the sky at a distance of two and a half *tālas*.
It is called a "mandala" because it pertains to the Lord of the Mandala. This, however, is the *vaiśākha* [stance] for driving horses.
Based on the context of "larger than those elephants," the birds referred to here should be understood as Garuḍa and others, who are the largest [of all].
Having extended his right foot five tālas from this very [position]. || 67 ||
One should assume the *ālīḍha* stance, and Rudra is its presiding deity;
whatever action is performed in this posture is characterized by heroism and ferocity.
Successive verbal altercations caused by anger and resentment, as well as the clashing of wrestlers and the sizing up of enemies; (69)
Likewise, there is the charging forward and the discharging of weapons;
having drawn back the right foot and extended the left foot. (70)
The turning from the *ālīḍha* posture is known as *pratyālīḍha*.
One should discharge the weapon held in the *ālīḍha* posture by means of the *pratyālīḍha*. (71)
Indeed, the discharge of various weapons must be performed by the practitioners;
furthermore, four principles regarding the discharge of weapons should be understood here. (72)

The Bhārata, the Sātvata, the Vārṣagaṇya, and the Kaiśika—by this very [description], he indicates the sitting upon the thighs (*niṣaṇṇorutva*) as well as the triangularity (*tryaśratva*) of the two. That by which the ground is licked or touched on all sides is *ālīḍha*. *Saṃpheṭa* means conflict or rivalry.

The characteristic of the *ālīḍha-parivarta* has been stated thus far; however, this is said for the purpose of clarifying the specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*). "Contracted" (*kuñcita*) means the opposite of extended;
here, the foot is further both turned upward and contracted. Now, it was indeed stated that the performers must effect the discharge of weapons.
Regarding its application by practitioners, [the text states] "of the principles" and so forth (p.
However, in the *Bhārata*, it says: "In the Kaṭicchedya [tradition], but in the Sātvata, there is the Pādacchedya. (73)
In the Vārṣagaṇya style, however, there is a cutting of the chest, while in the Kaiśika style, there is a cutting of the head;
by these methods employed by practitioners, various *ācarīs* arise.
The maneuvers (pravicāras) should be employed for the discharge of various weapons, using the rhythmic movements of the limbs (aṅgahāras) that rely on correct logic and arise from logic itself. (75)
Since battles take place, therefore rules of conduct have been established;
[one should hold] the shield in the left hand and the [weapon] with the right. (76)
Taking up the weapon with the hand, one should then perform the movement;
having properly extended both hands, one should indeed draw them back again. (77)
The shield should then be whirled from side to side,
and the wielders of the weapon must also perform a circumambulation of the head.

Likewise, the striking of a weapon against the cheek or the side of the face, and [the action] resulting from physical exertion (*vyāyāma*); according to their respective names, these constitute the remaining varieties within the classification of *vṛtti*. Or, according to Ārṣagaṇya, they belong to the *ārabhaṭī* style. In the term *kaṭicchedya*, the suffix *kṛtya* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*); it refers to the cutting of the waist or similar locations belonging to another.
There are four [types of] transgressions regarding those who are to be slain. "By these" means that, characterized by these principles,

one should perform the *pravicāras*— the excellent and diverse specific movements involving the discharge of weapons— as well as the *pariśrāntis*, which consist of *cārīs*, *vyāyāmas*, *khaṇḍas*, and *maṇḍalas*.
He demonstrates the meaning of the word *nyāya* [method/proper manner]: "By means of *nyāya*, that is, by the propriety of the limbs, those which are the examples of the limbs...
Furthermore: "And with the sword in hand, and with a graceful winding motion. (79)
The wise should perform the circumambulation of the head with the *kheṭaka*;
such is the deliberation to be made regarding the discharge of weapons in Bhārata. (80)
And I shall explain the detailed analysis of the Sātvata [weapon] according to the rule;
such indeed is the analysis prescribed for the sword and the shield. (81)
O Sātvata, the weapon must indeed be applied only from behind;
and even in the Vārṣagaṇya [system], the movement follows the sequence of the Sātvata.
The whirling of both the sword and the shield is performed;
likewise, the sword should be brought around the head in this manner. (83)

The unwrapping of the chest or, alternatively, of the shoulder should be performed with the weapon; whatever deliberation is prescribed for the *bhārata* [mudrā], that same should be applied in the *kaiśika*. (84)
Having thus caused [the weapon] to whirl, one should strike it down solely upon the head.

Because they proceed from the very principle (*nyāya*)—which consists in the attainment of the nature of binding the opponent—they are therefore called "principles" (*nyāya*). Furthermore, the word "ca" (and) following "atha api" means "moreover. By means of the encircling.

"Going," "leading," and "surrounding. "With the uncoiling" means the uncoiling of the weapon by the uncoiling of the wrist (*maṇibandha*). "From behind" means on the rear part of the body. Anticipating the objection that everything might follow from the context of battle, he says:
(114) These analytical investigations should indeed be applied in this manner through the graceful movement of the fingers. 85.
Bows, vajras, swords, and weapons should be employed for the purpose of liberation;
there is nothing to be pierced, nor anything to be cut, nor even the shedding of blood.
In a colored arena, weapons should be employed, yet there should be no actual killing;
the discharge of weapons by the wise should be performed as a mere simulation.
Alternatively, one should perform the *chedya* (cutting) according to the prescribed rules, accompanied by dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) and adorned with *aṅgahāras* that possess excellence of limb.

One should properly perform physical exercise accompanied by the *laya* and *tāla* rhythms; indeed, those who engage in such exercises must apply effort toward achieving aesthetic grace (*sauṣṭhava*). 89.
Excellence is declared to be the defining characteristic when it is applied according to the sequence of execution;
for all beauty is indeed eternally dependent upon excellence.
For one whose limbs lack grace does not shine in dramatic dance (*nāṭya*) or ordinary dance (*nṛtta*).

The suffix [-ya] here denotes a state (*bhāva*), meaning "it should not be pierced. Regarding the phrase "by mere designation" (*saṃjñāmātreṇa*): it refers to establishing a mere name so that another understands, "These two are fighting," or "These two are such-and-such," and so forth, even within works such as dramas.

By this, he shows that it is not inappropriate. Alternatively (*athavā*), the word indicates an alternative option. Regarding the "excellence of the limbs" (*aṅgasauṣṭhava*) which was mentioned, he states the preparatory means (*parikara*) for its accomplishment as "physical exercise" (*vyāyāma*).
Physical exercise consists of training the limbs at the very time when the limbs are fit for it.
(115) It is unwavering, not hunched, and likewise has well-proportioned limbs. || 91 ||
One should employ a posture that is neither too high nor with shaking feet, characterized by well-proportioned limbs;
wherein the hips are level with the ears, and likewise the elbows, shoulders, and head [are aligned]. (92)
A well-elevated chest indeed constitutes what is called "grace" (sauṣṭhava);
here, the middling and superior performers must always apply diligent effort. (93)
Indeed, all drama and dance are established upon gracefulness;
[this includes] the hips, the navel, the hands, and the chest being well-elevated. (94)
The Vaiṣṇava station is declared to be the square limb;
it consists of wiping, taking up, joining, and likewise releasing. (95)
The fourfold application of the bow consists of:
wiping, stroking, taking up, and the act of grasping. (96)
In this way, that which is called *tāla*—which has been assimilated as a constituent of the connection (*anusandhi*) of *druta* (quick) and so forth, as well as *cañcatpuṭa* and so forth—is recited.

"Sanna" refers to one whose limbs have reached a state of rest. The compound "kūrparāṃsaśiraḥ" is treated as a singular because it consists of parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*). "Tathā" means by way of similarity. Regarding the lowest [types] here...

He demonstrates autonomy with the words "by means of the middle and the best. He describes the excellence that constitutes the universal standard of proficiency as being fourfold—namely, by way of sequence and simultaneity—with respect to the hilt, the center, and the tip. Just as the procedures are according to rule in sword-fighting, so too are they in archery.

He shows that they exist. "Wiping" refers first to wiping the bow, then grasping it with the hand, then fixing the arrow to it, and then releasing it. When physical exercise is undertaken, there is the excellence conducive to it, as well as the bow which has come up in connection with it.
Joining, the placement of the arrow, drawing back, and release— these should be performed with a body anointed with oil and rubbed with gruel. (97)
The wise one should perform physical exercises on a wall or likewise in open space;
since the wall for practice is the *mātṛkā* (the foundational matrix), one should therefore rely upon a wall. 98.
One should cause the person to perform exercises by stretching the limbs against a wall;
for the sake of strength, one should likewise employ nasal medication (nasya) and the procedure of enema (vasti).
Foods that are unctuous, as well as juices and drinks—
life is sustained by food, and life itself is established in the vital breath (prāṇa).
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing yoga, one should be diligent regarding food;
[for otherwise] the body becomes impure, utterly exhausted, and excessively tormented by hunger and thirst. (101)

Having mentioned the ritual action (*karman*), he describes the practice (*prayoga*) itself as physical exertion (*vyāyāma*) with the words "anointed with oil" (*tailābhyakta*). Here, "oil" (*taila*) refers to sesame oil. "Barley-gruel" (*yavāgū*) is barley-food. A "training session" (*yogyā*) is so called because it is capable (*prabhavati*) of leading to "union" (*yoga*), that is, a specific connection with knowledge. And for him, the procedure for enemas (*vastividhi*) consists of [applications] with oils, clarified butter, and so forth, according to place, time, and constitution.

It should be understood from Āyurveda that "rasaka" refers to meat broth (*māṃsarasa*), which is to be consumed; this is the connection. And "pānakas" (drinks) are to be "unctuous" (*snigdha*); this is the connection. Anticipating the doubt, "What is the use of this [prescription]?", he says:
"They are dependent upon diet. By the phrase "one whose body is impure," he implies one whose limbs have not been purified by emetics and purgatives.

He shows that one has the qualification for physical exercise [only when fit]. (p. 117) One should not engage in physical exercise when the body is impure, nor when one has drunk excessively, nor likewise when one has eaten too much.
With steady and graceful limbs and a broad, symmetrical chest. || 102 ||
The wise man should cause a person who desires physical exercise to perform it;
thus, when engaged in exercise, the procedure for *cārī* (dance steps) should be carried out. 103.
Hereafter, I shall explain the various classifications of the mandalas.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Rules for the Cārīs," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.

And even in the case of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*). "Exhausted" (*praklāntam*) means [exhausted] by honey, fatigue, and so forth. "Of the immovable ones" (*acaleḥ*): wherever it is applied to an action, the meaning is "by those who have attained full development" (*prāptapariṇatibhiḥ*) right there. "Sweet" (*madhuraiḥ*) means graceful (*lalitaiḥ*).

"Action of the limbs" (*aṅgakriyā*) means the accomplishment of the limbs (*aṅgasiddhiḥ*). Thus, concluding [the chapter], he introduces the next chapter with the term "(conceptualization)" (*vikalpanam*).

I shall explain in what manner they are perceived through their diversity; thus, as a sutra, [the author] indicates the incalculability of those whose nature consists of the succession of movements extended according to the limbs, and those whose nature is the mandala.
Thus, having established that another chapter is introduced for the purpose of providing a mere illustration by way of a sutra, [the author] concludes: "May there be auspiciousness!
Having thus explained the tenth chapter in brief, Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, though his own purpose has been fulfilled through the remembrance of Śiva, acts for the sake of others."
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Varieties of Cārīs," in the Abhinavabhāratī, a commentary on the Nāṭya-veda composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the Great Māheśvara.
Śrīḥ.
Śrī Nāṭyaśāstra, Chapter Eleven.
These noble [steps] have been correctly explained by me for the purpose of releasing the *śaratra*;
now, understand here the *maṇḍalas* born from the combination of *cārīs*. || 1 ||
The *atikrānta*, the *vicitra*, and likewise the *lalitasaṃcara*;
the *sūcīviddha*, the *daṇḍapāda*, and likewise the *vihṛtālātaka*. (2)
O best of the twice-born, understand now the movements performed in the air—namely the *vāmaviddha*, the *salalita*, and the *krānta*—as well as those performed on the ground. (3)
The *bhramarārakandita* (the bee’s hum) and the *āvarta* (the whirlpool) should follow next;
they also call these the *samotsarita* (the simultaneous advance) and the *eḍakākrīḍita* (the ram’s play).
I bow to the power of the Great Lord, which always manifests the manifold variety of the spheres of existence and likewise creates that which is most near.
I must not omit even a single chapter, however brief the portion to be recited may be;
for this is a primary hymn to the All-pervading Lord, the Soul of the Universe, while the others are incidental.
The connection is that there are mandalas for the discharge of weapons. Regarding the word "here" (iha), it refers to this chapter;
having heard it, understand from the direction of that revelation other [mandalas] as well, for such is their general definition:
they are born from the combination of *cārīs*. Their form—
The *aḍḍita*, that which is called *śakaṭa*, as well as the first *ardhaka*,

These ten [types of sites] have also been declared here by name as those situated on the earth;
hereafter, I shall describe their characteristics in due order.
Having generated the first foot and performed the *udvāhita* movement, one should perform the *alāta*, the *vāmaka*, and the *pārśvakrānta* with the right foot. (7)
Furthermore, one should perform the needle-step on the left and the side-stride on the right;
then one should give the needle-step on the left and the backward stride on the right. (8)
One should again rotate the needle, the left [hand], and the triad;
likewise, the right [hand] is turned upward, as is the left fire-brand (alāta).
It must indeed be demarcated by an external border;
furthermore, the residence is extended, as is the staff-foot on the right.
This should be understood as the *vyāyāma* (exertion) once the *maṇḍala* (formation) has been transcended.

Among the movements for combat, this is mentioned first because of its preeminence; it is likewise characterized among the *maṇḍalas* by an abundance of movements performed in the air and on the ground. "The first" refers to the right [side].

By the partial definition "raised" (*udvāhita*), he indicates the *śakaṭāsya* [hand-gesture]. The same applies elsewhere. By "three-fold" (*trikantva*), he refers to the *bhramarī*. With the left foot, one performs the external *bhramaraka*.
But having first performed the *janita* [mudrā], one should perform the *nikuṭṭana* with that very same [mudrā]. || 11 ||
Having performed the *āspandita* with the left foot, one should step across with the right;
then one should place the left foot in the *sūcīpada* position and step away with the right.
The left [hand] is "trembling" (bhūrja), the right has "transgressed" (atikrānta), the right is indeed "upturned" (udvṛtta), and the left is "like a firebrand" (alāta). || 13 ||
Then there is the side-step with the right foot, likewise the needle-step with the left movement;
the throw-out with the right [foot] and the withdrawal with the left. (14)
One should employ both the "external bee" and the "distraction";
this should be known as the variegated maṇḍala in the practice of physical exercise.
Having placed the first foot with the knee raised, one should apply the *sūcī* step; then the left foot, having moved away, should again be positioned at the side. (16)
One should again give the left *sūcī* and perform the triple rotation;
then the *pārśvakrānta*, and again the first [step], the *atikrānta*, and the left [foot]. (17)
Having performed the sequence beginning with the needle-step (sūcī), one performs the withdrawn step (apakrānta) on the left;
then again the side-step (pārśvakrānta) and the first step, followed by the overstepped step (atikrānta) on the left. || 18 ||
The movement should be defined and performed with the external *bhramaraka*;
this application of *cārī* is to be employed in graceful movements. (19)
One should place the needle-step on the left foot and perform the triple-turn;
then there is the side-stride, followed again by the first, the left over-stepping, and the very same [over-stepping].
Furthermore, one should perform the *sūcī* (needle) step first, then the *apakrānta* (stepped-back) with the left foot;
then again the *pārśvakrānta* (stepped-to-the-side), and then the first [step] again, in the *sūcīviddha* (pierced-by-a-needle) mandala.
But having first been generated, that sequence of the staff (daṇḍakrama) should come into being;
one should again give the left needle and rotate the triad. || 22 ||
The *udvṛtta* and the *dakṣiṇa*, the *alāta* and the *vāmaka*, then the *pārśvakrānta* and likewise the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*. (23)
Furthermore, in the *daṇḍapāda* posture within the *maṇḍala*, the left leg is extended forward while the right leg is bent;
the left [foot] forms a needle-like point with the three joints rotated.

"Āspandita" refers to the *cārī* known as *spanditā*; others call that very same movement *askanditā*. "Daṇḍakrama" refers to the *cārī* called *daṇḍapādā*, such as the *trikāvarta* and others, because it is recited at the end [of the list], it pertains specifically to the position of completion.
First, having performed the *janita* with that same [foot], one should perform the *nikuṭṭaka*;
then the *āskandita* with the left foot and the *udvṛtta* with the right.
One should place the left foot in the *alāta* position and the right foot in the *sūcī*;
then, the left foot is again in *pārśvakrānta* and the right likewise in *ākṣipta*. (26)
Having balanced the triple-joint (trikam), one should extend the staff-like leg;
one should place the left foot like a needle and rotate the triple-joint. || 27 ||
The first [step] is the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*, while the left is both *atikrānta* and *eva*;
this application of *cārīs* occurs in the *vihṛta* maṇḍala. (28)
One should perform the sequence beginning with the needle-step (sūcī), followed by the withdrawn step (apakrānta) on the left;
then again the first side-step (pārśvakrānta), and the firebrand-step (alāta) on the left.
Then, having performed these movements in turn within the mandala, which consists of six or seven [circles], with graceful strides of the feet; || 30 ||
The connection is that the *maṇḍala* known as *daṇḍapāda*, which relies upon the *bhramarī*, is located there.

By the term *nikuṭṭaka*, the *talasañcara-pāda* (foot moving on the sole) is indicated. *Udvṛtta* refers to the *cārī* such as *ūrūdvṛttā* and others. *Samāvartana* is a complete turning by means of two *bhramaras*, one to the right and one to the left.
By means of these movements, employed alternately six or seven times, having circled around the perimeter in the four directions, [one proceeds] with intermediate steps as follows: (p. 123)
One should perform the first [step] as *apakrānta* or *abhikrānta* on the left;
then again the first on the left as *apakrānta* and likewise as *atikrānta*. || 31 ||
There should be the *pādabhramaraka* in the circle of the flaming wheel (*alātamandala*);
having performed the sequence beginning with the needle-step (*sūcī*), one indeed withdraws the left foot.

First, the staff-step (daṇḍakrama) is performed; then the left-hand needle-step (sūcīkārya-vāmaka) should be performed; then the triple-turning (trikavivarta), and the right-hand side-stride (pārśvakrānta). || 33 ||
One should make the left leg drawn back and the right leg like a staff;
with that same right [leg], the hip should be turned outward.
Having performed the needle-like left-step, one should rotate the triple-step;
the fire-brand-step (alāta) should be on the left, and the side-stride (pārśvakrānta) on the right. || 35 ||
Furthermore, when the left [hand] has passed over in the mandala pierced by the left,
one should apply the initial sequence of the needle, and the left [hand] should be withdrawn.
Then the first [leg] is stepped across the side, and that same one is terrified by the arm;
then the left leg is stepped across, and likewise the right is drawn back. (37)
Furthermore, the left [foot] is stepped across, and likewise the right is bent;
then again the left is like a firebrand (alāta), and the right is stepped toward the side. (38)

One should again perform the needle-like movement with the left foot while the right foot has stepped away; then, having moved forward, the left foot should again be employed in the graceful gait (lalitasaṃcara). || 39 ||
This movement of the feet should be performed in the Lalita Maṇḍala;
having made the *sūcī* step, the left foot is then drawn back.
Then, having performed the first *pārśvakrānta* on the left side as well,
one should traverse the mandala in succession by means of these *cārīs*.
Then one should place the left [hand] as a needle, and the right [hand] should not move forward;
for this is how the mandala is arranged when walking according to one's natural gait.
This "krānta" (stride) is to be understood by name by the practitioners of drama;
these ten alone are to be known here as the "ākāśagāni" (sky-going movements). 43.
Hereafter, I shall declare the characteristics of the terrestrial [mudrās] as well:
the first should be produced by action, and it should be motionless on the left.
Furthermore, the one called Śakaṭa (the Cart) is the first, and the left [foot] is also extended; such is the connection [of the verse].

By the word "number" (saṃkhyā), repetition is indicated. This is a qualification of that which has just passed, namely, that it moves gracefully (lalitaṃ sañcarati); for this very reason, this is the name of the Maṇḍala. And "he" (sa ca)—he...
This is the meaning.
125) First, the *bhramaraka* should be performed, and one should rotate the *trika*. || 45 ||
Furthermore, if the left [arm] throbbs and the right one is like the face of a cart,
and the left one recedes toward the back, it likewise bestows the Bhramaraka [sign].
That very [hand] should be made motionless; this is the *bhramaramaṇḍala*.
The first *bhramaraka* should be performed, and the left one should be raised. (47)

The *trikavivarta* (turning of the three) and the *śakaṭāsya* (cart-mouthed) [gestures] are performed with the right [leg]; that same [leg], when the thigh is rotated, becomes the *ūrūdvṛtta*, while the left [leg] is drawn back.
The right hand should perform the *trikavivarta* and be vibrated; the left hand should form the so-called *śakaṭa*, and likewise there should be a clapping. (49)
This is called Āspandita; in the *vyāyāma* known as the *yuddhamaṇḍala*, one first performs the *janita* step and then strikes with the left foot.

Furthermore, one should rotate the triad consisting of the *āspandita*, the left-hand *śakaṭa*, the *vāmaka*, and the first *bhramaraka*. || 52 ||
The left [foot] should follow behind in a circular revolution;
having first assumed the *samapāda* stance, one should extend the two hands. (53)
Having indeed entwined and untwisted [the hands] continuously at the upper surface,
and having placed the first [hand] upon the hip, one should rotate it in succession.
Furthermore, one should extend [the limbs] counter-clockwise in succession; having performed the movement by circling with this gait, one should then [enter] the mandala in turn.
And this circle of exercise is to be known as "the descent," performed with feet joined together and likewise pierced like needles. (56)
Having circled the mandala in due order with the "play of the ewe," with powders, with single revolutions, and with the "piercing and casting away" of the needle.
One should know the *elakākrīḍita* as that which is designated by the term *khaṇḍamaṇḍala*;
having performed the *savyamudghaṭṭita*, one should perform the rotation with that very same [movement]. (58)
By that same [method], one should perform the *askandita*, the one called *śakaṭa*, and the *vāmaka*;

Furthermore, the left [foot] should be contracted, while the first [right foot] is drawn back; the left [foot] should be made into a *bhramaraka* [step], and the first [foot] should be leaping forward (*āskandita*).
With that very [movement], one should perform the *āsphoṭana*; this is the *aḍḍhita* maṇḍala. Having first performed the *janita*, one should likewise perform the *nikuṭṭaka*. (61)
That same [stance] is called the cart (śakaṭa), and the left [leg] should be in the āskandita position;
with the feet positioned in the cart stance, one then performs the circular movement (maṇḍala) in succession.
The battle formation known as the "Cart" (śakaṭa) should be understood as a circular array used for exertion;
having first been formed, it should then be charged forward. 63.
The left [foot] moves backward, while the right is called the cart-step (śakaṭa);
having circled the mandala in succession with these movements, one performs the *cārīs*.
This mandala, measuring one and a half [units], is to be understood as applicable even in close-quarter combat (niyuddha).
Having first formed the needle-step (sūcī), one then performs the leftward withdrawal (apakrānta).
Today, Vāmaka likewise was terrified by serpents;
having wandered about with feet terrified by serpents, he even [traversed] the mandala.
The wise should understand that the *piṣṭakuṭṭa* movement is performed by the dancers in a circular formation (*maṇḍala*),
having circumambulated the circle with all their feet moved like those of a blue jay.

The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "also. Beyond this, one should employ further circles. To the question "How? they say: "Equal" (*samāḥ*).

These sections, along with their mandalas, should be performed here by practitioners with the mindset of a teacher,

Those skilled in the art recognize that actions preceded by the sweetness of playful gestures are accompanied by instrumental music.

Here, he demonstrates examples for the application of *āryā* verses in various combinations, even when they are joined with one another.

"He becomes fit for practice. He also shows the predominance of the *khaṇḍas* by saying "the *khaṇḍas*.
By the phrase "followed by instrumental music" (*vādyenānugatāni*), he refers to the movement that follows the instrumental music (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.282).
Thus, in contrast to the fourth chapter concerning dance (*nṛtta*), he declares the predominance of movement in drama (*nāṭya*). May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on Mandalas, in the Abhinavabhārati, a commentary on the Nāṭya-veda composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the Great Māheśvara.

Thus, when engaging in physical exercise, one should perform the visualization of the maṇḍala;
hereafter, I shall explain the movements as they exist in their natural state.

Having performed the ritual descent there, preceded by the sounding of musical instruments and vessels, we ever praise that state of the Supreme Self— the goal wherein the injunctions find their ultimate rest in the Vedanta— which is the embodiment of the essence of the mass of Great Bliss.

In order to establish the connection with the present context, he makes a formal declaration regarding what is about to be described in its proper sequence, beginning with the word "evam" (thus). When there is a combination, that is, a mixing together, of *vyāyāmas* (exercises) and *cārīs* (steps) suitable for mutual conjunction, it is possible to construct *maṇḍalas* (circles), even though they have not been explicitly mentioned.

Having understood this, one then desists. In that regard, although the application of the bodily [expressions] to rasa and bhāva has already been performed through their respective divisions (*vibhāgaśas*), and thus even when they are mixed, it ought to be stated separately by way of their individual application;
nevertheless, the Sage, intent on the welfare of his disciples, shows the direction [of the procedure] starting from the head down to the feet.

The actions involving the joining of the limbs have been described; now, intending to reveal the application of that bodily configuration which arises through the power of their union—whether in motion or at rest, as there is no other mode—he first promises to explain the application of movement, since the context of the *cārī* and *maṇḍala* movements pertains to the activity of the mind. And movement depends upon the nature [of the character], the sentiment (*rasa*), the state, the location, and...

And it must be stated with regard to the proper time (*kāla*), because it is designated for each individual person. In that context, the procedure (*prakriyā*) is stated first; this very point is indicated by the word *tu*, which is a synonym for "as far as" (*yāvat*) and signifies sequence (*krama*), moving in both directions like the eye of a crow (*kākākṣivat*). [An objection is raised: "In that case, what is the fate of one who has not entered?"

He indicates the commencement of the application with the words "therein, the mounting" (*tatropavahana*). When, in accordance with the limbs [of the ritual], there is a recitation endowed with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the path during the entry of the *prakṛtis*—[this is the mounting]. (p. 130) 2.
When the *dhruvā* has commenced and the curtain has been withdrawn, the entrance of the actors—giving rise to various purposes and sentiments—should take place. (3)

Having thus engaged in that well-known conversation, when Dhruvā had properly commenced—how so?—having performed it endowed with the three forms beginning with "being preceded by instrumental music" (*bhāṇḍavādya-puraskṛtatva*); these three are adverbs. *Tantrī-bhāṇḍa* is stringed instruments being played; *puṣkara-vādya* is percussion instruments. *Mārga*...

The term *deśa-rasa* is an avyayībhāva compound used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). Having made it so that every description of a location— such as a house or a garden— and every specific mental state such as love (*rati*) and the like is endowed with [the performance],
that *dhruvā* (song) is likewise that in which there is an "entering" (*āveśana*), meaning an entry into the intellect, for the various types of characters, such as the noble (*uttama*) and others.

Having done this, the following is meant: by means of similes such as the swan and so forth, the particularity of the *prakṛti*, the particularity of the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*), and the particularity of the garden and so forth must necessarily be bound to the *dhruvā*.
When the *dhruvā* has thus proceeded and is established in this manner, the cloth is removed.

When the curtain has been removed, the actress is turned away from the stage with the thought that she has come from the dressing room to the assembly; by the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that there is a further introductory song (*upohana*) at that time. The entry into the *dhruvā* occurs at the medium tempo (*laya*).
"Valitayā"—Kohala has designated this as "valanikā" because it involves a turning in the performance—and it consists of singing in dry syllables (*śuṣkākṣara*).
Immediately upon entering, one should act with appropriate posture, gaze, facial coloration, and so forth,
in such a way that the audience’s immersion in the primary rasa arises instantaneously through the process of "denotation of the associated" (anvitābhidhāna). [The song is] thus sung.
Upon hearing a single *gamaka* that has reached the forefront of the *grāmarāga* being sung,
one comes under the power of perceiving the essential reality (*tattva*) of the entire scale (*grāma*).
Others, however, read the text as "endowed with the kalās according to the path," and they explain both [readings] as being supplementary.
In the *mārgas* such as *citrā* and others, those *kalās* consisting of two, four, and eight *mātrās* are spoken of in the *grāmas* such as *acalitaka*;
and in the *kalās* such as *vādyākṣaras*, although there are also *adhruvas* for the performers (*pātras*).
Having established the Vaiṣṇava posture— whether in the highest or the middle [position]—
the chest should be well-elevated, level, and square.
One should perform [the mudrā] when the upper arms are relaxed, neither too raised nor too low;
the region of the neck should be made such that the head is tilted like that of a peacock. || 5 ||
One should apply it to the top of the arm when it is eight finger-breadths from the ear,
and the chin should likewise be situated four finger-breadths from the chest.
The two hands should likewise be positioned at the hips and the navel;
the right hand should rest upon the navel, while the left hand remains on the hip.
The distance between the two feet should be made two tālas and a half;
the lifting of the foot, moreover, should be performed according to its own prescribed measure.

Nevertheless, this is merely a statement of possibility; or rather, it was stated thus because of the context concerning the superior and middling [types]. For those *dhruvās* and *praveśas* belong to those two, or they are indeed included by the word "and" (*ca*). One view is that they are equal; the other position is that it refers to the place (*sthāna*).

In a triangle, [the height] is one and a half *tāla*s; this is the Vaiṣṇava [measure]. When the image is seated, it must be steady and serene, neither too uplifted nor too low; the tendency to go downward must be avoided with effort.
To teach precisely this meaning of the verse, he states the clear method in two and a half verses beginning with "The region of the neck," and so forth.

Wherein the head is well-formed, beautiful, and curved like that of a peacock while standing at ease—this is the *cāturaśrya* (square) posture; the *khaṭakāmukha* (sword-hilt) is when [the right hand] is placed at the navel; and the *ardhacandra* (half-moon) is when the left [hand] is so positioned. Furthermore, this is not a seated position (*upaviṣṭasthānaka*), but rather a standing position (*sthitasthānaka*) due to the propriety of its immediate sequence in the progression of movement.

To demonstrate this, he says: "the distance between the feet. The meaning is that one should perform exactly that which was indicated as the definition of the *sthānaka*—namely, "the distance between the feet is two *tālas* and a half"—and nothing else, such as sitting down. In that context, immediately after the *sthānaka*, he introduces the movement (*gati*) with the words "lifting of the foot," for that is appropriate.
p.
132) There are four *tālas*, two *tālas*, and likewise one *tāla*.
The four *tālas* belong to the gods and likewise to kings. || 9 ||
The *dvitāla* is the tempo for middle [voices], as well as for women and low-voiced men;
furthermore, there are the *catuṣkala*, the *dvikala*, and the *ekakala*.
For the best [singers], the pause consists of four beats; for the middling, it should be two beats;
and likewise, a pause of one beat is proclaimed for the low [singers]. (11)

It should be performed according to the future characteristic (*bhāvilakṣaṇa*) and the delimitation of place and time (*deśakālapariccheda*). Furthermore, the tempo (*tāla*) for the performer (*pātra*) is by means of one's own hand-measure; this is the meaning.
In that regard, he first states the delimitation of place: "one *tāla*. *Tāla*...
"The *tāla* is known as that which is measured by the middle finger [extended] between the thumb and the middle finger.
Having thus designated it according to the sequence of numbers,
[the author] now begins its practical application, because the entire range of performance finds its rest in the supreme nature that constitutes the locus of the *sthāyin* (the permanent emotion).
He states the application [of the rule] with the words "But the four *tālas*... The word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "also" (*api*), because [the movement] may sometimes be otherwise.
The word "likewise" (*tathā*) serves to dispel the possibility that kings might possess a gait similar to that of the gods.
Because they are mentioned in association with women and low-born persons, they should be understood as being base. For it is of them...
