Because it is indicative (liṅgitvāt), one should not conceive of it as being anything inferior; "according to beauty" means according to the requirements of dramatic convention (nāṭyadharma). Having stated the restriction regarding place, he now states the general restriction regarding time as well, beginning with "the four-beat [time] indeed. Likewise:
And thus, by that upward lift, the falling of the foot is defined as consisting of four *kalās* for the best [type of dancer];
the meaning is that this is the general rule (*utsarga*), since for the middle and inferior types, it is prescribed according to a sequence of halving those values.
Having observed the slow, the medium, and the fast tempos, as well as the pauses, the wise expert in drama should employ the movement according to its inherent nature. (12)

In this regard, the four *gītis*, beginning with *Māgadhī*, will be described; since among them, starting with *Ardhamāgadhī*, the three varieties beginning with *Citrā* are applied in sequence. One should understand that the general rule for all *dhruvaka* meters—that five *nimeṣas* constitute one *mātrā*—is the default path obtained from the general definition of a *kalā*.
When there is a specific designation, by that fixed measure, the foot-fall consists of four *kalās*. Likewise, regarding the adoption of the best [meter], a *dvipadī* was stated by Kohala:
"The *dvipadī* of the best [poets] shall be endowed with four long [syllables]."

In this regard, because there are two feet through the processes of lifting and dropping, the definition is as follows: by means of the division of the *dvipadī* (two-footed) meter, the falling of the foot occurs with the word "dhig ḍidhiṃ. Here, in the *dhruvaka*, there are four *kalās*; for the duration of "dhigaḍadhiṅ" is indeed [the time of] ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, not [that of] ha.

The duration of a consonant is distinct from the duration of a vowel; and because those [consonants] are mobile when following a heavy syllable (*guru*), like the clatter of a sword-blade, those who know this regard it as *tripuṭa*. For in that case, in a form such as *tāgaḍudhiṃ*, the short [syllable] is one *kalā*, which consists of three *mātrās*, while in the fourth, the heavy syllable, there are two *mātrās*.

And the morae (*mātrā*). In every such case, this type of application regarding the apprehension of immediate succession (*samanantara*) is difficult to perform due to the absence of rest; therefore, for the sake of establishing rest in the postures and movements, one mora situated in the middle, consisting of a pause, has been conceived as the means of piercing the target (*lakṣyavidhi*). By virtue of that, such [a practice] is described.
Or rather, let it be for now that [the syllables] appear as four *kalās* in rapid tempo; here, according to the path of the *citramārga*,
the rule of the four-*kalā* foot-fall is required, because otherwise it would lack the beauty of both the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the illustrated example (*lakṣya*).

Now he states the remainder of the rule regarding the time of dissolution (*layakāla-niyama*) with the words "sthitam" (abiding) and "vilambitam" (protracted). Having said "samavekṣya" (having observed), he explains that this refers to the differentiation of the categories beginning with *prakṛti*; he demonstrates that very point by saying:
"Consciousness is considered to have slow, steady, and protracted tempos, as well as intermediate tempos."
It should be understood as being produced by such qualities as fortitude and profundity, whether they pertain to the literal or the figurative sense;
[this refers to] "according to their respective natures" (p.
The gait of those endowed with fortitude is supreme; the gait of those considered mediocre is middling;
and the gait of the most base is rapid.
The three abodes are to be applied according to the predominance of the [three] constituents (sattva). || 13 ||
This indeed is the rule to be understood regarding the measures (kalā), time-units (tāla), and tempo (laya);
now listen, O sinless ones, to the application of the movement of the gaits once again. (14)

However, one should not apply [qualities such as] caste and so forth merely for the sake of a superior proclamation, even though they are fabricated— such as the fact that Vidūṣaka is twice-born yet remains impure;
for even if something is superior, if it is somehow otherwise, it is as if it does not exist at all, despite being abundant.

The meaning is that this has been stated as something well-known in the world. Not only is there a distinction of parts based on *prakṛti*, but intending to refer to the distinction of mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*), he says: "And the three degrees of intensity are to be applied by means of the strength of the *sattva*.

*Sattva* here refers to the mental modification; by means of it, [the tempo is determined]—quickly even for a superior person in battle and the like, or slowly even for an inferior person in grief and the like.
[The tempo is] slow (*vilambita*). Now, he shows that this same rule applies to the *dhruvā* meter used for movement that follows such [a tempo], stating:
"But this very... Here, the rule for *tāla* follows the movement; it was stated in the section on *tāla* that others [hold] otherwise.
The compound *kalātālalayaḥ* is a *madhyamapadalopa* (elliptical) compound, meaning "that *tāla* and *laya* which is accompanied by *kalā*s."

Therefore, this is the meaning: even in the *dhruvātāla*, the rules for *kalās* and the rules for *vilayas* follow the *gati* (movement) alone. For this very reason, following this [principle], Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa, Gopāla, and others have elaborated in works such as the *Tāladīpikā* the application of the *dhruvātālas*—which is the consensus of the ancients—regarding the categories of *bhaṅga*, *upabhaṅga*, and *vibhaṅga*.
It has been criticized; however, we shall examine that in the chapter on *dhruva*, so let it rest for now.

Thus, having stated the restriction of place and time, he applies it to the present subject: "Listen again to the movement in the gaits"—the connection is that one should listen again to the diversity (*vaicitrya*) or the application (*prayoga*) of movement within the various gaits (*gati*). This is the composition (*saṃghaṭanā*).
The meaning is that it has not been stated [otherwise].
On the other hand, in the case of the supreme gait (*uttamagati*), the action [is such that] the knee is level with the hip.
Furthermore, in the applications of the *yuddhacārī* movements, one should place it level with the breast. || 15 ||
Then, with graceful side-steps accompanied by musical instruments,
he should proceed five steps toward the corner of the stage.
Then one should perform the piercing with the left hand and the scattering with the right;
having turned around for the second time, one should then proceed to the next corner.
There too, piercing with the left is distraction, as is [piercing] with the right;
therefore, one should proceed facing the vessels, moving by those very steps.
Having thus performed twenty-one steps by going back and forth,
one should then perform the piercing with the left foot and the scattering with the right.

Regarding the phrase "but in the case of the natural state" (*svabhāve tu*): by means of the particle *tu*, which indicates a distinction, it is shown that while a four-beat measure (*catustālatva*) is prescribed for the *manrthagati*, a three-beat measure (*tritālatva*) applies to the *svabhāvagati*, and a five-beat measure (*pañcatālatva*) must also be performed for the *dīptagati*.
He describes the arrangement of the movement of those gaits with the words beginning "with side-strides" (*pārśvakrāntaiḥ*).

Lifting the contracted foot and raising it to the side, one should place it with the foot in the *udghaṭṭita* position; this is the *pārśvakrāntā* (10-32), the *pārśvakrāntā* *cārī*. [It is performed] at the northeast corner of the stage.
"The second corner" refers to the north-west; "likewise" means in the same manner. "In the other" refers by extension to the other two corners.

And this five-step sequence has been explained previously (A 5.73). "Piercing" (*vedha*) is the placement of the needle-foot upon the field of the heel. "Leftward piercing" (*vāmavedha*) is that which has its opening pierced inward, for the sake of attaining perfection.

Having moved along the corners, he says that those situated in the Brahma-position must not be transgressed. And this, on the expanded stage, Bharata states, should be performed as a coming and going, a movement of the feet.
In a triangular field with a square-colored border, the movement is indeed square.
When one proceeds accompanied by equal [beats], there the support of *laya* (tempo) should be applied;
it may be four beats (*catuṣkala*), or two beats (*dvikala*), or likewise again one beat (*ekakala*).
Now, he who proceeds surrounded by those of middling and low status [should move] four beats, then half a beat, and likewise again one beat. (22)
Furthermore, the wise should determine the gait of Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, kings, Pannagas, and Rākṣasas by means of the measure of four tālas. (23)
The middle course is prescribed for all those who dwell in heaven;
even among them, those who are haughty have a destiny equal to that of the gods.
The movement of five steps is the general rule for all cases. He also states an exception: "in the theater, [the distance is] extended.

By the word *bharata*, there is indicated—by way of metaphorical usage—the connection through learning or lineage. Regarding the phrase "with goings and comings," the restriction of five steps applies to a limited direction; however, in a single spot, there are two [steps].
It should be understood that these are "steps of the feet. And in the case of a protracted [movement], there are repeatedly five steps.

In this very context, regarding the various measures of the *pātarī*, the *dvibhaṅga*, *caturbhaṅga*, and so forth are primarily [discussed]. Desiring to explain the specific details of the mixed movement (*vyāmiśragati*), he concludes the discussion on the even movement (*samagati*).

"By those who are equal" (*yaḥ samaiḥ*)—the meaning is "in that very way," that is, by means of equality. He speaks of the mixed state with the word "now" (*atha*). "Surrounded" (*parivārita*) means intended to be expressed as being superior (*uttamatvena*). Therefore, even when gods and others are being relied upon by a virtuous person, this rule does not apply to another in that case.

Because of its predominance: in that case, when there is a fall of the highest foot (pāda), there is one [beat] for the middle and the low [feet], and four for the highest. And for this very reason, he states the conclusion—accompanied by the specification of the highest—in order to raise a question for the sake of establishing certainty regarding the division into four *tālas* and so forth.
"Of the Daityas, Dānavas," and so forth. "Of all" refers to the divine messengers and others. "Those who are haughty" refers to Mātali and his like.
The sages said:
"When men become kings, how can they have the destiny of gods? To this it is replied: how is it that this destiny will not belong to kings? (25)

Now, with regard to the performance of dramatic action, divine characters are to be understood as "divine," those who are both divine and human as "divine-and-human," and those who are purely human as "human. || 26 ||
The nature of the gods is divine; that of kings is indeed divine-human;
while that which is known in the world as otherwise is proclaimed to be purely human. || 27 ||
Kings are declared in the Vedas and the inner sciences (adhyātma) to be born from portions of the gods;
thus, there is indeed no fault here in emulating the gods. (28)
This rule must be observed regarding going according to one's own will; however, in cases of emergency, sudden calamity, or anger, no such restriction is prescribed. (29)
However, performers must effect the movement of all characters—whether superior, inferior, or middling—by resorting to different states of being. (30)

Kings are born from portions of the gods; they are emanations of portions of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Their preeminence has been declared in the Vedas, as well as in the treatises on inner science (*adhyātmaśāstra*) and the Vedāntas. (This is an imitation: because of the description of the gods and others, it is said that this is the "Secret of Virāja and Viddharāja."
The meaning is that there is no deficiency in imitating the gods. "This" refers to the four-quarter [meter] and so forth. "Moving at will" means movement according to one's own inclination.

"Agitation" (*saṃbhrama*) means excitement; here, "calamity" (*utpāta*) refers to insanity and the like. "The stated measure" means having the form already described. He refutes this very point: "Two for the highest [meter], one... and so on.
For the middle [note], it is half [the duration] of the low [note]; by the power of the different states, for all [notes], it may be either a quarter-kalā or even half of that kalā. (p. 138)
Having attained another state, it performs the various activities of movement.
Where there are four *kalās* in the *jyeṣṭha* [measure], there should be two *kalās* in the *madhyama*;
where there are two *kalās* in the *uttama*, there should be one *kalā* in the *madhyama*. (32)
Where there is one *kalā* in the middle [of the sequence], there shall be half a *kalā* for the lower ones;
in this manner, one should apply the practice to those who are dull-witted by reducing it by half and half again.

In one afflicted by fever, in one afflicted by hunger, in one exhausted by austerity, in one possessed by fear, in one filled with wonder, in one displaying feigned indifference, and likewise in one endowed with longing; (34)
In the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), as well as in grief (śoka) and in moving about at will,
the movement should be performed with a steady tempo (sthitalaya), falling within the interval of more than one kalā.
"The movement of the *prakṛtis* is based on *kalālaya* and *tāla*. However, it is more appropriate [to say] "it falls entirely.
By the statement "in low [notes], there should be half a *kala*," this quarter-part of a *kalā* was indicated by the sage Bharata.
Those who know the definitions say that the *vṛtta* form is fast (*druta*); as for the fifth part, it is according to the rule already stated.
That same [movement] is joined with four [units of time] when preceded by the cessation of breath and so forth;

thus, he shows that there is even a further increase beyond the four-unit measure. "Afflicted by fever," etc.: one who is possessed by fear becomes paralyzed (ūrustambha), for otherwise his gait would be described as even more rapid. "Astonishment" refers to the paralysis caused by it.

This is the meaning. Regarding *avahittha* (concealment): for those who possess feigned fortitude, it is indeed possible to make their artifice appear well-knit. In that case, there is only an intensification; for it is precisely from this [intensification] that experts recognize artifice. That very variety of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) which is fully endowed with the eagerness of excessive devotion is called *vipralambha* (love-in-separation).

Up to "moving at will" (*svacchandagamana*) means wandering about for play without any specific purpose. Regarding "in excess" (*adhika*), the prefix *adhi* has the sense of "excess. Some read it as *adhikalām*; it refers to an abundance, specifically the excellence of the fourfold nature, which is the very essence of the protracted vowel (*pluta*) and the pause (*virāma*).
Furthermore, when accompanied by anxiety, the movement should be performed with four *kalās*;
likewise in cases of illness, longing, fear, and being terrified. (36)
In cases of agitation and joy, in matters requiring haste, upon hearing something undesirable, in instances of reproach, and when witnessing a marvel. (37)
Moreover, in matters of urgent necessity, when one is suffering, when searching for an enemy, when pursuing one who has committed an offense, and likewise when following after wild beasts; || 38 ||

In the increase of the *pāda*, there is an understanding of the *tāla* through an increase in number; that is, in which [verse] the foot-fall (*pādapāta*) is such that its measure (*parimāṇa*), consisting of an interval of *kalās*—such as six, eight, and so forth—is extended (*vikṛṣṭa*) and augmented (*adhikṛta*).
For this very reason, in the course of investigating the occasion of drinking (*āpāna-prasaṅga*), he will say:
"Six *kalās* must not be performed, nor likewise eight *kalās*; for those who know it, the falling of a foot [in such a case] would cause distress to the woman. (12.172).
This is because of the statement "four, half, and one *kalā*" and because of the prohibition of the sevenfold [measure].

It indicates the absence of the three-fold and five-fold time-units (*tāla*). For those who know *tāla*, the equality arising from the application of raising and lowering measures of unequal durations is indeed the underlying secret (*upaniṣad*);
and that [secret] it makes clear here.

Thus, in these [melodies], there is a measure exceeding even six *kalās*, and likewise, in the performance (*parikrama*) of those [songs] tranquilized by austerity (*tapaḥśānta*), there is what is called the *ullasana* dissolution, which has been described by Kohala and others as having an extremely slow temporal limit. Having thus stated the excess of *kalās*, he says "the desire of one who is unwell," etc., to show that there is also a deficiency. In the case of one who is unwell...

For when there is an intense urgency regarding a secret desire—such as when one hears of something undesirable concerning a kinsman and so forth, and then proceeds quickly to their side—or when there is a delay or protractedness regarding the sight of a wonder, this is not considered a fault. *Atyaya* means transgression; its purpose here is the swift accomplishment [of the goal].
That which is not desired but must necessarily be done is performed with haste; however, the distinction is that a good deed performed with haste is indeed something desired.
A wise person should thus employ these movements in a modified manner;
however, that movement which belongs to the superior ones should not be applied among those of middling capacity. (39)
One should not apply to base persons that same course which is intended for those of middle standing.
[This is the] measure. Although everything is obtained by this much, there is nevertheless an elaboration for the sake of instructing the poet and the actor.
The offense to be enacted belongs to an enemy other than [the hero], or rather, it is the offense committed against someone such as a teacher or elder; and from that—
"He has transgressed regarding forms" means he has committed an offense concerning these and other such types, including pride and the like.

"Deficient" (vikalām) means that which lacks its full measure of parts (kalā); although even a quarter-part (*turyā*)—which is half a part—is not to be disregarded there, even a third or a sixth part of that may occur. For this very reason:

There is no redundancy with the rule "in cases of agitation, sudden occurrence, and anger, [the pause is] at the fourth half-measure," because that [rule] does not apply to this case, whereas the present one applies to a situation involving an uneven division of measures. For instance, in the *mattagati* meter, in the performance of the *khaṇḍaka* by Śekharaka—
specifically in the phrase *gahiduṃ dhi*— the *mātrā* occurs at the third [syllable], which is the name of the third [measure].

"Dhaṃ dhag" is the first beat; "tsuka" is the second; "dhi" is the third; and there is no equality among these. By this, through the determination of the equality, deficiency, or excess of the *kalās*, and by the designation of the division of equal and unequal *kalās* as *bhaga*, there arises variety through the adoption of heavy (*guru*), light (*laghu*), quick (*druta*), and protracted (*pluta*) durations. This also—

The established arrangement of *bhaṅga* and *laya*, which is comprised within the various types and expansions (*prakāra-prastāra*), proven by its application to illustrative examples (*lakṣya-siddha*),
and consisting of the syllables and their meanings intended to be conveyed— this arrangement,
well-known by the term "path of impact" (*āghāta-mārga*) regarding subjects such as the *dhārā-bandha*, is indeed clearly evident.

It has been shown. That [explanation] regarding the definition of the measure of time (or the measurement of the *kalās*) has become like the "bath of an elephant" [i.e., excessive and redundant]; thus he says: "But as for the course of the highest ones... The word *tu* has the sense of *eva*; the meaning is: "by this very sequence of others. This is what is meant: by showing [an example] without restriction, a restriction [is established].
Nevertheless, when there is an excess of *kalās*, for the best [type] there are six *kalās*, for the middling there are four *kalās*, and for the lowest there are two (*kalās*).
The movement should be amorous, arising from a state of natural desire. (40)
The path of seeing the female messenger (dūtī) should enter the circle of the stage;
and by means of the needle-gesture (sūcī), one should perform the representation based on the meaning. 41.
Adorned with pleasing garments, as well as perfumes, incenses, and powders,
he was beautifully decorated with garlands possessing the sweet fragrance of various flowers.
One should move with graceful steps, both those that have passed by and those that are stationary, endowed with elegance and following the rhythm and tempo.
The hands should also be made to follow the feet by the performers;
[this is done] by raising the hand and then dropping it, alternating between the two feet. 44.

Latā: Even where a lesser portion has been prescribed, there too the highest [quality] receives one full measure (*kalā*), the middling half a measure, and the lowest a quarter of a measure; so how could there be any confusion?
Having thus explained the progression according to the distinction of the *prakṛtis*, [the author] first proceeds to demonstrate it with respect to the *rasas*.

Describing those subjects that serve human goals and relate to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), he first speaks regarding the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) out of its preeminence, beginning with "the gait is amorous" and so forth. "Natural desire" means unhidden longing. Once the basis of the matter is established, the repetition of the term "hinting" (*sūcā*) refers to the intense contemplation of a charming object.

To demonstrate that it produces wonder, he shows that one should apply the *sūcī* (needle) style in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment, without omitting even a single portion, chewing it over and over again like something already tasted. For in the *yuddhavīra* (heroic-in-battle) and other such sentiments,
it is appropriate to maintain focus on the primary element alone, while those occurring in between [are treated differently].

Because other duties must not be disregarded, and because if they were disregarded, there would arise the contingency of neglecting one's teacher, maternal uncles, brothers, kinsmen, and so forth; and because the meaning of the phrase "those who follow the inner path" is to avoid the "needles" (sūcīs) in the dance.
(142) Now understand further the conduct regarding the "concealed" lover:
one who has dismissed his attendants, one who is relaxed, and likewise one who is accompanied by a female messenger (dūtī). || 45 ||
The lamp of Nirvāṇa was not excessively adorned with ornaments;
likewise, it was slowly accompanied by a messenger with garments resembling the ocean tide.
But one whose desire is concealed should proceed with silent and slow steps;
apprehensive of noise, he should remain intent on looking about.
With his body trembling and filled with apprehension, he stumbles repeatedly;
[the phrase] "let me not take refuge" is incorrect. For even that [refuge] would be useless, for how could there be a mere hint (*sūcā*)?
Immediately after the hint, he describes his natural course of action: "the dancing girl and so forth"; *sugandha* means a beautiful fragrance.

In the phrase "with various flowers for the companions," there is an absence of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). "Salalita" means accompanied by grace (*savilāsa*). "Endowed with *sauṣṭhava*" means possessed of the elegance of the limbs. "Laya" refers to the slow tempo (*vilambita*) and rhythmic measure (*tāla*), such as the four-beat (*caturaśra*) and so forth.
Furthermore, although the supreme gait is generally endowed [with these qualities], it is now described again in its specific details.

The state [of *bhāva*]: where, having made an inquiry, a desire is expressed in the context of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), as in the case of the King of Vatsa and others toward Sāgarikā, or otherwise, as in the case of Rāvaṇa and others toward Sītā; there, with a trembling body, faltering speech, and so forth—due to the influence of the fourth stage of love—the longing for the beloved results in an action such as that described by the words "the lamp has gone out."
By the words "fearing the sound" (*śabdāśaṅkī*) and so forth, [the author] indicates the *kalā* that has been divided, and thus describes the *gati* as being a mixed application (*miśraprayoga*).

Now, Kohala and others state that the *dhruvā-tāla* named Subhadra has precisely this kind of erotic subject matter; for its expansion (*prastāra*) consists of a mixture of *druta* and *laghu* beats. Thus it is said: "clothes equal to the time (*velā*)."

In the *Candrāloka*, [the heroine] is described as veiled in white garments, her limbs made lovely by a mass of camphor powder, and adorned with abundant ornaments primarily of pearls; these are the characteristics of her dress and so forth. However, in the case of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation), the movement of the passionate woman is mixed with pathos (*karuṇa*).
(143) But regarding the *raudra* (fierce) sentiment, I shall speak [of it] with respect to the hosts of Daityas and Rākṣasas. || 48 ||
O best of the twice-born, their single, stable rasa is the Furious (raudra);
it should be understood as both the Furious of Costumes (nepathyaraudra) and likewise the Furious of Limbs (aṅgaraudra). (49)
Likewise, the Raudra [type] is conceived as threefold, including that which is born of its own nature;
it is that whose body is drenched in blood and whose face is likewise moist with blood. (50)
Likewise, that fierce one born of the costume had flesh in his hands;
he possessed many arms and many faces, and was crowded with various weapons.
He is proclaimed to have a massive body, to be tall, and to have a fierce appearance;
he has red eyes, tawny hair, is black in color, and possesses a distorted voice. || 52 ||
Then, fierce by nature and intent on reviling, he [struck] with feet raised at a distance of four tālas and brought down with force. (53)

Because it is consistent with the *cāri* (transitory mental state), it is not mentioned separately. Having thus described the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in relation to desire for sense objects within the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), he now defines its movement in the furious sentiment (*raudra*), which is of the same nature, stating: "But in the furious sentiment...
To dispel the doubt as to with what intention that which was spoken regarding Daityas and others was said, he says: "It is one and the same..."

Now, one might ask: "Is there not ferocity in them even without anger? We reply: "Yes. If one asks, "How so?", [the author] says, beginning with "the ferocity of costume" (*nepathyaraudra*) and ending with "their inherent nature" (*svabhāva*), in order to have it relished according to the principle stated in the Chapter on Rasa (*rasādhyāya*).
Thus, it is stated that they possess only a single rasa, and this has been explained in detail in the Chapter on Rasa.
Regarding the phrase "raised at intervals of four *tālas*," some maintain that the mention of "intervals of *tālas*" refers to the space between the second *tāla*.
However, the Upādhyāyas state that here the word *tāla* denotes a measure of time rather than a measure of space;
thus, the falling occurs in less time than it takes for the raising. Following this:
(144) This same course of action should be followed by those who are like them. || 54 ||
But where the ground is unpleasant, defiled by cremation grounds and battlefields, one should employ that gait for the representation of the loathsome sentiment. 55.
In some places with feet about to fall, in others already fallen far away; with feet performing the *elakākrīḍita* movement, falling one upon another.
The gait for the *vibhatsa* (terrifying) sentiment is said to be performed with hands following those very [steps];
whereas in the *vīra* (heroic) sentiment, it is accompanied by the cutting action and the movement of the feet.
By asserting that these [sentiments] possess a natural intensity (*saṃrambha*) arising from their inherent nature (*prakṛti*), their movement through uneven paths is authorized.

Thus, Kohala and others, by means of the two-fold characteristics of *kalā* and its meaning, describe the circumambulation (*parikrama*) in the *raudra* and other sentiments through dance movements such as the *utphulla*. Those of this kind are Bhīmasena and others, according to this [tradition].

This indicates that even in the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*) of battle, this same course [of action] applies. Now, amidst the descriptions of the fierce intensity of the wrathful sentiment (*raudra-rasa*), he describes the course based on the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) arising from the exertion of human effort:
"But it is unpleasant," etc. It takes the form of a cremation ground, fashioned from headless trunks (*kabandha*) fallen in battle and other such things. Therefore...
Thus, by its falling nearby, it indicates [the stages] such as *kalārdha* and *turyāga*;
by its falling at a distance, it indicates [the stages] such as *kalāsādhaka* and *kalā*.
Now, he states the movement of the hero (*vīra*): "Now, in the case of the hero... By "projection in extension," the inclusion of *syandita*, *apasyandita*, and *udghaṭṭita* is intended.
And therein, the application consists of *kalā*, half-*kalā*, and so forth. From that very source [arises] what is called *ullāsanikā*,
which is based on rapid movement and filled with various *cārīs*.
With side-steps, rapid thrusts, and likewise with needle-piercing movements. || 57 ||
One should employ the gait with a hurried pace using feet that have reached their full measure of movement; this is generally declared to be the sequence of movements for the superior [dancers]. (58)
Furthermore, I shall describe the gait of those who are middling and inferior:
in states of wonder and joy, their steps and strides are erratic.
Having reached the *rasa*, one should employ this [tempo] and others as well;

those who know the characteristics of performance call this *tāla*. It is that in which the movement is rapid (*druta*) for the purpose of reaching the intended location. When there is a state of being drawn out or fallen [into delay], such as in the case of a *mallaghaṭī* or a triangle (*tryaśra*), the movement consists of half-*kalā*s, *laghu*s, and *druta*s.

By this, it is indicated that in the *vīra* or *raudra* [rasas], there is a state of rapid movement due to the nature of touch. Regarding that, he states the movement with the words "by the divisions of time" (*kalākālagataiḥ*). By the plural number in the word "feet" (*pādaiḥ*), three footfalls are understood. Therefore, by proximity to both the *kalā* and the *kāla*, the movement is governed by the *tāla*; thus, those [beats] which have a light descent—or alternatively, one—[is intended].

A quick step (*laghupāta*), two successive rapid steps (*dvāvanyonyadrutapātau*), and a pause of exactly one *kalā*—such is the *utphullaka* circumambulation. And that is the sequence for both the heroic (*vīra*) and the furious (*raudra*) rasas. [Regarding the phrase] "of the superior [characters]":
is it not the case that the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) rasa alone has the superior as its object? Who has taught this to you?

Bībhatsa (the loathsome) is a means for achieving human goals; however, when there is a connection with the objects of the aforementioned rasas and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) among the highest [characters], he describes the conduct of those of middle rank as follows: "And in wonder. By the word "and" (*ca*), other transitory states such as agitation (*āvega*) are also included. "Vikṣipta" means gone here and there, mostly agitated, characterized by many quick and rapid movements.

[This refers to] one whose [movement] is circumambulation. Likewise, for those of middle capacity, wonder itself—existing as a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) and culminating in the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the marvelous rasa (*adbhuta-rasa*)—is their state. Furthermore, by the repetition of the word "thus" (*evam*), he shows that for those of superior capacity, even in the case of the marvelous, the previously described free movement of gait remains the same. Only in that case must wonder be produced through speech.

Regarding facial expression (*mukharāga*): when the laughter of superior persons ranges from a mere smile (*smita*) up to excessive laughter (*atihasita*), it constitutes their natural state (*svasthagati*).

However, for those of middling and inferior status, this same range constitutes derisive laughter (*apahasita*) and excessive laughter (*atihasita*), characterized by a distracted gait (*vikṣiptagati*).
Furthermore, those established in their station should then proceed with compassion toward the beings in the various realms of existence.
With his eyes choked by tears and his limbs likewise [trembling], he raised and dropped his hands while weeping with a loud sound. || 61 ||
One should proceed with the *adhyardhika* [rhythm] when resorting to a fresh and beloved [lover];
this [technique] should be employed by women, and likewise toward one of low character.
But for the noble, it should be performed with fortitude, accompanied by tears,
with long-drawn sighs, and likewise with upward glances.
In that case, neither excellence nor such a measurement is required;
rather, the movement of those of middling strength should be applied according to the prescribed rule.
"With his enthusiasm struck down by falling upon his chest, his consciousness bewildered by grief...

[He says: "Moreover," and so forth; thus, by way of this context, the gait suitable for swift laughter (*drutahāsya*) directed toward the Vidūṣaka has been described. Regarding the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*), however, it is stated again: "And the pathetic... [The text continues: "In the state of extreme distress... (*uvarārte*).

Although the manner of movement was briefly described by the verse beginning with "ceti" and so forth, the meaning of the word "again" (punaḥ) is that which will be stated [later]. With "steady steps," meaning slow; having made them "extended," meaning long; and with "abandoned," meaning cast aside;
with "upward glances," indicative of reproaching the gods; such a thing is not authoritative, therefore it is not [to be accepted] here.
In every respect, there is an absence of fixed rules; rather, the *pramāṇa* (tempo) consists of a fall (*pāta*) that is entirely unrestricted.

For this very reason, Kohala has demonstrated here a tempo called *jambhaṭikā*, characterized by a slow *laya*, three *laghu* beats, a difficult *tala*, and a pause consisting of a single *guru-pluta*. The fall from the chest occurs because of its curvature.
One should not walk with excessively uplifted steps when there is the downfall of a beloved kinsman. (65)
And during a deep strike, one should adopt a posture with relaxed limbs and arms;
the movement is characterized by a swaying body and steps that are stamped with powder.
When one is overcome by cold or assailed by rain,
the performers must employ a gait suited to a woman or a person of low character.
Having contracted his limbs, there was a trembling of them;
likewise, placing his hands upon his chest, he became hunched over.
Trembling of the lips and teeth, as well as the quivering of the chin,
should be performed slowly during the enactment of coldness and the act of walking.
Likewise, in terrifying situations, the wise should adopt the same gait as women, cowards, and others who are devoid of courage. (70)
In connection with *karuṇa* (the pathetic sentiment), he describes the movement [of the feet]: "The powders (*cūrṇāni*) are thrown up in measured amounts;

because they fall more than [expected], the feet are slightly raised (*adhyardhikā*), and thus there would be little interval [between steps]. In the *karuṇa* rasa, poverty and oppression are present; here, coldness and the occurrence of rain are to be expected. He does not describe the understanding [of this].

"And by cold. By the word "then" (*atha*), he indicates the movement toward cold and so forth through the relative deficiency of the power of those in the middle and superior [stages]. By the word "of them" (*teṣām*), he refers to the combined *mātrās*;
by the word "and" (*ca*), trembling and contraction are conjoined; and by the particle "only" (*eva*), excellence, symmetry, and so forth are indicated.
It is cast aside. "The two hands" means they take the form of a downward movement toward the hips.

Having gathered the limbs together and placed the hands upon the chest, whatever movement exists in the world for approaching someone, that performance of the gesture of cold (*śītābhinaya*) must be executed there.
By the performers—the actors—there should be a trembling of the limbs, the body becoming hunched, and so forth.

The connection of the words is as follows: having thus described the movement [of the gaze] in the pathetic (*karuṇa*) rasa and, by extension, in other rasas as well, he speaks regarding the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) rasa with the words "and those others. Those who possess excellence due to the propriety of their lineage and so forth; furthermore, those who are devoid of courage (*sattva*).
The eyes were wide open and flickering, the head was shaken, and with a gaze filled with fear, he looked toward both sides. (71)

Having bound the hands in the *kapotaka* posture with swift movements and the application of powders, one whose body has been entered [by the breath] and whose mouth is dry shall walk with faltering steps. (72)
This [practice] should be performed during pursuit, as well as during threatening and terrifying [the enemy], upon seeing a deformed being or hearing a distorted sound. (73)
This [gait] should be employed for women whose prowess has been eclipsed by men;
in some cases it is performed with steps about to fall, and in others with steps already fallen far apart.
One should employ the *elakākrīḍita* footfalls, dropped one above the other, along with the hands following those very feet, to enact the movement of those who are terrified. (75)

The conduct of merchants and ministers should be appropriate for the assembly, as follows—for example, Uttara, the son of Virāṭa. By the word "swiftly" (*drutaiḥ*), the *dhārālaya* and other such movements mentioned by Kohala are indicated.
"Following" (*anusaraṇa*) means approaching from behind the enemy. Of men...

Furthermore, it means that which has been brought forth with a resumed stride, yet with courage maintained at every interval. By this, even the heavy and light footfalls in the middle [of the movement] are indicated; thus he says:
"In some places by those about to fall," and so forth.

Now, the treatment of the *śānta-rasa* (the sentiment of peace) must be discussed. Since it brings about the beauty of dramatic performance primarily through its own nature, there are certain characters—such as merchants and others—who possess an internalized state of refinement (*saṃskāra*). This is according to the statement, "Merchants are both heroic and peaceful" (*vīrapraśāntā vaṇijaḥ*).
Furthermore, even episodes such as those beginning with *yati* are dominated by the *śānta-rasa* when they occur within the context of dramas and similar works.
He describes the destination of both these types of merchants with the verse beginning "vaṇijām" (of the merchants), and so forth. The term *sacivāḥ* means ministers.
By the word *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature), he refers to their form as it remains unmanifested in various instances. *Naiṣṭhikāḥ*...
Having placed the hand with the palm facing upward and the fingers extended like a bird's beak at the level of the navel. (76)
The first [hand] should be extended, turned upward, and placed at the side between the breasts;
it should not be seated, nor rigid, nor should it be slung across.
Having positioned the body in that manner, one should proceed by that sequence;
O Brahmins, with steps taken at intervals of two tālas.

The path should be prepared for the ascetics (yatis), the mendicants (śramaṇas), and others who are established in austerity, as well as for those who have undertaken the lifelong vow (naiṣṭhika-vrata).
He should have unfluttering eyes, looking only a yoke’s length ahead, with mindfulness ever-present, having composed his entire body. (80)
With a mind that is indeed unshakable and relying upon the appropriate outward signs,
he should be modest in dress and likewise wear saffron-colored garments.
First, the wise one should stand in the posture with both feet even,
and having made one hand four-finger-widths apart, he should likewise extend the other.
Having made his face serene and remaining under the control of the application, he should proceed with his gait while his body remains unbent, even when passing through a crowded place.

The meaning is that [the practice] was set in motion from the very beginning of the religious life (*brahmacarya*). A *yuga* consists of four cubits. "One whose mindfulness is present" means one in whom memory arises instantly through the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Indeed, because of their tranquility, the hearts of these people—merchants, ministers, ascetics, and so forth—are to be restrained; thus, in a secluded place, there is indeed a binding of the joints [of the body].
This [state] belongs to the best of those who bear the marks (liṅgin), who observe the great vows, and whose minds are intent upon the constant investigation of reality.
One should apply these very same qualities, though inverted, to others. || 84 ||
Likewise, the states of those following vows—even among other ascetics—are either bewildered or noble;
they may be bewildered, or they may be composed.
The gait of the Pāśupatas should be performed with feet placed like those of a cart and likewise extended forward, moving with a haughty stride.
Furthermore, in darkness or while traveling, the practitioners must proceed with their feet placed carefully on the ground and their hands used to show the way. (87)

The *liṅga* consists of the rosary, ashes, the loincloth (*kaupīna*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in others," this refers to those who exist in name only; in their case, however, a reversal [of these signs] should be understood as appropriate. For example, a restless eye and mind constitute the *liṅga*, whereas matted hair (*jaṭā*) and the like become the *liṅga* for others;
in this manner, other cases should be inferred. He clarifies the state of being accompanied by vows with the words "and wandering about" (*bibhrāntā*).
For the vow of the "insane" (unmatta) and others is indeed heard in the Āgamas; the meaning is that the goal is attained precisely through those [practices] appropriate to each.

Having performed the desired sequence (*kramaṇa*), the "goal" (*gati*) refers to the state of the Pāśupatas who observe the vows of the Supreme Lord; the meaning is that this goal is exalted (*udātta*). Alternatively, it refers to the state of supreme fitness.
For those who have entered upon the path of seeing Nākula, there is even the "insane vow" (unmattavrata), which has reached a state of delusion directed toward that very object.
Thus, the transition to another rasa has been described. And as for what others have recited following the Furious (raudra) rasa with the intention of [introducing] the Peaceful (śānta) rasa:
"Free from desire for form and the rest, contemplating the supreme means,

one proceeds with a wandering gait by means of feet consisting of four kalās and two mātrās. How is it that this, which is indeed meaningless and redundant, has been seen in the manuscript in this book?
It should be disregarded as being merely one's own fabrication.
Having thus described the movement according to the flavor (*rasa*), he speaks also according to the location (*deśa*): "In darkness" means moving in a state of blindness;
"with gliding [steps]" means devoid of downward casting; "by those showing the path" means by those seeking the way.
Even for one standing in a chariot, the movement should be performed with the *cūrṇapada* steps;
having likewise assumed the *samapāda* stance, one should proceed with the gait of a chariot.
Taking hold of the bow with one hand and the chariot-pole (kūbara) with the other, the charioteer, agitated by the whip and the reins, cried out, "O Lord!
Various vehicles should be fashioned according to their respective divisions;
one should proceed upon the stage with swift and powdered steps.
For one situated in a celestial chariot (vimāna), this very movement of the chariot should be performed;
to ascend, one should raise the body slightly, remaining with the face turned upward. 91.
One should also perform the descent (avarohaṇa) by reversing this very [process].

"By others" is the meaning. The phrase "the movement should be performed" is the syntactical division; he explains this with the words "by means of powdered steps" (cūrṇapada). The movement is by means of a standing position with feet together (samapāda-sthānaka) or by means of a chariot (ratha); one should go to that place, or the movement is characterized by the chariot.

It is like the expression "the common [term] for a laborer who speaks" (*akarmakara-bhāṣika*); this is according to the treatise. By the phrase "with powdered words" (*cūrṇa-padaiḥ*), he indicates that which was taught by Kohala: a composition consisting of many short syllables (*druta*) and abundant flow, ending with a heavy syllable (*guru*).
*Kūbara* is the pole; *yugandhara* is the yoke; *pratoda* is the goad; *preṣaṇaka* is the driver's command; *pragraha* is the reins; and *rathyāni* refers to the vehicles.

The various horses, oxen, donkeys, and camels, painted according to the propriety of their natural divisions, are to be executed by this very *sūta*; the meaning is that one should keep that picture-cloth in the hand of the *sūta* himself.
The word "quickly" (*drutaiḥ*) is used again for the purpose of defining a specific tempo (*laya*) for the *cūrṇapāda* verses.
By the phrase "on the arena" (raṅgamaṇḍale), he says this: in reality, that person performs the act of going on the arena itself;

likewise, here everything—that painting—must be made in the form of that chariot, consisting merely of words following the truth, by which it is perceived that "the chariot goes. This applies everywhere; for this very reason, he says, "even for one situated in a celestial vehicle" (vimānasthasya).

The meaning is: even of divine objects such as the Puṣpaka chariot that travels through the sky. Now, in connection with the topic of the chariot, he also mentions another ritual action, beginning with the words "to ascend" (āroḍhum). One should "raise up" (udvahet), meaning one should cause it to go upwards. By way of contrast, this refers to the downward-facing position, by lowering the limbs downwards.
By looking downward and by revolving the mandala. || 92 ||
And in the act of moving through the air, performers of drama should employ the *samapāda* stance as well as the *cūrṇapada* steps. (93)
And for one who would descend from the sky, one should cause this movement to be performed—
whether straight, extended, raised, lowered, curved, or whirled.
And as she fell from the sky in that manner, her arms were cast out, her movement was lost,
her garments were scattered, and her eyes were fixed upon the surface of the earth.
Furthermore, one should perform ascending and descending on palaces, trees, mountains, rivers, and uneven terrain as required by the circumstances.
Then, having ascended the palace with strides that have transcended [the ordinary],
one should raise the body and place the foot upon the rows of steps.
In that same manner, one should cause the descent and the body of this [image] to be fashioned; whatever proportions I have declared for the temple shall apply here in their entirety.
This is the meaning. Now, in connection with the celestial chariot (*vimāna*), he speaks of movement through the sky: "by looking downward.

Some say it is a circular movement like a whirling mandala. However, the teachers (*upādhyāyas*) maintain that it is by repeatedly circling the circular formations (*cārī-maṇḍalas*) belonging to those who move through the sky. "This" refers to what is about to be described.

The dance master should have it performed by actors who are upright, with straight and graceful shanks; for this very reason, [the movements] are extended, raised and cast down, with a winding gait, whirled and turned;
others read "elevated and bent," meaning they are elevated at the time of raising and bent at the time of lowering.

They explain: "it falls" (bhraśyate) means falling unintentionally. In *apaviddha*, the two arms fall in the shape of a swift swing (*tvarita-dolākāra*). He clarifies this by the phrase "by the force of the situation" (*arthavaśāt*), [saying] "having descended from the bank, then the body..."
(153) However, movement within water depends upon the depth of the water:
when the water is shallow, one must lift up the garment; when it is deep, one must move by drawing in the hands. (99)
With the upper part of the body slightly bent, movement is desired on a sandbank by repeatedly extending each arm and pulling through the water. (100)
With limbs stretched out sideways, being carried away by the water, with all her members agitated and her face tossing about—such is the desired gait. 101.
Even for one standing on a boat, the movement should be performed with swift *cūrṇapada* steps,
using the second foot which has stepped beyond and is slightly raised (*unañcita*).
Whatever [measurement] was prescribed for ascending a palace, one should apply that very same to mountains;
however, in that case, the projection (vikṣepa) alone should be the measurement for the feet (the base). 103.
One should perform the ascent upon the tree with steps that have been passed over and remain stationary;

one should cross over by means of this application. He explains this method as "crossing over" (*pratāraṇa*). As for the phrase "regard for the measure of water," he clarifies this by saying "in little water. "Excellence" (*utkarṣaḥ*) refers to leading upward when the water is abundant or great.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "the movement therein" refers to a gait characterized by the various movements of the hands, such as the *patāka*, *sarpaśīrṣaka*, and so forth. Regarding the gait of one being carried by water without conscious intent, he says: "stretching out," etc.
"Each one" means in alternation. It is a gait in which there is a state of agitation throughout the entire body.

"Ādhṛta" is said to be that which is carried across the scale once; it becomes so because of its lack of independence. However, some say it refers to being weighed alternately; that is incorrect, for that [alternating weighing] is what is called "pārśvata," and this is not the case here. Furthermore, since this involves water, he describes the movement on the water—namely, "parivāhita"—which would apply to crossing water intentionally, but not in this context. Due to the connection with water, he states the movement upon the water:
"Of one standing on a boat": having thus discussed the movement along a current as an incidental topic (*prasaṅga*), he returns to the subject at hand, namely "ascending a palace.
Now, [one might ask]: what is there in that case regarding trees, palaces, and so forth, on the stage (*raṅgamaṇḍala*)?
[The postures] known as sūcīviddha, apakrānta, and likewise pārśvakrānta. || 104 ||
One should apply this very same descent even to the rivers;
by this very procedure, the movement and activity [of the deity] should be performed. 105.
These [rites] should be performed according to the prescribed rules merely as a matter of designation;
for when it is said, "He is dead," what is there left for the performers to do?
Just as an elephant is controlled by seizing the goad, a horse by seizing the bit, and a vehicle by seizing the reins, so it is with others as well. (107)
In the horse-vehicle [mudrā], the movement should be performed with the Vaiśākha stance;
likewise, it is done with various circular footprints (cūrṇapada) cast one above the other.
The movement of serpents should be performed with feet joined in the svastika posture;
having made the *pārśvakrānta* step, one should then release the svastika here.

He says "by mere designation" (*saṃjñāmātreṇa*) to show that it is not to be viewed according to the analogy of a chariot, a painted cloth, or similar things. "Designation" (*saṃjñā*) refers to the mimetic representation (*abhinaya*) of mounting [the elephant] and so forth as previously described.
In this context, he shows the mimetic representation in other cases as well, starting with "by grasping the goad" (*aṅkuśagrahaṇāt*) and so on. By that—

Even in the absence of a painted cloth [depicting a chariot] and the like, the mimetic representation of the movement of a chariot and so forth is not logical; however, the sense is that such a representation may nevertheless occur due to its ease of execution. He analyzes what was stated as "joined with the svastika" by saying "pārśvakrāntam" (the side-step). Thus, movement has been described in relation to space. Now, however, following the context of serpents and the like:
The gait of a serpent is also [to be performed]; furthermore, the gait of a libertine, characterized by graceful amorous movements, should be performed as well.
With the feet slightly contracted and dropped inward toward the palms. || 110 ||
With the two hands joined in their own natural grace and following the feet,
having formed the *khaṭakāvardhamāna* mudrās, one should proceed with the gait of a libertine (*viṭa*).
The chamberlain’s role must be performed according to his specific stage of life;
one who knows the application [of dramatic technique] should employ such a movement for one who is not old. (112)
With feet raised to half the height of a palm tree and with straight supporting pillars [the legs], as if lifting up his limbs, he should walk as if stuck in mud. (113)
Now, the movement of an old man must be performed with a trembling body,
his life-breaths suppressed by the *viṣkambhana* posture, and his steps raised slowly.
Now, defining the *gati* according to the distinctions of stages (*avasthā*), he first speaks regarding the stage of the *viṭa* (the gallant) with the words "And also of the *viṭa*.
"One's own" (*svam*) refers to that excellence (*sauṣṭhava*) which is appropriate to one's nature. "A cloak" (*kañcuka*) refers to the mode of behavior (*vṛtti*) suited to his costume;

one who desires that for himself—by the addition of the suffix *kyac*—is called a *kañcukīya*. This explains what was stated [previously] regarding "the particularity of the stage of life" (*vayo'vasthāviśeṣataḥ*).

He analyzes that [state] as "thus" according to the sequence to be described. "Viṣkambha" means stability; the suffix -a- is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). "Carrying" (*samudvahan*) means drawing [the mind] forth with effort.
He teaches this very point by means of an illustration: "as if stuck in the mud. Therefore...
This is a compendium of the *khañjakahelāvilambita* and *laghu* meters as taught by Kohala, applied to the *yaṣṭi* and other types of *viṣkaṃbhaṇa*.
For even one who is emaciated must proceed with slow steps;
likewise, one seized by disease, afflicted by fever, exhausted by austerity, or overcome by hunger [must do so]. (115)
His vital breaths were suppressed; he was emaciated, with a thin and sunken belly, as well as a weak voice and hollow cheeks, and his eyes were likewise downcast. || 116 ||
One should perform the slow raising of the hands and feet, as well as the shaking and likewise the twisting of the limbs. (117)
Even for one who has traveled a long distance, his gait becomes slow and labored;
there is a contraction of the limbs and a rubbing together of the knees. (118)
For even on land, the gait of one carrying a body should be characterized by a predominance of drawing oneself along,
with steps raised slowly.
He may walk with a staggering gait and likewise breathe heavily;
overcome by fatigue and perspiration, he may even move with faltering steps.

However, for those who are intoxicated, the movement should be performed during the early or middling stages of intoxication—[that] by which breath and strength are possessed. "Wrinkling," "contraction," and "rubbing" are mentioned for the purpose of avoiding confusion with other [terms]. "Of the gross" means of one with a large body; it refers to sweat produced by fatigue.
(157) Reeling with the left and right feet, she moves backward. || 121 ||
When the intoxication has subsided, she indeed stands with unsteady feet,
her body reeling and her hands likewise faltering.
Even for one who is mad, the movement must be performed without a fixed sequence, characterized by many types of gaits and based on the imitation of worldly behavior. 123.
His hair is coarse and split, his body is covered in dust, he speaks of things without cause, talks excessively, and is full of agitation. (124)
He sings spontaneously, laughs, and does not even become attached to social company;
he dances with great joy, and furthermore, he plays musical instruments.
Sometimes it runs with speed, sometimes it stands still;
sometimes it sits, and at other times it lies down. (126)
Wearing various garments and having no fixed abode on the streets, he indeed becomes like one insane; for him, one should cause this state to be brought about.
Standing on the other foot, one should extend the leg with the staff-like posture;
likewise, having performed the bound movement (baddhācārī) and the svastika as well.
Having wandered around the mandala by means of this movement of the practitioner,
one should extend the outer circle at the corner of the colored powder.
Having performed the *trika* in a well-rounded manner and likewise the hand known as the *latā*, there shall be a gait with the feet accompanied by hands moving in reverse positions. (130)

However, for the purpose of the deceptive performance (*kuhakābhinaya*), three types of gaits should be performed by those who are lame, crippled, or dwarfish, through the employment of impaired limbs. (131)
One foot should always remain fixed as if in a lame gait, while the second foot should be moved along the surface of the ground with its toes leading.
With a steady foot, one should lift up the limb;
however, one should move by means of the other foot, not by the one currently used for standing.
One should sit down with the other foot and proceed by this same sequence;
this "limping gait" (khañjagati) should be employed in cases of wounds from a thorn or a splinter in the sole.
The movement [of the foot] should be performed with the sole turned upward and slightly bent;
likewise, for one who is lame, the body is seated and the shanks are similarly bent.
"With the feet moving in reverse" refers to the movement of the feet; likewise, it should follow the action of the hands.

Some say that *kuhakas* are base ascetics (*liṅgins*). By the word *kuhaka*, the sentiment of humor (*hāsyarasa*) is indicated. Regarding "in the sole," meaning on the sole of the foot, he describes the movement when there is a wound from a thorn or similar object there: "with the foot placed on its tip" is the *narkuṭa* [step].
In the *vāmana* (dwarf) gait, all limbs are held contracted;
neither a striding stride nor the lifting of the foot should be performed. (136)
She, whose nature is deceitful, should be portrayed as being smeared with powdered substances;
likewise, the movement of the Vidūṣaka should be adorned with the three types of humor. (137)
Laughter produced by the body is considered laughter arising from costume;
it involves one who is bumpy-toothed, bald, hunchbacked, lame, or deformed-faced. (138)
If such an entrance were to occur, it would be the "limb-laughter" (aṅgahāsya);
however, when one proceeds like a heron with upward glances and side-long looks, [it is the heron-gait].
And because of excessively long words, that [type of humor] becomes "limb-based" (aṅgahāsya);
however, "literary" (kāvyahāsya) humor is to be understood as arising from incoherent speech. (140)
Adorned with meaningless distortions, as well as vulgar speech, and decorated with rags, skins, ink, ashes, red ochre, and so forth; (141)

O Brahmins, he who would act in such a manner is merely a comic character born of his costume; therefore, having understood the temperament, the emotion, and the action according to their true nature— || 142 ||
One should analyze the movement of gait as consisting of various internal states.

Since the specific actor being introduced onto the stage in such a manner is called "entrance" (*praveśa*), it follows that this is "limbering" (*aṅgahāsya*). By the term "entrance," he demonstrates that this is a rasa specifically within drama (*nāṭya*) and not in the ordinary world (*loka*).
He explains that as being "unconnected," "meaningless," and "inappropriate" by the words "with meaningless and indecent [expressions]";

in the term *aślīlaiḥ*, the letter *ra* becomes *la* because it bestows (*rāti*) lack of splendor (*aśriyam*), that is, lack of beauty. Therefore, based on the three types of humor, in some cases one type is employed, and in others two.
Having placed [the syllable] born of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) on the left hand, one should place the curved [syllable] on the left hand. (143)
Likewise, one should again form a group of four on the right hand:
the side, the head, the hand, and likewise the foot. (144)
One should harmonize it measure by measure, following the rhythm and tempo;
for this movement of his is natural, while any other is born of modification.
Whether there is gain or loss, his gait should be steady; indeed, it should be performed with the circumambulation characteristic of low-born people such as servants and the like. 146.
Furthermore, those who are known as the lowest and possess various types of conduct [are described as]:
one side [of the body], the head, the hand, and likewise the foot. (127)
The movement of the letter *śa* must also be made unstable;

in some cases, by this sequence beginning with "all," the Vidūṣaka, having understood the nature of his master—whether he be a king, a minister, or a merchant—their disposition, mental state, and what ought to be done, should perform the division. And not [only] toward the king.
Upon his return, it is appropriate for him to speak in an indecorous manner; this should be inferred in all similar cases.

Having stated the account relevant to his movement, he describes that movement with the words "born of his own nature" (*svabhāvajāyām*), because it has been stated that when there is no possession (*anāveśa*), his gait is like that of a crane (*vakavat*). The tempo (*laya*) is slow (*vilambita*); the rhythm (*tāla*) consists primarily of long (*pluta*), short (*laghu*), and heavy (*guru*) beats.

This [state] is accepted here. Other [emotions], such as grief and the like, are generally produced by their own nature through the tempo of *druta* (quick), which exceeds the measure of time for a *pluta* (protracted) note. With the intention that even a transformation consisting of pride (*garva*) occurs, he says: "from loss and gain" (*alābhalābhāt*).
"Loss" refers to a loss following upon a prior gain. "Enjoyed" (*bhukta*) indicates clothing and so forth. As for fear and the rest...
When he has gone only a short distance, his gaze, which examines the purpose of his servants' activities, should bow down. (148)
By the touch of her garments and ornaments, by her repeated glances, by her limbs agitated with emotional transformations, and likewise by her hanging clothes and garlands; || 149 ||
The gait of Śakāra should be haughty and characterized by a stamping of the feet with powder;
his movement, intent on glancing about, should be employed for those of low birth. (150)
The sequence [is as follows]: (Regarding "of the Śaka too")—one whose speech abounds in the letter *śa* is a *śakāra*.

Others say he is an inhabitant of a region such as Śaka and so forth, characterized by the letter *śa*, as will be stated later: "the Śaka, the Ābhīra, the Caṇḍāla" (Chapter 17, Verse 60), etc. Others maintain that a *śakāra* is one of low disposition who has been elevated to a high position.
Regarding the verse on *adhyāhāra* (supplying an ellipsis): Even in the Prakrit language, the manifestation of the sound *śa* does not lead to excellence;
its manifestation in Apabhraṃśa is revealed only as a source of distress, like that of an ascetic woman.
And regarding this matter, I too have a verse:
"The composition of words that have become corrupted has shaken off the true Dharma; what talk can there be concerning the perception of one's own intended meaning?"
O Ordainer, what was placed in your heart when you brought Śakāra to such a state of preeminence?
Likewise:
"This very Śakāra, who is accessible to all people, clearly manifests his sovereignty over the head (the cerebral *ṣ*), since he has destroyed [all] defining characteristics."
"In this world, this succession of ill-sounding rumors regarding her whose body has been struck down— a report consisting of mere hearsay— is a cutter that shatters her fame.
Thus, in the *Pratijñācāṇakya*, the great poet Bhīma also refers to King Vindhyaketu as "Śakāra."
It is frequently employed [in this context]. In this case, the association with the touch, sight, and pride regarding garments and ornaments is considered afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
And because they avoid contact with the world and conceal their own limbs, those tribes of Mlecchas such as the Pulindas, Śabaras, and others [are so called]. || 151 ||
O best of the twice-born, the actions, movements, and behaviors of those birds, beasts of prey, and domestic animals are in accordance with their respective regions.
The movement should be performed according to the nature arising from each respective species;
thus, the movements of lions, bears, and monkeys must be executed by the performers. (153)
That [mudrā] which was performed by Narasiṃha, the powerful Viṣṇu,
having assumed the ālīḍha stance, with his body following that very posture.
Placing one hand above the knee and the other resting on the chest, looking toward all directions with the chin resting upon the forearm, [he remains] with the head erect. (155)
O Brahmins, one should move with strides that rise to the height of five palm trees during the time of wrestling as well as when entering the arena. 156.
This gait should be employed by performers for lions and other such creatures; for the remaining animals, one should apply the gait and posture according to the requirements of the context.

Furthermore, there is no one known as Śakāra who was born in an Ārya country; rather, the various tribes of the Mlecchas will be explained separately in the passage beginning with "As for the tribes of the Mlecchas... and so forth. Therefore, it is logical that the Śakāra mentioned here is indeed of such a [Mleccha] nature.

By the statement "by the powerful one" (prabhaviṣṇunā), this indicates that this movement belongs specifically to those bears, monkeys, and others—such as Jāmbavat, Sugrīva, Aṅgada, Hanumān, and their peers—who are characterized primarily by their descent [from heaven];
for others, however, it is according to their own respective species. "Of him alone" refers to the movement following the *ālīḍha* posture.
The meaning is "going to the left side.
[This applies] in applications for the purpose of mounting a vehicle and during entries onto the stage.
In this manner, these destinies of men should be applied by the wise. || 158 ||
Whatever [topics] have not been mentioned by me here are indeed to be grasped from the world;
beyond this, I shall explain the movements and gestures of women.
The postures, actions, movements, and modes of address for women, as well as the *āyatam*, the *avahittham*, and the *aśvakrāntam* [are now described]. (160)
These are the positions for women; now their characteristics are described:
where the left foot is naturally placed flat [on the ground]. || 161 ||
With another [arm] placed at a distance of one tāla, forming a triangle and situated on the side, where the face is serene and the chest is level and elevated; (162)
When the two hands rest upon the hips of a creeper-like posture, that stance is known as Āyata;
the right foot is even, while the other is triangular and situated on the side. (163)
The left hip should be raised and the stance should be extended during invocation,
dismissal, and likewise during the [recitation of] names.
One should employ this position during moments of reflection and feigned indifference; it marks the beginning of the entrance onto the stage and the scattering of handfuls of flowers. (165)
(164) The anger arising from jealousy toward me, the threatening gesture and the clenching of the fingers, the silence of prohibition, pride, and gravity, and the maintenance of self-respect; (166)
In this place, an examination of the various directions must be performed:
where one [the Sama] stands, the Vāma is situated there, and the other [the Tryaśra] is located on the flank.
When the left hip is raised, that is the *avahittha* (concealed) stance;
however, when it moves forward, it is triangular (*tryaśra*), while the other [stance] is receded and even (*sama*). || 168 ||
The foot is placed with an interval between the beats (tāla), while the three [other limbs] are slightly raised;
where one hand is called "the creeper" (latā) and the other is placed upon the hip. 169.

The *avahittha* posture has been fully described by the ornaments of the traditional scriptures as being employed in the depiction of grace (*vilāsa*), playfulness (*līlā*), coquettishness (*bibboka*), and the nature of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). 170.
This place should be employed when observing the path of one's husband;
this is remembered as the proper place for women in conversation arising from their own nature. (171)
In cases of certainty, satisfaction, deliberation, and likewise shame, one foot is planted firmly on the ground while the other is slightly raised on its forepart. (172)
Whether pierced by a needle or not pierced, that is called "trodden by horses" (aśvakrānta);
likewise, there is the "stumbling," the "reeling," and the "falling of the garments. (173)
Plucking clusters of flowers, guarding them, charmingly frightening [the lover], and hanging from the branches of trees. (174)
In this place, the following should be arranged for women by those who employ them:
[the act of] leaning against a branch, as well as grasping a cluster of blossoms. (175)
Furthermore, in the case of base men during their periods of rest, their station remains exactly as it was as long as their physical activity continues. (176)
If a particular posture (sthānaka) is broken during a dance and a new step (cārī) presents itself, then this rule for postures should be applied for both women and men. (177)
Furthermore, I shall explain their movement as it exists in its natural state:
having assumed a pose of concealment, one should place the left arm in a downward-facing position.
Having placed the left hand in the *khaṭakāmukha* position at the region of the navel,
one then raises the gracefully moving foot to the height of a *tāla*.
One should place the right foot on the outer side of the left foot;
at that very same time, the left arm is called "the creeper" (*latā*).
One should bend the right side and place it upon the surface of the navel;
then, having placed the right hand on the hip, one should twist the left hand upward.
The word *skhīlatam* means "fallen away" in a specific sense. Because it is mentioned without qualification, yet due to its predominance and primacy, it is called "that which has gone" (*tad-gati*).
Regarding the phrase "having assumed a pretense" (*kṛtvāvahittham*) and so forth, and the term "left" (*vāma*), the [posture] called *latā* is on the outer side.
At the region of the little finger;
then one should place the left foot and the right hand in the *latā* (creeper) gesture.
Then, with his head tossed up in sport and followed [by the other], || 182 ||
Then, with his body slightly bent, he should walk five steps;
such is the rule for men when circumambulating the stage-platform.
That alone should indeed be performed by those who stage dramas for women;
however, the six-beat measure (ṣaṭkala) and likewise the eight-beat measure (aṣṭakala) should not be performed.
Falling at her feet is known by the experts as "causing distress" for the woman;
such is the conduct that should be practiced toward young women by the wise. (185)
I shall now describe the destiny of those women who reside there:
having assumed a pose of feigned indifference, she places her left foot upon the edge of her hip. (186)
One should make the first [hand] curved, open, and turned upward at the navel and between the breasts;
it should not be seated, nor rigid, nor should it be rotated.

"Or rather, one should perform the *vāpa-vedha* according to the prescribed rule. By this, he indicates through extended application (*atideśa*) that whatever mode of movement for men has been described—

depending on the nature of their passion (*rasa-prakṛti*), place, and time— all of it is intended to apply to women as well, provided it is permeated by the aforementioned modes of graceful play (*vilāsa-rūpa*).

Regarding the measurement of space and time where the *śobhā* is elevated, he states a specific distinction here. This has already been explained previously: "The rule for the measurement of women does not exceed four *kalās*.
By the mention of eight *kalās*, it indicates that even among men there is no measurement greater than that. Otherwise—

Since the sixfold division (*ṣaṭkala*) is prohibited, there is a connection with the eightfold division (*kāṣṭakala*) by means of that prohibition. They are situated in the middle age; for this very reason, their middle form is to be restated. The first is the right.
It is "circulated" (*parivāhita*).
Having thus prepared the body, one should then proceed by that very same sequence;
even for servants, the movement should be performed with a graceful, swaying gait.
With her limbs slightly raised, her arms gracefully extended in a display of prowess,
she assumes a pose of feigned indifference while keeping her left arm bent and turned downward.
Placing the left hand in the *khaṭakāmukha* position at the region of the navel,
the "Half-Woman" gait (*ardhanārīgati*) should be performed, which is a mixture of the movements of both woman and man.
With limbs raised and graceful, and feet endowed with playful movement—
that which was previously described by me as the gait of the most excellent beings.
One should apply half and then half again of that [measure] for women and for cowards;
such is the movement and behavior of men who are middling, superior, or inferior.

That same [gait] should be performed by women with graceful steps. He describes the gait of low-born female servants as "with intervals," and so forth. "Moving with a whirl" refers to those affected by the changes of intoxication; it is a winding motion rich in turns, where the stride of the arms constitutes half of the woman's movement.

The third nature (*prakṛti*) is called "neuter" (*napuṃsaka-lakṣaṇā*); and by the intention of expressing an equal division, there is the compound "half-neuter" (*ardha-napuṃsaka*). Regarding the gait: the gait of men is characterized by a high pitch (*udātta*) and grace (*lālitya*), while that of women consists of four *tālas* and four *kalās*. For women of inferior rank, it consists of two *tālas* and two *kalās*.
Half of that [time] belongs to base men and their laborers, consisting of one *tāla* and one *kalā*.

Does this [rule] indicate the place for the best alone? No; it applies to middle and superior men, as well as to those who are not men (*apuṃsaḥ*). Whatever the gait and movement of these [men], that same [movement] belongs to women of the high, middle, and low classes.
In the same way, one should act toward those who perform that work; thus is the term "excellent" employed.
Even for children, the stepping of feet at will should be performed. (193)
In that [third gender], no excellence of performance should be sought as a standard by practitioners; rather, a third nature must be produced, known by the name "neuter" (napuṃsaka). 194.
Having abandoned the male nature, one should apply the female state there; the reverse should be employed by men, women, and eunuchs. || 195 ||
Having abandoned one's own nature and attained the state of that [other] here, whether by means of a pretext or even through play, as well as through deception regarding fearlessness; 196.
A woman may adopt the nature of a man, and a man likewise may adopt the state of a woman,
through fortitude, generosity, goodness, intellect, and similarly through action.
A woman, however, should represent a man through her dress, speech, and gestures.

Regarding the passage beginning with "even for children," he states the method for cases where the distinction between superior (*uttama*), middling (*madhyama*), and inferior (*adhama*) characters is not explicitly manifested in order to demonstrate that [the representation] is apprehended by everyone. "By attaining their state" (*tadbhāvagamanāt*): whoever perceives that which is of such a nature, it belongs to them alone.
This is its function. And regarding the adoption of the opposite [means], he states the cause for a specific purpose with the word "by means of a pretext" (*vyājena*).

A pretext (*vyāja*) is the employment of something as a means to accomplish a certain task; for example, a servant girl wearing the clothes of a maidservant at the place of an assignation for the sake of a Vidūṣaka. Or it is play, such as the assumption of the form of a beloved person by heroines.
"Because of deception," as for example, a servant boy assuming the dress of a woman in order to deceive Vidūṣaka.

Furthermore, by the inclusion of the word "also" (api), he demonstrates the reversal between male and female with respect to a hermaphrodite, and that of the latter with respect to those two. In this very context of reversal, there arises the contingency of a reversal of movement.
