He also speaks of the reversal of the representation of transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), the involuntary states (*sāttvika*), and the subsidiary limbs (*upāṅga*) in the phrase "by steadfastness and nobility" (*dhairyaudāryeṇa*).

Steadfastness and nobility are mentioned as general modes of representation; by these two, the [transitory] emotional states (*bhāva*) are indicated. By "intellect" (*buddhi*), the permanent state (*sthāyibhāva*) is meant; by "being" (*sattva*), the involuntary states (*sāttvika*); by "action" (*karman*), the subject matter of the postures (*sthānaka*) and so forth; and by "trembling" (*vepa*), the [subsidiary] limbs are indicated.

"Modes of expression" refers to the application of refined speech (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth in the verbal dimension; "by means of gestures" refers to the *tripatāka* and other hand postures used in the intermediate space.
He was endowed with the dress and speech of a woman, as well as her glances and gestures.
A man with a gentle and steady gait may assume the state of a woman; likewise, those women who are of low birth, such as the Pulindas and Śabaras. (199)

Furthermore, for those women who are established in vows, established in asceticism, or likewise established in the emblems [of their sects], their destination shall be one corresponding to that specific class. 200.
For women who are standing on the ground, one should employ the *samapāda* stance; this applies to those *aṅgahāras* that are elevated, as well as to the *āryās* or the *maṇḍalas*. (201)
These [gestures] should not be performed by women by those who know the application of dramatic art;
likewise, the rules for sitting should be observed by both women and men. (202)
Likewise, the reclining posture (śayanāśraya) is characterized by various states:
the feet are extended and slightly bent, and the sacrum (trika) is somewhat elevated.
When sitting in a state of composure, the two hands are placed on the hips;

since the posture for sitting consists of being situated in its proper place according to what precedes and follows, he describes that kind [of posture] as "the rule for sitting" (*tathāsanavidhi*). Likewise, when walking, there is also lying down.

The remainder [of the definition] is that it is a resting place for the body occurring in a prior and posterior sequence. With a span (*viṣkambha*)—that is, a width suitable for the *vaiśākha* stance—the two feet are "bent" (*añcita*), meaning their intervals are wide;

however, this does not involve the technical application of the characteristics of the "bent foot" (*añcitapāda*). It refers to the manner of sitting upon a seat, stool, or similar object by a person who is composed.

In this context, the connection is that "the triad should be elevated. By the word *iti*, it is indicated that the meaning of the sentence—namely, "it should be explained as that which is to be performed"—is intended. As for "the two hands," they are in the form of a crab (*karkaṭa*).
One foot is slightly extended, while the other remains resting upon the seat. || 204 ||
When sitting with anxiety, the head and sides are bent;
the hands rest upon the knees, and the head rests upon the shoulders. (205)
During the sitting posture of grief, he should have his senses and life-breath completely lost;
with his arms outstretched and relaxed, he should likewise lean against a support.
One should cause [the patient] to sit down in cases of fainting, intoxication, fatigue, exhaustion, and despondency;
with all the limbs drawn together, the feet and knees joined. (207)
When afflicted by disease or overcome by shame, or when sleepiness has come upon him, a man should sit in meditation;
likewise, he may adopt the *utkaṭika* posture, which consists of the joining of the buttocks and the heels.
During the ancestral offerings (pitrya), the pouring of water (nivāpa), the recitation of prayers (japya), at the twilight rituals (sandhyā), and even while seated,
one should again place the knee upon the ground in a fixed position.

In this collective dvandva compound, the reading is *indriyamātra* with the word *saṃpraṇaṣṭa*; however, if the reading were *manaḥ*, then once it has been designated as the object to be spoken of (*procyatve*), the connection must be established by supplying an ellipsis. The phrase beginning with *apāśrayanti* is what is relied upon (*āśritam*).
In the expression *upaveśayet*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in its own sense (*svārthe*), or the teacher (*ācārya*) is the agent; however, the teachers [hold that] the arms [are the agents].

They say that one should cause [the practitioner] to sit on a seat with [the legs] extended, thereby allowing them to rest. Because it causes the upper body to bend due to the separation of the knees from the state of being drawn together (piṇḍitatva), it is called *utkaṭa*; it is derived from the root *kuṭ* in the sense of "to bend. And here, there is a separation of the knees, while in the former case, there is contact with the ground by means of the buttocks.

The distinction is that neither of these two applies here. "Pitrya" refers to the water poured during the *śrāddha* and other rites; "water for libation to the ancestors" (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) refers to the giving of water by another for the purpose of receiving it, and the acceptance thereof. By the word "sandhyā," one means the recitation, meditation, and so forth appropriate to that occasion. "Viṣkambhita" means expanded or extensive. One [is thus described].
(171) One should act for the propitiation of a beloved and in the performance of fire-offerings (*homa*) and other rites while remaining with knees touching the ground and face turned downwards. 210.
One should go to visit the gods when there is business to be done, to appease those who are angry, in times of grief, during intense lamentation, or upon seeing the dead. (211)

One should cause it to be performed for the purpose of terrifying base beings, for the begging of those who are lowly, for the performance of fire-offerings and sacrifices, and for the sake of servants. || 212 ||
The rule concerning the postures (āsana) should belong exclusively to the observances of the sages;
likewise, the various rules for posture based on drama should be practiced accordingly. (213)
For women and for men, there is likewise the external and the internal;
the internal belongs to the king, while the external belongs to one who has gone outside. (214)
O twice-born ones, one should offer a lion-throne to the gods and to kings; likewise, there should be a cane-seat for the domestic priests and the ministers. (215)

The second knee should remain on the ground as it was, fearing that the mechanical device might move closer; this refers to the mantra to be performed there, which serves as an illustration for the performance of *homa* and other rites. "Approaching" means saluting. Regarding the phrase "and in grief," the term "of the low-born" (*nīcānām*) is to be connected with every instance here.

When the lowly behold the deceased at that very moment of intense wailing born of grief, the genitive case is used in the sense of mere relationship (*saṃbandha-mātra*), and since there is no possibility of both [the agent and the object] being present simultaneously, there is no restrictive rule. When base beings such as jackals and the like terrify the lowly, or when the lowly beg for something, [then too it is so].
The two knees are cast upon the ground.

Now, in connection with the arrangement of time pertaining to the seat, he states the rule regarding its constituent elements as "the rule for the seat" (*tathāsanavidhi*). The external [form] pertains to all people, while the internal is appropriate for kings.
A seat with a shaven head-design (muṇḍāsana) should be given to the commander-in-chief and the crown prince;
a wooden seat for the Brahmins, and a rug-seat (kuthāsana) for the princes. (216)
Having thus entered the royal assembly hall, one should perform the ritual pertaining to taking one's seat;
furthermore, I shall fully explain the rules for the seating of women.
A lion-throne should be given to the queens and princesses, a shaven-seat to the wives of the domestic priest and the ministers, and likewise, a cane-seat to the wives of the attendants.
Likewise, for the women who enjoy pleasures, there is clothing, skins, or even rugs;
and for Brahmin women and female ascetics, there is likewise a cushioned seat.
O twice-born ones, even for courtesans, a cushioned seat (masūraka) should indeed be provided; for all other women, however, there should be a seat made of the bare ground.
Thus should the internal procedure for the posture be understood, as well as the external one;
likewise, in the affairs of one's own home, the posture is prescribed according to one's preference.
The *muṇḍāsana* is a cleverly crafted cushion; the *masūraka* is a seat devoid of stuffing; the *kāṣṭhāsana* is a wooden seat; the *pīṭhaka* is a seat made of cane vines;
the *vetrāsana* is something distinct from a cane seat; the *vistārikā*—according to others—is a piece of colored woolen cloth that has become a common term [for a rug].
A *rājñī* is a royal courtesan; a *devī* is a daughter of the commander-in-chief or similar high officials who has been married by the king.

The *bhoginyaḥ* are those who have taken up maidens [as wives]. *Bhūmyāsanaṃ* means that the ground itself is the seat. By the word "thus" (*evam*), he indicates [the practice] is performed in the presence of the king; by the phrase "otherwise in one's own home" (*tathā svagṛhe*), he shows it may be done at one's own will. By the term *vārtā*, he indicates such things as the commander-in-chief’s going to the house of a minister, and so forth.
For those established in the observances, there shall be the rule for sages concerning the arising from the seat;
for those bearing the marks [of an ascetic], the rule for the seat must be performed in reliance upon their vows. (222)
One should employ a seat made primarily of grass, a shaven-head-shaped seat, or even a cane seat for the performance of oblations, sacrificial rites, and ancestral offerings. || 223 ||
Those local men who are endowed with noble lineage and learning should be accorded the honor of seats by kings in this world. (224)

One should provide an equal seat for an equal [guest], a middle seat for a middle [guest], and an extra seat for one who is superior; for one who is inferior, there should be a seat upon the ground. || 225 ||
In the presence of the preceptor, the king, and elders,
the wise should likewise use a seat made of earth or a wooden seat.
In boats, elephants, chariots, and vehicles, as well as on wooden seats upon the ground,
it is not a fault to sit together with one's guru, preceptor, or a king.

The ascetic (*yati*) who abides by his observances (*niyamastha*) has, for some, an abundance of ritual implements (*aṅgaviṣṭara*), while for another it is a deer-skin (*mṛgājina*). Regarding "those who bear marks" (*liṅginām*):

as, for example, the *brusī* (grass mat) of the Śākyas, the shaven head of the Śaivas, and the cane-bark garment of the Kṣapaṇakas. He states that very point with the words beginning "the *brusī*" and so forth. The elders (*vṛddhāḥ*) are beneficial for their station; they are in their vicinity.
Those elders who are useful for both visible and invisible regulations—for this very reason he says "family science" (kulavidyā).

Regarding the honor of the seat, [the instruction is] "let him sit here. In that regard, he states the classification: "equal" means one who possesses knowledge equal to his own caste; "equally" refers to the threefold expectation regarding the seat.

"Medium" means slightly less than that; "middling" means also less in size than one's own seat; "inferior" means [less] in comparison to oneself. "The ground together with the ground" is to be designated as "let him sit right here"—that indeed is the honor of the seat for him. "A wooden plank" means a single, long, sturdy bed-frame.
It is said "wood" in order to demonstrate [the material], but not [to imply] that it is made of wood.
174) [The movements are] contracted, even, extended, and turned.
The ritual actions on the bed are proclaimed as being both raised up and bent down. || 228 ||
When the knees are pressed against the bed with all the limbs drawn in,
this posture called ākuñcita should be employed for those afflicted by cold.
With the face turned upward and the hands likewise released toward the back,
the posture known as Sama (the Equal) is prescribed for one who is lying asleep.
Placing one arm as a pillow with the knees fully extended, one should assume the posture known as *prasārita*, which is for sleeping comfortably. || 231 ||
That which is situated face-downward is known as "inverted" (vivartita);
one should employ it in cases of wounds from weapons, death, being lifted up, intoxication, or insanity.
Placing the head upon the shoulder and likewise shaking the elbow—this is to be known as the *udvāhita* gesture used by the Lord in playful dalliance and speech. (233)
When both hands are placed upon the thighs which are slightly extended, this posture, known as *nata*, is prescribed for occasions of indolence, fatigue, and exhaustion. (234)

Now, regarding the posture of reclining (*śayanasaṃniveśana*): it is called "contracted" (*ākuñcita*) because of the bending of one's own body. Through the movement of the space between the arms and by virtue of lying on one's side, there is an upward turning of both the front and back parts of the body.
Not from another bed or arrangement;
this movement of the *gati* has been explained by me.
And that which has not been explicitly stated is to be established by the force of the meaning. || 235 ||
Hereafter, I shall describe the arrangement of the successive chambers for the circumambulation of the stage. || 236 ||

Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the *Śrī-Bhāratīya-Nāṭyaśāstra*, titled "The Movement of Gait. The phrase "according to the requirements of the subject matter" (*arthavaśena*) means according to worldly convention. Now, immediately following this concluded chapter, he speaks with a demonstration of the connection [to the next], saying "hereafter" (*ataḥ param*). Regarding that which occurs on the stage through circumambulation...

The application of that [calculation], namely the division of specific orbital zones (*kakṣyā*), has been explained in the chapter on motion within the *Parikramaṇavṛtti*. May there be auspiciousness!
Herein, he elucidates the chapter which reveals the rules for the various types of motion.
Abhinavagupta has become the pollen of the lotus feet of the Destroyer of Smara.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, on Gait, in the Abhinavabhārati, a commentary on the Nāṭya-veda, composed by the illustrious Great Māheśvara Ācārya Abhinavagupta.
[The twelfth chapter, with a reading order different from the Mātṛkā.]
This is the movement of gait.
Thus has been described the preparation of the mandala, a task produced by physical exertion.
Hereafter, I shall explain the gaits as they exist in their natural state. (1)
Having performed the ceremonial reception there, preceded by musical instruments and the sounding of vessels,
he should bring the subjects into the city according to the route and the appropriate sentiments.
When the *dhruvā* has commenced and the curtain has been drawn aside, the entrance of the actors—giving rise to various purposes and aesthetic sentiments—should take place. (3)
The Vaiṣṇava posture should be performed in the highest or middle degree;
likewise, the chest should be raised, level, and square.
When the shoulders are relaxed and not raised, one should perform [the mudrā];
the region of the neck should be made with the head tilted like that of a peacock. || 5 ||
The two arms and the head should be situated eight finger-breadths apart from the ears;
likewise, the chin should be situated four finger-breadths from the chest.
The two hands should likewise be positioned at the waist and the navel;
the right hand is placed at the navel, while the left rests upon the hip.
The distance between the two feet should be made to be two and a half tālas;
and the lifting of the foot should be performed according to its own natural measure.
It may be four tālas, two tālas, or likewise one tāla;
however, for deities as well as for kings, it should be four tālas.
The *dvitāla* is the tempo for middling women and those wearing the marks of religious orders;
furthermore, there are the *catuṣkala*, *dvikala*, and *ekakala*.
Indeed, the *catuṣkala* belongs to the superior, while the *dvikala* belongs to the middling.
And likewise, the descent of those who are base is proclaimed to be of a single moment; having observed the three tempos— slow, medium, and fast— the triple rhythm (laya-traya).
Just as one skilled in drama should employ movement according to the natural disposition, so too,
in a movement of the highest quality by its very nature, one should place the knee level with the hip.
In the movements of one engaged in battle, the knee should be level with the breast;
this rule must be observed for moving about at will.
In cases of agitation, rising [in anger], or wrath, no standard of authority is prescribed for the arrogant Daityas, Yakṣas, as well as Pannagas and Rākṣasas.
The wise should fashion the gait of the gods with a measurement of four tālas; for the remaining [deities], the middle gait is prescribed. (13)
Among them, those who are the most excellent have a destination equal to that of the gods;
as do the Pulindas, the Śabaras, and all the remaining Mleccha tribes.
One should observe the behavior and movements of aquatic creatures, deer, serpents, domestic animals, wild beasts, and birds, according to their respective habitats.

One should apply the tempo (gati) according to the disposition arising from the region and caste, while the wise observe the tempo as slow, medium, or fast, and likewise the rhythmic pause (laya). || 16 ||

One should perform the prostration at the feet correctly according to the sequence. A steady gait is for the highest [beings], a moderate gait for those of middle standing, and a rapid gait for the most inferior; these three tempos (layas) should be applied according to one's inner nature (sattva). || 17 ||
One should employ a four-beat pause for the superior [performers], a two-beat pause for the middling, and likewise a one-beat pause for the inferior. (18)
Where one proceeds with equal [beats] joined together, there the support of *laya* (tempo) should be employed;
namely, the four-beat (*catuṣkala*), the two-beat (*dvikala*), and likewise the one-beat (*ekakala*).
Then, surrounded by those of middling and low status, he should proceed; likewise, there may be a measure of four beats, half a beat, or even a single beat.
Thus, this rule for the movement of the digits (kalās) should be understood;
now listen, O sinless ones, to the application of the movement of the [soul's] course once again. (21)
Then, with feet gracefully stepped to the side and accompanied by instrumental music,
he should proceed five full steps facing toward a corner of the stage.
Having thus performed twenty-one steps by going back and forth,
one should then perform the binding of the left foot and the throwing out of the right foot.
On a long (rectangular) stage, Bharata prescribes the movement of the feet through coming and going;
on a triangular or trapezoidal stage, the movement of the feet is likewise triangular; and on a square stage, the movement of the feet is indeed square.
A swift gait should be performed when stepping with two *kalās* per foot;
in the *jyeṣṭha* [tempo], four *kalās* should be used, while in the *madhyama* [tempo], it should be two *kalās*.
Where there is two *kalās* in the highest [pitch], there should be one *kalā* in the middle;
the measure of *kalās* in the middle is thus, while in the lowest it is half a *kalā*. (26)
In this manner, one should apply a reduction of half and half again to the digits;
however, that movement which belongs to the highest [digits] should not be applied to the middle ones. (27)
One should not apply to those of low status that destiny which belongs to the middling;
rather, O Brahmins, I have described the destinies of the superior ones according to their respective natures. (28)
I shall further describe the destinies of those who are middling and inferior;
for merchants and ministers, their conduct should be performed according to their own inherent nature.
Moving with steps that had passed beyond [the previous range] and spanning two *tāla* intervals,
she placed her hand on the surface of her navel and performed the *kaṭakāmukha* gesture as she rose.
The first [hand], extended and open, should be placed between the side and the breast;
it should not be resting, nor stiff, nor indeed swinging. (31)

Having positioned the body in that manner, one should proceed according to that sequence of instrumental music; furthermore, the gait should be performed with laughter, as well as with the limping and the dwarf-like movements.
In performances involving two or half-kalās, regarding the representation of a *kuhu* (a woman with a protruding belly),
the gait should be performed as if limping, based on one leg being stiff.
Likewise, the second foot should be made to move on its forepart;
with that foot, the body should be raised while remaining steady.
And he may be seated while walking, or likewise supported by another foot;
this occurs in the case of the application of a limp, as well as from a wound caused by a splinter in the sole. (35)
Then, the movement should be performed with the foot tilted upward on its forepart;
the body should be made to sit down, and likewise, the shanks should remain extended.
And when walking with a dwarfed gait, all the limbs should be contracted; one must not overstep that [pace], nor should there be any tossing of the foot. (37)
She, being of a deceptive nature, should be portrayed with powdered footprints;
the movement of the Vidūṣaka as well should be adorned with the three types of comic sentiment. (38)
There is laughter arising from gestures, laughter arising from action, and likewise laughter arising from costume;
as well as those who are hunchbacked, lame, bald, protruding-toothed, or deformed-faced. (39)
O Brahmins, that which is such should be his limbs and face; but when he moves like a crane with upward glances and side-long looks, [that is another sign]. (40)
Furthermore, due to having excessively long limbs, he may become an object of ridicule;
yet he is adorned with rags, skins, ink, ashes, red ochre, and other such ornaments. (41)
O Brahmins, that which is of such a nature is laughter arising from costume;
however, laughter arising from poetry (kāvya-hāsya) is to be understood as resulting from incoherent speech. (42)
With various meaningless words and likewise with vulgar speech, the wise man, having understood his nature as well as his disposition, [should act accordingly]. (43)
One should analyze the movement of the gait, which consists of various internal states,
by placing the crooked [finger] of the left hand upon that which is born of its own nature.
One should likewise make the right hand four-fingered;
so too the one side, the head, the hand, and the foot. (45)
In due sequence, one should cause it to settle, following the rhythm of the layatāla;
this movement of his is born of its own nature, while any other is born of modification.
Likewise, upon obtaining and enjoying [wealth], and even when satisfied, one's destiny remains as it was;
for Śakra too, his destiny is that of a fickle-bodied being.
One should perform the contact with garments and ornaments for exactly five steps; then one should perform the piercing to the left and the scattering with the right. (48)
Having turned back, one should then go to the second corner;
there too, the piercing is to the left, while the casting is to the right.
Then, facing toward the vessel, one should go these very same steps;
having thus performed twenty-one steps in this manner of going and returning.
Then one should perform the piercing with the left and the scattering with the right;
this movement, occurring according to its natural state, should be employed by practitioners.
But when there is a connection with another state, understand that it is a movement;
likewise, in the case of one who is unwell, it is due to the absence of fear and terror. 52.
In cases of agitation, as well as joy, upon hearing something undesirable, when there is a lapse of time, in the act of reproaching, and at the sight of a marvel; || 53 ||
In matters of urgent business, when one is suffering, when seeking a path, when imitating those who are confined, and likewise when fleeing from wild beasts; || 54 ||
One should apply a two-mora duration to these movements;
such is the movement prescribed for divine beings and kings. (55)
To this it is replied: How could the destiny of kings be equal to that of the gods?
Their nature should be understood as divine, or else as otherwise—divine-human. (56)
Regarding the performance of dramatic action, it should be understood as human;
however, for kings, there may be a divine form consisting of divine beings or one that is both divine and human.
Any other worldly arrangement, however, is proclaimed to be human;
therefore, no fault exists therein in imitating the gods. || 58 ||
The gait should be performed as amorous, arising from a lover who is in his natural state;
it should likewise possess grace and be measured by four *kalās*.

Having been shown the way by the female messenger (dūtī), he should enter the performance arena; and with the needle-like gesture (sūcī), he should perform the representation based on the meaning of the subject matter.
Adorned with delightful garments, as well as perfumes, incenses, and prepared powders,
and with various fragrant garlands, he was fully embellished. (61)
Then one should walk with graceful steps, rising after having stepped forward,
endowed with elegance and following the rhythm and tempo.
The hands should also be made to follow the feet by the performers;
now learn further regarding the gait in secret love-making.
Having dismissed the people there, accompanied by his female messengers,
he was like a lamp of nirvāṇa, yet not entirely devoid of ornaments.
Clad in garments resembling the ocean tide, Śani returned slowly;
anxious and fearing a sound, he was intent on looking back behind him.
With his body trembling and stumbling again and again,
the anxious man would go along, desiring to see his beloved person.
This course of action for superior men should be performed by the wise;
now I shall further explain the course for those who are middling.
To one afflicted by fever, afflicted by pain, exhausted by ascetic toil, or overcome by fear;
likewise to one who is wounded, traveling in disguise, or even one who is feigning indifference.

Likewise, when accompanied by thought, when established in one's natural state, and when eagerness has been withdrawn, the movement should be performed steady and slow, arising from the support of the instruments [of action]. (69)
In times of fear, when terrified, when intoxicated, or likewise when apprehensive;
when ill, when joyful, or in anger—one should act with fourfold agility. (70)
Through repeated gazes at the sight of that bewildering marvel, with the trembling of his limbs and the pulling of his garment; (71)
The movement of the letter Śa should be well-knit with its feet in powder;
however, even for a thick [letter], the movement should be such that it draws the body along. (72)
With her limbs raised up and her steps hanging down, she moves with a staggering gait and likewise heaves many sighs. (73)

And it should always be performed with the *cūrṇapada* verses, O best of the twice-born; furthermore, for those of low status such as female servants and others, it should be performed in this manner.
(182) Those who are known as the lowest— possessing various types of conduct and evil livelihoods—
[are those whose] side, head, hand, and even foot [are missing]. (75)
One born of a low family and designated as a servant should direct [the mind] toward that state;
one’s focus should be on observing those of inferior birth. (76)
With her movement of speech impaired and her entire body restrained,
she was just like one of her own kind, yet she was able to draw herself along by her body.

In moments of agitation and joy, one should employ a gait with striding steps that are wide-stridden; having reached a state of laughter, one should likewise employ other [gaits] characterized by speed.
Furthermore, in the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa, the movement should be characterized by steady steps; likewise, one should be tearful, with eyes full of tears, and with the limbs drooping. (79)

One who has been subjected to the *utkṣiptaka* penance should travel with his bowl lifted; likewise, he should go with loud lamentations, or else by the *adhyardhika* method, due to his association with a newly acquired unpleasant person.
This indeed should be employed toward women and toward those of base character;
however, for superior persons, it should be performed with tears and accompanied by fortitude. (81)
With long-drawn sighs and upward glances,
one should not strive for physical grace there, nor should the prescribed measurements be observed.
One should not walk with feet raised too high when a beloved kinsman has fallen;
and during a severe blow, one should adopt a posture with relaxed limbs and arms.
With a swaying body and a gait with mincing steps, this is called the gait of a chambermaid, distinguished specifically by her stage of life. (84)
Whether it be large, medium, or even small,
the pillars should then be erected with their bases rising from the *arhat* level, standing upright and well-proportioned.
As if lifting his limbs, he should walk as though sunk in mud;
such is the manner of movement to be adopted by an old man whose body trembles. (86)
With the movement of her gait obstructed and her breath suspended, with her steps raised slowly, she was thus overcome by the cold and struck by the rain. (87)
One should always perform the movement with practitioners who are women or of low character, by contracting the limbs and shaking them. 88.
Placing both hands upon her chest, her body likewise bent like a hunchback,
she trembles her teeth and lips and quivers her chin. (89)
The movement should be performed very slowly when acting out the need for coolness;
likewise, when it is hot, the movement should be employed as agitated by burning heat.
Accompanied by the contraction of the eyes, perspiration, and the withdrawal of the limbs,
it is likewise characterized by *atikrāntas*, *apakrāntas*, and *elakākrīḍitas*.

Those skilled in dramatic performance should employ these, as well as others, such as the *krama* steps, the *abhiyaya* movements, and the *cūrṇapada* steps, within the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa-rasa*).
I shall now describe the Furious Sentiment (raudra-rasa) with respect to the hosts of Daityas and Rakshasas;
O best of the twice-born, for them, that single sentiment is the permanent emotion (sthāyin), namely the Furious.

The Furious (raudra) [sentiment] is to be known as threefold: that arising from the stage costume (nepathya), likewise that arising from one's own limbs (svāṅga), and that which is innate (svabhāvaja). Thus the Furious is proclaimed. || 94 ||
He whose body is drenched in blood, who has a face made hideous by a fierce expression, and who likewise holds flesh in his hand—that is the Raudra [sentiment] arising from costume. 95.
He is described as having many arms and many faces, crowded with various weapons; he has a massive body, is exceedingly tall, and his limbs are fierce. || 96 ||
With red eyes, tawny hair, a dark body, and a distorted voice, this one is fierce by nature, speaking with terrible threats. (97)
The movement should be performed in this manner, with feet raised four *tālas* high and dropped at intervals of three *tālas*; and the same applies to all other movements of that kind.
O best of the twice-born, the single dominant sentiment (sthāyī rasa) of these [dramas] is the Furious (raudra);
it is held to consist of combat, laughter, and likewise the Erotic (śṛṅgāra). (99)
Likewise, wise men should adopt a cautious gait even toward those who are fearsome—such as women, cowards, and others who are devoid of strength. (100)
With his wide-open, flickering eyes and shaking his head, he looked toward his sides due to a mind agitated by fear. || 101 ||
Having formed the *kapotaka* hand gesture with swift, powdered words, one whose body is smeared [with ash] and whose lips are parched should walk with faltering steps. (102)
This [mudrā] should be employed in imitation, as well as in threatening and quarreling;
likewise, when observing a distorted state of being or hearing a distorted sound. (103)
This [gait] is to be employed for women, and it displays the prowess of women;
in some places with steps about to fall, and in others with steps already drawn back and fallen.

One should employ the gait of those very same [elephants] among the frightened, using feet that move in the "sporting of the elk" (elakākrīḍita) fashion, falling one upon another, accompanied by corresponding trunk movements.
But where the ground is unpleasant, defiled by cremation grounds or battlefields, one should perform the enactment of the loathsome sentiment (*bibhatsa*) in that location. (106)
In some places with steps about to fall, in others with steps already fallen far apart,
and in others with steps completely overstepped, he should proceed toward that loathsome path.
Likewise, in the *vīra* [rasa], it should be performed with the throwing of the feet, characterized by rapid movement, pierced [with gestures], and filled with various *cārīs*. 108.

One should employ movement in a state of impetuosity by means of steps that involve the crossing of the sides, the swift piercing, and likewise the needle-piercing, all in accordance with the musical divisions (*kalā*) and time-measures (*tāla*). 109.
The gaits of the Vita, however, should be performed with graceful strides,
using feet slightly contracted and dropped inward to the beat.
Endowed with the excellence of the stage, the hands should likewise be placed at the hips;
having formed the *khaṭakā* and *vardhamāna* hand gestures, the movement of the *viṭa* should be performed.
For those with emaciated limbs, the movement should be made with slow steps;
likewise for one seized by disease, afflicted by fever, exhausted by austerity, or overcome by hunger. (112)
His vital breaths are obstructed, and he is always thin-waisted;
his voice and cheeks are emaciated, and likewise his limbs are withered. (113)
One should slowly perform the lifting of the hands and feet there, as well as the shaking and the relaxing of the limbs. || 114 ||
Even for a traveler, the gait should be performed with slow steps, by means of the contraction of the face and the pressing together of the knees. 115.
The wise should always employ the gaits of the low and the middle classes,
with feet raised only to the height of a palm, and likewise with them contracted and extended.

Those ascetics established in the stages of life (āśrama), and whoever else is devoted to austerity— sages and forest-dwellers alike who are firmly established in lifelong vows (naiṣṭhika-vrata)— [all these are present]. (117)
One's gaze should be steady, looking only a yoke’s length ahead;
one should maintain constant mindfulness and keep the entire body under restraint. (118)
With an unshakable mind, he proceeds taking refuge in the *liṅga*, dressed in modest attire and likewise clad in saffron-colored garments. (119)
First, the expert in dramatic performance, standing in the *samapāda* posture,
should form the *caturaka* hand gesture and likewise extend it.
Having made his face serene and remaining under the control of the preliminary practice,
the ascetic should likewise perform the movement with his body well-seated.
This [conduct] belongs to the best of those who bear the marks [of asceticism], those who observe the great vows;
whereas in other mark-bearers, these very qualities are found in their reverse order.
Likewise, the movement of other ascetics (liṅgins) should follow their respective vows;
one should employ the hands accordingly as well. 123.
Vibhrāntā, hyadāttā, vikrāntā, and likewise vihṛtā;
with feet positioned like a cart-mouth and likewise with them extended forward. || 124 ||
The movement of the Pāśupatas should be performed with a wandering gait;
indeed, for those established in the *liṅga*, such a movement must be practiced by the wise. 125.
One should move like a blind man in the darkness, practicing yoga with feet that creep along the ground while guided by the hands. 126.
Even for one standing in a chariot, the movement should be performed with the *cūrṇapadakrama* (the foot-stamping sequence);
having assumed the *samapāda* (even-footed) stance, one should proceed with the gait of a chariot.
Holding the bow with one hand and the arrow with the other, his charioteer likewise remains occupied with the whip and the reins. (128)
Various instrumental accompaniments should be performed according to their divisions;
one should proceed to the performance arena with swift and powdered steps. 129.
For one situated in a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), the gait should be like that of someone riding a chariot;
he should lift his body slightly as if to ascend, and likewise remain with his face turned upward. (130)
One should also perform the descent (avarohaṇa) by doing the reverse of this very [procedure],
by looking downwards and by turning around the mandala.
And in moving through the sky, one should perform the movements of gait;
likewise, by means of the standing posture with feet together, or else with the "powdered-foot" steps.
Furthermore, for one who has descended from the sky, one should fashion this [funeral] path with straight, extended, raised, lowered, crooked, and winding sections. (133)
As she wandered, her arms were obstructed from moving through the air,
her garments were scattered, and her eyes were fixed upon the surface of the earth.
On account of necessity, the wise should ascend and descend trees, palaces, mountains, rivers, and uneven terrain. (135)
Then, having ascended the palace with steps that have been traversed, the wise man should raise his body and his foot before placing it upon the stair. 136.
Likewise, in the descent, one should release the measurement of the body with the second foot, which has stepped forward and is slightly bent.
As for the ascent to the temple (prāsāda), one should cause that to be performed among the deities and others;
however, in the case of mountains, O dear one, there should be only an upward projection of the limbs.
The ascent on the tree should be performed with steps that have passed beyond [the previous height], rising up,
pierced like a needle, stepped away, and likewise with side-steps.
In this manner, the descent of the deities should be performed in rivers and other such places;
likewise, it is prescribed for temples, and the same applies to the ascent.
One should indicate trees, palaces, and mountains by means of mere signs;
however, movement within water depends upon the measurement of the water's depth.
In shallow water, movement is desired by lifting up the garments; in deep water, by drawing them with the hands; and when crossing a ford, by slightly bending the upper body. (142)
Stretching out each arm one by one and repeatedly pulling at the water, she was carried away by her own current as she was stretched out sideways. (143)
A gait characterized by the swaying and shaking of all the limbs is desired;
even for one standing on a boat, this gait should be performed with rapid, rolling steps.
The movements and activities should be performed according to this very procedure;
these should be carried out in accordance with the rules, even if only by way of designation. || 145 ||
One should know an elephant by the seizing of the goad, a chariot by the seizing of the reins, a horse by the seizing of the bit, and a boat by the act of disembarking. (146)
In the horse-vehicle [mudrā], the movement should be performed with the Vaiśākha stance,
as well as with the "pounded foot" (cūrṇapada) steps, falling one upon the other.
The posture of the serpents (pannaga) should be performed with the feet positioned in the svastika;
having executed the sequence of side-pressing, one should likewise join the svastika.
The movement of those who are intoxicated should be performed during the early or middle stages of intoxication,
by means of the left and right feet, through swaying and retreating.
With feet that mostly stumbled against the sky and were unstable,
her body reeled, and likewise with hands that were trembling.
Even for one who is mad, the gait should be performed according to no fixed sequence;
it should be characterized by many movements and based on the imitation of worldly behavior. 151.
One whose hair is coarse and bristling, whose body is covered in dust, who speaks of things without cause, who talks excessively, and whose speech is erratic; 152.
He was one who sang and laughed excessively, wearing various strange ornaments,
and was constantly devoted to dancing, singing, instrumental music, and conversation.
Sometimes he runs with speed, sometimes he stands still;
sometimes he sits down, and sometimes he lies down. (154)
Wearing no garment for a long time and having no fixed dwelling on the streets,
he should perform this gait with the gestures of a madman.
Having stood with the *nūpura* foot, one should extend the *daṇḍapāda*;
then, having performed the *udvṛttā* posture, as well as the *svastika*. (156)
Having traversed the mandala by means of this movement of the hands, one should employ curved and circular movements at the corners of the performance area. || 157 ||
Having performed the triple movement with grace and the hand known as the creeper (latā),
one should proceed with the gait of a swan using hands and feet in reversed positions.
Performers should employ the gaits of the lion, the elephant, and the monkey, which were created by the powerful Viṣṇu, the Man-lion (Narasiṃha). 159.
Having assumed the ālīḍha stance, with the body following that very posture, one should extend the knee upward and keep one hand positioned [there]. (160)
Having tilted the head and placed the chin upon the top of the arm,
one should proceed with strides each measuring five *tāla*s apart.
In wrestling, in times of danger, and likewise upon entering the arena, this gait should be employed by performers when dealing with lions and other such creatures. (162)
Furthermore, one should cause the positions of the remaining [deities] to be made according to their respective functions;
however, elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth, should be made merely as symbols. || 163 ||
In applications for mounting vehicles, in entering the stage, and so forth—thus should these gaits of men be employed by the wise. (164)
Those [gestures] which have not been mentioned here are to be understood from the scriptures and common worldly practice.
Hereafter, I shall explain the movements and gestures of women.
The postures, activities, movements, and modes of address for women, as well as the *āyatam*, the *avahittham*, and the *aśvakrāntam* [should be understood]. || 166 ||
In the āyata posture, the right foot should be even, the other [left] foot on the side should be triangular,
and the left [foot] should be bent toward the side of the hip.
Alternatively:
"The left" refers to where the foot is naturally positioned.
Another [pillar], triangular in shape, is placed at an interval of one palm-span and situated on the side. || 168 ||
That posture in which the face is serene, the chest is level and elevated, and the two hands rest upon the hips like creepers is to be known as *āyata* (the extended). 169.
The commencement of the descent into passion, the scattering of handfuls of flowers, the anger arising from jealousy that destroys me, and the threatening gesture with clenched fingers. (170)
In this place, one should maintain silence characterized by the depth of the pride of negation, while adopting a guise of concealment;
it is appropriate here to direct one's gaze toward other quarters.
One should employ this posture during invocation, dismissal, as well as in descriptions, reflection, and feigned indifference. (172)
When one stands balanced, with the left side forming a triangle and the other side situated on the flank,
such that the triple-joint (trika) is elevated on the left, that is called avahittha.
This, however, is the proper place for women in conversation arising from their own nature, as well as in matters of certainty, satisfaction, deliberation, and likewise in shame. || 174 ||
When one foot is standing flat and the other is here with its sole turned upward—whether pierced like a needle or not—that is called *aśvakrānta* (the horse-step). 175.
This position is for use when stumbling or reeling, when holding up a slipping garment, on a variegated seat, or during graceful movements, as well as for protection. (176)
It should be performed when leaning on a branch, as well as when grasping a cluster of blossoms;
likewise, it should be done during pauses and even when stamping the feet. (177)
A stationary posture (*sthānaka*) lasts only as long as movement continues; once the movement ceases, it is no longer a posture in dance, but becomes a *cārī* [step] combined with the dance. (178)
O best of the twice-born, the rule for the placement of women should be performed correctly in this manner;
furthermore, I shall describe their destinies as they abide in their natural state. || 179 ||
Having assumed the *avahittha* posture, one should place the left arm facing downwards at the region of the navel, while the right hand is in the *khaṭakāmukha* position. (180)
Then, having gracefully raised the right foot to the height of a palm-tree span,
one should place it on the outer side of the left foot.
At that very same time, one should bring the left arm, known as the creeper (latā),
toward the side, and then place the right hand upon the region of the navel.
Having placed the right hand on the hip and having raised the left,
one should then place the left foot and the right hand in the *latāhasta* (vine-hand) position.
Then, with the head gracefully tossed up and followed by a slight inclination of the body, one should walk five steps.
Whatever procedure is prescribed for men when moving about the stage and its platform, that very same must be performed by the practitioners of drama for women as well. (185)
Six beats and likewise eight beats should not be employed;
for those who know the art, such a falling of the foot would result in exhaustion for the woman. (186)
This indeed should be the course of conduct for women of various classes as determined by the wise; now I shall fully describe the courses for those women who reside in their own homes.
Having assumed a pose of concealment (avahittha), one should place the left foot against the hip;
then, one should extend the first [right] leg, arching it upward, between the navel and the breast.
Without sitting down, without being stiff, and without swaying the body at all,
one should proceed with the limbs in that very same initial manner.
Even for female servants, a gait that moves with a slight swaying motion should be performed,
with the limbs slightly raised and the steps taken with a graceful, sidelong toss.
Having assumed the *avahittha* posture, one should place the left arm facing downwards at the region of the navel,
while the right [hand] is in the *khaṭakāmukha* position.
The gait of Ardhanārī should be performed by both women and men combined,
with limbs that are noble and graceful, and feet endowed with playful charm.
O wise ones, that supreme goal which was previously described by me for the noble,
one should cause women and cowards to attain half of that, and half again of that.
Whatever gait and movement belongs to superior, inferior, or middling men,
that very same should be performed by women with graceful strides of the feet. (194)
Even for hair, one may perform independent rhythmic movements of the feet;
in that case, no elegance need be observed, nor should such a standard of measurement be applied. (195)
The third nature, known by the name "neuter," should be fashioned; having abandoned the male disposition, one should apply the female mode of being there. 196.
But as for the inverted application in the case of male, female, and neuter, one should abandon the nature of one's own self and join it with the nature of another. (197)
By casting off their own nature through play or deception, a woman may assume the nature of a man, or even a man may assume the state of a woman. (198)
Then, through grace, goodness, intelligence, and likewise through action, a woman should indeed represent a man by means of gestures, speech, and movements. (199)
A man should adopt the behavior of a woman by employing feminine dress and speech, by means of glances, looks, and smiles, and by adopting a soft, languid gait. || 200 ||
As for those women who are of low birth, such as the wives of Pulindas and Śabaras—for them also, a course of action corresponding to their own caste must be performed. || 201 ||
Furthermore, for women who are established in vows, established in austerity, established at a sacred emblem (liṅga), or even those residing in the sky, one should employ the *samapāda* stance.

Those graceful movements of the limbs (*aṅgahāra*) which are overly exuberant, as well as the noble circular formations (*maṇḍala*), should not be performed by women by those who know the application of dramatic art. (203)
Then the rules for seating must be observed for both women and men; likewise, there are various dispositions associated with the use of beds and seats. (204)
The natural posture (*svastha*), the slow and languid (*mandālasa*), the exhausted (*klānta*), and also the drooping and weary (*srastālasya*);
likewise the *viṣkambhaka*, the *utkaṭika*, and the *muktajānu*—these are the postures (*āsana*). (205)
The *jānugata* and *vimukta* [positions] are for standing and sitting;
furthermore, their characteristics and their application will be explained.
With the feet slightly extended apart, the chest somewhat raised, and the hands placed upon the hips or thighs—one should remain composed during a seated posture. (207)
One should employ this [mudrā] during the enactment of innate nature (svabhāva), as well as when sitting at ease, and whenever all the internal states (bhāvas) are manifested. || 208 ||
With one foot slightly extended and the other resting upon the seat, and the head likewise turned to the side—that posture is indeed the "Slowly Languid" (mandālāsa). || 209 ||
In reflection, as well as in longing, in world-weariness, and likewise in separation, and in disputes and the like—this state should be employed by practitioners. (210)
With the hands resting on the chin and the head resting on the tops of the arms, with the senses and mind completely withdrawn—this should be known as the "exhausted" posture. 211.
One should indicate this state for one who has been seized by force, one who has been defeated by an enemy, and one who is exhausted by grief and filled with longing. (212)
With hands drooping and loosened, the body likewise languid, and the eyes similarly weary from exhaustion—that is what is called "drooping and languid. (213)

It may occur in cases of fatigue, exhaustion, intoxication, fainting, and among those afflicted by disease; likewise in delusion, when there is fear for one's life, and in times of deep despair. (214)
In the posture named *viṣkambhana*, the feet are extended apart (*viṣkambhita*), the arms are bent at the thighs (*añcita*),
and likewise, the eyes are closed. (215)
Through the gaze fixed upon one's own chest, one dissolves in yogic meditation;
and by abiding in one's true nature, the state of the actors is attained.
Placing the two feet together and sitting evenly, without touching the ground, is to be known as the utkaṭikāsana posture. || 217 ||
This place should be established for ancestral rites, for meditative recitation, for the performance of fire-offerings and other rituals, as well as for the act of ritual sipping (ācamana).
When one knee of this very person is placed upon the surface of the earth, this posture, with the knee released, should indeed be known as the āsana by the wise. || 219 ||
In order to appease beloved ones who have been offended by her actions,
and likewise for the cleaning of paved floors and the anointing of the ground.
One should adopt the posture known as *jānūgata*, with both knees touching the ground, when paying homage to the gods and when propitiating those who are angry. (221)
In intense grief and wailing, upon seeing the dead, in terrifying base beings, and in the begging of the lowly; (222)
That which falls upward from the ground is known as *vimukta*;
it should be employed in striking, as well as in sudden onset and in crying out. (223)
Likewise, the rules for seating based on the drama should be performed according to the prescribed ritual;
this applies both to women and to men, and likewise to those who are external and those who are internal.
Likewise, the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) is to be employed for gods and kings;
similarly, the cane-seat (vetrāsana) belongs to the chief priest and the ministers. || 225 ||
A shaven-seat (muṇḍāsana) should be provided for the commander-in-chief and the crown prince;
a wooden seat for the Brahmins, and a rug-seat (kuthāsana) for the princes. || 226 ||
But those men who are local residents and distinguished by their family lineage and learning— honors and seats must be offered to them by the royal preceptors.

In the case of equality, the seat should be equal; likewise, in the case of mediocrity, a mediocre seat. In the case of superiority, a superior seat; and in the case of inferiority, a seat made of earth. || 228 ||
In the presence of the preceptor, the king, and elders, the wise should likewise use a seat made of earth or even a wooden seat. (229)
On boats, elephants, chariots, and on the ground, as well as on wooden seats,
it is not considered a fault to sit together with one's guru, preceptor, or a king.
Having thus entered the royal assembly, he should perform the ritual of taking his seat; likewise, he should attend to all the subjects' matters arising from their knowledge.
This rule regarding the adoption of postures applies to men;
hereafter, I shall fully explain the rule for the postures of women.
The lion-throne belongs to the Great Queen; for the [other] queens, there is the muṇḍa-seat;
and for the wives of the domestic priest and the ministers, there shall likewise be the cane-seat.
For sisters, however, a seat made of cloth, leather, or a rug should be provided;
for Brahmin women and female ascetics, moreover, a seat of woven grass (paṭṭāsana) is appropriate.
O wise ones, even for courtesans, a cushioned seat (masūraka) should indeed be provided; however, for all other women, there should be a seat made of the bare ground. || 235 ||
In this manner, the rule regarding the seat should be understood for those in the inner apartments as well as for outsiders;
likewise, in matters concerning one's own household, the seat is permitted according to one's preference.
For those sages established in the observances, the rule regarding the seat shall be as follows;
for those bearing the sectarian marks, the procedure for the seat must be performed in reliance upon their vows.

One should employ a seat made mostly of grass or a seat of muñja grass, or even a cane seat, for the performance of fire-offerings and sacrifices, as well as for rites pertaining to the ancestors. || 238 ||
Contracted, even, extended, turned, raised, and bent—these six positions of the body one should designate as the postures for lying down and sitting. (239)
When the knees are pressed against the bed with all the limbs contracted,
this posture, known as Ākuñcita, should be employed by those afflicted by cold.
With the face turned upward and the hands likewise released toward the back,
the posture known as *sama* (even/equal) is prescribed for one who is asleep. (241)
Placing one arm as a pillow with the knees fully extended, one should assume the posture known as *prasārita*, which is for sleeping comfortably. || 242 ||
That which is situated face-downward is known as *vivartita*;
one should employ it for those who have been wounded by weapons, the deceased, the uprooted, the intoxicated, and the insane. (243)
Placing the head upon the hand and likewise shaking the elbow—
this is to be known as the "raised" (udvāhita) gesture, performed by the Lord when entering with playful grace.
When both hands rest upon the shanks which are slightly extended, this posture known as *nata* is prescribed for states of indolence, fatigue, and exhaustion. (245)

When the stage is wide, Bharata should perform the movement of the feet with forward and backward steps; on a triangular or square stage, these movements should always be made with even strides according to the requirements of the subject matter.
The first [element] is the costume, which must correspond to one's age; the movement and gait must correspond to the costume;
the recitation must follow the movement and gait; and the acting must be performed in accordance with the recitation.
This movement of the gaits has been described by me; that which was not mentioned must be accomplished according to the requirements of the situation.
Hereafter, I shall explain the division of the circumambulation of the stage according to its successive sections (kakṣyās). || 248 ||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Movement of Gait," in the illustrious *Nāṭyaśāstra* of Bharata.
The Thirteenth Chapter of the Nāṭyaśāstra:
Regarding those three types of theatrical pavilions (nāṭyamaṇḍapa) which were previously described by me.
Having understood their classification, one should then apply the appropriate enclosure.
The body, however, manifests various activities characterized by the distinctions between its internal and external layers;
it is expert in both defilement and purification.
May the lion-marked one, whose gait is like that of the sun, be victorious.

Here, although all the modes of activity (*vṛtti-pravṛtti*) have been indicated following the discussion on dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), and the *kakṣyā* has been signaled at the very end of the performance (36), the subject matter of this chapter ought to be stated immediately after the exposition of the fourfold representation. Nevertheless, such a procedure is required for each type of representation; without its exposition—

It must be stated that [the definition] would have been expressed as consisting of its constituent parts (*aṅgika*) alone. However, since the general term is used in that enumeration, there is no way to enumerate each one individually; moreover, such an enumeration would be overly cumbersome. Therefore, the reason stated by one who argues thus—that there is no separate status for the *kakṣyā* and so forth because of the transgression of the sequence—is unestablished (*asiddha*).
On the contrary, contradiction [arises] because it results in each [element] being applied individually;

since sequence is not a word-meaning (*apadārtha*) and is not established by the meaning [of the words], it is improper for it to subvert the primary word-meanings established by direct audition (*śruti*), as Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa has stated in this context that the authority of syntactical connection (*vākya*) is set aside by direct audition (*śruti*).

It is established because there is no contradiction and because the sequence occupies the middle position, as it is the cause for the application of the form of the transition (gati), which were previously proclaimed by me at the door of the dressing room (nepathyagṛha). (p. 197)
The placement of their instruments must be performed by the practitioners in the center.
The division of the zones (kakṣyā-vibhāga) is to be explained by means of the movement around the stage platform (raṅgapīṭha-parikrama).
Therefore, its mention at this very juncture is appropriate; through that [movement], it becomes an integral part of the dramatic representation (abhinaya-aṅgatā).
Those three locations and those three speakers must be described. Among them, first—

The intention behind this mention of the "girdle" (*kakṣyā*) is as follows: here, motion (*gati*) depends upon a destination to be reached; and while a location—such as water, land, and so forth, including its many internal subdivisions such as level or uneven terrain—is possible in the mere context of poetic meaning, it is simply not possible in the actual place of performance. Therefore, this [mention] is for the purpose of avoiding that [objection].
The examination of the enclosures (*kakṣyā*) must be performed. For this very reason, it was stated at the end of the previous chapter:
"I shall explain the correct division of the specific locations, which is useful for the movement in circumambulation.
To demonstrate this connection between the chapters, he says: "But those which were previously... The word "but" (*tu*) indicates distance [from what was previously mentioned].

Indicating the priority [of the first chapter], he recalls the subject matter of the second chapter with the words "of them," the intention being that this applies to each one individually. Having understood— that is, having known by way of division— the specific part of the pavilion consisting of the inner pedestal (antaraṅgapīṭha).
One should employ a specific location suitable for entering the *kakṣyā* (the inner chamber) and establish a connection through its division.

According to the requirements of the dramatic space (*nāṭyadeśa*), once the *prakoṣṭha* (the outer courtyard) is set aside, that which remains is precisely where the *caturaśrīya* (the square area) is located.
For this very reason, the arrangement of the *kutapa* (carpets or rugs) occurs on the left and right sides, while the division of the *kakṣyā* occupies the remaining space.
He asks, "What is the division of the stage? and replies with the words beginning "those at the door of the dressing room," and so forth.
(Regarding the word "previously"): this refers to what was proclaimed in the second chapter concerning the musical instrument (*bhāṇḍa*) together with its drum and the triple-pipe (*tripuṣkara*).
He then asks, "What follows from that? and replies, "the division of the enclosures (*kakṣyā-vibhāga*). By means of that instrument, that which is surrounded and occupied—

Having avoided that [area], the remaining portion of the stage platform (raṅgapīṭha) must be designated as the spatial division for activities such as exiting, entering, and moving about, extending up to the spectators.
For by the progression of the stage, another enclosure (kakṣyā) indeed comes into being here. || 3 ||
Houses and cities are to be known according to their division of courtyards;
likewise are gardens, groves, rivers, hermitages, and forests.
The earth and the oceans, the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving, the seven continents and the various mountains for many years—thus [he saw]. || 5 ||
And likewise Āloka and Loka, as well as Rasātala;
and the abodes of the Daityas and Nāgas, as well as houses and palaces.
It must be transferred. Now, what is the division of places? He says: "by means of movement" (*parikrameṇa*).

That by which they move is "movement" (*parikrāma*), namely the arrangement of steps (*cārī*) and so forth. By virtue of that, even for a single portion of the stage, there arises the relinquishing of different places; as in: "one should lift up the cow to mount it."

By the passage beginning with "with the foot having stepped beyond" (12.102), its specific nature as a palace, a mountain, and so forth is established. Now, one might object: on a stage floor that is not devoid of vessels and other objects, how can there be a determination of different locations based on a specific sequence? To this he says "no," [introducing] the division of the enclosures (*kakṣyāvibhāga*).
In this manner, other locations should be conceived within a distinguished and cultured region;

these are recited as illustrations for the sake of the memory of poets. Houses and so forth are further exemplified through the divisions of earth, heaven, and the netherworld (pātāla) for the purpose of comprehensive inclusion.
Even though "the three worlds" has already been mentioned, this enumeration of descriptions is for the sake of further clarification.

Now, one might ask: in every application, are all those residing in the three worlds possible [to be included] due to the distinction of locations? He shows that this is not so with the words "or in a city," and so forth. By means of particles (*nipāta*), forests and other such places are directly indicated even if not explicitly stated. Likewise...
Whether in a city, or in a forest, or in a village, or even on a mountain—
wherever news may circulate, there one should employ the *kakṣyā* (the enclosure or strategic arrangement).
One should likewise designate a location that is either external, intermediate, or internal; and whether it be distant or near.
Those who have entered the arena first should be known by the wise as the "inner" ones;
those who enter later are to be understood as being on the outer part of the enclosure.
But he who, desiring to see them, enters the circle of the stage,
should then offer himself while facing the south.

This indicates repetition and so forth. Wherever a narrative—a report derived from the power of past events—should proceed with excellence, one should cause that specific division of space within [the performance] to proceed; that is to say, one should display it upon the stage, but not everything. It was stated "in a particular place," not "on the stage. He shows the distinction:

Regarding the passage beginning with "bāhye ca" and so forth: when there are three parts (*bhāga*), one should conceive of space and so on in one particular part, and therein imagine the distinctions of distance and so on; the meaning is that one should conceive of them through a process differentiated by greater or lesser extent. He defines the distinction between external and so forth with the words "pūrvapraviṣṭāḥ," meaning those who existed previously.

Those who have previously entered as the primary [members] are called "internal" (*abhyantara*); thus, a specific designated location is the "inner enclosure" (*abhyantara-kakṣyā*). However, even one who was previously entered as the primary [member], when entering the primary [assembly], is simply at the end of his own enclosure. But the place for those who enter later is the "outer enclosure" (*bāhya-kakṣyā*).
The middle enclosure (*madhyamā kakṣyā*) is that specific location toward which those who have entered first approach;
this means that for one who has entered previously,

there is a division of the house, garden, and so forth, appropriate to the plot of action (*itivṛtta*), right within his own place, and for one who enters later as well, [it occurs] together with the one who entered first.

Until the gathering occurs, there is only observation within the middle stage (*madhyamakakṣyā*), such as the movement and circumambulation; for the purpose of that gathering, the division of the stages (*kakṣyāvibhāga*) is interrupted once they have gathered. Thus, he explains the procedure for the gathering with the words "But of those... referring to those who have previously entered.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the object.
200) For from that [place] should be the opening of the vessel and the entrance to the dressing room.
That eastern direction must always be mentally conceived through the application of dramatic performance. || 11 ||
And whoever should depart from that place, he should proceed in that very manner;
for by that man, an offering has already been made to him.
If he has already departed but must re-enter that house for some purpose, the man from whom he received [the gift] should exit by the same path by which he arrived. (13)
Alternatively, he may go with that very person for the sake of the plot;
likewise, he may enter the stage either alone or accompanied.

The meaning is that he stands looking toward the southern side of the one who entered first, such that he turns his back to the spectator; this is the sequence for the southern region and so forth for the sake of their engagement, whereas it is the opposite elsewhere. Furthermore, the word *atha* indicates the sequence that brings about the constituent parts of the engagement.

Therefore, he said this: facing north is primary, while the offering of oneself toward the south is described as it truly occurred according to the sequence of events; such is how it is composed. The meaning of the word "tu" (but) is that [the offering] takes place in the outermost enclosure itself, together with those who have already entered. He asks: what indeed is the southern direction here? He says:

The compound *yatomukham* means that the direction in relation to which the opening of a vessel faces is the "east. Now, one might object that the opening of a vessel is difficult to measure; therefore, he says it is the "door. When taking up the stage attire (*nepathya*), whatever main entrance of the house serves as the point for bringing in the vessels, its status as the "front" is made manifest during their re-arrangement.
By means of indicating their preeminence. "By that very [means]" means by way of conjunction with another character who has already entered.
Furthermore, when those two are entering, one should specify another chamber (*kakṣyā*).
By means of circumambulating the stage, however, another enclosure (kakṣyā) is prescribed. || 15 ||
He should travel together with those of equal status and surrounded by those of lower rank; furthermore, the female messengers should indeed be directed to go ahead. (16)
That same ground may be made extensive by many circumambulations;
one should thus determine it as either intermediate or proximate for those very [circumambulators]. (17)
Whether in a city or a forest, on a mountain or even in the ocean,
one should perform the journey of the divine beings, or again in another continent within the year.
Whether by means of a celestial chariot traveling through space, or again by means of illusion, or else through various activities performed for diverse purposes. || 19 ||
In a drama, there is the movement of divine beings in disguised forms upon the stage;

likewise, whether it be external, intermediate, or internal, that very same ground differentiates [space] as "far" (*vikṛṣṭa*) or "distant" (*dūra*), and so forth, through the arrangement of the relative magnitude— intermediate or small— of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), and not merely through smallness alone.

This is indeed established by multiplicity. By the passage beginning with "or in a city" and ending with "by means of performance," he demonstrates that there is yet another variety of movement. In dramatic performance (*prayoga*), the travel of divine beings—those of celestial origin, ranging from Piśācas up to Brahmā—to locations such as cities or islands occurs solely through the sky.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "The task is to be accomplished by means of a celestial vehicle (*vimāna*) that travels through the air, or by means of illusion (*māyā*) whose form is invisible, or by other actions such as seizing [someone] by force for various purposes.
He says "drama" (*nāṭaka*) to show that this is not the only method for divine beings, but that there is also another; by the word "disguise" (*vepa*), he does not...

The ground appears as the body of the bow; by that, when the true forms of the gods—whose essential natures were concealed due to the cause of favoring them with the granting of boons and other such acts—are revealed, they become visible to human beings. At that time...
When these [beings] are seen by humans due to some specific cause, (p. 202) || 20 ||
(Whether in Bhārata, or in Haimavata, or in Harivarṣa, Ilāvṛta, Ramya, Kimpuruṣa, or even in the Northern Kurus. || 21 ||
The movement at will among all the divine regions is proclaimed;
however, for human beings, movement is ordained only within Bhārata. || 22 ||
If a man must go to a distant place on account of some business, he should be designated by another in a *praveśaka* through the marking of a scar. (23)
Having determined the duration of the day, one should predict the attainment of the task;
however, if the task is not attained, the cutting of her [the thread’s] mark is prescribed.
In a one-act play, a single act should be composed to last for a moment, a muhūrta, a watch (yāma), or even a day, following the requirements of the plot and the seed (bīja).

When the marking [of the stage] is completed, whether for a month or even for a year, they may move about upon the ground during the performance of a drama; "movement" (saṃcara) refers to the ground itself because one moves (*saṃcarati*) upon it. However, he says "for the divine beings" because this is the general rule among the gods. But in the Purāṇas, this—

He says "the general rule" (*sāmānyavidhi*) with the words "in Bhārata," meaning that it does not apply to [regions] such as Ilāvṛta and so forth. He states the continent for the sake of its practical application.
After one year has passed, the ritual that relies upon the lap should be performed.
Thus, in the land of Bhārata, the stages should be performed according to practice;
now learn of the course of humans as well as that of the divine beings. (27)
On Kailāsa, the best of mountains, situated upon the back of the Himavat,
there were yakṣas, guhyakas, and those who are the followers of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
The Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas are all known to dwell in the Himavat;
and on Hemakūṭa, the Gandharvas together with their hosts of Apsarases are to be found. (29)
All the Nāgas—Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka—are on Niṣadha;
the wise should know that the thirty-three hosts of gods are on Mahāmeru.
On the blue mountain made of lapis lazuli dwell the perfected ones and the Brahman-sages; the White Mountain is said to belong to the Daityas and the Dānavas.
The Pitṛs as well are to be known as residing upon Śṛṅgavat;
these indeed are the most excellent mountains, for they are divine abodes.

"Haimavatāḥ" means that their movement is mostly in the Himavat; this applies everywhere in the same way. "Nīla" refers to a particular mountain, and its qualification is "made of lapis lazuli" (*vaiḍūryamaya*); this is for the sake of the poet's instruction.
It is the abode of the divine beings, from the Piśācas up to the Brahmās.
The division of their zones within Jambūdvīpa shall be as follows; however, they have no activity or task to perform through their own individual karmic prowess. (33)
However, the distinction among them is as it is in the world of humans;
all the activities of the gods must be based upon human affairs. (34)
However, their state of being unblinking is not something that should be employed by performers;
for in this world, both the emotions (*bhāvas*) and the aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*) are established solely upon the gaze. (35)
For a state of being is first indicated by the gaze and subsequently manifested by the limbs.

Now, [the author] says "of them" (teṣām) to show that it is possible to perform that journey which is appropriate for the divine mountains in other worlds; the word "and" (ca) implies that even for the divine beings, [this is possible] just as it is in Jambūdvīpa.

The meaning is that "movement" (gati) is characterized by the specific locations of the various enclosures (kakṣyā). He clarifies this with the words "not of them" (na teṣām). The meaning is that their specific limitation (pariccheda-viśeṣa)—that is, their attendant service (paricāra) surrounding them—should not be made manifest. Alternatively, "limitation" (pariccheda) refers to knowledge; that [knowledge] whose objects are distant, concealed, and so forth, should not be displayed. How then? He says:

This entire state must be enacted as belonging solely to the human realm; how so? Just like the world of humans, in the descent of portions [of divine beings] into the human world, the conduct of the leaders such as Rāma and others is nothing other than something preeminent, transcendent, yet entirely appropriate for a human being. In that very same way...

The meaning is: "even for those [beings] who possess many divine states. It is "unblinking" (*animiṣa*) because they do not blink; their form is not at all an effect [of worldly causes]. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. The reason for this is stated here: he clarifies that "the states" (*bhāvāḥ*), namely the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) and the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), are perceived only through sight, by saying "in sight" (*dṛṣṭau*). That which was indicated is the indicative representation (*sūcābhinaya*) itself.

"It is manifested" means that it becomes clearly evident when it is endowed with the specific [factors] such as the *vibhāva* (determinants). For this very reason, this same point—which is also the probandum (*sādhya*)—is stated again by the phrase "not their activity," because of its primary importance.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the division of the sections has been declared by me;
furthermore, I shall again explain the characteristics of the modes of activity (pravṛttis). (36)
And fourfold is the mode of performance (pravṛtti) declared by the practitioners of drama:
Āvantī, Dākṣiṇātyā, Pāñcālī, and Oḍhramāgadhī. (37)

Here it is asked: Why "pravṛtti"? It is said: Because it makes known the various livelihoods, customs, languages, and behaviors in different regions on earth, it is called *vṛtti* and *pravṛtti* in the sense of reporting.
Here it is asked: Just as there are various regions on earth...

Thus, because the general outline (*uddeśa*) is beneficial to all, everything is subsequently included within that summary; therefore, although the division of sections (*kakṣyāvibhāga*) was not explicitly indicated [in the outline], it has nevertheless been shown immediately after the chapter on movement (*gatyadhyāya*) in the context of the progression of the *cārī* movements. Now, [the following is presented].
The triad beginning with *tvāṅgika*—namely, *upayoga*, *dharmya*, and so forth—has been enumerated; among these, the detailed examination of the *vṛttis* will occur later.

The reason for this we shall explain in the very chapter on *vṛtti* (Chapter 20). Although *dharma* was enumerated first, nevertheless, by the statement "wherein *vārttā* proceeds," [it is indicated that *vārttā* takes precedence].
Furthermore, in connection with the mention of the distinctions between regions as conceived through the division of the *kakṣyās* (courtly zones),
the activities undertaken based on those regional divisions are implied; moreover, when an actor enters, there is a division of the *kakṣyās*,
such that the Southerners (*Dākṣiṇātyas*) and the Westerners (*Āvantyas*) enter by the northern gate, while others enter by the other gates.
