The phrase "saveyana" (having understood) thus implies a division of activity and a distinction of introductory sections (*praveśaka*).

Having considered that those [sections] must also be explained immediately thereafter—both by their position and by their utility—the author says "fourfold," meaning that activity arises from that. The term "questions" refers to the inquiry "from what? (*kasmāt*).

Now, he states the meaning of the fourfold inquiry, beginning with the word "pṛthivyā" (of the earth). "Pravṛtti" (activity) refers to the well-known variety of dress, speech, and customs found in specific regions. The construction there is as follows: in each respective region, whatever dress (*veṣa*), that is, attire; speech (*bhāṣā*); or custom (*ācāra*), which is the worldly practice according to secular treatises; or livelihood (*vārtā*)—[these constitute activity].

They proclaim that livelihoods such as agriculture and animal husbandry bring about the worldly renown of all sciences, beginning with those of the earth; for it is because of this engagement with external objects [that such renown occurs].

How is it that these [four means] are established as being fourfold, given that their application (*prayoga*) possesses identical characteristics? It is said: That is true; their application does indeed possess identical characteristics. However, because the world consists of diverse regions, dress, languages, and customs, [the Buddha] acted in accordance with worldly convention for one who relies on a livelihood.

I have declared that drama is fourfold: Bhāratī, Ārabhaṭī, Sāttvatī, and Kaiśikī. The word "pravṛtti" refers to engagement in knowledge—that is, complete or exhaustive understanding. This [fourfold nature] exists in the world.
In such passages as "the activity of Rāma toward Rāma," the term *pravṛtti* (activity) occurs.
Now, regarding the question of number, he states his own intention with the words "when. As for "countries":
although it was stated that there are four types of activity, this does not mean that there are only four countries. This much has indeed been stated for now.

Anticipating the objection that [the other modes] have been omitted because they are subordinate, he says: "It is called 'performance' (prayoga) because its characteristics are the same," with the words "by the great ones" being understood as the ellipsis. "Performance" (prayoga) refers here to drama (nāṭya). This is the common nature of these four modes of activity, shared by all performances among those four which possess identical characteristics.

In your view, however, no other legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) has been shown. And thus, just as the consideration of the world—which is common to all—is quickly set aside by greed, anger, and delusion, so too is it in the present case. But surely it was stated that the fourfold common application is used here, and no other procedure enters into this?
You are forgetful; you do not remember what was said at the end of the *pūrvaraṅga* (in chapter 5):

"This *pūrvaraṅga* is to be performed by the Avantikas, Pañcālas, Dākṣiṇātyas, Oḍras, and Māgadhas. Thus, it was stated that this serves as the point of conception for the performance of the *pūrvaraṅga*.

In that very context, he states the reply preceded by an admission, beginning with "But that is true" and ending with "of trembling and so forth," using the word "admission" (*abhyupagama*) and the word "place" (*deśa*) to denote their occurrence.
The word "of these" (*āsām*) has already been explained. He states the reply starting with "However" (*kiṃtu*). This is what is meant:
This fourfold [classification] is dependent on *vṛtti* (mode of application), that is, it relies upon *vṛtti*. Now, what is *pravṛtti*?
For by means of the applications (*prayoga*) based on *vṛtti*, the regions (*deśa*) are designated. (p. 207)

The fourfold mode of performance has been brought forth and the preliminary application has been initiated. In this regard, those from the South (Dākṣiṇātyas) abound in much dancing, singing, and instrumental music; they are characterized by the Kaiśikī style, and their bodily gestures of expression are clever, sweet, and graceful. For example:

Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Mekala, and Pālamañjara—regarding each of these, he states that there is no "acceptance" (*abhyupagama*) or "application" (*pravṛtti*) therein, in accordance with the conventions of the world. For the world is fourfold: the Southern Region (*dakṣiṇāpatha*), the Eastern Region (*pūrvadeśa*), the Western Region (*paścimadeśa*), and the Northern Land (*uttarabhūmi*).
This division is not without foundation, for it arises from similarity;

thus, among the Southerners (Dākṣiṇātyas), the Kaiśikī style occurs due to the abundance of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra). Among those in the West, including the Āvantyas, the Sātvatī style exists because of the predominance of righteousness (dharma). But among the Easterners...

The *bhāratī* and *ārabhaṭī* styles of dramatic composition are characterized primarily by the grandiosity of speech and the ostentation of words. However, in the *uttarabhūmi*, even when there is a combination of *bhāratī* and *ārabhaṭī*, they are capable of admitting an entry of a trace of *kaiśikī*, as it will be stated: "But the performance has little purpose for song" (13.51). By the word "purpose" (*artha*), its objective is meant.

Dancing, instrumental music, and so forth—thus, the fourfold division of the world that exists based on the similarity of these various mental states is precisely what has been described here. Now, why was this summary adopted? He says: because the world...

Since it is endowed with various languages, customs, and so forth, who could possibly speak of it word by word, or be able to learn, practice, employ, or even observe it? Furthermore, since this drama has the movement of the mind as its primary element, it is only right to speak of that alone. Clarifying this very point, he says "the Bhāratī [speech]," and so forth.

In performance, regarding the movements of speech and limbs, those regions which are established and well-known in the world as being based upon these [styles] are to be known as the Dakṣiṇāpathas. || 39 ||
The Kosalas and Tosalas, the Kaliṅgas, Yavanas, and Khasas;
the Dramiḍas, Āndhras, Mahārāṣṭras, and those born in Vaiṇṇa and Vānavāsa. || 40 ||
One should always employ those who are from the southern regions located between the Southern Ocean and the Vindhya mountains.
The people of Avanti, those of Vidiśā, the Saurāṣṭras, as well as the Mālavas, the Saindhavas, the Sauvīras, the Ānartas, and the Sārvudeyakas; || 42 ||
The Dāśārṇas, the Tripuras, and likewise the Mārtikāvatas—
these always maintain the activity of the Avanti region.
Such is the meaning. By the word "ca" (and), the word "tataḥ" (from that) is drawn forward. Relying upon those four examples well-known in the world, Brahmā produced this formulation.
This text has been explained by the ancient commentators by taking these very four as illustrative examples, and therein they have stated a refutation based on their dissimilarity.
For since the activities of the fourfold [senses] and so forth possess causes,
this illustration— by being cited in commentaries merely as "the elephant's bath"— has been rendered neither complete nor coherent; let this matter rest for now.
The term *kaiśikī* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which *kaiśikī* [intonation] predominates.

Because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*), or even if there were coreferentiality, because there is no prior mention of the masculine gender (*bhāṣitapuṃstva*) within a common form (*sāmānāyām ākṛtau*), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur. [It means] "produced from hair" (*kaiśair nirvṛttā*). In those [cases],...

The derivation beginning with "bhavet" (it would be) is merely for the sake of etymological explanation; we shall explain this in brief in the twentieth chapter. Since the term "Dākṣiṇātyas" (Southerners) is already established by the fact that they reside in the regions between the Southern Ocean and the Vindhya mountains, the separate enumeration of those various regions is intended to indicate the intermediate areas and the mountains [between them].

(209) Relying upon the *sāttvatī* and *kaiśikī* styles of performance (*vṛtti*), the enactment [of these] should take place; it should not be otherwise, for that is how it must be performed by the practitioners.
The Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Vatsas, Uḍras, Māgadhas, Pauṇḍras, Nepālakas, as well as those of the Antargiri and Bahirgiri regions. || 45 ||
Likewise, the Plavaṅgamas, Maladas, Mallavartakas, those beginning with the Brahmottaras, the Bhārgavas, and the Mārgavas are to be known [as belonging to this lineage]. (46)
The Prāgjyotiṣas, Pulindas, Vaidehas, Tāmaliptakas,
Prāṅgas, and Prāvṛtis employ here a woman from Oḍhra and Māgadha.
Furthermore, those other eastern regions which are celebrated in the Purāṇas—in them, this Uḍhamāgadha mode of speech is indeed employed. (48)
The Pañcālas, Śūrasenas, Kāśmīras, and those from Hastināpura;
the Bāhlīkas, Śākalas, as well as the Madras and Kauśīnaras. || 49 ||

Those who dwell in the Himalayas and in the northern direction of the Gaṅgā—this is for the purpose of including regions through the exclusion of the Mlecchas of Kaccha and other such areas, according to the usage of poets;
it is the same in what follows. Regarding "the eternal and the non-eternal": this sequence of mental fluctuations is seen to be beginningless according to the distinction of regions.

The meaning is that the inherent difference [in dress] appropriate to different regions—manifesting in the form of garments and ornaments—is indicated by the phrase "mostly," which suggests that this will not be the case here due to a lack of evidence, and so forth, through dry reasoning (*śuṣkatarka*).
The word "this" refers to those from Avanti, Prāgjyotiṣa, and Kāmarūpa. By the word "ancient" (*purāṇa*), he indicates that it was not preceded by [any prior] tradition (*āgama*).
The Turuṣkas, the Āraṭṭakas, and the Darakas—
among those very regions they have taken refuge, Pāñcāla is preeminent. (50)
In the Pāñcālamadhyamā, however, the Sāttvatī and Ārabhaṭī [vṛttis] are prescribed; its performance involves little singing and is characterized by agitated movements and prowess. (51)
Their movement upon the stage is twofold:
entering by circumambulating to the right, and likewise entering by not circumambulating to the right. (52)
The Āvantī and Dākṣiṇātyā styles involve a clockwise circumambulation,
whereas the Pāñcālī and Oḍhramāgadhī styles involve an entry by the left (counter-clockwise).
In the Āvantī and Dākṣiṇātyā [styles], the northern side-door is used;
however, in the Pāñcālī, Oḍhra, and Māgadhī [styles], the southern door should be employed.

The Khaśas and others have already been included within the Madhyama [country]; however, because they are excluded from common usage (*vyavahāra*), they were not recited by name. The phrase "one who has little knowledge of the *Gītārtha*" permits the *Kaiśikī* style only in a minor degree. In that regard, the Uḍras to the south near the ocean and the Māgadhas to the north serve as the boundaries for the eastern regions.
Because it possesses both of those [qualities]—being situated between [the two regions] and being afflicted—it is called *auḍhramāgadhī*.
For this very reason, with the intention of showing that the people of *auḍhra* and *kaliṅga* subsist on both, it is enumerated among the two modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*).

Those who exist within the mountains are *antargirāḥ*; [this form arises] by applying the possessive suffix *matup* (which becomes *ra*) after the word *giri* according to the rule *gireśca senakasya*.

The form [of the ritual] is described in the *Vājasaneyi-saṃhitā*. Since there is no place for circumambulation other than to the south and north, the two movements—starting from "not one" (*naikatyāt*)—are unified and designated as a single performance.
In that regard, the Southerner enters by the northern door, circumambulates toward the western direction, then toward the southern, and from there toward the eastern.

Then one should circumambulate toward the north. Having circumambulated, one should offer self-surrender in that very direction. As it has been said: "facing south. Then, having reached the east from the north, then the south from there, and then the west, one should exit by the northern door alone. Thus...
The Pāñcālī style is the opposite of that found in the Sāttvatī and others.
Furthermore, these [styles] should be employed by performers in a unified manner.
And having also considered the assembly, as well as the place and the time, along with the purpose and the reasoning. || 55 ||
In whatever regions whatever conduct is prescribed, a knower of those [rules] should employ forms corresponding to that conduct in those places. (56)
Furthermore, these [qualities] become unified in drama and similar works;
having observed the abundance of the modes (vṛtti), one should perform each respective action accordingly. || 57 ||

Thus, her entry and exit would be through the southern gate, proceeding clockwise; that is, the entry from the south would be right next to the vessels situated within the inner enclosure. In this way, there is an "entry by the left" (apasavya).

He states another distinction with the words "become one" (*ekībhūtā*). Regarding the term "(the assembly)" (*pārṣadam*): having observed this variety—whether it be primacy based on ownership within the assembly, or that arising from place, time, purpose, the examination of a greater number of vessels, or what is appropriate [to the occasion]—there may even be a mixture [of elements].

It should be performed; thus he says, "unified," meaning they follow the principal [style]. In this way, there is utility for the transition within the performer. Showing that [utility] even regarding each individual *pravṛtti*, he says, "In which regions," and so forth; the meaning is that the *pravṛtti* is that *vṛtti* which exists in those dramatic works (*rūpaka*).

In that particular region, O leader of Kashmir, a *nāṭikā* is not appropriate because it is suited to the Southerners (*dākṣiṇātya*) primarily through the *kaiśikī* style. If there is a lack of propriety regarding the region, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is absent due to the disruption of the audience's perception caused by the exclusion of the actions characteristic of that place. Furthermore, aesthetic flavors are the very life-breath of drama, as is proficiency [in their application].
Or else, there might be a suspicion of untruth, which would indeed destroy the application [of the argument] by striking at its very root;
with this intention, he says "tadvṛttikāni" (those possessing that mode of operation).

Those dramas, such as *nāṭaka* and others, in whichever specific types of dramas the particular mode of operation described for certain regions occurs—those dramas are referred to by the word "teṣu" (in those).
The poet and the drama must be composed with the primary focus on the hero situated within that [particular] region;

for this is the basis of the performance (*prayoga*) denoted by the term *nāṭya*. Here, the word *nāṭaka* does not refer to a specific type of dramatic form (*rūpaka*), but rather to the art of drama (*nāṭya*) itself. As it is said:
(On page 212:

"In a group, when one [element] is predominant, the wise person should complete the activity by means of the remainder; likewise, when others are predominant, he should complete the activity accordingly. || 58 ||
Furthermore, the application based on drama should be understood as being of two kinds:
the delicate and the piercing, both relying on the principles of dramatic performance. (59)
That which consists of piercing limbs and movements, characterized by cutting and piercing in combat, abounding in illusions and sorcery, and joined with puppets and costumes; (60)
That which is performed by many men and few women, and likewise consists primarily of the Sāttvatī and Ārabhaṭī styles, is indeed the *āviddha* dance-drama.
The *ḍima*, the *samavakāra*, the *vyāyoga*, and likewise the *īhāmṛga*—these should be known by practitioners as having the designation "āviddha" (interlaced). (62)

Regarding the phrase "those occasions for laughter which arise from the action in a drama" (A-22): here, the *nāṭaka* elevates the spectators through aesthetic immersion (*saṃveśa*) and through discernment (*vyutpatti*), as well as the performers through their entry into that state of being. In the reading "the *nāṭaka* is made" (*kṛta*), [it means] the limbs are cast about because of this for the application of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*).
At the time of naming, others— desiring that the word *naṭa* [be treated] like *kaṭha* and so forth as a *caraṇa* (Vedic school)—

say that because the work of the *naṭas* is praiseworthy, the suffix *vuñ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.126 (*gotracaraṇācchlāghātyākāraprātipadikāt*) since it qualifies [the word] through praise and the like;
and since the gender is worldly (*laukika*), one should not suspect that this *vuñ* is exclusively [restricted to that].

"Strītva" means womanhood. "Āviddha" means intense; it refers to that in which there is the "hāra," or the seizing, of the limbs. "Āhava" is a primary battle characterized by cutting and piercing, wherein heroes challenge one another.
"Indrajāla" refers to the transformation of form and so forth, produced through illusion, mantras, and stratagems.
*Pusta* refers to that which is made from wood, clay, or similar materials, such as a figure created through manual dexterity or likeness.
Likewise, we shall explain *āviddha*—the nature of feminine actions and forms—within its own specific context. *Śaurya* is fearlessness.
This application should be performed by gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas,
as well as by those arrogant men who are endowed with heroism, valor, and strength. (63)

The drama (nāṭaka), along with the play-within-a-play (prakaraṇa), the monologue (bhāṇa), the farce (vīthī), and the act (aṅka)—these indeed possess delicate performances and are based on human characters. (64)
Now, however, in the case of an external performance, the stage may sometimes be located even in the intermediate directions, provided it is free from a viewing gallery, by the command of the patron.

Heroism, enthusiasm, strength—which is a bodily quality—and valor [are qualities] among humans.

One who adopts variety in the activities of the poet and the actor in order to bring about an excess of passion and preeminence is called a *nāṭyadharmī*.

If drama were to consist of such things as the imitation of innate dispositions and the portrayal of various men and women, it would be considered merely a worldly practice. || 72 ||

This is what he says with the words "the substratum (dharmin) is twofold. The meaning is that it has been stated and indicated. By the word "previously," he refers to the occasion of the summary and classification [beginning with] "the sentiments (rasas) and the transitory emotions (bhāvas)" (A 6–10). It characterizes the worldly phenomenon (*lokadharmin*) as "having attained the state of being an intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvabhāvopagata*), and so forth. That which is the existence of something by way of its own intrinsic nature—such as the permanent (*sthāyin*) or the transitory (*vyabhicārin*)—is what it is endowed with.
To the question "How so?", he says "pure" (*śuddham*). Because of its purity, it is not [mixed] with one's own conceptual constructions.

Because it is mixed, one should thus purify it; having purified it through worldly talk— that is, what is well-known in the world— the action, the conventional usage, or the narrative therein, that which is appropriate as a drama to be performed or enacted is "worldly dharma" (*lokadharminī*).

There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because of the metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of the property (*dharmin*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*) as non-different. Having rendered [the body] devoid of finger-gestures (*aṅgalīlā*), such as turning [the hands], and so forth—
just as in the case of falling by one's own nature, striking, making sounds, or the opportunity for dispute— one who [acts] with a banner (*patākā*) and so on...

It is endowed with the performance of extraordinary speech and action, possesses supreme essence and intense emotion, features graceful gestures and dramatic postures, and is characterized by the defining marks of the art of dance.

That which is endowed with vocal ornaments (*svarālaṅkāra*), which rests upon persons who are not in their natural state, and which is accompanied by guile; and that which, through the diversity of woman and man, involves the woman as the one to be acted upon (*prayojyā*) while the woman alone is the agent (*prayoktrī*), whereas in the case of the man, the man himself is the agent— such unpracticed behavior is called "worldly conduct" (*lokadharmin*).
Because of the designation of those properties (*dharma*), or because poetry is of the nature of a composite whole, the mind is the substratum (*dharmin*) whose parts are constituted by those two.
This is what is meant: when the poet describes merely the facts as they occurred, and the actor [performs them]...

He employs [these], but he does not introduce the variety of coloring created by his own intellect; at that time, to that extent, that portion of poetry and that portion of performance are based on worldly conventions (*lokadharma*), and therein the substratum (*dharmin*) exists.

Whether in the representation of meaning (*arthābhinaya*), they take the form of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) or the form of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), as stated in the *Daśarūpaka* (10.10) and elsewhere.

He speaks of the entrances (*praveśa*) in relation to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). For the nature of poetry and drama is either conformity with the world or the employment of variety; as for what is here called "the manifestation of this state," let that matter rest.

Now, he defines *nāṭyadharmī* as "endowed with an action that transcends the literal statement. This refers to an action consisting of the imaginative construction of a plot (*itivṛtta*) that is appropriate for pleasing the audience, which goes beyond the words of historical accounts and the like. For instance, by Rājaśekhara, the banishment of Rāma was [imagined] through the fabrication of a reality involving Daśaratha and Rākṣasa; that which is endowed with such imaginative substance (*bhāvasattva*) is [the dramatic convention].

The meaning is that it remains having transcended the mental state of its own inherent nature, being joined with another mental state imagined by the poet. Just as, for example, in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*, Vasantaka transcends the mental state of his own inherently fickle jester-nature and employs a gravity and dissimulation appropriate for a minister.
Transcending the speech of natural expression, that which remains is like the refined Sanskrit of a queen;
such is poetry (*kāvyam*). Within this poetry lies the dramatic principle (*nāṭyadharma*):

having applied the characteristics of drama (*nāṭyalakṣaṇa*) to that which pertains to the actor (*naṭagata*), one performs graceful movements (*aṅgahāra*) with playfulness, characterized primarily by beauty.

It is captivating, endowed with principal dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*), and likewise joined with the application of musical notes and ornaments in the recitation; furthermore, it is that wherein the male performer does not remain in his own natural state,
but rather assumes the strength of a woman— the male actor therein not abiding in his own form.
If the drama were to be of such a nature, it would indeed be known as the "actor's duty" (nāṭyadharmī). || 74 ||

Whatever object in the world is fit for application and is employed here, whether it possesses form or is expressible in words—that is traditionally known as the dramatic element (nāṭyadharmī). || 75 ||
When a statement spoken by one nearby is not heard by another, yet what was not spoken is nevertheless heard, that is known as the dramatic convention (nāṭyadharmin). || 76 ||
Mountains, vehicles, celestial chariots, shields, armor, weapons, and banners are employed in embodied forms; that is traditionally known as the dramatic convention (nāṭyadharma).
"When one has performed one *bhūmikā* and then performs another after an interval—either due to skill or because they are identical—that is remembered as *nāṭyadharmī*. (78)
Rather, it is employed by a woman; that is the nature of an actor. By saying "it might be," he expresses a possibility and says this:

one should not say that this is merely a conventional fiction, but rather that it is indeed possible. It is useful for pleasing the virtuous and useful for the matter at hand; for even in the case of words spoken in close proximity, [the distinction remains].
In the world, it never happens that one hears what has not been heard by others;

That which is impossible there may indeed be possible for a phenomenon.

as in the *Māyāpuṣpaka*, where it says, "Then enters the Curse of Brahmā. People hear what is spoken in *janāntika* (aside) and *apavārita* (whispered), as well as what is unspoken, namely speech from the air (*ākāśabhāṣita*).

"In space and so forth" refers to the sky and similar elements. And this division of the zones (kakṣyā-vibhāga), which relies on various rules and is described as situated upon the stage-platform, shall indeed constitute the dramatic convention (nāṭyadharmin). || 83 ||

One should always employ the drama according to the dramatic conventions (*nāṭyadharmī*). That which is incomplete in form is employed by means of wood, cloth, painting, and so forth. "With graceful movements" (*lalitaiḥ*) means those set in motion by *vartanās* (movements of the limbs) supported by the four types of *karaṇas* (postures), such as the *āveṣṭita* (twisted). The term *vidhāna* has a distinct meaning here from that in verse 1.118 of the first chapter, where it was explained as referring to the definition of drama (*nāṭyalakṣaṇa*) within that very chapter. this is a collective *dvandva* compound. "Passion" (*rāga*) is the delight of the audience. This applies if it pertains to the dramatic conventions (*nāṭyadharmyā*).

"of all, it is innate. The word *hi* (for/indeed) indicates the state of being a reason. Therefore, the innate state (*sahaja-bhāva*), characterized as a worldly phenomenon (*lokadharma-lakṣaṇa*), is said to belong to everything by virtue of its status as a fixed foundation, like a wall, for the action that accords with the innate [state] within the nature of drama (*nāṭyadharmya*). It is a constituent part (*aṅga*).

The forms of progression, the characteristics of the qualities (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*), the activities of ornamentation, the ornaments such as similes (*upamā*) and so forth—[the author] concludes the meaning of the chapter with the words, "Thus is the division of the sections. here, the dramatic quality (*nāṭya-dharma*) is primary because everything else is submerged within it. These are the logical arguments (*yukti*).

Vowels (*svara*) are the *ac* letters; consonants (*vyañjana*) are the *hal* letters; and phonemes (*varṇa*) are the collections of vowels and consonants (*ajjhal*). May there be auspiciousness! [Salutation to] the lotus feet of the one whose crest is the orb of the cool-rayed moon.

This commentary on the description of the characteristics of the various floors, marked by the figures of the courtly pavilions, has been composed by one whose hair is purified by the *kiñjalka* nutmeg, and who bears the name Abhinavagupta.

Chapter Fourteen:
O best of the twice-born, that which was previously described by me as the enunciation of speech (vāgabhinaya), [is now concluded].
I shall explain its characteristics, which arise from vowels and consonants.
Effort must be exerted in speech, for this is considered the very body of drama; indeed, it is through the limbs, costume, and inner disposition that the meaning of the words is revealed.

Now begins the fourteenth chapter: We bow to that Lord, the bestower of boons, whose abode exists in two ways yet is eternally divided, who gathers all objects of the universe, and for whom the organ of the hand is the cause of worldly activity.

Following the physical (āṅgika) representation, the verbal (vācika) variety is now to be defined; this is because it serves as the vital breath that animates the drama and because it provides the essential content for the previously mentioned physical representation.
Thus, he establishes the connection between the chapters with the words "that which is the verbal representation" (yo vāgabhinayaḥ). Verbal representation is speech itself.

The verbal representation (*vācikābhinaya*). It was previously defined in its true nature in the sixth chapter, because that [chapter] primarily concerns designation (*abhidhāna*). Here, he states the reason: "That which must be performed in speech" by the poet at the time of composition and by the actor at the time of performance. Why? He says: "(This belongs to the drama)" for this indeed—
The *tanu* (body) [of drama] is so called because it serves as the foundation for the entire performance (*sakalaprayoga*),
because it supports instrumental music, song, and acting, and because it is itself of the nature of acting (*abhinaya*). This has been demonstrated.
This very point was stated by us at the very beginning of the discussion on the *upāṅgas* and *abhinaya* (Chapter 8).
As for what some assert—that words are extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) with respect to mental states (*cittavṛtti*)—that is incorrect.
For instance, regarding the claim that "rasas and so forth are not denotable by words because there is no positive concomitance (*vyatireka*)," [we reply] that all...

The absence of exclusion (*vyatirekābhāva*) with respect to words is unproven; for we have stated in the seventh chapter that the commonality of the four modes of representation (*abhinaya*) operates everywhere toward the clarity of external cognition.
Now, even in the absence of verbal expressions such as "erotic" (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth, there is still the apprehension of that [meaning].
Her cheek, pale as the stalk of a ripened reed, resembles a white lotus closing in the winter season;
her eye and her bimba-like lower lip are exhausted by the cessation of her sighing.
O slender-limbed one, your body extends the life-force of the God of Love.

And in such cases as these, this very absence of reciprocal pervasion [is the reason]. That too is incorrect; for even by this much, it is easy to state that there is another cause for that cognition, just as in the case of a scorpion and so forth. If it is argued that "the scorpion is one thing and the one born from a cow is quite another, being produced from a scorpion," then here too the same applies. For the nature of the word *śṛṅgāra* is not such that...

The cognition [of rasa] is exactly the same as that from other [sources], and it is not the case that there is no cognition of it from the word *śṛṅgāra* in the expression *śṛṅgārahāsya*; for otherwise, the verse would incur the status of being like the "cawing of a crow" (*kākavāśita*). Indeed, who can obstruct the communication of what is established and what is to be accomplished by a word functioning according to convention?

Even the name of the "probandum" (sādhya) is a source of intimidation; furthermore, regarding the fact that it must be expressed by the word "probandum" in such instances as "this [emotion] acts as love," "it laughs," or "it acts as pathos," what more need be said? This is certainly necessary, otherwise, in cases such as "having gone to Dvāravatī," [the meaning would be lost].
(On page 222) The descriptive restatements "with longing" (*sotkaṇṭhayā*) and "eagerly" (*utkaṃ*) would be entirely fruitless, because if that [state] were not touched upon,

it would be impossible to evoke its attendant moods (*anubhāva*). Furthermore, this is so because the distinction between the permanent moods (*sthāyin*) and the transitory moods (*vyabhicārin*) must be perceived.
As she departed, turning her neck with a downward glance,
resembling a lotus flower whose stalk has been twisted,
that fawn-eyed woman smeared him with both nectar and poison.
"In my heart, [her] sidelong glance is as if deeply buried" (*Mālatīmādhava* 1.32).
In such cases, even the cognition of the *anubhāva* (the indicative effect) would become difficult to attain; what then can be said of the *rasa*?

This is because words such as "curved," "turned back," "deeply buried," and so forth—which constitute the very lifeblood of the verbal expressions of the *kaṭākṣa* (sidelong glance)—are present in these actions.
Because there is an absence of actual action;
the same principle applies to such expressions as "as if dissolved," "as if reflected," or "as if painted.
Likewise: "The body of Lakṣmī, with its embrace of the neck withdrawn without haste and accompanied by a sigh, and with its arms languidly drooping..."
For several days, her body remained with eyes fixed solely in languid gazing.
When a living being, even though happy, becomes filled with longing upon seeing beautiful things or hearing sweet sounds,
it is surely because his mind remembers them from a time prior to his awakening.
Affections formed in other births remain steadfast;
even the Daughter of the Mountain, though her eyes were closed in sleep and her limbs languid with intoxication, revealed her inner state through her gestures. (Śākuntala 5.2, p. 223)
In such works as these epics— which are like reflections of the moon that rises from the ocean of the hearts of connoisseurs—

the states such as laughter, languor, longing, sleep, intoxication, arrival, desire, and so forth, which constitute the very life [of poetry], appear as if devoid of passion, because they are untouched by words and their nature is not produced by the excitants (*vibhāvas*).

It would be nothing more than a fanciful fabrication, like the play of a crooked crow. If it is argued that the very nature of established entities is expressed by words through the notions of "arising therein" and "experiencing that," and thus they possess a nature to be accomplished by that [action], [we reply] that this is because both [words] touch upon the substratum called "action" through the medium of one or the other property, according to convention.

If it is argued that the action exists for the sake of establishing [the state] because the non-contact with the second property is equal for both [the river and the bank], then what is this partiality toward one of the two properties regarding a subject (dharmin) possessing both properties? Furthermore, it is not the case that this action lacks the property of being established; otherwise, the sight of the bank would never occur.

Or else, there would have to be an understanding of a metaphorical application (*gauṇīpratipatti*) [of the word "state" (*bhāva*) to the emotion]. But even that is impossible, because the basis for such a metaphorical application—which must necessarily be brought forward by some word—is not touched upon by any word at all.
Therefore, its meaning is indeed touched upon by words such as *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and so forth, which denote established entities; it is not, however, [touched upon] otherwise.

The state of being a poet (*kavitva*) consists indeed in the composition of poetry—a continuity characterized by the grace of a well-constructed sequence—such that everyone would otherwise be a poet; it does not consist in the mere communication of mental states (*cittavṛtti*).

As for the claim that the scope [of poetry] is limited by words such as "erotic" (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth, this cannot be established except through the recollection of linguistic convention (*saṅketasmṛti*).

We know of no other intervention [between cause and effect] than this sequence characterized by temporal priority and posteriority; thus, when the convention that "this is the fruition" is grasped, why would there not be such a cognition? By this, the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is refuted.
Furthermore, even from the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and the like do not arise without being encompassed by the complete process of poetry.
"Just as these two, standing in the garden, casting glances at one another and scratching the ground with their feet, have met together upon reaching each other."
Therefore, in the case of incompleteness, the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is equal [for both]. As for those [qualities], however, they are indeed established.

Furthermore, that which was set forth by the teachers in the *Kāvyakautuka* in the verse concerning the enumeration of rasa—beginning with "ityādi"—should not be accepted as having the meaning already stated.
In this world, the scriptures consist of speech and are likewise grounded in speech;
therefore, there is nothing higher than speech, for speech is indeed the cause of everything. (3)

Vocal representation (vācikābhinaya) is to be understood as that which is produced by nouns, verbs, particles, prefixes, secondary derivatives, and compounds, and is joined with euphonic combinations (sandhi) and case-endings (vibhakti). || 4 ||

But if this is so, should "speech" (*śabda*) also be included in the *rasa-sūtra*? This would lead to the situation where one searches for a child already sitting on one's lap. For if "emotional states" (*bhāva*) were included here, what would not be already encompassed by the statement:
"which he manifests through speech, body, and being" (7-7)? And by way of repetition, [the term] "speech" (*vāk*) is indeed included right there.

[The term] *chedaḥ* [is used]. He says this by way of a collective conjunction. This very [speech] is useful, but it is the fourth means (*gopāya*), consisting of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), and is the cause of the universe.
The Blessed Goddess Bhāratī said: "They are called 'consisting of speech' because their culmination lies in speech, which is the form of the fruit.

To the question "Why?", she says: "Because here, the existence (*sattva*) of entities is established by their connection with being, their own essential nature, their purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), and so forth."

That which constitutes the nature of cognition centered upon that [object], namely the taking of an oath as its refuge, is the supreme sovereignty and autonomy of that cognition; it consists precisely in self-reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), which bestows the distinction from insentient matter.
This has been clearly explained by our supreme Guru in the *Pratyabhijñā* and other works, and by us in our commentary thereon.
And in the context of the shattering of the doctrine of duality and so forth: thus, speech alone is the illuminator and it is that very same speech which is the sustainer;

for illumination itself is, in the ultimate sense, liberation (*nirvāṇa*). As it is said: "Speech is indeed all," and "Speech alone is all the worlds," according to the Śruti. Furthermore, the nature of [the universe] as a transformation (*vivarta*) of sound and so forth has been established therein.
Therefore, you, beginning with Bhartṛhari and others, should follow this here; for speech possesses all forms, and thus even historical narrative (itihāsa) [is included].

These [distances] have indeed been stated by relying on the method of calculation. || 82 ||
One should apply the meter for all poetic meters (*chandas*) in this way by means of triplets (*trika*).
For there, eight triplets are to be known by their names as the positions and the syllables. (83)
Three syllables are to be understood as a *tri-ka*; this is conventionally established in all meters as being composed of heavy (*guru*) and light (*laghu*) syllables at all times. (84)
The syllable *bha* has a heavy (*guru*) vowel preceding it; for the syllable *ma*, there are three heavy vowels;
the syllable *ja* has a heavy vowel in the middle; and likewise, the syllable *sa* has a heavy vowel at the end. (85)

The *repha* (r) shall be light and medium; likewise, the letter *ta* is light at the end. The letter *ya*, however, is preceded by a light syllable, while the letter *na* consists of three light syllables. (86)
These eight triads should be known by name as originating from Brahmā;
furthermore, they have been [grouped] for the sake of brevity and in consideration of the measurement of the meters.

Furthermore, other lineages such as the *samā* and others, which have emerged from these, are described by their metrical characteristics (*vṛtta-lakṣaṇa*) as being both without vowels and with vowels. (88)
A single heavy syllable is to be known as "gu," and likewise, a light syllable is remembered as "la.
The fixed division of words is designated by the technical term "yati. (89)

A syllable is heavy if it is long (guru), protracted (pluta), or followed by a conjunct consonant; likewise, it is heavy if it has an anusvāra or a visarga, or if it is final. However, in some cases, even such a syllable may be light.
For these [Vedic meters], the measurement beginning with the gāyatrī is fully established; indeed, those [meters] arising from ritual application (prayoga) generally do not exist here. (91)
In the Gāyatrī, two triplets (of eight syllables each) are to be known; the Uṣṇih has one syllable more;
the Anuṣṭubh is to be known as having two more; and in the Bṛhatī, there are three triplets.
A *paṅkti* has one syllable more [than a *gāyatrī*], and a *triṣṭubh* has two syllables more.
The Jagatī consists of four triplets, and the Atijagatī follows that with one additional [syllable]. || 93 ||
The Śakvarī has two more [syllables] than that; the Atiśakvarī is known to have three more.
Likewise, the Aṣṭi has one more, and the Atyaṣṭi is said to have two more. (94)
Dhṛti is declared to consist of six trikas, with two additional syllables;
Kṛti is said to have two more, and in Prakṛti there are indeed seven trikas. (95)
Ākṛti has one more [syllable] than that, while Vikṛti likewise has two more;
in Saṃkṛti there are three more, and Abhikṛti would have eight with one added.
The *utkṛti* meter should be understood as having two more [syllables] than the *gaṇa* count; one heavy syllable is called "ga," and two heavy syllables are traditionally known as "gāu. (97)
A single short syllable is to be known as "la," and two short syllables are recorded as "lā. The other two quarters may have more than two syllables or even fewer syllables.
It is designated as *svarāṭ* by the wise, and indeed as *virāṭ*, when one foot of a verse consists of one syllable more [than the others]. (99)
If the other three feet are equal, it is proclaimed as *bhurik*; however, if one foot of that *ṛc* is deficient by a single syllable, [it is called *nyūnā*]. (100)
When three feet are equal and the other [foot] is different, that is proclaimed as *nivṛt*.
Now, the *sampad* and other [measures] of these meters will be correctly explained. || 101 ||
The foot, the pause, the deity, the station, the syllable, the letter, the vowel, the rule, and the meter—such is the rule pertaining to prosody. || 102 ||
(244) That arrangement of meters in which the syllables are neither in excess nor deficient is designated as "sampad" (perfection). || 103 ||
That point where the meaning reaches its completion is known as a *virāma* (pause).
Then, one should aggregate those [syllables] measured by the standard of prosody, starting from one and so forth in sequence, by means of doubling and other such sums.
One should place it on top of that; this is a concise method for revealing the total number of meters.

Just as in the case of three syllables, having condensed them, there is a single number due to a single throw; so it is with twenty-six syllables—here, according to the stated sequence, there is doubling up to the maximum. Thus, the summary is: two in one syllable, four in two syllables, eight in three syllables, sixteen in four syllables, and so forth.

By this very method, one should determine the reading in the text through investigation. The meter is not fulfilled as it would be in the *uṣṇik* here, because one additional syllable is stated to be in excess; in the *anuṣṭubh*, two [syllables] are [in excess].

In that case, the seeds of the triads must be made as heavy or light syllables alone. And so, if there is one [syllable] in excess—whether it be a heavy or light syllable, or two heavy syllables, or two light syllables, or a light and a heavy syllable, or a heavy and a light syllable—that is what he means by "that which is one in excess."

He explains the verse beginning with *glāvi* with the words "not indeed excessive. The meaning is that the meters *sampad*, *svarāṭ*, *virāṭ*, *bhurik*, and *nivṛt* have their origin in the Veda alone, and not in poetry.
And a *pāda* is proclaimed to be a fourth part of the verbal root *pad*. (104)

The third libation is indeed the head, consisting of the Jāgata [meter].

"Śārdūlalīlā is used among the Easterners, and Mandākrāntā among the Southerners," and so forth. however, because they are of no utility here, we have not recorded them. As for the phrase "composed for the Blessed One" (*bhagavate kṛtaḥ*), it refers to those [verses] such as the *Grodaka* and *Toda*, which, by being sung, produce an excellence of beauty; this is a *śloka*.

The Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti; || 113 ||
The Triṣṭubh and the Jagatī—this is the first divine group; likewise the Atijagatī, the Śakvarī, and the Atiśakvarī. (114)
Aṣṭi, atyaṣṭi, as well as dhṛti, atidhṛti, the group [of meters]; and likewise kṛti, prakṛti, ākṛti, and vikṛti. (115)
Saṃkṛti, abhikṛti, utkṛti, divya, and mānuṣa—furthermore, regarding these meters, there is the application of the rules for their expansion (prastāra). || 116 ||
I shall fully explain the characteristics of both the lost and the indicated [meters],
as well as the *prastāra* specified by syllables and likewise that stated by measures.

By the word "pāṭhena" (by recitation), he explains [the term] "divya" by means of the word "iti," which has the sense of "in this manner. "First" is because, in the *stotra* and *śāstra* hymns, one predominantly observes only seven meters. The meaning of "among the gods" (*deveṣu*) in the phrase "in the praise of the gods, etc.
(*devastutyādau*) is that this group consists of the gods as the speakers. The word "group" (*gaṇa*) is the second [term], meaning "the group" in contrast to the "divine" (*divya*).
Therefore, among human speakers, this [style] generally belongs to the third type, which pertains both to divine-human beings such as Rāma and others,
and to kings. Therein, by the word "basis" (*saṃśraya*), he indicates everything including the meter and so forth, because it is a collective designation for that group.
The *prastara* is also mentioned; it means spreading out or unfolding. "Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) means the number of marks.

"Gone" (*gata*) means lost, such that it is not known by its very nature; whereas "indicated" (*uddiṣṭa*) is known by its nature but not by its number. By means of the method for knowing those, the "lost" and so forth are established as pure (*śuddha*).
When two syllables are mentioned, such as "glau," they refer to the phonemes; when two morae are mentioned, they are likewise mixed.
In the *prastāra* (metrical expansion), one should place a short (*laghu*) syllable beneath the first long (*guru*) syllable. (118)
The heavy syllables should be placed at the beginning and likewise at the end;
first, with heavy syllables, and finally with light syllables. (119)
Regarding the *vṛtta* among all meters, the procedure for the *prastāra* (metrical expansion) is as follows:
having placed a heavy syllable below [the first position], then place two [units] each, as previously described.
This method of arranging the *prastāra* (metrical expansion) is declared to consist of syllables and is to be applied constantly;
the *gaṇa* (metrical group) is specified by the number of *mātrās* and is constructed from *mātrās*.

The two mixed [syllables] are to be understood as *glau* according to the distinction of their individual characteristics; thus they are characterized by a group of morae, a heavy syllable (*guru*), and two light syllables (*laghu*). 122.

In this regard, the *prastāra* (metrical expansion) is twofold, consisting of that which pertains to syllables (*varṇagata*) and that which pertains to morae (*mātrāgata*). He illustrates these: "Two *glau*s" refers to a heavy (*guru*) and a light (*laghu*) syllable according to the rule of syllabic count; those two, being measured by the number "two," are called "morae" (*mātrika*) in the calculation of morae. Because they are not modified by anything else, they become mixed with one variety.

Therefore, he states the method for the *prastāra* as well: "Below the heavy [syllable]," and so forth. Below the very first heavy syllable, a light syllable must be placed for every [position]. Where two parts are mixed in an odd number, then it is done twice;
thus the *mātrā-prastāra* is repeatedly demonstrated. In the calculation of *mātrās*, there are those consisting of three *mātrās*, four *mātrās*, and so on.

A collection is merely a number; among these, the first is the *prastāra* (the expansion), which is to be defined separately by the count of light syllables. Here, the heavy syllable (*guru*) must be placed at the very beginning of that number. However, where two parts are mixed within an odd number, there the first [part]—

The other [syllable] is light, while the remainder is heavy; this is the same as in the *varṇaprastāra* (the expansion of syllables). However, because of the statement "only the number of *mātrās*," in the placement of multiplication, the *mātrās* must be added in the preceding case. Where there is a *varṇaprastāra*, it has indeed been illustrated even when the *mātrās* are uneven. But the second [case], he says, is "heavy" (*guru*).

The singular number is used for the plural, meaning "the heavy [syllables]. By the word "and" (*ca*), the two light syllables are included, and by the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the other three varieties consisting of four mātrās are likewise understood. (Āryāṇāṃ, p.
For the noble ones (āryās), however, a four-mora expansion (prastāra) is prescribed;
for the gītakas and so forth, likewise, a five-mora [expansion] is desired.
Placing the *vaitālīya* at the forefront, as well as those beginning with six *mātrās*, the three-syllable groups (*trikās*) should be known as being composed of light and heavy syllables. (123)
The division of the groups of morae, however, depends on heavy and light syllables.
From the last form, which has been doubled, one should subtract two from each [position] for every heavy syllable. (124)
Having doubled the count of the light syllables, one should indicate them by their total sum;
the first [meter] is to be known as having all heavy syllables, and it is designated as "sama" (even).
The *kośa* (treasury) section, however, ends with the lightest [meter] among all; the remaining sections consist of mixed [meters] throughout.
Having combined the count of the equal meters (*vṛtta*), one should apply that same number [to the others].
One should indicate the odd-numbered [gaṇas] as being less than the [total] count, and the even-numbered ones as equal.

The meaning is that there are fifteen varieties of *gaṇas* in the *prastāra*; thus, the fifth *mātrā-gaṇa* is eightfold. Likewise, the sixth is here [treated] in the same way within the *varṇavṛttas* (syllabic meters) once they have been laid out; however, in other cases...
The division of *gaṇas* is determined by *mātrās*; based on that, the status of heavy (*guru*) and light (*laghu*) syllables is established independently.
Regarding this, he states what has been indicated: "from the doubled," and so forth. All of this should be understood as applying only to *varṇavṛttas*.
Observe the distinction: having added one unit at a time, doubled it, and again twice—thus repeatedly.

Having doubled even what was already doubled, and having completed the final [calculation], one should subtract the numbers associated with the heavy syllables (guru) for the masculine [meter] (or "spread them out"). Having added together the numbers associated with the light syllables (laghu),
one should indicate the count by means of that accumulated total, specifying that "this many is this variation," as follows:

Such is the differentiation of operations for a four-syllable [meter], which occurs when the count exceeds the number of light syllables; having thus clearly multiplied both the even and the odd [syllables], [one proceeds]. (127) p. 250
One should understand the deficient signs in brief for the odd-numbered ones, having assigned the numerical sequence beginning with one to the meters. (128)
One should fill the subsequent group with the preceding one as far back as possible; having done this for all the following groups, there is the filling of the preceding ones. (129)
Having established the determination of the short syllables for all the meters by placing one [syllable] after the other in reverse order from the end, [one should proceed]. (130)
Know, moreover, the number of those with equal feet in brief.

Now, for the purpose of knowing the light syllables beginning with one, he constructs a table (pīṭha), starting with "the first is all-heavy" and so forth. The term "treasury" (kośa) refers to the group of divisions situated between the beginning and the end; that shall provide the determination by means of the number of this light syllable.
For example, regarding the four-syllable [meter] with the first two syllables being heavy: there is the all-heavy, the all-light, and those with one, two, or three light syllables;
these are briefly of four, six, and four types respectively. By mixing these numerical values, the total number is obtained as sixteen varieties for the *cara* (four-syllable) meter.

Regarding the numerical positions, he states another method: "beginning with one" (*ekādikām*). One should place "one, two, four," and so forth, above the syllables of the meter. Therein, one should perform the mixing of the subsequent [number] with the preceding one, until the total sum of the *gaṇas* is reached; and that sequence beginning with one should be mixed with one—thus it is.

The number of even meters (*samavṛtta*): one should multiply the number of light syllables in this manner by sixteen. Then, one should subtract the number sixteen from that product. By that [subtraction], for four-syllable meters, there are one hundred and twenty *ardhasamavṛtta*s; having multiplied that number as well, one should subtract it from the product.
And by that [calculation], "thousands" and "eighty hundreds" constitute uneven meters (*viṣamavṛtta*) consisting of four syllables.
Having divided the measure of half a meter (*vṛttārdha*) by half, [the counts] follow in due order. (131)
Place a light syllable there, and likewise a heavy syllable with a following 'sa' (sibilant);

One should place heavy syllables in those positions where light ones and so forth were prescribed;
such are the meters that have been described here by me, O best of the twice-born. (133)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Prescription of Meters," in the section on Vocal Representation within the *Bhāratīya Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now, regarding the statement "the measure of half the verse" (*vṛttārdhaparimāṇam*) used to describe what is lost: one should divide the number by two.

Where an odd number does not complete the division, one should add one more for the sake of completion. Thus he says, "in due order. In that regard, the Guru states: "By adding one, there is effort and heaviness; otherwise, it is light."

By means of division (*chedana*). Thus, repeatedly until the syllables are complete, according to the rule: in the case of four syllables, what is the fifth division like? First, from the division of the number five by one more than itself (*saika*), there is a long (*guru*) syllable; again, from the division of the number three by one more than itself, there is a long syllable; from the equal division of two, there is a short (*laghu*) syllable; and from the division of one by one more than itself, there is a long syllable.
By this, such is the fifth division.

Concluding this, he introduces the next chapter with the word "evam" (thus): "The poet should introduce or compose in the poetic illustration (*lakṣya*) those [figures] which are subordinate or primary according to the analyzed classification. May there be auspiciousness.
The servant named Abhinavagupta, who is the bee at the lotus-face of Pārvatī and the source of her three eyes, has composed this treatise on prosody.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, on Prosody, in the Abhinavabhāratī, a commentary on the Nāṭya-veda, composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the great devotee of Maheśvara.

I bow to that form of the eightfold Lord Śiva which consists of speech, from whom all meters originate, and without whom there would be no poetic compositions— the elixir for the ears of those born under the sacred thread.

Regarding what was stated [in verse 14.133], "one should arrange the syllables," he began to explain the classification based on their suitability for recitation with the words, "Thus, the meters... The connection is as follows: "Learn the *vṛtta*s among these meters that are suitable for application in drama. This is done by means of the rules governing heavy (*guru*) and light (*laghu*) syllables.

Those meters (*vṛtta*) in which there exists the quality of being audible (*śravyatā*) are called *śrāvya* because their meaning is intended to be heard; here, the suffix *-kta* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*). Since it was established in the preceding chapter that [the meters] beginning with the *gāyatrī* are fit for ritual application, he begins with that very point: "Now, at the beginning," while in the middle [of the meter], there is a light syllable by implication. By means of the *gāyatrī*, it is the *gāyatram*; thus, in this chapter—

In the *mālinī* metre, there shall be one [short syllable] in the sixth position and a second [long syllable] at the foot;
such a metre is well-known by the name *mālinī*.
When the foot consists of six syllables, and the second syllable is light while the remaining syllables are heavy, that is considered *mālinī*, as for example:
"By means of abundance of bathing and perfumes, and the application of garments and ornaments..."
It is evident that you are this well-known Mālinī.
Where the second and the fifth syllables are established as light, and the remaining syllables are heavy, that is named Mālatī, as follows: || 9 ||

When the second, fourth, and fifth [syllables] are short, the characteristic of *cilla* is accepted; thus, two types of textual readings are observed. Furthermore, both are recited in the manuscripts for the sake of meditation. It is well-known by this name and possesses a celebrated form.
The meaning is that it is praiseworthy.

My mind has entered into that; here is the account of what occurred in Siṃhala.

Where the fourth, second, sixth,

"That *anuṣṭubh* meter in which the last two syllables of each quarter-verse are *ma-ga-u*, and there is a pause at the end of the verse, is always called *vidyunmālā* by the wise.
When the sky was pervaded by dark clouds heavy with water and thundering with rain, [the elephant] roared.
This garland of lightning, vying with the rays of the sun, wanders through the quarters of the sky.
The fifth, seventh, and last [syllables] are long in the eight-syllable foot; this meter is to be known by those who understand prosody as *cittavilāsita*. (26)
With these marks of teeth, radiant through the power of your smile,
your face, O fair-limbed one, eclipses the full moon.
When each foot consists of nine syllables and there are three heavy syllables at the end,
that meter is known by the name Madhukarī.
(If there are six short syllables here, and the letter *a* occurs at the end of the *nidhana*,
it is the *madhukarī* by name, which has the structure of the *budhajanabṛhatī*. || 29 ||)
Beholding the forest covered with various clusters of blossoming trees and exceedingly rich in fragrance, the female honey-bee wanders about delighted. (30)
In a verse consisting of ten syllables per quarter, that which has three long syllables at the beginning and three at the end is to be known as the *paṅkti* meter called *utpalamālikā*.
If there are three heavy syllables at the beginning,

and the letter 'a' at the end of the *paṅkti* meter;

Just as— on this head of yours, which was then so lovely and enriched with lapis lazuli, crystal, and gold,

Where the second, fourth, sixth,
and eighth syllables in a ten-syllable foot are short, that is Śikhisāriṇī.
Those various parts which abide in their own nature possess their own inherent beauty: the petals have the luster of lapis lazuli, while the filaments within them are like shimmering gold.
That [meter] in which the two *rg* [feet] are situated in the first and third [quarters], and likewise both are supported by the *pāda*,
is the *Paṅktiyoga-supratiṣṭhitāṅgī*.
She was known by the name Mayūrasāriṇī. (35)
"Just as you have no union with men, nor any other sign of sensual enjoyment,

When the first, fourth, last (ninth), seventh,
and likewise the tenth syllables are long in a *traiṣṭubha* foot, that is the *dodhaka* meter.
If there are *gaṇas* of "bhau" (—uu) and "tu" (u—u), and the *yati* occurs at the third and fourth syllables, that indeed, by name, is called the *dodhaka* metre; so they say.

[the gait] with the movement of stumbling forefeet and the graceful play of limbs reeling from intoxication.

The *dodhaka* meter is a metrical form sung very slowly. (*Eṣa iti*) means:
having heard the roar which is equal to the strike of a drum.

(258) Where the first two syllables, as well as the fifth, eighth, and likewise the final (twelfth) syllable of the verse are long, and there is a long syllable in the eleventh foot, that is *moṭaka*, as for example: [40]

But when those same [syllables] are joined with light [syllables] in the *traiṣṭubha* meter, it is to be known as *upendravajrā*, provided that in this case the first syllable is exclusively light. (44)
*Upendravajra* is its point of comparison; thus, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is applied.

*Upendravajra* is compared to Indra’s bow (the rainbow); this is an *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison). By your smile, your radiance, and your delicate nature—these qualities are worthy of your beauty; yet, are you Upendravajrā? 45.
Where the first, third, last (twelfth), seventh, and likewise the ninth syllables are long, and the eleventh syllable in the foot is also long, that is the *rathoddhatā* meter. (46)

In the *atiśakkara* meter, that [verse] in which the first, sixth, tenth, and thirteenth syllables are short is to be known as *nāndīmukhī*. (93)

For example: the body licked by the nails, the lips and cheeks marked by teeth-nails,
and the head with flowers intermingled and hair disheveled and beautiful.
This gait is weary, and even this face has eyes that are agitated; oh, how praiseworthy is her conduct, so exquisitely graceful and full of amorous gestures! 100.
In the Śikhariṇī and Garuḍī meters, there are five syllables following the first [foot], then twelve followed by thirteen, and finally seventeen in the last foot. (101)
When that very *pravaralalita* consists of four [syllables] in each of its three groups, and the *lau-ga* occurs at the end of the quarter, it is called *atyaṣṭi*;
when there is a division by six, provided it is arranged according to the path—
When this [meter] occurs with such a distribution of syllables, it is indeed called *śikhariṇī*.
For example:
"Your hip shines like a sandbank on the expanse of a great river."
Likewise, his face with its two eyes is like a lotus accompanied by bees;
perceiving this and that, he—whether it be the cloud or indeed the elephant—performs a grace befitting an elephant.
O slender-limbed lady, your touch is like a shadow—delicate and not harsh;
yet, O mountain-like woman, you appear radiant with the two breasts that are like peaks.
Where there are five light syllables at the beginning, and likewise in the thirteenth, fourteenth, sixteenth, and eleventh [syllables], that is the Vṛṣabhaceṣṭita metre. (104)
If indeed, in each quarter, the syllables *ma*, *ra*, *sa*, *la*, and *ga* are arranged in sequence,
and if the pause (*yati*) occurs after six syllables and again after ten,
and if it is composed as a basis for the ease of employing the *atyaṣṭi* meter—
The Vṛṣabhalalita metre is to be known, as is the Hariṇī. || 105 ||
Just as a bull, arrogant with the pride of rutting, having heard and heard the roar of the rain-clouds, stamps the earth with the thrusts of his horns and bellows in response.
Surrounded by his own young females, he wanders fearlessly from stall to stall, and performs various graceful movements like a bull upon the grassy meadow.
Where the fourth, the tenth, the thirteenth, the fourteenth, as well as two others—the eleventh and the twelfth—are long (guru). || 107 ||
When the seventeenth foot consists of the remaining [syllables] as light, that [meter] is to be known by the name Śrīdharā. || 108 ||
If there are two *mo* and two *bha*s in the quarters, and those two *ga*s have entered [the middle], and if there is a break joined with ten [syllables] and likewise another with four;
And that [line] consisting of eight syllables, clearly defined by its phonemes, should be known by the hosts of twice-born sages as being "Śrīdharā" by name.
[One should worship her] with baths, powders, fragrant and sweet-smelling scents, perfumes, and incense.
O beloved, with other flowers fashioned upon your head, with various arrangements of garments, and with diverse jewels set in gold resting upon your limbs,
you truly shine like Śrīdhara, whose abode is the lotus.
The first, fourth, sixth, tenth, and last syllables are heavy;
this is the *vaṃśapatrapatita* meter, with pauses after the tenth and seventh syllables.
For example:
"This elephant, surrounded by its young, plays upon the slopes of the mountain peak amidst a thicket of trees and shrubs bent low with the weight of blossoms."
O beautiful one, hearing the roar of the clouds, he becomes joyful; equal to the speed of the wind, he once again performs the "falling of bamboo leaves. (112)
In a foot of seventeen syllables, the second, the last (seventeenth), the sixth, the eighth, the twelfth, as well as the fourteenth and fifteenth [syllables] are short. (113)
That [meter] in which the long syllables are many and the remaining short ones are few should be known by the name Vilambitagati. 114.
When the *jsau* and the *trika* have each occurred twice and are supported by the *pāda*, and likewise when the *yo* and *largau* are supported by their respective *nidhanas*.
When that [gait] is preceded by excessive exertion, and even a practitioner moves with a natural slowness, it is then called *nānta* by the twice-born.
Furthermore, she whose eyes roll and whose necklace is widely scattered—

With your lower garment trailing and your feet stumbling as you moved, you were weary from the slow pace; yet, my dear, it was not for the sake of my own pleasure that I made you walk with such a languid gait, rendered helpless by intoxication through my great passion and deep affection for you.
The first five, the fifteenth, the twelfth and eleventh, the fourteenth, and likewise the last two syllables are long; this is known as the Citralekhā meter when it possesses these characteristics.
For example:
with many abundant ornaments made of various jewels placed upon her limbs,
and with delightful body-pastes rich in diverse fragrances that arouse passion.
With hair adorned by abundant bathing, filled with flowers, and with various dyes for your garments—my dear, what need is there for much more? In brief, you shine here like a painted picture.
The last [syllable] and the seventeenth, the sixteenth and the fourteenth, the thirteenth and the twelfth, as well as the sixth and the eighth. || 119 ||
That [meter] in which there are three heavy syllables at the beginning of the nineteenth foot, while the remaining feet have light syllables, is indeed the Śārdūlakrīḍita. 120.
(SMAU JSAU TAU and GURU are the *prayoganityā* [fixed applications] in which the three [syllables] are situated;
p.
274) the first [meter] has a pause at the end, while the other is to be known as having four triplets [of syllables] and seven [syllables].

That state which the exceedingly steadfast always resort to, and which is ever dear to poets—that indeed should be known as *śārdūlavikrīḍita* by those skilled in meters and poetic genres. For example: (Here follows the verse in *śārdūlavikrīḍita* meter.)

Struck by hundreds of various weapons and slain by *tomara* lances, their life-breaths and weapons fallen away, their bellies, feet, arms, and faces pierced through— the enemies were utterly destroyed by those various extraordinary qualities such as fortitude, energy, and prowess.
O destroyer of enemies, your conduct in battle shines like the "tiger's play" (śārdūlavikrīḍita).

O one of auspicious mind, as long as this fierce lion of disease and old age— with its claws upraised and its mane bristling— does not violently seize you, you must, having conquered your senses, apply your mind with your whole being every day to the practice of generosity and ethical discipline, which bring about both heaven and liberation.
Death does not take away your life, which sports like a tiger among the deer of living beings.
Having first [omitted] the fourth, the sixth, the seventh, the fourteenth, as well as the fifteenth, the sixteenth, and likewise the final syllable; 124.
These [syllables] would be heavy, while the remaining ones are light;
when such is made in a quarter-verse, it should be known by the name Suvadanā.

If the feet are properly composed with the syllables *ma*, *ra*, *bha*, *na*, *ya*, *bha*, *la*, and *ga* in their respective order, and there is a pause (*viccheda*) after the seventh syllable, followed again by a pause consisting of seven syllables;
and if this [meter] possesses both *kṛti* and *śliṣṭa* syllables and words— [then it is the Vaitālīya].
Therefore, among the classes of meters, this one has been described here by the learned under the name *suvadanā*.
For example:
Her eyes are languid with grace at the corners, resembling lotus petals; her eyebrows are arched like a bow;
her cheeks and lips are lovely; her waist is slender; her teeth are even, well-aligned, dense, and glossy;
her ears hang down to her shoulders; her chin is slightly inclined; and her nose is most beautiful.
It is evident, O fair-limbed one, that you alone have been created as a woman of beautiful countenance in the world of mortals.
The fourth, as well as the sixth, the seventh, and the fourteenth;
the eighteenth, the seventeenth, and again the fifteenth. (128)
In this [meter], the syllables at the end and the penultimate position are heavy, while all others are light;
when there are twenty-one syllables in a quarter-verse, it is named *sragdharā*, as follows: || 129 ||

If the *mra*, *bhna*, *ya*, and *ya* [gaṇas] are properly arranged in triplets at the feet, and if there is a pause (*yati*) after the previously taught number of syllables and again after every seven syllables,
then that is the *vṛtta* known as *Prakṛtimanugata*, as prescribed by those who know the truth.
It should be known that the *sragdharā*, beloved by poets, is defined by its metrical pattern as follows:
[A verse] consisting of mangoes, *aśoka* trees, lotuses, *kuravaka*, *tilaka*, *karṇikāra*, *śirīṣa*, *punnāga*, *pārijāta*, *bakula*, blue water-lilies, *kiṃśuka*, and *atimukta* flowers; |||
Scattered with these various kinds of flower-fragrant seasonal clusters of blossoms,
the earth of this best of men shines today like a woman wearing a garland.
The fourth, the first, the sixth, the tenth, and likewise the twelfth, as well as the sixteenth and the eighteenth, and finally the concluding [syllable]—these are the heavy syllables. 132.
When there are twenty-two syllables in a foot and the remaining syllables are short, that should be known by the name Madraka, as follows. || 133 ||

When the *bhrau* are placed in the feet, then by the rule of succession, *triko*, and thereafter *nrau* in the arrangement of the form; and furthermore, after that, *rucirau*, and again *nagau* in the subsequent construction;
and that [verse] composed of ten and eight syllables, with a pause (*yati*) constantly applied in all four [feet]—[this is the Vasantatilakā].
Indeed, this very Madraka style has been described by wise men skilled in the application of drama:

it is characterized by leaping with one hand and foot while the second hand performs gestures; it is well-bowed, sweet with the playing of flutes and mṛdaṅga drums, and follows various diverse movements in many ways.

O fortunate one with the face of the moon, today you dance according to the Madrakā style, with graceful movements and gestures of the wise, your steps agitated by charm and filled with the sentiment of the erotic.
Furthermore, the last [fifteenth], the nineteenth, the seventh, the thirteenth, the eleventh, the seventeenth, and the fifth are the heavy syllables. (136)
And if the remaining [syllables] are light, it is known by name as the *Aśvalalita* metre, just as in the case of the *Chuva* [variant] of the *Vikṛti*. || 137 ||

If the syllable *na* is placed at the beginning of the foot and the syllable *la* is likewise placed at the end, and if *ja* and *bha* are then applied three times in succession, and the two middle feet are likewise arranged;
And if the *yati* occurs at the tenth syllable as well as at the eleventh, then this is proclaimed here by the hosts of sages of pure conduct as the *Aśvalalita*. (138)

A vast army has assembled, teeming with various horses, elephants, chariots, and infantry; it is spread wide with hundreds of arrows, spears, lances, clubs, and iron maces, and equipped with many weapons.
Frightened by the sound of weapons discharged by hundreds of enemies, the soldiers are filled with apprehension, and all directions are agitated by fear.
Having observed the horse’s graceful movement at the front of the battle, you have displayed its full excellence.
The sixth, the eighth, the eleventh, the fourteenth, the twentieth, the seventeenth, and likewise the twenty-third. (140)
These [syllables] should be light, while the remaining ones are heavy;
when there are twenty-four syllables in the quarter, it is the *meghamālā*, as for example: [141]
If, indeed, there are two triplets (triads) situated at the feet [of the verse], followed by three triplets called Kṛttikā,

and if there are likewise *rā*s (long syllables) in succession with pauses after every seven [syllables] in these three [sections], then one should know that this is another variety of Āryā, known as Pañca.
p.
278) Constantly adhering to the body, it is likewise always perceived by the wise in its conditioned state;
therefore, those learned in the treatises have designated this here as "Meghamālā," just as [the meter] Daṇḍaka is defined.

Driven by the force of the wind, possessing a fierce and deep roar, girdled by rows of cranes, resembling a mountain in its lofty form, and born from the womb of waters dark as great blue collyrium— this [cloud] approaches.
With the bow of Indra as its bright girth-band, radiant with the lightning-flash as its armor-strap,
and spreading across the expanse of the sky, the cloud-bank of the rainy season shines most intensely.
The first, the fourth, the fifth, and the sixth, as well as the ninth, the tenth, and the final syllable, should be heavy. (144)
When there are twenty-five *gaṇas* in the quarter, and the remaining syllables are light, that [meter] should be known by those who understand meters as being named *Krauñcapādī*. || 145 ||

If there are *sa* and *bha* in the first foot, and likewise *ga*, *na*, and *ja*, and if indeed four *ga*s are placed [in the remaining feet], and if a heavy syllable (*guru*) occurs at the end (*nidhana*),
and if it is further characterized by a pause (*cheda*) after five syllables at the beginning, and if indeed the pause occurs again after ten syllables— [this is the *Śārdūlavikrīḍita*].
In the arrangement of the meters, this *kroñcapada* has been composed by the hosts of gods, the hosts of ancestors, and the hosts of sages.
p. 279) For example:
He who, it is said, [destroyed] the excellent sacrifice of Dakṣa, in which the Soma had been spilled, the ladles were gone, and the pitchers were removed—

May that eternal enemy of the hosts of Daityas consume your entire host of enemies, as he once did the sacrifice— striking down the sacrificial post, casting away the *caṣāla* ornament, scattering the grass, removing the fuel, and depriving the offerings of cattle and cooked rice— with an arrow swiftly released from his bow, causing the assembly of gods and ancestors to depart.
She who has tawny eyes and reddish-brown hair,
who is fond of strife and daily harsh in her entreaties,
and whose limbs are covered with very long, thick veins.
Her body was transformed, her gait exceedingly crooked;
her thighs were long, her cheeks sunken,
and her heart was occupied by a pair of very small breasts.
A woman marked with the footprint of a curlew must be avoided by one who certainly desires unending happiness in this world. (148)
The first eight syllables should be heavy, as should the nineteenth, the twenty-first, and the twenty-fourth along with the final syllable; this is how it should be understood. (149)
These [syllables] are heavy (guru), while the remaining ones are light (laghu);
in a quarter-verse of thirty-six syllables, that is called *bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita*. (150)
In that [system] where the mothers and the sages are eternally recited in succession,
and where the three [groups] are indeed stated in order within the thirty-five and the twenty-nine; if indeed...
If, after four [syllables] and then eight,
the two final syllables *ga* and *la* are joined,
it is called *manujadayitā*, provided it rests upon the *utkṛti* meter.
Known in the world by the name *Bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita*, this meter is celebrated for its purpose of causing the mouths of poets to blossom. (151)
For example— having beheld Tilottamā, endowed with beauty, created by the gods, and possessing the graceful gait of an elephant in rut.
As he moved clockwise to see [the deity], Hari made his head turn with many faces and countless eyes;
sighing deeply, he gazed inwardly at the face of her breast.
Having likewise beheld her beautiful hips,
as well as the excellent jeweled golden bracelet placed upon her back by the Lord of the Gods, which resembled the undulating movement of a serpent; || 152 ||
(The phrase "endowed with form") refers to the *bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita* [meter], which is placed in the hand of the Blessed One.
281) That which is known by the name *daṇḍaka* consists of more syllables than the *utkṛti*.
That [group] beginning with Meghamālā consists of nine; and at the beginning are Kā, Guhā, and the three Rtrikas.
