Just as the earth— crowded with joyful people and abounding in mines of abundant crops— pays homage to you.
The Vindhya and other mountains, whose forests of *hintāla* and *tālī* palms have been lopped off by the trunks of elephants, pay homage to you;
they are now covered with pearls burst forth from oyster shells and spat out.
The oceans, filled with joyful aquatic creatures and strewn with pure [gems], pay homage to you with their wave-hands bearing fruits; the great rivers seem to proclaim your fame. (154)
O best of the twice-born, these even meters have been described by me;
now I shall further state the characteristics of the uneven and half-even meters.
Where the quarters are unequal, arising from various meters and joined together by the combination of feet, that meter is known as *viṣama* (irregular). 156.

By the phrase "arising from various meters," he states that while the definitions of meters with identical *chandas* (prosodic measures) have been composed separately for each quarter-verse (*pāda*), those that are irregular (*viṣama*) should be inferred by oneself.

In a *vṛtta* (metrical verse), two feet are even and two are uneven; likewise, in an *ardhasama-vṛtta*, [the first and third, and the second and fourth, are respectively even and uneven]. When all four feet are uneven, it is called an *viṣama-vṛtta*. || 157 ||

A *vṛtta* is called "half-equal" (*ardhasama*) when its feet consist of pairs that are either short-first or long-first, or alternatively, when they are long or short, provided those pairs are respectively even and odd. (158)
When the first quarter is established, the even [meter] is established; the uneven [meter] is that which applies to all quarters.
One should know the half-even [meter] to be that which occurs in two [quarters]; this division, however, is according to the quarters.
I have already explained the varieties of even meters by means of *chedas*;
now I shall fully describe the characteristics of uneven meters by means of triplets (*trikas*).
"In the *naidhana* [finale], it is optionally desired in either the first or the second foot; thus, in brief, is the *anuṣṭubh* [defined]. (161)

If the first quarter consists of sa, ga, and u; the second of sra, u, and two gurus (l); and the odd and even quarters consist of three triplets (trikas) [as defined by the preceding rules], that is to be known as Pathyā. 162.
For example:
"O beloved, you who hold your deities, friends, and kinsmen dear;
you who delight in giving what is wholesome—dear to me, you are my beloved. (163)

"Two are equal" refers to the first and third, as well as the second and fourth. "Two are unequal" refers to the first and second, as well as the third and fourth; this [phrase] contains an internal repetition (*vīpsā*). Regarding the word "two," it is characterized by the term "established" (*siddha*); the remainder is that it is to be characterized as "applying to all quarters" (*sārvapādika*). This also applies to the word "of two. "Cæsura" (*cheda*) means division within the quarters.
(An enumeration of the even meters: Those various divisions that have been enumerated among the even meters are now declared.
283) If there are *mra* and *ga*s in the first quarter, and *yū*, *sa*, *la*, and *ga*s in the second;
In the first quarter, there are the gaṇas rbha, la, and ga; in the third, likewise; and in the fourth, ta, sa, la, and ga. || 164 ||
For example:
"Neither conduct, nor friend, nor one who cherishes the virtues of kinsmen—you are in every way and in all respects as disagreeable as unwholesome food, O beloved. (165)
For this is the definition of the *ayuji* [meter], whereas that which is the opposite is to be known by name as *pathyā*, just as follows: || 166 ||
O river, what is the use of your anger toward Rāma?
You have no purpose for him either; you are perverse and not beneficial—by whom, O dull-witted one, have you been deluded?
Where the fourth syllable from the beginning consists of three short (laghu) syllables in an even position,
that *anuṣṭubh* should be known by the name Capalā, as follows.
For instance:
"Indeed, her most beloved does not wish to hear what has been spoken by her friend;
this fickle woman is merely describing an image of Nārada. (169)
The *vipulā* meter is to be known as occurring in the even [pādas], due to the lightness of the seventh syllable;
however, for some, the *vipulā* occurs everywhere, specifically in the seventh syllable. (170)
O beloved, whose face resembles the full moon, your breasts are firm like diamonds in their center and resemble golden jars; your hips are broad and expansive. 171.
Just as the Ganges, when the clouds arrive, floods the earth,
uprooting the trees on its banks and flowing with vast currents. || 172 ||
"O thief born of a family of extreme timidity, you have come to another's house at night like a cloud; you deserve to be bound. (173)
Thus, indeed, there are various combinations of *pathyā* meters,
formed by pairs of even and odd feet, or otherwise by the remaining three types of feet.
A trika consisting entirely of light syllables, even if it has a heavy syllable at its end, is never desired;
however, in this [meter], it is traditionally taught that a light syllable must precede the fourth syllable from the beginning. (175)
When the first quarter consists of light syllables and the last three quarters always have heavy syllables, that is called Vaktra by the wise. (176)
For example:
"O fair-browed one, your face—with its lower lip bitten by teeth, its corners of the eyes languid from staying awake, and exhausted by the enjoyment of love—is most beautiful to behold. (177)

(Regarding "ending with a guru"): That [foot] ending with a guru is entirely light; we do not accept [the feet] *na* and *trika*. Following the first syllable, and above the fourth syllable, however, there should be a preceding light syllable, and the letter *ya* should not be employed.
(Thus, this [meter] is called *sarvaviṣamā* by name; it is an *anuṣṭubh* according to the differing opinions of those who know it, as well as by its three and four syllables. 178 ||
In each quarter there are sixteen mātrās, divided into four parts; those who know the meters recognize this as the Vānavāsikā gāthā. (179)

With unsteady steps, her limbs trembling, and charming with movements faltering from passion—where will you go at the time of love-making, O fair-thighed one? Are you perhaps a courtesan? (This is the *Anavāsikā* meter), where the first and third quarters consist of the *sjau sgau* [ragaṇa, jagaṇa, guru, guru] arrangement.
In the Ketumatī [meter], the wise always state that there are ganas consisting of bha, ra, na, ga, and ga. || 181 ||
Tell me, why does this face of yours— trembling-lipped, with startled eyes, rosy cheeks, and lotus-petal eyes— possess a beauty eclipsed by anger, resembling that of Ketumatī?

In the first [pāda] of Vaktra, which has no prior [meter], there are two *na*s, a *ra*, and two *la*s; in the second, there are a *na*, a *ja*, a *ra*, and a *ja*; and the remainder is exactly as before. (183)
In the first and third quarters, the *gaṇas* are proclaimed to be *ra*, *la*, and *ga*; whereas in the second and fourth quarters of the Aparavaktra meter, they are *na*, *ja*, and *ja*. (184)
Just as the orb of the moon is obscured by clouds when its surface is veiled by the waters of a river—
O moon-faced one, why is it that today this face of yours, which is otherwise so lovely, has turned away from me?

Where the first quarter consists of na, ra, ya, and two ras (n r y r r), and likewise the other [second quarter] consists of na, ja, ja, and a ga (n j j g), that is the Puṣpitāgrā metre, provided the remainder is as before. (186)
For example: [the tree] with its beautiful branches shaken by the force of the wind, resounding with the cries from the throats of joyful cuckoos.
O fair-limbed one, behold this forest with its blossoming tops, its sounds being sung by the bees.
Sja, sla, and cāda; likewise nsa, jga, śna, jla, and ga; and again sja, sja, and ga—these three groups of three syllables are proclaimed as the [varieties] of the Udgatā meter. || 188 ||
For example:

"O fair-limbed one, this line of hair upon you shines most brilliantly; it is like a cluster of blossoms on the mango tree of Love, or like a swarm of bees emerging from the flower that has flown out from the hollow of your lotus-navel."
In the third [quarter], the ganas are remembered as *sjau*, *slau*, *ca*, *tato nsau*, *jgau*, *nau*, and *sau*;
while in the fourth, they are *sjau*, *sjau*, and *ga*. These are the ganas of Lalitā.
Just as:

"O Goddess, with your beautiful garments and lovely sprout-like hands whirling in graceful agitation, your face possessing the splendor of a full-blown lotus, you shine forth, weary from the exhaustion of amorous play. (191)
In this manner, these meters, both even and uneven,
should be employed by the wise in dramas and other poetic compositions. (192)
There are other meters as well that have been mentioned here in summary;
however, those should not be employed here, for their beauty is destroyed [in this context]. (193)
One should employ those [elements] which are prohibited here in the case of song;
however, regarding their application in connection with the *dhruvā*, I shall explain their various alternatives.
Thus, the definition of *vṛtta* has been stated by me in brief;
hereafter, I shall indeed declare the definition of the *āryā*s as well. (195)
Pathyā, Vipulā, Capalā, Mukhacapalā, and Jaghanacapalā—these five are proclaimed as the Āryās. || 196 ||
I shall now fully explain for these [vowels] the determination of their duration and quantity, as well as their characteristics, rules, and the qualities inherent in their variations. (197)
The *yati* (caesura) should be understood as a pause; a group (*gaṇa*) is traditionally held to consist of four morae (*mātrā*).
In the even feet, the second and last [syllables] are short (*yuk*), while in the odd feet, the others are remembered as being long (*apara*).
Devoid of the middle guru and endowed with four qualities, an odd number of syllables should be employed;
however, an even number may be used as desired.

If it is objected that [these meters] have lost their beauty, how then are they to be employed? He says: "Those which are prohibited here"—because song (*gīta*) is not being recited (*pāṭhyamāna*), it does not require the aesthetic quality of being audible as found in metrical verse (*vṛtta*);
rather, for the purpose of joining with the rhythm (*tāla*), the equality of the meaning must necessarily be maintained through the *mātrās*.
A restrictive rule is established therein:
the sixth [vow] indeed possesses two alternatives, while the Naidhana is fixed as one.
But when it refers to a subsequent meaning, it would be the sixth; however, in the case of a single mantra, it is simply that alone. || 200 ||
But the sixth, which consists of two short syllables, should be heavy in the middle; likewise, that which is entirely light is designated as *yati*. || 201 ||
The second and subsequent [syllables] are to be known as light; there is a pause (yati) at the seventh and fifth [syllables].
Alternatively, the pause is prescribed at the first and last [syllables], or at the fifth. (202)
That [verse] in which the *pathyā* occurs in all three feet is indeed the *pathyā*;
furthermore, the other, known as *vipulā*, should be understood by its characteristics of caesura (*yati*).
That [meter] in which the odd-numbered *gaṇas* consist entirely of heavy syllables (*guru*), while the even-numbered *gaṇas* have a heavy syllable in their middle,
is to be known as *capalā*.

The first [half] should be known to consist of thirty [mātrās], while the other consists of twenty-seven; the total aggregate of mātrās for both halves should be understood according to this division. (205)
And if these thirty [units] of his were doubled,
one should assign three other syllables according to the division of the count.
These have been briefly indicated as having the designation "light" (laghu), according to the sequence of all such syllables of the noble ones. 207.
(289) All Āryā verses are proclaimed to consist of seven and a half gaṇas;
furthermore, in the Naidhana [meter], the sixth gaṇa is fixed as one of two possible varieties. || 208 ||
Alternatively, that sixth *gaṇa* which consists of a single *mātrā* is called *paścāt*.
However, that sixth *gaṇa* which has two *vikalpas* and has a heavy syllable (*guru*) in its middle is [called *dvivikalpa*]. || 209 ||

Just as the first [meter] consists entirely of light syllables and relies on pauses at the count of seven, that second [meter] consists of two light syllables and has its pause at the seventh [syllable]. (210)
Devoid of the guru and madhya [mātrās], it should be endowed with four gaṇas; an odd-numbered gaṇa is to be employed, and that very same even-numbered gaṇa as well.
If the first and third quarters consist of twelve mātrās each, that is *pathyā*;
indeed, the other *vipulā* is said to be endowed with the characteristics previously mentioned. (212)
As for the favorable type:

she whose eyes are red and soft like lotuses, whose hair is white, long, thick, and soft, and whose hips are broad and soft while her arms, shoulders, and belly are slender—such a woman is favorable to whom? (i.e., to everyone).

The half [verse] consists of eight groups, and seven of these groups end in a long syllable (*s*). Since the sixth group of four morae (*caturmātra*) may be of two types, he describes its single variety later: "In the half [verse], when the sixth group is to be made, one short syllable (*laghu*) must be placed in its position. This means that in the middle of the [sixth group], there is a *ja* (a short syllable between two longs).

The *sarvalaghu* consists of four short syllables (*laghu*). In that case, the pause (*yati*) occurs after the second [syllable] among the shorts; immediately thereafter, the commencement of the quarter-verse (*pāda*) should be made. Furthermore, at the end, there is a pause following the first [syllable], and a pause occurs when the fifth *gaṇa* is completed.
The "odd *gaṇas*" refers to the subject matter consisting of the first, third, fifth, and seventh forms. The "even *gaṇas*" (refers to the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth).

The meaning is that the letter *ja* is not to be excluded there, as it is equal to *ca*. A division must be made within each of the two halves consisting of three *gaṇas*; that [division] is called a *pāda*. Thus he says: "The first and third *pādas* consist of twelve *mātrās*. In the first half, the three *gaṇas* constitute the first *pāda*, and in the second *pāda*, there is another set of three *gaṇas*.
The third quarter: *pathya* means "suitable for the path. (p.
290) An example of *vipulā* is as follows:
A maiden is auspicious if she possesses broad hips, face, breasts, and eyes, with copper-colored lips, hands, and feet, and long noses, cheeks, foreheads, and ears. 214.
When the second and the fourth [syllables] fall in the middle of a heavy syllable, it should be known as *capalā*, just as in both halves [of the verse]. (215)
Moving with haughty strides, speaking harshly, her body trembling with the signs of passion, she knows [the way], being full of flesh, fond of wine, and fickle in every respect. (216)
For this [meter] has its characteristic in the first half, and it is [determined] by the mouth;
however, in the second half it is *capalā*, and that is [determined] by the hips.
An example of one who is talkative in the presence of her husband:
"Though she is talkative in the presence of my noble husband, nevertheless she is not unfaithful to me;
for she is skillful in household duties and likewise suffers when I am in distress. (218)
An example of the *jaghanacapalā* meter is as follows:
"O deer-eyed one, you are fickle; O fair-thighed one, you are fickle before this face which resembles the mirror of the moon.
You are the very essence of Love, yet you were not previously captivated by my beautiful hips. (219)
If this characteristic is observed in both halves [of the verse],
it should be known by those who understand meters as *sarvataścapalā*.
The first and third feet should consist of twelve mātrās each;
the second foot should have eighteen, and the last foot fifteen. || 221 ||
Having attained the application of the expansion of the four and five types of tetrads specifically, one should demonstrate their abundance. (222)
The last [verse] consists of fifty-five syllables, and likewise the first consists of thirty; thus should the Āryā be recognized here by practitioners according to the total number of its syllables.
Furthermore, out of thirty syllables, there may be three light syllables; the remaining ones are counted as heavy. Thus one should indicate [the count] everywhere.
And for all the noble syllables, according to their sequence, and for all the meters (jāti) and prosodic feet (vṛtta), [the calculation] is preceded by the number of the subsequent one. 225.
Having performed the calculation of the metrical units (vikalpa), one should indicate the total number by summing them up;
the Āryā-gīti consists of eight gaṇas, with half of it being a single [unit]. || 226 ||

In order to demonstrate the variations of the noble ones (*āryas*), he says "the expansion thereof" (*tatprastāra*): "Having reached the application of the expansion of the fourfold groups, which are specifically of four and five types, one should demonstrate their abundance."

For those situated in odd positions, there are four types of groups of four; for those situated in even positions, there are five types. One should examine the abundance of the *prastāra* (metrical expansion) of the Āryās caused by the mutual intermingling of these specific varieties. The final [verse] should be made entirely light.
There are fifty-five syllables in the first half and twenty-nine in the second, making twenty-six [in the latter part].
O you whose mass of tawny hair is fashioned with all the digits of the circle of the most cooling-rayed one;
O you who have placed the daughter of the best of mountains upon your chest—victory, victory to you, Śiva!
In the second [foot], there are two short syllables; in the sixth position, there is a short syllable, and likewise three short syllables.

Here, for the purpose of knowing the designations of all the *mātrāvṛtta* meters, he says: "Of all these indeed. Having first performed the calculation of the varieties of options (*vikalpa*), one should perform a multiplication (*guṇasaṃhanana*) by means of the subsequent number. What [is produced] by that...
The *piṇḍa* occurs; by that one should state the number.
But in the other half, the sixth *gaṇa* is not desired to be light.
Thus, indeed, by means of various meters arising from diverse metrical feet.
Furthermore, poetic compositions should be fashioned so as to be endowed with thirty-six characteristics.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Investigation of Metres," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.

In that regard, there are five varieties for all [the feet] taken together; four varieties for the uneven [half]; six varieties for the sixth [foot]; one variety for the second half; and one variety for the eighth [foot]. Here, the multiplication of the subsequent figure by the preceding figure results in sixteen positions for the other figures, which constitutes the attainment of the total number. Among those, by means of four...

One should understand that by multiplying five by twenty, one gets two hundred; by multiplying four by that [two hundred], one gets eight hundred; and by multiplying those qualities by twenty, one gets sixteen thousand, and so forth. Thus it is said: "The noble ones should be known as nineteen hundred thousand."
In measurement, it is eight crores, twenty thousand, and [eight hundred].
"It is not light," meaning that, as in the first half, in the second half as well, the sixth *gaṇa* consists of two varieties in the *Āryāgīti*.
Concluding the subject matter of the chapter, he introduces the forthcoming topic with the words "by meters" (*vṛttaiḥ*), and so forth.

By the phrase "the forest of poetry" (kāvyavanī), he says this: just as when a palace, walls, or similar structures are to be built, the ground comes first, so too when a poem is to be composed, the rules of grammar and prosody—which serve as the foundation—are like the ground;
and by arranging the "appropriation of the field," the "resort to meters," and so forth, one constructs that which stands in place of the walls.

The application of characteristics is like the work of a painter; it involves the arrangement of the qualities of ornamentation, the designation of features such as windows and air-holes, the classification of the ten types of dramatic forms (*daśarūpaka*), the description of their utility,

the modulation of the voice such as the *kāku* (intonation) and other melodic leaps, and the nature of the performance according to the scriptural rules— thus [it is defined] by fourteen [topics], and so forth.

It is explained in six chapters; therein, two chapters will be the prescription of the definitions of meters (*vṛtta*). Even though, at the time of composing a poetic work (*rūpaka*), for one whose wisdom is fully matured—

"Nevertheless," they say, "the appearance of sequence is merely imagined through the intellect of analytical abstraction. The teacher [Upādhyāya] maintains that the sequence is simply this: the mastery of the practice appropriate for the composition, the accomplishment thereof, the realization of the meaning through performance, and the ascension into that performance; this itself is the sequence.
As they say:
"For those who desire to ascend the path already trodden by the great poets,
there is no way to the summit of the ladder of perfection without recollecting the touch of each step," and so forth.
For when there is a transgression of the proper sequence, great errors and corruptions occur for those composing dramas and similar works;
indeed, not everyone is a Vālmīki, Vyāsa, Kālidāsa, or Bhaṭṭendurāja— even among them, such things happen.

The excellence of knowledge arising from the breaking of the family [of ignorance] is produced by the proficiency of latent impressions (saṃskāra) developed through the gradual practice acquired in previous births; may there be auspiciousness!
Thus, in the fifteenth chapter, the manifestation of the hidden meaning has been performed by Abhinavagupta for the meditator upon the Supreme Lord.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Rules for Dramatic Styles," in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on the *Nāṭya-veda* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the Great Śiva-worshipper.
The Śrī Nāṭyaśāstra,
Chapter Sixteen.

Adornment, the collection of syllables, beauty, pride, the praise of virtues, encouragement, illustration, etymological explanation, the recounting of qualities, excellence, and the statement of reason [are the types of praise].
The success of false determination through similarity, the collection of words, lamentation, and desire;
as well as narration, entreaty, prohibition, and inquiry—
And there are also the appearance of examples and doubts. || 2 ||
I bow to that Śiva, accomplished by the ancient sages, by whom the manifold characteristics and ornaments of the realm of forms are made manifest.
(Now,) it has been stated that poetic compositions (*kāvyabandha*) should be endowed with thirty-six characteristics;

however, while the paths (*mārga*)—namely the qualities (*guṇa*), ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), and so forth, as well as the styles (*vṛtti*)—are well-known in poetry, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not. Furthermore, the application of the terms "characteristics," "qualities," and "ornaments" to poetry is not [universally] established in the same way as they are for a person.

[The connection] of a person [is established] due to the difference between the body and consciousness; since bracelets and the like are different from that [person] as well, [the same applies to] poetry at the time of its re-composition.
Blessings, pleasant speech, deceit, forbearance, acquisition, remorse, compliance with one's purpose, and reasoned justification.
Conciliation and lamentation are to be employed. || 3 ||
These thirty-six characteristics,
which are indeed reckoned as ornaments, have been declared by those who know them to reside within the aesthetic sentiments and meanings of poetic compositions.
But they should be applied correctly according to the specific humor (rasa). || 4 ||
Furthermore, at the time of their acquisition, or when they exist as actualities, those [qualities] are not counted [among the ornaments]; for even Daṇḍin,
by stating "they declare the ornaments to be those properties that produce the beauty of poetry," and by identifying *prasāda* and the others specifically within the midst of the qualities (*guṇas*).

It is thus indicated that [such a distinction] is impossible even regarding the division of *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras*. This is true; however, for the sake of establishing the capacity for composition and analysis, one must necessarily resort to a conceptual division, even if it is merely imaginary. Regarding that conceptualization, there are conflicting views; some say: "In this regard..."

The qualities (guṇas) reside first in the self consisting of consciousness, and they necessarily manifest within the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) and others; thus, because they are established separately, they are called ornaments (alaṅkāras). That which is established separately and resides in the body is the definition [of an ornament], by which the beauty of the body is produced. And that is of an accomplished nature (siddharūpa).

Or it may take the form of a predicate, as in "dark-complexioned" (*śyāmā*) or "walking slowly due to intoxication. This very thing is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and it is embellished [by figures of speech]. Poetry joined with ornaments does not shine without definitions.
Due to the distinction between the action, the expressed meaning, and the object of comparison, this definition is twofold; for example: "The dark-complexioned one with large eyes..."
And [it is said], "moving like a rutting elephant.

Others, however, hold that the very sections of the narrative (itivṛttakhaṇḍala) are designated as both the "limbs of the junctures" (saṃdhy-aṅga) and the "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa). This is due to a difference in the causal basis, through the connection between what precedes and what follows, regarding the matter introduced by the seed-plot (bīja).
At the conclusion of the *nirvahaṇa* [sandhi],
on page 296,
they are designated as *sandhyaṅgas* (subdivisions of the junctures) because they serve as mutual connectors, by virtue of their utility for specific aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*).

The application of terminology regarding the limbs of style (*vṛttyaṅga*) is designated by the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) because it serves the purpose of renown and praise for the poem, just as the lines on the feet of a great man are characterized by the presence of a noose, a banner, and so forth. As it is said in that very same work:

"The characteristics themselves are the seeds, the purpose, and the fulfillment of the sequence; thus, through the logical establishment of the attainment of the fruit, these are the links of the connection.
(Some maintain that in poetry, there is either the infusion of qualities such as the "noble and calm" (*dhīrodātta*) or the stylistic treatment of the description of the subject matter.)

Thus, in this matter, according to the first view, the meaning characterized by function (vṛtti) culminates in the division of qualities and so forth residing in the principal personage who is the subject of the description within the poem; whereas, according to the second view, it consists of the entirety of that which is being described. This is the meaning defined by its function.

It is divided into three types according to the classification of poetry. However, according to the view of some: the first impulse of the poet, which consists of his creative intuition (*pratibhā*), brings forth the *guṇas* through the power of that activity; for it is only through such intuition that there arises the capacity to manifest aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the capacity to compose with qualities such as sweetness (*mādhurya*).
According to Sāmānyaka:
"The ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) are to be accomplished by a second operation, which is synonymous with 'description'—namely, the thought: 'By means of this word, I shall describe this object.'"

The third movement of the poet consists of the thought, "I shall unite these words with these meanings"; it is upon this that depend those [qualities] which reside in the body of poetry— consisting of both word and meaning— and whose very acquisition of self is dependent upon it.

Regarding that which was stated— namely, that "definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) are functional in nature, serving as refinements of word and meaning, and possessing the operation of manifesting the ten qualities such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia) to be described [later]"—
it is said therein: "This [excellence] which resides in word and meaning, which have become its body..."
"The wise know that the characteristics [of poetry] have been demonstrated by her in poetry.

Thus, even in poetry, there exists a certain smoothness (*snigdha*) of both sense and word, which, being established as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), is capable of manifesting qualities such as *śleṣa* (coalescence). Thus [it is said].
"...by means of gestures, ornaments, similes, and indicative marks.
Thus, in this view, the distinction between the characteristics of *guṇas* (excellences) and *alaṅkāras* (ornaments) arises from the different functions of the poet.
Others, however, maintain that [this applies] to dramatic compositions whose nature will be described hereafter.

One should define the *rūpaka* (drama) for the sake of establishing the poet’s own skill; first, practice must be applied to the method of composition, and its definition is initially incomplete at the head [of the work], but gradually it becomes such that the dramatic subject matter is a poetic composition [defined by its characteristics]. And by that—

This is because it consists in the application of describing what is transcendentally beautiful. For instance, there are certain types of literary compositions that primarily consist of a multitude of poetic qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), such as the one called *Meghadūta* (The Cloud Messenger) and its like; others are similar.
Some, however, say that the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are the properties of the composition itself, while [others say they are] the particular intention of the poet.

Others, however, consider it to be the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Some maintain that the definition is the application of qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) according to their specific respective places.

Others, however, have stated: "That specific type of dramatic representation which is seen in poems—naturally beautiful even without depending on ornaments and the like—and that quality which is the cause of its beauty, possessing its own characteristics, is itself the *artha* (meaning) in the form of a specific body of poetry; this is the *lakṣaṇa* (defining characteristic)."

They state that there is a division [of figures] due to the infinity of similes (*upamā*), illuminators (*dīpaka*), and metaphors (*rūpaka*). By the word "but" (*tu*), they indicate that "variety" (*citratva*) is not the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the meaning.
However, the opinion of others is as follows: just as *tantra*, *prasaṅga*, *bādha*, *atideśa*, and so forth are well-known in the Mīmāṃsā system...

The position that the definition consists of a specific exclusion of sentences, and likewise that it consists of the collection of definitions such as ornaments which exclude specific types of poetry—this view does not differ from the second position. However, among these positions, upon adopting any one of them, the qualifiers do not coherently fit together by any clear path. But this [following]...
The subject matter consists of ten aspects.

It was stated previously that "here, the meanings of poetry are the *rasas*. Furthermore, there are three etymological derivations for the term *kāvya*: that which is to be described (*varṇanīya*), that which is to be expressed through words (*śabdanīya*), and the work of the poet (*kaveḥ karma*). By this, [the treatise covers] the denoted object (*abhidheya*), the means of expression (*abhidhāna*), and the act of expression (*abhidhā*).

Furthermore, having been accepted, it persists; moreover, the operation of the word (*śabda-vyāpāra*) is threefold: the operation of the signifier (*abhidhātṛ-vyāpāra*), the operation of the signified (*pratipādya-vyāpāra*), and [the operation of the aesthetic relish]. Among these, the word’s capacity to convey a meaning capable of manifesting rasa consists merely in its own transition into the auditory organ.

Because it possesses the capacity to produce the fitness for perceiving that aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through its state of being inseparable from it, a second phoneme or word that recurs— being denotable by the term "quality" (*guṇa*)— is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) when it serves as a cause of beauty for the preceding phonemes or sounds. The same applies to the meaning (*artha*).

That which is the cause for the manifestation of rasa is a quality of the object (*arthaguṇa*); that which expresses another entity, such as the moon [expressed] by the face, is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*); and that which consists of the threefold operation of denotation (*abhidhā*) is the province of the various types of indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
For instance: "This [is] by this..."
With this procedure, with this intention, and for the purpose of generating such a cognition, the poet proceeds, thinking, "I speak by means of words";
he thus composes poetry endowed with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). In that context, *rasa* consists of the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛtti*).

The threefold function of denotation (*abhidhā*), which effects a variety of meanings by indicating various factors of aesthetic emotion (*vibhāva*) appropriate to each rasa, is expressed by the term "indication" (*lakṣaṇa*). This is their general definition. And just as stoutness is an indication (*lakṣaṇa*) of the breasts but a bad sign (*kulakṣaṇa*) for the waist, so too is something being denoted [in this manner].

By means of a certain form appropriate to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), such as the form of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, it indicates that very sequence of objects through indication (*lakṣaṇā*); however, in other cases, it possesses its own specific characteristic. Therefore, all figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) and poetic qualities (*guṇa*) are distinct from that collection. Likewise, even its own primary meaning (*svārtha*) sometimes consists of the mere object (*artha*).

In some cases, the ornament resides in the meaning; in others, in the word; and in yet others, the meaning itself—though devoid of any formal process of ornamentation—is inherently beautiful. Thus, the function [of poetry] pertains to these three types [of expression]. Through these means, there occurs the enhancement of words by way of the denotative function (*abhidhā*), the denoted meaning, and their respective qualities and ornaments.

Indeed, speech characterized by the function of denotation (abhidhā), which effects a manifold synthesis of meanings through words, of words through meanings, and likewise through other meanings, is precisely that which is called indication (lakṣaṇā), as it mounts the primary burden of leading toward nirvāṇa.

Therefore, as it was previously stated that "compositions of poetry (kāvyabandha) should be made endowed with the thirty-six characteristics," the intended meaning is that the characteristics themselves are primary, while the qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṅkāras) are secondary, being incidental to them.
We shall clarify this in the explanation of the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).

Therein, in order to state those characteristics, he first speaks in four verses beginning with "ornament" (*vibhūṣaṇa*) and ending with "according to the sentiment" (*yathārasam tu*). These are the emotional states (*bhāva*), namely the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*), as they correspond to each respective sentiment.

Among those [meanings], that meaning which consists in the transformation of the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) into rasa— those objects such as gardens and so forth, having reached another purpose by being transferred to the function of denotation (*abhidhā*), attain the state of being the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so on for that specific rasa; these are they.
"Characteristics" refers to the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). For this very reason, it has been stated that their proper application in poetry constitutes their scope.
Bhaṭṭanāyaka also, having learned those very [characteristics], [described] that which is dominated by the function of denotation (*abhidhāvyāpāra*).
It has been stated that "poetry" (kāvyam) is so called by relying on the predominance of the word; therein they recognize the *śāstra* as distinct.
But when it is joined with the reality of the meaning, they call these two an *ākhyāna*.
"When both [word and meaning] possess the status of qualities and the function is predominant, there is what is called 'poetic speech' (kāvyagīḥ). Thus [it was said]. Bhāmaha also stated:
"This very speech of the speaker is entirely such that by means of it the meaning is brought forth," and so on (2.75).

And in the ultimate sense, activity alone is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); however, that [activity] is determined by way of its object. Since it is accepted as such, the object is also a defining characteristic, as is the activity. For those who know this and are devoted to its practice, upon the immediate perception of an object consisting of such poetry, [it is realized] at once.
It appears [as follows]: there is a purpose for this [distinction] by means of inference elsewhere, intuition, and self-awareness.
For indeed, the activity of one well-trained in skill shines forth in the vision of that poetry.
And the phrase "thirty-six" is intended to exclude anything else.

Because other [figures] existing within the hearts of poets are innumerable, this enumeration of their number is intended to show that, for the most part, the illustrative examples (*lakṣya*) are pervaded by this much, and that the poet should pay attention to this extent. Thus, according to another view, even the Sage Bharata himself has presented them differently through various names and definitions.
And because he conducts his practice accordingly, a difference is observed in the manuscripts themselves, which we shall demonstrate;
however, the order of the recited topics follows the tradition passed down through our own lineage of teachers.
That which is adorned with many ornaments and qualities,
like well-placed physical decorations, is known as "ornamentation" (bhūṣaṇa). || 5 ||
In that regard, he states "by ornaments" (*alaṅkāraiḥ*) in order to define *vibhūṣaṇa*.

*Vibhūṣaṇa* is the definition consisting of the poet’s activity of adorning [the work] with qualities and ornaments as if they were placed there after having distinguished them—having deliberated upon the distinctions of location, place, time, state, person, and so forth. It is called *bhūṣaṇa* (ornamentation).
By means of that [the word], there is also the operation upon the word and its meaning.

This is what is meant: here, by the statement "qualities and ornaments are the objects," the subjects—which have been made the content of poetry—are established as having the state of being excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, which constitute the specific objects of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

They are capable of being explained as follows: for instance, in works such as the *prahasana* (farce), where the sentiment of humor (*hāsya-rasa*) predominates, the definition and the poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) apply even when the speaker, the performer, or the listener is a dry *śrotriya* (Vedic scholar).
To illustrate this, in the *Pādatāḍitaka*, with reference to a *śrotriya* listener, even the speech of a *viṭa* (libertine) [is considered valid].

The statement regarding the *nirguṇa-puruṣa* (the person devoid of qualities) alone enhances its beauty, as in: "Do not carry it away with a mace; do not burn it with the fire from a granary. However, the employment of what is improper occurs in cases such as the *karuṇa-vipralambha* (pathos of separation), for example, in the case of a *yamaka* (rhyme/pun).
Today, scorched by the fire of separation from her beloved, she is consumed;
yet alas, she is further tormented by the destruction of the mango tree.
As for the settling [of the mind] upon the object,
it is as follows: "She is as if dissolved, as if reflected, as if painted, as if engraved within, as if carved out, and as if fashioned from adamantine cement" (from the *Mālatīmādhava*).

In this world as well, this [poetic] imagination is indeed nothing other than the supreme [source], for it is the very life-breath of the state of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) and the various stages of love (*kāma-avasthā*), since it consists in the emergence of diverse mental constructs regarding the beloved, which are illuminated by the intense immersion in extraordinary passion.
It is established that poetry endowed with sweetness (*mādhurya*) and clarity (*prasāda*) indeed enters the path of the ear;

for this [quality] is pleasing to those of delicate mental disposition and is thus the benefactor of the entire range of *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras*, being the very nature of the poet’s activity, and it is by virtue of that [activity] that—
The definition known as *vibhūṣaṇa* (ornament) also touches upon the word, its meaning, and their function;
the teacher Ānandavardhana himself has clearly delineated this very point:
"Having observed [the sentiment], it is placed within the *śṛṅgāra*, which constitutes the soul of *dhvani*."
The category of ornaments, beginning with metaphor (rūpaka) and so forth, attains its true meaning [through this].
(300) Where there is a description of various meanings through few, yet skillfully joined, syllables—
that too should be known as a collection of syllables designated by the term *lakṣaṇa*.
Having said this, [the author] proceeds in order:
"The grasping and abandoning [of elements] occur through the intentness of the desire to speak, never as a matter of primary status;
and at the proper time, they are not pursued for the sake of excessive elaboration" (*Dhvanyāloka* 2).

This has been explained by us in detail in the *Sahṛdayālokalocana*, which is a commentary on that [work], through this collection of textual passages accompanied by examples. Those who take interest in it should consult that very work. However, we have not elaborated upon it here, for people might become weary due to the excessive bulk of the text resulting from such incidental discussion.

Now, he speaks of the "peace of syllables" (akṣara-śānti) in the verse beginning with "whereby by few. By the word *akṣara*, the predominance of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā-śabda*) is intended, because in arbitrary words the very form (*svarūpa*) itself is the ground for their application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*).
Therefore, it is "variegated" precisely by being characterized as being composed of only a few syllables that are joined together and arranged in various ways, as described.

The meaning, which attains the state of being a determinative cause (*vibhāva*) and so forth appropriate for that rasa, is described in order to cause it to enter the hearts of the listeners; the poet's operation consists of the collection of syllables, because those syllables are the cause of that [description].

For instance, the syllables "māninī" (the indignant woman) lead to the realization of that very same [emotional] state in the context of separation through jealousy; "taruṇī" (the young woman) in the context of longing; and "varatanuḥ" (the beautiful-bodied one) in the context of union. Although their etymological derivation is simply "it exists" (*asti*), nevertheless, in the final analysis, words such as "māna" and the others must ultimately consist of nothing more than roots and suffixes.
Regarding the nature of chance (*yadṛcchātva*), it is the mere collection of syllables that is primary; an example of the predominance of the word "chance" is as follows:
"Out of confidence, [he placed] the head of the lord of monkeys at the feet of Akṣa, the slayer."
Having playfully placed the body of the golden deer upon his lap, with its remaining parts resting against his skin,

he sits here with his ear lent to your younger brother’s words; he gazes at the corner of your younger brother’s face with a glance from the edge of his eye, while that sharp arrow, the destroyer of the race of demons, has been drawn by him with reverence.

It was stated that this was due to the power of [Rāma] granting sovereignty preceded by the killing of Vālin, who was primarily characterized by friendliness, based on [Sugrīva’s] trust, and so forth. Furthermore, as for the one who killed Akṣa— even alone, he performed the burning of the Aśoka grove and the destruction of the Rākṣasa army.
It has been stated that he too is where the primary nature (pradhānaprakṛti) resides. By the words "on the skin" (*tvaci*), the account of the slaying of Mārīca is indicated.
By the words "the arrow" (*vāṇam*) and so forth, it is stated that his great esteem lies in that very [matter].
This refers to the adverse turn of fate regarding the domain of the Rākṣasas.
Having established the meaning through proven facts, an unproven point is then demonstrated;
where the meaning is smooth and diverse, that is designated as *śobhā* (beauty). (7)

And what need is there to mention the preeminence of that which has its own function in this context? "Well-prepared" means that even though it had been made crooked by the weight of the intense friction of many battles, it was again employed out of great respect for the field [of combat]. "In your younger brother's mouth" refers to the excellence of political strategy (*nīti*) employed as a means of sowing dissension against the enemy faction.

The opposite is as follows: "He has lent an ear"—this refers merely to his listening, but in his heart there is not even a trace of respect for him, whose splendor blazes with such intense energy. "This one"—referring to him who stands nearby with a profound and steady appearance—even though he is not [actually] present in this matter.

For this very reason, some agitation [of the mind] has been mentioned; hence it is said to be "graceful" (*salīlam*). In this regard, the beauty of the meaning exists even without the effort of constructing an ornament (*alaṅkāra*); this is precisely what is meant by the definition. Now, it might be objected: "Is it not stated that the quality of *oja* (vigour) consists merely in the meaning being intentional (*sābhiprāya*)? What then of these 'splendors' (*śobhāḥ*)?"
If it is argued that since the meaning (*artha*) is insentient (*jaḍa*), how can it possess an intention (*abhiprāya*) such that it belongs to both the speaker and the listener?
And if so, how can it be said to be a quality (*guṇa*) residing in that [meaning]?

If, on the other hand, it is said that its quality consists precisely in its capacity to imply another entity (*vastvantara-ākṣepakatva*), then that other entity which is implied—[is it the same as the original meaning?]...
Even the quality of being "suggestive" (*ākṣepakatva*), which consists in an indirect intention, arises solely through the power of the poet’s mental operation, because it is so arranged;
for such a state occurs when a literal mode of expression is inappropriate. Therefore, *prauḍhi* (boldness) exists in reality only as a property of the speaker;
let the term be applied figuratively at will—enough of this prolixity.
And because these characteristics are intermingled, the object of characterization (lakṣya) is seen [as such]; however, the examples should be understood with regard to their predominance.
Now, as for "beauty" (śobhā): "by means of established meanings," etc. For example:
The belly becomes slender through the reduction of fat, and the body becomes light and fit for exertion;
yet the minds of living beings are observed to be subject to transformation by fear and anger.
And that is the excellence of archers, if their arrows strike a moving target.
"For they say that addiction is false; how could such a diversion as this [hunting] be considered an addiction? (Śākuntala 1).

Here, by means of the first three quarters—which consist of well-known matters appearing beautiful through their very familiarity—the author has fashioned the subject matter of hunting in its entirety; thus, even though that subject matter is unfamiliar and inappropriate [in the context of a king's conduct], it becomes appropriate.

And it has been described as manifold; yet no poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) exists here [in that sense]. Rather, that which is maintained by the poet's activity through many words and logical arguments for the sake of the plot (pp. 302)—[is what constitutes the essence].
That which does not remain steady is designated as *abhimāna* (ego-conceit). || 8 ||
When virtues arising from various meanings are being proclaimed, and no faults are mentioned therein, that should be known as "Praise of Virtues" (guṇakīrtana).
The charming arrangement of meaning arises solely from the operation of word and sense;
it is for the sake of definition that this "beauty" has been described, since even an unattractive meaning becomes beautiful by means of this method.

Now, as for pride (*abhimāna*): "But [the moon] being held by many," as in my own verse: "If the rays of the cool-rayed moon are indeed masses of nectar, why do they so utterly scorch my heart? Or perhaps they are inflamed by their long association with the mass of *kālakūṭa* poison."
Do they not take away one's life-breaths? Or are they warded off by the syllables of the mantras of the most beloved’s whispered conversation?
For what else is this state but a web of torment, rendered helpless by delusion?

For here, such a connection between the meaning and its object has been made that, even when being held by logical arguments for action and joined with the results, it does not remain fixed in the heart;
or, even when being warded off, it does not turn back. This one of yours is bound.

Such an object, being extraordinary (*alaukika*), is the means (*upāya*) for that much [expression], because the poet does not in any way accept the relation of *upamāna* and *upameya*; rather, by stating what is intended by the speaker, there is the expression (*abhidhā*)—characterized as naming (*abhidhāna*)—which consists of the thought, "What indeed have I said? That too is certainly not so."

This very same thing has also been described by others under the name "similarity" (*sādṛśya*): "That which arises from the description of objects seen, heard, or experienced, which produces agitation, and is designated as 'conformity' (*sārūpya*), is called similarity. Thus it is said.
For it is heard that the moon possesses the quality of being a source of nectar (*amṛtakaratva*), yet it is also the brother of the *kālakūṭa* poison;

and the neutralization of poison by mantras is observed and personally experienced. That which arises from such delusion (*moha*) and so forth constitutes a similarity in the present context; through this worldly perception, there is an identity of circumstance, and thus a disturbance is established within the heart.
It produces [an effect]: "If the moonbeams are like nectar, then why do they affect the body in such a way?
and so forth with other examples.
Now, the praise of qualities (*guṇakīrtana*): "By the qualities being proclaimed," and so on. (For example)—
By your virtues you are Pṛthu; by your form you are Rāma, Nala, and Bharata; in this great battle you are Śatrughna, and likewise Janaka stands here.
The wise should recognize encouragement as that which is composed of clear meanings that generate enthusiasm, relies upon similes, and is embraced by well-known [examples]. (10)
Where, by the observation of even a single word, very many others that have not been explicitly mentioned also attain completion—that is known as an "exemplification" (udāharaṇa). || 11 ||
Thus, bearing the form of ancient kings through your virtuous deeds,
how could you not be Māndhātṛ, even though you are a god who has conquered the three worlds?

For in this case, various individuals such as Pṛthu, Rāma, and others—when their qualities arising from their origins are being celebrated—their inherent defects are not imagined. Thus, when it is said "you are Pṛthu," certain defects such as the milking of the earth might be understood by implication; or when it is said "you are Nala," even his addiction to gambling would be perceived.

The same applies elsewhere. For this very reason, there is no fault here regarding the primary element. When it is defined as "by means of qualities" (*guṇaiḥ*) meaning "by means of good conduct" (*sucaritaiḥ*), then there is beauty; thus, the definition is indeed called "the praise of qualities. Since it remains supported by *śleṣa* (punning), the definitions indeed embellish the figures of speech (*alaṅkāras*) as well. We shall explain that immediately hereafter. In another reading:
"In that [work] where many persons who possess an abundance of virtues are designated by their names,
that indeed should be known as 'glorification of virtues' (guṇakīrtana).
This has a clear meaning.

Now, regarding encouragement (*protsāhana*), [it is defined] by the phrase "by means of generating enthusiasm. By the expression "wherein there is the resorting to or seeking out of a comparison," it is shown that even when such a comparison is sought out, its presence [is still required]. For example, in the work of Bhaṭṭendurāja:
"O Bull of Hara, victorious is your mother alone, whose birth in this world is peerless."
In this [place] dwells even the Supreme Lord himself, together with his son, his retinue, and his inner harem.

Even *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) is included here; its distinctiveness is produced solely by the characteristic of encouragement, as in the examples "Just as Lakṣmī... and "And you are that Murāri...". This has been read elsewhere as *priyavacana* (pleasant speech).
"That speech uttered with a serene mind for the purpose of honoring those worthy of worship, in order to manifest one's joy, is called *priyokti* (affectionate speech).
Now, the example: "where even of one... as follows:
Is this a mound of earth, or is it a mountain that has been uprooted? Whose heart would it touch?
If the three worlds have been conquered by me through asceticism, what does it matter if it is done with my arm?
Etymology is said to be of two kinds: the true and the untrue. That which is preceded by established proof is true, while that which is not proven is untrue. (12)
Everything is well, or rather, you obstruct [all hope] for Rāma, who is emaciated by separation from you,
if you do not discharge that arrow whose tip was soaked in the blood from Vāli’s chest as it was marked by your teeth.

For here, when the crushing of Vāli’s chest by the iron bar-like arm of Rāvaṇa is cited as an example, once that matter has been understood through his own contemptuous attitude, [it follows that] his defeat, the seizing of that very chest for destruction,
his wandering through the four oceans, and his subsequent abandonment out of mere compassion— all this constitutes a lack of retaliation.

Furthermore, "pride" (abhimāna) is understood as "arrogance" (darpa), and so forth. There is also a distinction regarding the combination of syllables (*akṣarasaṃhati*): in that case, the substitution of one word for another word that ought to be used is seen, as when one should say *hanumataḥ*, one says *akṣasya hantuḥ*; but here, in the example from his own section, it is *tvaddanta*. Others [hold a different view].
They recite:
"Where meanings are established by skillful persons through the demonstration of a statement joined with a similar meaning— that is remembered as an example (udāharaṇa)."
Whatever statement is uttered by those who are equal [in status] and who exist at that same time, that indeed is the meaning in terms of its result.

Now, regarding *nirukta* (etymology/definition): *nirukta* is of two kinds. Accomplishment (*siddhi*) is acceptance by means of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). That which is established by that [characteristic] is true; anything other than that is untrue. An example is as follows, from my own work:
"He who, at the festival of heroes on the battlefield, somehow brought the bewildered [foe] to the path of truth..."
He is Satyārjuna, yet his name is Kṛṣṇa; thus, all such renown is indeed false.

The truthfulness of the two names applies elsewhere, whereas their lack of truthfulness applies to their own respective objects. Nor is this meaning a case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), for that occurs between two words of equal number [of meanings]. For example, in the phrase “gāvo vaḥ pāvanānām,” the word *go* is well-established through beginningless usage in both the sense of rays and in the sense of cows. In the present case, however, a convention has been established regarding one thing being something else.
In this manner, examples for both the distinct and the non-distinct [cases] of the true and the untrue should be cited. Elsewhere, the reading is as follows (p.
"The praise of qualities attributed to the inferior by means of comparison with the superior..."
That speech which is uttered for the purpose of establishing the meaning previously stated through faultless words is cited as Nirukta.

Since it was previously stated that a certain external meaning is expressed for the sake of establishing [the word], that which is called "nirukta" (etymology) because it expresses the state of being blameworthy (*avadyabhāva*) would here be nothing more than a mere verbal explanation (*nirarthaka*). For example: "Truth (*satya*) is so called because it pleases (*rañjanāt*) all beings."

Now, the description of qualities (*guṇānuvāda*): "Description of qualities" refers to a comparison based on the attribution of superior qualities to that which is limited; it is an exaggeration of those qualities. For example:
"O King, the earth has been protected by you, just as the sky is protected by Indra."

Now, is it not the case that this is merely the figure of speech known as the "object of comparison" (*upameya*)? To this it is replied: for the variety of figures of speech is indeed established by their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Those very varieties of simile (*upamā*) which have been delineated by even the learned, such as Daṇḍin and others—in those cases, whatever distinguishing element there is, such as the object of desire to express (*ācikhyāsā*), the locus (*saṃśraya*), or the determination (*nirṇaya*), that is [the basis of the distinction].
Such [a figure] is counted as a distinct ornament (*alaṅkāra*). Even if it were so counted, there would be the consequence of its falling under *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) or *saṅkara* (blending).

If you argue that it is merely a matter of meaning (*arthamātra*), then that alone constitutes the definition. For instance, when kingship is analyzed and examined, it is established in this way: [it consists of] ornaments such as crowns and qualities such as valor.
The collection of characteristics such as a broad chest and so forth constitutes both the king—the one adorned—and the quality;

likewise, poetry too is characterized by that. Therefore, it should be understood that all [features] other than the qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṅkāras) are "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa). For instance, in the first half of the verse, "There is [a mountain] in the north," the characteristic is indeed what is called a narrative (ākhyāna).

[Objection: "If that is so, then the application of the definition [of poetry] exists everywhere; what, then, is the purpose of this objection? [Reply: This is indeed pleasing to us, for all such [instances] are poetry endowed with poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*). [Objection: But in the case of 'The Vāhīka is an ox' (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), even though there is an application of metaphor (*rūpaka*), why is it not considered [poetry]?

[Reply: Because of the absence of the description of defects, the possession of excellences (*guṇa*), the presence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and so forth—if you say this, we have been led into a difficulty."
Let it be that the fault has been uprooted by you yourself;
however, elsewhere the reading is:
"By various designations of qualities employed for various purposes."
"An excess of qualities may occur here through either sweet or harsh means.
306) That which is distinguished from the highest object is also remembered as *atiśaya* (excellence). || 13 ||
The meaning is that among many things being spoken, there is the determination of the significance of one [particular thing];
whether by means of sweet songs (*guṇaiḥ*) or harsh ones, or by means of excellent things serving as points of comparison—
those qualities employed through their designations are what characterize the "falling away of qualities" (*guṇānipāta*).
Now, *atiśaya* (excessiveness)— meaning "distinguished from the latter half"— is a distinction even from the meaning already stated, as in the case of Bhaṭṭendurāja:
"Only as many words as were taught by the deceitful female messengers..."
Having very quickly committed as many offenses before her husband,
she then began to act according to the whim of the Mind-born (Kāma); such is this indescribable,
lovely manner of one whose innocence is adorned by love.

In this regard, Ātreya has stated that the object of supreme love is even more distinguished than the self; furthermore, there is an underlying intention at every step which must be discerned. Nor is this a case of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), because it is possible [for such excellence to exist].
Or rather, we shall explain immediately thereafter that this too is a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) by its very definition. However, elsewhere it is recited as follows:
"Having praised many qualities common to ordinary people, that wherein a distinction is praised should be known by the wise as *atiśaya* (excellence).
Now, [the example] with its cause is: "of many who are speaking," and so forth. Of many...

Disregarding those who speak [otherwise], and taking as one's objective the determination of a single, unique point of meaning that must be established, the statement of what is already proven through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or comparison (*upamāna*) is the "introductory statement" (*upakṣepavacana*).
It is accompanied by a reason, as in: "This is how it appears to me," for example, in the case of Bhaṭṭendurāja:
When the day has ended, some say the rays of the moon have entered the ocean, others that they have gone to see other worlds, and some declare them to have become united with fire;
yet this is false, O dear friend, for it lacks witness, as the intense heat is directly perceptible.
I believe, moreover, that the sun now dwells within the hearts of the women traveling on the road.
The statement of a proven analogy is designated as the "reason" (hetu). || 14 ||
An indirect indication (*apadeśa*), however, arises from that which is beyond the senses through imitation;
it should be understood as similarity resulting from having a common basis with the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). (15)
Where there is a determination of a thing possessing a similar meaning by means of meanings that have never occurred before;

(*"of one"* means unique or uncommon). (*"With a proven object of comparison"* refers to the root *ḍu miñ* in the sense of "casting down," which serves as the object of comparison). There is another reading elsewhere:
"That by whose power of purpose a sentence becomes a means for establishing a further meaning—concisely stated and captivating to the mind—is designated as 'the cause' (hetu).
Thus, that by which [a meaning] is properly cast or projected into the heart is "samāsa" (compression); it is expressed by way of that logical justification (upapatti).
Now, regarding conformity (sārūpya): "An indication (apadeśa) occurs with respect to something imperceptible because it arises through imitation. As in my own [verse]:
"It is perceived as having the luster of thick saffron juice made red with vermilion..."

That brilliance in the eastern quarter, which possesses a curvature and is to be licked by the pair of eyes— this very light, assuming the state of mature rays, has become a sprout from a fingernail-tip scattered upon the cheek-slab of the bride of the approaching twilight, marking the limit of her future departure.

In this context, "that which" (*yat*) refers to an imperceptible object that is not fully understood in its true nature; it is indicated through a mere imitation or concealment, being pointed out by means of a definition such as "rendered with vermilion" (*saindūrīkṛta*),
and so forth— referring to an object whose act of seeing possesses a corresponding instrument endowed with valid cognition (*sapramāṇaka*).

Similarity (*sārūpya*) is the defining characteristic [of a simile]. Even on the full moon day, a curved line—the portion of the moon—is perceived at the time of twilight because it is partially obscured by the mountain of sunrise. Nor is this a metaphor, because of the absence of an object of comparison; for it is the very object of comparison that is indicated by the first half-verse. However, in other manuscript versions...

The recitation is described according to the location, according to the time, and according to the form; whether it be perceptible or imperceptible, it is described exactly as it was seen. Thus it is said.
A perceptible object is described as if it were imperceptible, in accordance with its place, time, and form.

Now, regarding false determination (*mithyādhyavasāya*): it is that [cognition] which, by means of objects never before experienced, [grasps] another object that is non-substantial and similar to those [unreal] objects.
When there is the activity of the speaker, this is what constitutes certainty; as it has been said by me alone:
"That which is a false determination is declared to be the definition of poetry. (16)
When the name of one among many principal [deities] is proclaimed, that which effects the accomplishment of a single purpose is celebrated as "Siddhi. (17)

That which is highly praised through many words possessing a single meaning should be known as *padoccaya*; however, that whose meaning is composed of various meanings is [also called *padoccaya*]. (18)

He who seeks the fulfillment of his desires from a wicked person surely oversteps that very source of happiness; for by forcibly offering the sixth object of sense—which is devoid of its proper sphere—into a blazing fire, he would achieve his aim.
By this definition of poetry (*kāvyalakṣaṇa*), it is shown that in poetic works there necessarily occurs an abundance of inversions of worldly norms.
He shows this. Others, however, read it thus: "The alteration of investigation, as well as that of the seen and the unseen, where [it occurs] due to doubt, is distracted error."

"Vicāra" means that which is deliberated upon; its meaning is "the unseen" (adṛṣṭa). Here, "doubt" (sandeha) refers to error (bhrama), or else it refers to "misapprehension" (viparyaya), which is a state of being otherwise. For even doubt, in reality, is nothing but misapprehension, as it presents the true nature of an object in a form other than what it actually is.

Now, regarding the accomplishment (*siddhi*): "and among many principal [deities]. Among those who are well-known, there is one who is not so well-known; when his name is proclaimed, that proclamation—characterized by the inclusion of him as a means for the sake of achieving the purpose of his uniqueness—is what is intended.
It is called *siddhi* because it is the cause of accomplishment (*siddhi*). As it is said:
"O auspicious one, Bhadreśvara, the celestial river, yourself, and I—these are now the essence of the three worlds here in the realm of living beings."
Bhadreśvara is among the best of gods, the Gaṅgā is among rivers, and I am among kings who are exceedingly afflicted with suffering.

In this context, the expression "you and I" is not well-established [as a single entity]. By being included among well-established things, it establishes the proof of commonality. Now, as for the mention of the words: "by many qualities having a single object"—that is, by many [qualities] that reside in a single intended meaning.
When a thing is praised by means of those properties which have been accepted as its denotable meanings [by words], solely by way of being characterized by them—how [is this]?
Having presented one's own person through arguments based on similarity with another, that which consists of speaking with intense meaning is proclaimed as *ākranda* (lamentation). || 19 ||

A "collection of words" (*padoccaya*) is that in which there is an accumulation (*caya*), meaning an abundance or excellence (*utkarṣeṇa*), of a gathering of words whose nature is composed of various meanings and whose form has been perceived. [It describes] the essence-less cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and the three worlds from which the jewel has been stolen.
How have you resolved to make the world devoid of light, the creation of human eyes fruitless, Cupid shorn of his pride, kinsmen reduced to seeking refuge in death,
and the entire universe a withered wilderness?

For here, the purport (*tātparya*) of the words— which function as intermediate sentences that produce intermediate cognitions— is unitary, whereas their individual meanings are distinct. Regarding the word *pada*, others read it as "a quarter" (*pāda*) meaning "a part."
The meaning is exactly as stated previously.

Now, regarding *ākrandanā* (lamentation): "having presented one's own person" means that after first placing before another one's own intention by means of methods that connect it with similarity—concerning a matter that is intense and directly inexpressible—one speaks of it all around; that is, a clear articulation.
The definition known as *ākranda* (lamentation) consists primarily in the manifestation of one's own internal state. For example, from my own work:
"O traveler, why do you hasten? Behold! The night, pale as she yearns to kiss the moon, reveals before her a state of passionate longing."

Or rather, even if it is placed before those who are spoiled by the enjoyments of the city, that happiness— delightful through the enjoyment of the unrefined and charmingly natural— is not recognized.

Here, by the latter half [of the verse], the speaker expresses her own intention—which is primarily characterized by delusion and thus remains unspoken—namely, that the enjoyment of food, sleep, and so forth in the village is most delightful. Having placed both her lack of relish for that [enjoyment] and her intense self-love for him at the forefront, she reveals her deep passion through a comparison with the story of the moon. Others...
They recite:

"When things that are not perceptible are brought into contact [with cognition] by means of metaphors or similes employed with equivalent meanings, that is proclaimed as 'equal reasoning' (tulyatarka)."
By the first half [of the verse], similarity with another is stated; the meaning is that it is the making known through contact with the self-nature (ātmabhāva) which is not directly perceptible.
The manifestation of the meaning closely connected to a state of being residing in the heart,
through the telling of stories concerning others, is known as *manoratha*. (20)

Whether it is composed through questions asked or even those not asked, that which provides a definitive conclusion should be known as *ākhyāna* (narrative); this is its characteristic based on the drama (*nāṭaka*).
Now, as for *manoratha*—it refers to a state residing within the heart. For example:
"O son, you have climbed the *pāṭalī* tree, which is difficult for a naked ascetic (*nirgrantha*) to climb.
Having climbed it, you have fallen down; who will [save] you? Who will [save] this village?"

In this instance, even while ascending the tree, a certain man longing for union with a wicked and unchaste woman is awakened by the disclosure of his own intention through the mediation of an elderly, clever woman;
she does so by pointing toward something else that is currently at hand. For this very reason, *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) is also included within this very figure.

Indeed, what logic is there in the claim that "in the case of an ornament, the state of being the object to be ornamented is non-existent in both ways"? For as for the definition, it exists precisely because it is a definition.

Now, the *ākhyāna* (narrative): "Whether asked or even unasked," and so forth. It is that in which many [points] are determined following a series of questions, such as in the dialogue of speech and reply beginning with "O Lord, O proud one, release me at the braid," where the determination occurs through expressions resembling questions or by stating matters that are possible or impossible. For example: [Example omitted per instructions.]

When it was said, "This Rāma has attained supreme renown in the worlds through the quality of his prowess," [the interlocutor] wondered, "If he is so famous, why am I not aware of him? and thus explained:
"Is it because of the reversal of our own fortune that Your Majesty does not know him?"
Anticipating the question, "What is the cause for its success? it is further explained: "That which generates anger at the beginning and increases joy at the end."
Where there is further agreeable speech, that is proclaimed as *yācñā* (a request). || 22 ||
If, when actions have gone astray, something proceeds [to correct them] and is restrained by those who know the proper course of action, that is proclaimed as *pratiṣedha* (prohibition). || 23 ||
By the words "the panegyrist [praises] the fame of the realm," and so forth;
by the phrase "based on the drama," he indicates that it is characterized by being frequently observed. Others read:
"Endowed with sentences of great excellence which accomplish the meaning of the sentence."
Fame is said to arise from many things well-known to the world.
This is clear.
Now, regarding the request: "That which first generates anger," etc. By the first half-verse, the beneficial is explained.
By that, first, that thing which is harsh at present but bears good fruit in the future is described; and then, the pleasant.
From the word "again" (punaḥ), it follows that after the beneficial comes the pleasant again—thus [the teacher] instructs the one to be awakened.
A request made with the intent of awakening [the recipient] is *yācanā-yācñā*. For example, my own:
"The ground before me is thorny; the trees are mostly full of many dangers;
moreover, this sun seeks union with the lady of twilight."
Therefore, O traveler, having rested here in this dwelling, enjoy what is customary for villagers;
then in the morning, after long reflection in your mind, you shall decide whether to stay or go.
However, there is an alternative reading:
"That compliance with another which is performed through pleasant words and beneficial speech,
as well as through verbal and physical actions, is declared to be *dākṣiṇya* (courtesy)."
Now follows the prohibition: "in the case of contrary effects. As in Amaruka’s [verse]:
312) "Where, by means of words arising from outward form, one [conceals] oneself or another..."

Here, the engagement in an adverse action is expressed by the third quarter; the heroine’s knowledge of the matter is stated by the first half-verse, yet her prevention [of that action] is declared by the fourth quarter. Others, however, recite:

Thus, regarding the sentence, the sentence-meaning is a negation; and since a river-flood is observed to be indicative of approaching rain, the negation is effected by means of the expression of something similar.

Here, by means of *ākāra*—which indicates intention through such devices as intonation (*kāku*)—words are brought forth, their power being manifested.
The meaning is "sentences. Others read the first quarter-verse as "where it is endowed with bhāva and rasa."

Deceit (*kapaṭa*) is characterized by a collection of elements that overpower and disparage, consisting of the misinterpretation or denial of a meaning stated through equivocation. In the *Mālatīmādhava*, there is Makaranda’s assumption of Mālatī’s disguise; in the *Nāgānanda*, Jīmūtavāhana’s deception by Śaṅkhacūḍa; and in the *Chalitarāma*, which was composed by an enemy, there is Sītā’s assumption of the disguises of Mantharā and Kaikeyī as employed by the Rākṣasa Lavaṇāsura.

In this context, all three types of *chala* (quibble) are accepted here due to their commonality with verbal figurative usage.

"Non-origination of what has already been attained"—this refers to faults (*doṣas*) that have [already] been attained. The phrase "of faults" means those things which, because they are seen to be logically inconsistent with origination, are non-substantial (*avastubhūta*). As in the verse beginning, "How could one remain under the sway of anger," and so forth; or as in: *na hi krodhasamudbhūtaṃ doṣaṃ kaścit prapaśyati | yatnena hanyate pūrvaṃ tasmāt krodhaṃ vivarjayet ||* For no one perceives a fault produced by anger; it is destroyed beforehand through effort.
