Here, the term "meaning of the treatise" (*śāstrārtha*) is an indicator for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "Possessing a happy conclusion" (*svanta*) means that in which there is a beautiful end, namely, certainty.
Now, regarding "reasoning" (*yukti*): it is that connection of meanings by which something is established. For example:
What indeed is this other ocean of loveliness here, wherein lotuses float together with the moon,
and wherein the temples of elephants seem to emerge?
Where others [are like] plantain stalks and lotus stems.

Here, by means of a conjunction characterized by mutual beauty and harmony— consisting of great and excellent eyes, faces, and so forth— the object, which is the unprecedented river-form, is established as being connected through a single resting point.

This is the reasoning regarding the *yojana* and so forth. If it is argued that there is a suggested (*pratīyamāna*) metaphor (*rūpaka*) here, what of it? It has been stated more than once that the very nature of the body (*śarīra*) consists of this [suggested meaning] alone. There is a reading by one school:
Where one sets aside a fault and connects a merit with the purpose,
or conversely, praises a merit despite a fault, those who know the characteristics of poetry recognize that as *kārya*.
That which wipes away an offense born of unprecedented anger through sweet speech for the sake of service is proclaimed as conciliation (sānunīti). || 38 ||
"For that meaning which was never before [established], yet is imagined from what is perceived, and which captures the heart of the world—that is called 'intention' (*abhiprāya*).
Now, as for the "purpose" (*kārya*): "wherein one removes a fault. Having removed the fault, [one establishes] the quality.

The meaning is that when one applies [a person] to what is desirable, or having set aside the praise of virtues, applies them to faults, and then employs them for one's own purpose by relying on that [fault]. The first example is: "First, the embrace of trees and creepers sheltered within oneself, then avoidance by travelers," and so forth. In the second case...
O Lord of the Universe, may you grant me prosperity; what else could be a greater service rendered by You than this? For You have fashioned me as something truly extraordinary.
Furthermore, for those traveling on long journeys, water was scattered in such a way that it reached as far as your fame has spread throughout the three worlds.
By some this has been called *gahana* (the obscure). Others, however, read it as follows:
"When another meaning is perceived upon the statement of a different matter, that which is endowed with the sweetness of expression is known as *arthāpatti* (presumption)."

For when it is said, "Indeed, a great service has been rendered by you here; and travelers have been given abundant water," the phrase "O Lord of the Universe" (viśvaprabho) is repeated for the sake of further reflection, resulting in the attainment of another meaning.
Now, as for conciliation (*anunīti*): the phrase "produced by unprecedented anger" (*apūrvakrodhajanitam*) refers to the production of an extraordinary (*sātiśaya*) and unprecedented anger.
That which is an offense—for example: "I shall say 'Be gracious,'" this is appropriate only when there is no anger. (Ratnāvalī 2.19, p.

When something is employed with words well-known for their conventional meanings but used by others with different names, and it is connected to a different sense, that should be known as *paridevana* (lamentation). || 39 ||
Others read as follows:
"The meaning of the sentence is established by many sentences that are endowed with excellence and are well-known in the world; this is proclaimed as 'established renown' (prasiddhi)."

Now, regarding lamentation (*paridevana*): "that which is expressed by the name of another due to faults. For example, in the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*, certain faults such as the exile of Rāma and so forth are attributed to the name of Daśaratha; yet, by means of those very words whose meanings are well-known, the speech employed actually refers in its ultimate sense to the connection with the Rākṣasa alone, and not [to Daśaratha].
Regarding that lamentation of Daśaratha, [the text says] "The elder of kings, having cast [himself] under the power of women... and so forth.

When other meanings expressed by different names are employed—that is, made to accord with well-known meanings—and are connected to the heart of another through their purpose (*artha*), that is "by way of purpose" (*arthena*). This refers to the connection or the act of connecting those meanings.
That lamentation is appropriate from the perspective of ultimate reality—as for example:
"Look at this riverbank before us! Here, it is said, Hara was struck impetuously on the crown of his head with the *gāṇḍīva* bow by Kirīṭin during our sport."
Having heard this wonderful tale of the Lord of Subhadrā on Mount Himavat,
he very slowly adorned his own two mighty arms.

Regarding the purpose stated here as the observation of the bank, which involves the activity of Dhanañjaya: no connection with any fault toward the King has been produced in my heart; rather, since we are equal in being human beings, is there not a deficiency in my prowess compared to Arjuna? What is the use of that ornamentation? For this [ornament] belongs to those who hold office. Thus it is said therein.
The purpose is the heightening of supreme propriety (*aucitya*). Others read as follows:

"Where one's own self is celebrated through various matters concerning the faults of others, or where someone else is mentioned even though not previously spoken of—that is called *kṣobha* (agitation)."
The faults of another consist of those various objects;

by means of those [faults] which have become the causes of another's virtues, even the unseen object—the Self—is proclaimed as being "other" through the state of being seen, or as some other thing distinct from the Self. This agitation arises from the movement of the heart. This very [state] is "attainment without being stated."
Simile, Illuminator, Metaphor, and likewise Alliteration—
these four are proclaimed as the ornaments of poetry. (40)
Whatever is compared through similarity within poetic compositions, that should be known as *upamā* (simile), which rests upon the commonality of qualities and forms. (41)
"That wherein the entire remaining meaning is understood through the context alone,
even without words, is proclaimed as *siddhi* (accomplishment). Thus,
in the composition of the *Dordaṇḍamaṇḍana*, everything— including the excellence of manly prowess, pride, and so forth— is understood from the context alone.
And since this intention belongs only to those who are superior, this definition is stated at the end because it is what is to be attained.

Thus, it has been said that whatever collection of meanings exists through the power of the poet's operation, even if it departs from its worldly nature—that alone is the definition [of poetry]. Now, the ornaments (alaṅkāras), which are like the body [of poetry], must be discussed.
He introduces that [subject] for the purpose of defining it with the words "simile" (*upamā*) and so forth. First, in poetry, the definition is the body;

among its parts, there are three elements belonging to the domain of meaning (*arthabhāga*), such as simile and the rest. Just as a beautiful woman is adorned by a necklace that exists as a distinct entity, so too is she adorned by the moon as a point of comparison (*upamāna*) or by similarity to it, through the flickering nature of the poet’s imagination.

Because it undergoes transformation, it is precisely by means of something already established as distinct that the face and other features of the woman under description are beautified; thus, that [transformation] itself is the ornament (*alaṅkāra*). And its existence is threefold: through the complete and manifest relationship of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*). And where [this occurs] among the letters...

In the figure of speech known as *saṃnidhi* (conjunction), the object of comparison (*upamāna*), the object compared (*upameya*), the indicator of that relationship, and the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) are sometimes unified by means of an implicit [comparison]; in such cases, the designation "metaphor" (*rūpaka*) is applied.
For the principle holds that a word employed in its primary sense (*padārthe*) implies its meaning through the function of "as if" (*iva*). However, in some instances...
The understanding of the simile arises from the force of the state of simultaneous occurrence, as in the *dīpaka* figure;
and this is merely an illustration of other varieties of its manifoldness.

The opinion of the Upādhyāya, however, is as follows: the variety of figures of speech arises from the power of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). For instance: through connection with the characteristic named "reiteration of qualities" (*guṇānuvāda*), there is the figure "Praise-Comparison" (*praśaṃsopamā*);
through that named "Excellence" (*atiśaya*), there is "Hyperbole" (*atiśayokti*); and through that called "Desire" (*manoratha*), there is "Indirect Praise" (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*).
Through a false determination, there is *apahnuti* (concealment); through a similarity in action, there is *tulyayogitā* (parallelism). In this manner, other figures may be inferred.

Furthermore, due to the mutual variation among the definitions [of these figures], their diverse manifestations are infinite; for instance, *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis) arises from the conjunction of *pratiṣedha* (negation) and *manoratha* (desire). And so too is the expansion of *upamā* (simile).
That "every [figure] is an ornament" is indeed accepted by the learned.
322) That [ornament] should be employed with one [word] for one [meaning], or again, with many [words] for one [meaning].
Likewise, one [should perform it] for many, and many [should perform it] for many. || 42 ||

That [simile] which occurs when a single [quality] rests upon a single [subject], such as "Your face is equal to the moon," and which shines like the stars together with the moon, would be the *śaśāṅkavat*. (43)
That [simile] which has a single subject and multiple objects is proclaimed as the "Equal Purpose" (tulyārtha), such as that which occurs in the case of hawks, peacocks, and vultures. (44)
That [simile] based on drama (nāṭaka) occurs when one [subject] is compared with many;
it is to be known as occurring when many [subjects] are compared with many, such as "elephants like clouds. (45)

Therein, he defines *upamā* (simile) with the words "whatever [is]... By the phrase "while poetic compositions—meaning poetic definitions—exist," it is shown that [the statement] "like a cow is a gavaya" is not this ornament (*alaṅkāra*). For "composition" (*bandha*), "weaving" (*gumpha*), "eloquence" (*phaṇiti*), "indirect speech" (*vakrokti*), and "the activity of a poet" (*kavivyāpāra*) are indeed synonyms. Furthermore, a definition is not useless even if it is devoid of an ornament.
Furthermore, a vast number of illustrative paths have been shown here.

Indeed, there is no poetry whatsoever that is devoid of *guṇas* (poetic excellences), as the Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) serves as an example; for it is precisely to demonstrate their non-rejectability that clarity (*prasāda*) and the other qualities are treated by means of the terminology of *guṇas*.

For without that [suggestion], there is an absence of the nature of poetry (*kāvyatva*). However, the "beautiful substratum" (*sundarāspada*) is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the body [of poetry]; it is to demonstrate that poetry indeed exists even without similes (*upamā*) and the like, that the term "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) is used for similes and so forth, but not in the same explicit sense as it is used in common worldly usage.

There is a separate establishment [of the definition]. For some say that all *alaṅkāras* (ornaments) are properties (*dharmas*) that bring about the beauty of poetry by means of a staff (*daṇḍin*). By the word "whatever" (*yatkiṃcit*), the purpose of the action (*kriyārtha*) is connected, not the object (*karman*). Since the act of "viewing in proximity" (*upa-samīpe prekṣaṇa*) can also occur due to other causes, he says "by way of similarity" (*sādṛśyena*). It is compared (*upamīyate*).

Thus, when the object of comparison (*upameya*) has been stated by this [word], that which "brings about" (*ākriyate*)— that is, illuminates (*dyotyate*)— the common property (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*), namely the quality (*guṇaḥ*) or the relation (*saṃbandhaḥ*), by means of similarity (*sādṛśyena*),
is the word "quality-bringer" (*guṇākṛtiḥ*), such as *iva* and so forth; and that [simile] in which such a word is employed is [defined as *guṇākṛti*].
Praise, censure, and that which is imagined as similar,
as well as something slightly similar— simile (upamā) is thus to be known as fivefold. (46)
An example of praise:
"Upon seeing that large-eyed woman, the lord of men rejoiced,
as if she were the very embodiment of the perfection achieved by the sages through arduous effort."
As for censure:
She embraced him, who was devoid of all virtues and possessed a harsh complexion, like a creeper in the forest embracing a thorny tree scorched by a forest fire. (48)
An example of the imaginary (kalpita) [metaphor] is as follows:
"Exuding the water of their ichor, moving with playful slowness, the elephants shine like moving mountains. (49)
An example of similarity is as follows:
"Whatever deed has been done by you today, acting in accordance with another's will, that shall befit you alone, for it is the work of a human being. (50)

[It is] the locus of human effort (*kṛti*). Here, he demonstrates the application of the definitions to these [examples] in sequence with the words "among them, the application of the definition is the same" (*teṣu lakṣaṇayojanaṃ tulyaṃ te*), and so forth.

Having thus stated the divisions of that [simile] according to the difference in number between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), [he proceeds] by means of the difference in their bodily forms (*śarīra*).

He states the varieties of the body [of simile] with the words "and praise" (*praśaṃsā*) and so forth. Because the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is praiseworthy, it is called "praise-simile" (*praśaṃsopamā*). This applies everywhere in the same way.
Mobile mountains are conceived as the intended standards of comparison because there is no other [standard] with which they could be compared.
Thus, in this case, it is imagined by means of similarity (*sādṛśya*). Others read "asādṛśī" (dissimilarity), and they explain it as follows: "slightly similar," for example— [p. 324] —just as:
"With a face like the full moon, eyes like the petals of a blue lotus, and the gait of an elephant in rut—this friend of mine has arrived. (51)
These varieties of simile should be understood by the wise in brief;
those remaining which have not been mentioned by means of the definitions are to be grasped from the world and from poetry. (52)
That which illuminates words having various distinct meanings, when they are joined together within a single sentence, is called *dīpaka* (the Illuminator) here. 53.
"O Brahmins, that which is pervasive, sweet, and adorned with all [excellent] qualities in poetry or drama is known as the *dīpaka*. (54)

Here, the object of comparison (*upameya*) is expressed; thus its etymological derivation is: "that which is seen as if equal" (*samāna iva dṛśyamānaḥ*), and so one perceives oneself as it were. Where the object of comparison itself functions as the standard of comparison, this is the "similar" (*sadṛśī*);
such a standard of comparison becomes "somewhat similar" (*kiṃcitsadṛśam*). Where the indicator of similarity is manifest—

There is no such category, nor is there a merging of two entities in their entirety as in a metaphor; therefore, it is said that [the simile] is "partially similar" (*kiñcitsadṛśī*) because its suggested meaning is equal on both sides. He illustrates this with the verse beginning *saṃpūrṇa*. Through the force of the compound rule stating that the seventh case-ending is used when the first member is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the status of being the standard of comparison is understood therein. In that regard:

Here, there is an elision of the final member of the compound because it is taught as being conditioned by the co-occurrence [of the suffix], just like the elision of *sa* when the suffix *kyaṅ* follows.

Thus, there is an elision of the final member in the expression "her gait is like that of an elephant in rut. This very phenomenon is seen in both common usage and in poetry; these varieties should be understood through their definitions so that they may be adopted by oneself.

[The examples] are possible. Regarding the statement "those not mentioned here are to be taken from common usage and from poetry," others say this is redundant because [the category of] "the rest" was already mentioned.
Now, concerning the *dīpaka* (illuminator): "of various subjects and meanings. Those which are various...

Those whose nature consists of other words, sentences, and terms, which serve as the substrata for those topics under discussion, and whose meaning is such that they possess the status of being meaningful—[of such things] there is a mutual expectancy.
Just as lakes are never empty of swans, trees of flowers, lotuses of intoxicated bees,
and garden groves of social gatherings, so too were they always made non-empty in that place.
That form which is fashioned by one's own imagination, possessing corresponding parts and characteristics,

endowed with some degree of similarity— that indeed is *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification). That which, through the coloring of various substances and so forth, rests upon qualities that serve as the basis for comparison [is another kind].
That which is joined with the description of form is known as *rūpaka* (metaphor). || 57 ||
For example:
those women with lotus-faces, possessing the luster of white water-lilies, and with eyes as beautiful as blooming blue lotuses;
The women at the ponds shone as they conversed with one another here, while flocks of swans warbled.

Regarding the term *kṣāṇām* (of those): that which, through its correct excellence, serves as an illuminator (*dīpaka*)—fulfilling the desire for action, quality, genus, and so forth—is called *dīpaka*. Since it performs such a function by means of a single intermediate sentence while remaining unconnected [to others], it is so designated because its nature is like that of a lamp; this is the meaning.

Now, regarding *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification): "constructed by one's own conceptualization. That form of the face, consisting of the moon, which is constructed by one's own conceptualization, is what identifies (*rūpayati*) the other; thus it is *rūpaka*. It has two divisions: that which is joined with all parts being equalized through the assumption of another form, or that which is identified as possessing some degree of similarity. Here too—

Some others argue that [the definition] is applicable where there exists a substance (*dravya*) or the like that is well-known to be manifested in one part (*ekadeśavivartin*), being figuratively represented as another form due to a similarity of form (*rūpasādṛśya*). In this context, the reading *yaḥ* (who/which) is appropriate; for by that [reading], the status of a compound simile (*samāsopamā*) in examples such as *padmānanā* ("lotus-faced") is excluded.
The repetition of sounds, however, is considered *yamaka* (rhyme) when occurring at the beginning of metrical quarters and so forth;
listen as I explain its specific varieties. (59)
The *pādāntayamaka*, the *kāñcīyamaka*, the *samudgayamaka*, and likewise the *vikrāntayamaka*. (60)

The twin [mountains] Cakravāla and Saṃdaṣṭayamaka, as well as the swan-families acting as jesters—since even that which is not embellished is understood [as such], this portion is an example of the second [type]. The reading here is "anyonyamiha" (mutually here); however, if the word "iva" (like) were used, it would suggest a simile (upamā) or a poetic fancy (utprekṣā).

Or rather, this is a "fancied simile" (*kalpitopamā*). Since the component of the simile does not manifest, that which is called "conceit" (*abhimāna*) is defined as such by the authors of the *alaṅkāra* treatises; they declare it to be an ornament because there is no distinction between the object to be adorned and the adornment itself. Otherwise, it would simply be that [conceit] itself.
Regarding this, some read as follows:
"That which is joined with the construction of form (or description), based on qualities of comparison through the blending of various substances and so forth— that is known as *rūpaka* (metaphor)."

And they explain [it as follows]: this is an etymological definition of the term *rūpaka*. It is that wherein there is a reliance upon a comparison (*aupamya*) by virtue of its being a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*) rather than the primary element (*pradhānatā*). Having thus established it, *rūpaka* is the description of one form (*rūpa*) after having determined it through another form (*arūpeṇa*). To the question "How is that determination made?", he says: "even by means of that which is manifold (*nānābhūta*) and distinct (*pṛthagbhūta*)."

The attachment [of a word] to its substance (*dravya*), like that of lac to crystal, is what is meant; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the various distinctions such as error (*bhrānti*), secondary usage (*gauṇa*), and indicative usage (*lākṣaṇika*) are included.
Thus, having demonstrated the figures of speech (*arthālaṅkāra*) in connection with the definition of the object (*artha*) as a domain, [the author proceeds].

He states the nature of the verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) as follows: "The repetition of words (*śabdābhyāsa*), however, is *yamaka*. The word "however" (*tu*) indicates its distinction from the ornaments of meaning (*arthālaṅkāra*). By the word "word" (*śabda*), everything is included—syllables (*varṇa*), phrases (*pada*), and parts thereof.

Consequently, alliteration (*anuprāsa*), such as that found in the *loṭīyā* meter and so forth, is subsumed by this very definition. Two [identical] things of the same kind are called "twins" (*yamau*).

Because it has that as its nature, it is *yamaka* (chiasmus). By means of this, the repetition of one syllable or word—whether immediately following or separated by an interval—that produces beauty is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). It is like a pearl being set in a particular setting alongside another suitable pearl, a ruby, or the like.

Or it is the falling among good men who are seated together in a suitable manner, or [the presence] of another good man. Regarding the word "at the beginning" (*pāde*), he says that because there is an option for [the repetition] in the middle, at the end, and so forth, there is no fixed rule for its placement, in order to include forms such as *anuprāsa* (alliteration) and *lāṭīya*. This is what is meant by "the observation of a distinction."
(327) Furthermore, there is the *pādādiyamaka* (repetition at the beginning of the quarters) and likewise the *āmreḍita* (repetition). || 61 ||
The *caturvyavasita* and the *mālāyamaka*:
these ten types of *yamaka* should be known as based upon drama. (62)
Where there is a syllable identical at the end of four quarters, that should be known by name as *pādāntayamaka* (end-of-quarter rhyme), as for example: || 63 ||
At the end of the day, the solar disc in the sky, its circle of rays withdrawn,
appears copper-red as it lingers there like a sphere of molten gold.
Just like the orb of a young woman’s breasts. || 64 ||

Victorious is the Lord Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the worlds, who endured the blow of the mace of the lord of the Daityas; he is the conqueror of gods and demons alike, the crusher of the foremost of the Asuras.
Where there are two identical feet at the beginning and likewise at the end of a verse...
This should be known by the wise as the *kāñcīyamaka*, as follows: || 66 ||
In each watch (yāma) of the nights— those possessing the moon, those flowing [with time], and those whose essence is manifest and unmanifest—
the meaning is that of the specific enumerations and characteristics; the "syllable" (akṣara) is both one and many, being unified.
He whose flood is a circle of rays; his golden wheel is a circle of refined gold.
Whether it be in full bloom or not, whether accompanied by bees or without bees.
The beautiful woman is both astonished and smiling.
When an entire metrical verse is completed by means of only one half [of the repeated pattern], that should be known by the name *samudgayamaka*, as for example: [68]

The magnificent elephant of the great forest shines with tusks as pale-white as the *ketakī* flower; the magnificent elephant of the great forest shines with tusks as pale-white as the *ketakī* flower. (69)
When, having stepped over each foot, two feet are identical, it should be known by the name *vikrānta-yamaka*, as for example: [70]
Having previously been an elephant like a mountain with two peaks, he became like a mountain without peaks due to the loss of his tusks. || 71 ||
When the final syllable of the preceding quarter is identical to the initial syllable of the following quarter, that should be known as *cakravāla* by name, just as follows: || 72 ||
Belonging to the most excellent women—brides and young maidens—it stands as their retinue;
every womanly form is clearly manifest, its features slightly revealed. Belonging to the moonlit nights, it smiles at every watch (yāma) of the night.
For when a flower has blossomed, whether it is accompanied by bees or not, one marvels;
thus, this elephant shines with such a face whose two teeth are as radiant as *ketakī* flowers. Likewise, he is one whose two tusks are white like *ketakī* blossoms.
That excellent forest, in the form of an elephant, shines forth. In this matter, the Sage did not take into account a difference in meaning;
thus, that [interpretation] is unestablished. We have understood the intention of others through etymological derivation and other means.
[The words refer to: "that which has two horns" and "that from which the horn has departed. These were gathered in battle.
Having become a unified body and ascended to the sky, they were struck by their enemies—the birds—with arrows following one after another, until they reached the end of their existence.
When the last [foot] is equal to one of the two middle feet, and the first foot is equal to it, that should be known by name as *cakravāla* throughout, as follows: (73)
Likewise, the mountains were struck down by enemies, repeatedly shattered by birds following their feathered arrows,
and all were piled up in battle like funeral pyres.
Mounted upon [their elephants], they were struck down by palms against palms.
Where the first two syllables in a foot are identical,
that should be known by name as *saṃdaṣṭa-yamaka*, as for example [in the following verse].
Look, look! By whatever quality of his he brings me under his control, by that very quality he brings me under his control whenever he comes within my sight.
Where there is an identical syllable at the beginning of the first foot,
it should be known by the name *pādādiyamaka* (initial-foot alliteration), as for example [in the following verse].
Viṣṇu creates all beings; Viṣṇu withdraws all creatures;
Viṣṇu brings forth the three worlds; Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of the worlds. || 78 ||
Where the final word of a quarter-verse is stated twice in succession here, that is to be known as the *yamaka* named *āmreḍita* by the learned. (79)

They were struck down. He describes the manner of their striking: "Those [demons], whose wings were severed, were further struck by the talons—the wing-arms—of birds such as vultures, like mountains [struck] by birds; they were strewn over and covered by these very [talons].
The phrase 'nihatānāmastaṃ lānti taiḥ' (they take the setting/death of those struck by them) is to be disregarded due to its grammatical difficulty."

(330) Your yawning and sighing occur again and again; how is it that you remember [him] at every step? And since this meditation of yours recurs so frequently, it is certain that you have passed the night without him, indeed without him.
Where all the quarters consist of a fixed number of syllables and are equal, that should be known by the wise as the meter named Caturvyavasita. || 81 ||
This indeed is the time for elephants; this indeed is the time for elephants.
This indeed is the time for elephants, or this indeed is the time for battles. || 82 ||
Where a single consonant is joined with various forms and vowels, that should be known by those skilled in poetry as *mālāyamaka*. || 83 ||
As follows:

May Halī, Balī, Halī, Mālī, Khelī, Mālī, Salī, and Jalī—the wielder of the plow, the strong, the one with the plow, the garlanded, the playful, the garlanded, the gentle, and the one who subdues—along with Bala, the powerful, and Māla, the mace-wielder, protect you! (84)
For that beautiful woman, who delights in the physical embrace of love,
bold in private, might delight her lover with supreme passion at night, even if his mind were otherwise intent.
If the dawn, the enemy of darkness, does not rise before me. || 85 ||

This is the season related to the *vāraṇapuṣpa* flowers, namely the autumn (*śarad*). Or, when there is well-being (*anāmaya*) for the *vāraṇas*—that is, the elephants—and in the absence of disease, for those enemies who possess the warding off (*vāraṇa*) or prevention [of harm], this is their time, that is, their end (*kṛtānta*). Alternatively: [this is] the time of the *vāraṇas*. When there is well-being for the *vāraṇas*, the elephants, and in the state of being free from sickness, this is the time—the end—for those enemies who have the warding off or prevention of the *vāraṇas*. Or: [this is] the time of the *vāraṇas*. When there is well-being for the *vāraṇas*, the elephants, and in the state of being free from sickness, this is the time—the end—for those enemies who possess the warding off or prevention of the *vāraṇas*. Or: [this is] the time of the *vāraṇas*. When there is well-being for the *vāraṇas*, the elephants, and in the state of being free from sickness, this is the time—the end—for those enemies who possess the warding off or prevention of the *vāraṇas*. Or: [this is] the time of the *vāraṇas*. Obscure meaning, redundant meaning, meaningless, contradictory meaning, tautological meaning, overwhelmed meaning, deviating from logic, irrelevant subject matter, broken euphony, and loss of word— these are indeed the ten defects of poetry.

That which is expressed by synonymous terms and is known as "the hidden meaning" (gūḍhārtha), wherein that which is not to be described is described, is intended as "the other meaning" (arthāntara). || 89 ||

It has been stated previously that the characteristics (lakṣaṇas) possess primacy; he concludes that very point with the words "by these characteristics," the meaning being that they are joined to the activity—the relishing of rasa—those [characteristics] which constitute the nature of the determinants (vibhāvas) and so forth, as it was stated below that these include serenity (prasāda) and the rest. He states what remains to be said after this: "ataḥ param" (beyond this).
In some manuscripts this section appears later, yet it is observed to be widely known [in its current position];

therefore, we explain it accordingly. In that regard, concerning the quarters of the verse, the sentence, and their meanings, there is—as in the case where one ought to say "Daśaratha"—an expression by means of a word that is in fact a synonym, though it is forcibly constructed as such.
Regarding the term *adhikanavavimāna*: for words used by chance (arbitrary names) do not admit synonyms.
An example of a different meaning is: "O fair-browed one, your sidelong glance spreads thought, delusion, and the bodiless god [Kāma] within my body.
Here, Kāma is accepted through the word *cintā* (thought) and so forth; thus, even that which is not directly describable has been described. As for that which...
Excessive description of irrelevant matters arising from a tangential discussion is a defect of composition;
since this has been refuted by the prescription of the rules for the constituent parts of a literary work (*sandhi-tadaṅga-vidhāna*), it does not merit further examination here.
Furthermore, one should recognize as defective that which is devoid of meaning, incoherent, leaving the sense incomplete, contradictory in meaning, vulgar, and indeed plebeian. (90)
Where a different intended meaning is found through another [literal] meaning, the experts in poetry call that too "poetry with distinct meanings" (bhinnārtha). || 91 ||
That which is a non-specific designation is known as having a single meaning;
it should be understood as having the sense of "repeatedly traversed" when it is compounded with a word. (92)

An example of that which is devoid of meaning (*arthahīna*) is: "Even now my mind remembers the mango trees of the Bhogavāyā [river], which are clever in the arts of love. Here, there is a lack of connection (*asaṃbandhatā*) due to the contradiction between the preceding and following parts of the statement. Or, for example:
"That great-souled one, by the power of fortune, has reached the great path. For in this case, there is a specific [lack of coherence].
The determination of a matter depends on the context, as it is also possible that [the meaning] was [intended] due to the influence of misfortune.
A different meaning is threefold; therein, "tolerable" refers to where the meaning [is understood] despite the intervention of a remote connection, for example—
"One should consume goat's milk and the like to destroy a long-standing fever born of impurities that has arisen from the king [of diseases] and is produced by the aggravation of the three *doṣas*.
Thus is the rustic (*grāmya*); for example: "O blessed lady, serve me; I shall give this to you. The third...

An example of a different meaning (*bhinnārtha*) is as follows: having said, "If this were not Rāvaṇa," one then asks, "Where, indeed, are all virtues found everywhere? For here, the undesirability of Rāvaṇa has been indicated; however, by the phrase "where, indeed," it is differentiated through the negation of the opposite.
An example of identical meaning (*ekārtha*) is: "white as the kunda flower, the moon, a pearl necklace, or the laughter of Hara. For all these have the same purpose;

for poetry does not proceed like a treatise (*śāstra*), with the intention that "someone might learn something specific" through instruction. An example of an overflowing meaning (*abhiplutārtha*) is:
That king was skilled in statecraft; the lake was adorned with water-lilies, the beauty of spring was beloved by all, and in summer, the *mālatikā* flower arrived.

In this case, because the meaning is completed in each quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is a state of "leaping over" (*abhipluta*); since there is no submergence due to the unity of the sentence, [the *yati*] does not occur within the middle of a word.

That which deviates from logic and is devoid of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) should be understood [as such]; where there is a disruption in the metrical structure, that is called "the uneven" (viṣama). || 93 ||

That which lacks the phonetic coalescence (*anupaśliṣṭa*) is proclaimed as "disconnected" (*visandhi*); and that which is devoid of phonemes due to the improper joining of vowels and consonants should be understood as "deprived of words" (*śabdacyuta*). (94)
These defects of poetry have indeed been fully proclaimed by me; the excellences, characterized by sweetness and loftiness, arise from their opposites. (95)
That which deviates from logic, contradicts place and time, and contradicts the arts and sciences (*kalā-śāstra*), for example:
"In Suvīra there is a famous city named Mathurā, whose surrounding lands abound in filberts and coconuts," and so forth.

An example of the uneven (*viṣama*) [juxtaposition] is: "O, do you see her resting upon the palace, wearing a garland of dense flowers," and so forth. If this is considered a fault, then it is improper when the connection between two [words]—which is threefold, consisting of immediate contiguity (*nairantarya*), the application of analysis (*vicāra-yoga*), or mutual merging (*anyonya-laya*)—is not properly established.
Or that which gives rise to harshness and so forth, wherein an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) is traditionally recognized by the sages;

among these, some are eternal defects (*nityadoṣa*), such as an incorrect word, while others are non-eternal, such as the vulgar (*grāmya*), because it is most desired in contexts like humor. This is what he means by saying "according to the gross" (*yathāsthūlam*). [This refers to] the sequence.
An *avyayībhāva* compound is formed with an indeclinable (*avyaya*). By that [rule], each subsequent [example] follows. These are the gross faults;
and as for the hidden meaning, it is to be employed in cases such as riddles (*gūḍhārtha*), secret letters, enigmatic verses (*prahelikā*), and the "flag" (*patākā*) stage-setting.

In a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is a different meaning, such as in the case of "the destruction of wealth" (*arthanāśa*) and so forth. In comedy (*hāsya*), there is a divergent meaning when the speaker is a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) and the like.

In the communication of meaning to another, these faults—namely, tautology (*ekārtha*), excessive prolixity (*abhiplutārtha*), deviation from the established meter in cases such as madness, and lack of euphonic junction (*visandhi*) within its own proper domain—are each considered defects in their respective order of occurrence. In this context, as long as there is comprehension of the intended meaning, that much is acceptable; however, a corrupt word (*apaśabda*) is indeed a fault, because it results in the absence of any comprehension of meaning whatsoever. For it [the corrupt word] does not...
One may employ any particular language that conveys the intended meaning, provided there is no lack of clarity.

Now, he declares [the presence of] excellences (*guṇas*): the meaning is that for these [languages], excellences arise from the removal of those very defects; it is the destruction of faults that constitutes excellence. Is this so without distinction? No, he says: [excellence is defined by] the characteristics of sweetness (*mādhurya*) and loftiness (*audārya*).
(334) Coalescence, clarity, evenness, concentration, sweetness, vigor, and softness of word.
The manifestation of meaning, loftiness, and charm—these ten are the qualities of poetry. (96)
The mutual cohesion of words connected with a desired set of meanings is designated as *śleṣa* (punning conjunction). || 97 ||

"Maṅka" refers to those [faults]. This is what is meant: if this "mouth of poetry" (the opening) is free from these defects and is radiant, then even if it is devoid of other qualities and ornaments, it is said that by virtue of its adherence to the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it does not deviate from being poetry.
He shows that there are other qualities as well by stating "cohesion (śleṣa), clarity (prasāda)," and so forth. The meaning of the word "of poetry" (kāvyasya) is:
of the word, of the sentence, or of the meaning residing in both. Then he explains cohesion (śleṣa) with the words "by means of a desired collection of meanings.
This refers to the arrangement of the constituent parts of the meaning through a connection imagined by the poet.
*Śleṣa* (paronomasia) is the quality consisting in the fitness (*upapadyamānatā*) of a meaning that is indicated by a word which has already accomplished the desired collection of meanings;
as illustrated by Vāmana: [text follows].
Seeing his two beloveds seated upon a single seat, he approached from behind with reverence;
under the pretext of a playful concealment, he closed the eyes of one while slightly turning his neck,
as her heart blossomed with love and her body was covered in horripilation.
The rogue kissed another woman, whose cheek-surface was radiant with a suppressed smile.
In this matter, although the objective—

characterized by the simultaneous winning over of the hearts of two heroines— is beyond the reach of mere imagination, it has been so skillfully established that it ceases to be a ground for incredulity; therefore, even though this sequence is circuitous, it does not cause distress to the heart.
Because it becomes prominent and sinks into the heart of everyone;

And that which is naturally well-connected is proclaimed as *śliṣṭa* (the "coalesced"). || 98 ||
Even where a word or a meaning is understood by the wise without being explicitly stated, that [quality] is celebrated as *prasāda* (clarity), due to the harmonious union of words and meanings. 99.
