the Śakāra dialect should be employed, along with a slight touch of the forest-dweller (Vānaukasī) speech.
The speech of those living in the settlements of cattle-herders, horses, goats, sheep, camels, and so forth is Ābhīrī; that of the Śabaras is Śābarī; and that of the forest-dwellers is Drāmiḍī. (56)
The Māgadhī style is used by tunnel-diggers and others, by those making secret pacts, by horse-guards, and also for the self-protection of leaders in times of calamity. (57)

In the case of drama (*nāṭya*), however, others say that because this [language] is intended for illustration, even Paiśācī and other dialects may be employed. The connection is with "those residing in the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*) of kings.
For gamblers, it is "those who play" (*dīvyatām*). *Śakāras* are those of low birth who, by virtue of their wealth, are full of pride.
The language abounding in the letter *śa* is the Śaka language. A *pulkasa* is a *ḍomba*; others say he is a *mṛtapa*.

"Vanecarī" means belonging to forest-dwellers; that is, [the language] of those who live in the woods. "Tunnel-diggers" are those who break through walls (*sandhicchedakṛtaḥ*). "Kārā" is a prison. "Vyasana" refers to when some misfortune has occurred, lest the world [should find out about me].
With the intention that "he will come to know [this]," the leader should not employ the Māgadhī language even for his own protection;
for the prohibition of the Draviḍa and other such dialects applies specifically to those who are distinguished [in learning].
In the performance of drama, poetry composed in the languages of tribes such as the Barbaras, Kirātas, Āndhras, Dramiḷas, and others, should not be employed. (58)
Regarding those regions proclaimed to lie between the Gaṅgā and the ocean,
one who knows [the rules] should employ a language in which the sound 'e' predominates.

One who knows [the regional dialects] should employ a language rich in the letter 'na' in those regions situated between the Vindhya mountains and the ocean that have come down in the sacred scriptures.
In the regions of Surāṣṭra and Avantī, and in those lands to the north of the Vetravatī river,
one should construct [a city] primarily consisting of squares.
Those people who have taken refuge in Himavat, Sindhu, and Sauvīra are known as those in whom the letter *u* is predominant; one should employ that dialect among them.
On the banks of the river Carmaṇvatī and those places that rely on Arbuda,
one should always employ speech abounding in the syllable *oka*.
Thus, the rules for language should be applied according to the requirements of the drama; however, whatever has not been mentioned by me here should be adopted from common usage by the wise. (64)
*Sipu* is to be found among the *Draviḍas*, specifically those belonging to the *Barbara*, *Andhra*, and other regions associated with them, located in countries such as *Bhaṅgela*.
"Between the Gaṅgā and the ocean" indicates the eastern region;
"between the Vindhya and the ocean" refers to Southern *Saurāṣṭra*; and [the phrase] "in the regions of *Surāṣṭra* and *Avanti*" [indicates the western region].

The western [direction] is [defined] by the Vetravatī and so forth, while the northern is [defined] by the [Vāk]. By the single word "vākyavidhāna" (the formulation of the sentence), the entire meaning of the sentence is made clear.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the rules for the formation of speech have been declared by me; now, furthermore, learn the worldly rules for the construction of sentences.
Learn now from me those persons who are to be addressed in a drama by superior, middling, or inferior characters—whether they be equal, superior, or inferior [to the speaker]. (66)
Even those great-souled great seers who are gods among the gods must be addressed as "Bhagavan," and so too must their wives.
Those who are gods, those who bear sectarian marks, and those who uphold various sacred scriptures—
these should be addressed as "Bhagavan" by both men and women.
One should address a Brāhmaṇa as "Ārya," a king as "Mahārāja," a teacher as "Upādhyāya," and an elder as "Tāta. (69)
Kings should be addressed by Brahmins as "O King" (Rāja);
for that is what they must endure, since the twice-born are traditionally held to be worthy of honor by rulers of the earth.
The minister should be addressed as "Brāhmaṇa" by Brāhmaṇas, or as "Amātya" or "Saciva" by others;
however, he should always be addressed as "Hīnarārya" by all other people.

The term "sentence" (*vākya*) is used with the intention that [the words] are made to have mutual form—that is, they are connected; for there will be the formation of words (*pada-vidhāna*). "Gods of the gods" means those who are to be praised by the gods. "Likewise" (*tathā*) refers to the Blessed Lady (*bhagavatī*) in her feminine aspect. "Those who have not heard much" means those who are not learned. "It must be forgiven" means it must be accepted. "Minister" (*saciva*) [refers to] the king’s...
The minister [says]: (p. 380) One should converse with equals using the name by which they are designated.
But the superior one, having addressed those who are inferior along with their retinues by name, [should do so]. || 72 ||
Likewise, men and women appointed to official duties, as well as artisans and craftsmen, should indeed be addressed in that same manner. (73)
One should address a superior as "mārṣa"; one slightly inferior as "mārṣaka"; an equal as "vayasya"; and a lowly person as "haṃho" or "haṇḍe. (74)
A charioteer should always address his master as "Venerable One" (āyuṣman);
one who is tranquil is called "Ascetic" (tapasvin), and he is addressed as "Virtuous One" (sādhu). (75)

One should address a master as "svāmin," a crown prince as "kumāra" or "bhartṛdāraka," and a gentle person as "somya" or "bhadramukha"; one should speak thus to those of higher status, while addressing an inferior with "he. (76)

"By name, together with his retinue" means that the superior king, having taken up his own name along with those of the inferior kings—such as "O Vatsarāja, pearl-jewel of the Lunar dynasty," and so forth—should address him. Alternatively, there is the reading *saparihāsam* ("with jesting"); here, "jesting" (*parihāsa*) indicates satisfaction, and thus flattery and the like should be employed on the occasion of such satisfaction.

Even by those of low status, a king may be addressed by name, as in such examples as: "While Udayana rules the earth, what room is there for calamities? Artisans (*kāruka*) are those such as stūpa-builders and the like;
craftsmen (*śilpin*) are those such as painters and the like. The vocative form "bhāva" is intended here; thus, it does not appear in any other case-ending.

The statement "it is improper [to use the vocative]" is incorrect; for even in cases such as "friend" (*vayasya*) and so forth, the vocative case is intended everywhere when addressing someone at the start of a conversation.
One who is equal to, or even lower than, inferior persons should be addressed with "haṃho" or "haṇḍe. From the word "ca" (and),...
Even without [these],
if one's action, craft, knowledge, or even birth [is such], (p. 381) [one attains it].
Indeed, he should be addressed by that name by the performers at the beginning of the drama and other such works. || 77 ||
A disciple or even a son should be addressed by his father or his teacher using such terms as "vatsa," "putraka," or "tāta," whether by name or by lineage. (78)

The Śākyas and Nirgranthas are to be addressed as "Venerable Sir" (Bhadanta) by those who speak to them; however, other heretics are to be addressed with their own specific titles according to their respective traditions. (79)
The king should be addressed as "Devā" by his servants and subjects;
however, the sovereign of the whole earth should always be addressed as "Bhaṭṭā" by his attendants.
O King, a lord of the earth should be addressed by sages as "rājan" (O King), or with a suffix indicating descent; or he may be addressed as "vayasya" (friend) or "rājan. || 81 ||
The Vidūṣaka may address the Queen and the female attendant as "bhavatī"; likewise, the Vidūṣaka may be addressed by the King by name or as "vayasya. (82)
A husband should be addressed as "Noble Son" by all women during their youth;
at other times, however, the lord of the earth should be addressed as "Noble Sir" or "Great King."
By the word "he" [is meant]: occupation, such as agriculture and so forth; knowledge, such as the three Vedas and so forth; birth, lineage, or country;
the Śākyas, the followers of Sugata, the Nirgranthas, and the Kṣapaṇakas; and the "others," namely the heretics such as the Pāśupatas and so forth.
One's own tradition (*svasamaya*) is, for example, the address among the Pāśupatas as "Bhāpuṣan" or "Bhāsarvajña," and so on.
Likewise, in some cases, it is by means of words such as "vākya" (speech) and so forth; or by means of a patronymic suffix, as in "Kaurava" and so forth, or the address "Great King.
Elsewhere than in youth, there is the designation "Noble Son" (Āryaputra) used by a father-in-law; by this, his youth, which is appropriate for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), is expressed.
p.
382) An elder brother or an older relative is to be addressed as "Noble Lady" (āryā), while a younger brother is to be addressed like a son.
(Furthermore, women should address him as "Desirable One" [kāmyā], and warriors as "Prince" [rājaputra]. 84.
Thus indeed should the speech of men be performed by the actors in drama;
now I shall further explain how women should speak in the play. (85)
Ascetic women and deities should be addressed as "Bhagavatī" (Venerable Lady);
however, the wife of one's guru should be addressed as "Sthānīyā" (Lady of the Household).
In a drama, a woman who may be approached should indeed be addressed as "Bhadrā" or "Vṛddhāmbā";
however, all wives of kings should be addressed by their attendants using the term "Parijana."
In drama, the learned use the terms *bhaṭṭinī*, *svāminī*, and *devī* [for a queen];
however, the term *devī* should be used for the chief queen by the king or by his attendants. (88)

Furthermore, those who remain as enjoyers (bhoginī) should be called "mistresses" (svāminī), while those who are maidens (kumārī) should be addressed by the female attendants as "the daughters of our masters" (bhartṛdārikā). || 89 ||
One's own sister should be addressed as "sister" (svasā), and a younger sister as "child" (vatse);
a Brahmin woman, one who dwells in the [monastic] marks, and one observing vows should be addressed as "Noble Lady" (āryā).

A younger brother should be addressed by an elder brother like a son, using terms such as "dear child," "father," or "little son. The phrase "addressing men" serves as a concluding summary that implies a greater number [of cases]. Although addressing women was also determined in the middle [of the discussion] with the word "poor things" (*tapasvinyaḥ*), it was previously stated there that "their wives" (*teṣāṃ yoṣitaḥ*); therefore, it is not the case here that [the rule applies] even when they themselves are not poor.
This is a repetition. A teacher’s wife is to be honored; other women who occupy a similar position are also venerable, being slightly older.
[The term] *patnī* refers to one who shares in religious duties.
A wife should be addressed as "Āryā" or by her son's paternal name; likewise, friends of equal status should address one another as "Halā. (91)
A woman who is of high status should be addressed as "servant" or "strike";
and a courtesan should be addressed as "actress" by her attendants.
Indeed, a courtesan’s mother should be addressed as "Mother" by her attendants;
a wife should be addressed as "Beloved" by her husband, or by anyone other than a king. (93)
The wives of priests and merchants should always be addressed as "Āryā";
poets should always employ names that signify those respective characteristics.
Those names of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas which may be innate and not well-known in drama should be used according to their lineage and occupation. (95)
For indeed, poets have composed works in poetry that provide both pleasure and protection;
one should employ the names found therein as if they were bestowed by merchants. (96)
(The Kāpālikas, however, are declared to have names ending in -ghaṇṭā).

Because she is a wandering actress (*cāriṇī*), the noble stage-manager (*sūtradhāra*), who has been initiated into the great sacrifice of the science of drama (*nāṭyaveda-mahāsatra*), addresses her as "Noble Lady" (*ārye*). She is called "Māṭharaputrī" by the name of her father; "Somaśarmajananī" refers to the mother of her son; [and finally] she is a courtesan (*veśyā*).
One's own attendants should address [a woman] as "Ajjuke" (O Ajjukā).

The term "always" implies that even during her youth, she should be addressed as "Āryā" by the family priest and others, or as "Bhāryā" (wife) by her husband. Regarding the "innate names" (*autpattikāni*), these are those which are assigned by oneself; for this very reason, they are called "declared," having meanings corresponding to their specific characteristics.

The ritual acts should be endowed with meanings that indicate the subject matter at hand. He clarifies this very point through an illustration, beginning with the words "of the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya" (brahmakṣatrasya), and so forth.
One should likewise apply names derived from valor to those who are brave. || 97 ||
The names of the king's wives should always consist of words signifying victory;
one should assign the names Mitrā and Senā to the courtesans.
In a drama, the attendants should have names derived from various flowers;
one should also assign auspicious names to the male servants (ceṭas). 99.
One should indeed employ names of profound meaning for those who are supreme, because their actions will be in accordance with those names. (100)
One should apply names for the remaining [deities] as well, in accordance with their birth and activities; thus have the names of both men and women been truly declared. (101)
In this manner, poets should always prescribe names:

those indicating heroism and nobility, such as *Bhīmaparākrama* (of terrifying prowess); those intended for victory, such as *Śubhalakṣaṇavijayavatī* (possessing auspicious marks and victory), and so forth; and those such as *Devadatta*, *Vasantasenā*, *Vidagdhamitrā*, and the like.

Regarding courtesans: names such as *mālatī*, *mallikā*, and so forth, which denote various flowers—the mention of "flowers" here is an indication that includes their clusters (*mañjarī*)—and even names such as *cūtalatikā* (the mango-creeper) are seen.
Names for the sake of auspiciousness include *siddhārthaka* (white mustard) and so forth. Names of profound meaning include *akṣobhya* (unshakeable) and so forth.

With the intention that there is no burden [imposed] by convention, he asks; here the answer is that [the name] conforms to its own nature (*svarūpa*). For a name indeed arises by embracing its own essential form through the power of the will of the Lord (*īśvara*). Thus, when a syllable of a name is afflicted by planetary influences, malevolent spells, mechanical devices, or ritual acts, or when it is the object of pacifying (*śāntika*) or nourishing (*pauṣṭika*) rites and so forth, it is exactly so.

The intended meaning is that the fruit arises for the person. Thus, the actor endowed with poetic skill, having understood the rules of language and all the actions without exception, [should perform].
Thereafter, one should employ the recitation (pāṭhya) endowed with six ornaments.

Now we shall describe the qualities of recitation (pāṭhyaguṇa). They are as follows: seven musical notes (svara), three registers (sthāna), four types of vocal coloration (varṇa), two kinds of intonation (kāku), six ornaments (alaṅkāra), and six auxiliary parts (aṅga).

Now we shall explain their characteristics. With this intention, he says: "Having understood the rules of language, then... which means that having first mastered those [rules] and composed poetry, one should employ the recitation in performance. However, if there is another poet, then...
The designation "pāṭhya" (recitation) should be understood as being used in the sense of an agent because it is the fundamental basis.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with six ornaments," the six factors here intended by the word "ornament" are tone, pitch, phoneme, pause, ornamentation, and the limbs [of performance]; for it is poetry adorned with these that is called *pāṭhya*.

For it is in this way that the nature of what is to be spoken (vaktavyatva) pertains to the material (upādāna): if it is to be recited, it must convey the entire meaning intended by the speaker; and all of that depends upon the phonetic qualities such as accentuation (*svara*) and so forth. Therefore he says "the qualities of what is to be recited" (*pāṭhyaguṇān*); for "qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) are those things which are beneficial (*upakāraka*).
The meaning is that whatever has been taught [previously] serves as an aid.

He explains this according to the order of enumeration, beginning with "In that regard" (*tatra*) and so forth. We shall elaborate upon the matter of musical notes (*svara*) in the section concerning song (*geya*). In this context, within the various modulations (*kāku*), the notes themselves are what truly provide assistance. That which constitutes their accompaniment—

However, when the vowels are in their natural state (*prakṛtibhūta*), the quality of *kāku* (intonation) is produced within them. In this context, by the word "place" (*sthāna*), the substratum for the production of their own nature is indicated.
[This occurs] through the forms of the acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), and tremulous (*kampita*) accents of the vowels.

It has been shown that what is useful for recitation (*pāṭhya*) is merely the contact with high, low, and middle registers, having abandoned that resonance (*anuraṇana*) which consists primarily of attachment (*rakti*) to specific tones.
For if the attachment pertaining to musical notes were relied upon as the primary element in recitation, then it would become the activity of singing (*gāna*).
It might be argued that there is no recitation; if it is claimed that there is a distinction among the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) due to the absence of complete musical notes (*svara*), [we reply:
they are indeed called the seven notes (*saptasvara*). (p. 386)

The notes *ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, *pañcama*, *dhaivata*, and *niṣāda*— these are to be applied to the aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*). For example, even though they are not complete in their tonal structure, they are still recognized as "song" (*gāna*) because of the commitment to singing, as in the cases of the *ṣāḍava* (six-note scale) and *auḍuvita* (five-note scale).
Even when there are three or four musical notes (*svara*), the perception of singing still occurs, as in the case of artificial flutes which have three notes,

and in the *Bhinna-ṣaḍja-bhāṣā* and *Kālindī* scales which have four notes. Therefore, disregarding the quality characterized by aesthetic attachment (*rati*) for the sake of distinguishing it from mere singing, [one must consider] the contact with the points of articulation (*sthāna*) such as the chest (*uraḥ*) and so forth.

The mention of the vowels here is for the purpose of stating that they are the primary [factors] in this context; otherwise, since there exist qualities such as the acute (*udātta*) accent which are distinct from the seven musical notes (*svara*), their mention would be purposeless.
As for the slight restriction of the body-parts and the constriction of the throat-cavity belonging to the qualities of the acute accent and so forth—

Regarding the statement beginning with "saṃvṛtā" (concealed), the purpose was stated so that there might be [the application of] ornaments such as *ucca* (high pitch) and so forth upon the attainment of qualities like the *udātta* (acute accent) as recited in the rules of phonetics (*śikṣā*). Even in that case, if our stated purpose is not accepted, we do not understand what would be achieved by the attainment of those qualities.

Now, if this is so, what is the purpose of denoting the vowels? It is said: since the *dhruvā-gāna* is the very life-breath of the performance, the application of the generic portion (*jātyaṃśaka*) will take place therein; therefore, this [specification] is now for the purpose of dispelling the doubt as to whether it should be entirely abandoned at the time of recitation.
The purpose of this exposition of the musical notes (*svara*) here is that the recitation must be performed by making primary reliance upon the notes that reside therein.
Thus, when the distinction from *upagāna* (accompaniment) has been established, [the text proceeds] by means of the presentation of external objects.

Or, through the surrender of the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛtti*), the *kāku* is designated according to the distinctions of meaning and rasa in order to attain the state of being an *abhinaya* (acting) and an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion). For this very reason, the nature of *kāku* alone is the pervasive element everywhere, because it serves as the primary factor in excellence. And thus, even in the subsequent [discussion of] ornaments such as *ucca*, *dīpta*, and so forth—

The sage will employ the word *kāku* itself [to express this]. The term *alaṃkāra* (ornament) refers here to those things that produce assistance (*upakāra*) and lead to perfection; *alam* has the sense of sufficiency (*paryāpti*), not the sense of physical decoration (*bhūṣaṇa*).
As for the "limbs" (*aṅga*), such as pauses (*viccheda*) and so forth, they serve to nourish the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the meaning (*artha*), and the function of beauty (*śobhā*) and the like.

"Only *kāku* is the benefactor"—thus, in the ultimate sense, this *pañcamī* is completed by means of various other forms; and since it is through *kāku* that what is being recited is led toward its appropriate meaning—whether conscious or insentient—by means of being directed [toward it] as a performance (*abhinaya*), *kāku* alone is the primary element here. And so, at the end of this chapter:

"He will bring [the discussion] to a conclusion"; thus it is said that "the varieties of *kāku* have been explained. Otherwise, if it were merely a concluding summary of what falls within the group of six ancillary factors (*aṅga-ṣaṭka*), or if it were simply a description of other ancillary factors, then everything would be inconsistent. Therefore, *kāku* alone is the primary element here.
For teachers indeed justify a conventional meaning by attributing it to a form that does not possess that sense.
But how could there be such a modulation of voice (*kāku*) if one disregards the heard meaning? Regarding this, others have said:
"In this matter, the nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*) must be observed; for there is nothing that is impossible when it is actually perceived. We, however—

We reply: here, as for this [rule], the notes *madhyama* and *pañcama* are to be employed as the *kārya-svaras* (notes of action) for *hāsya* (the comic) and *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic), respectively, by the first [author]. (103) p. 387)
Likewise, Ṣaḍja and Ṛṣabha are used in the heroic, furious, and marvelous sentiments;
furthermore, Gāndhāra and Niṣāda should be employed in the pathetic sentiment. (104)
And the *dhaivata* note should be employed in the *bībhatsa* (disgust) and *bhayānaka* (terror) sentiments.

There are three places [of articulation]: the chest, the throat, and the head. And it is said: "Speech, which is devoid of specific forms such as phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth, is produced by the vibration of consciousness through the arousal of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."

It is established that sound, being of the nature of resonance (*nāda*), is understood through the Vedānta and other scriptures as mental fluctuations such as joy and sorrow, or as the intention behind injunctions and prohibitions— either by virtue of its being an inferential mark (*liṅga*) of those effects or through identity (*tādātmya*).
And thus, even for other animals such as deer and dogs, fear, anger, sorrow, and so forth arise upon hearing a sound.
Thus, this comprehension of mental modifications and so forth from sound is, for its part, inference.

As for these particular phonemes, they—being like knots within the word which consists of the universal nature of that sound—are dependent upon other causes distinct from the initial effort; for that very reason, even when another [meaning] is not intended, they appear otherwise.

Therefore, they are capable of being employed and are thus observed to deviate [from their literal meaning]. Sound, however, is like a sudden breaking forth of facial coloration and horripilation; it is not otherwise established, and it certainly subverts a word-meaning that is otherwise established. As it has been said: "O timid one, by saying 'I have no fear,' he reveals his [inner] state."

The word "fear" (*bhayam*) prescribes a different mode of the sentence-meaning by imparting a specific nuance; we shall discuss this further under the verse beginning with "O Agni," so let it rest for now. In any case, it is established that *kāku* (intonation) is the primary element in recitation. Here, by the phrase "in the comic and the erotic," etc., the connection with the various types of *rasas* is indicated.
By restating what is yet to come, he shows that the application of the *kāku* follows the vowels that are quickly established;
then he shows the bases for these vowels with the words "three places. [Objection:

But at the time of recitation, where the phonemes (*varṇa*) are cerebral (*mūrdhan*), how can there be the production of a vowel whose place of articulation (*sthāna*) is the chest? The same applies elsewhere.
It must be stated: it has been said that the seven notes (*svaras*) constitute the nature of speech which consists of deep resonance (*mandranāda*);

and that speech, having been produced from the chest (*uraḥ-sthāna*), striking the head, manifests a cerebral (*mūrdhanya*) phoneme whose form is permeated by that deep resonance. And this remains so even though [the phoneme] has the head as its place of articulation (*mūrdha-sthānatva*).
Its high pitch results from its elevated position. For the place of articulation for the production of the consonants is indeed different;
it is another location, namely the interior of the head, extending only as far as the nasal cavity. However, the production of vowels occurs in the expanded and unexpanded [spaces] of the head.
Furthermore, in the case of the physical lute, the modulated tone (*kāku*) arises from three places alone: from the chest, the head, and the throat. (106)

As they are produced in the body, they attain a state of high pitch; thus, the qualities of high, low, and middle pitch arise for vowels, even though their forms are produced through the differentiation of all the locations of sound (*sthāna*).
In that context, although the differentiation of locations is already implied by the mention of "vowels" (*svara*), the locations are mentioned again [in the verse] for the sake of emphasis.

This is for the purpose of excluding the sixty-six distinct locations [of articulation]. Likewise, there are twenty-two locations in the chest (*puraḥsthāna*) where the *śrutis* and *svaras* reside; the same applies to the throat (*kaṇṭha*) and the head (*mūrdhan*). We have already stated that with such [articulations], there can only be a clear singing (*gāna*) and not recitation (*pāṭhya*). For this very reason, the word "quality" (*guṇa*) is not [applicable here].

The word *dharmavacana* refers to the qualities of recitation; however, it also refers to the place of the instrumental means (*upakaraṇa-vacana-sthāna*), for that which serves as an instrument is indeed an instrumental means. Furthermore, some explain the passage beginning with "In the case of the *śārīrī* lute" and so forth as follows: here, the intonation of meaning (*artha-kāku*) conveys the understanding of injunctions, prohibitions, and other such meanings, whereas the intonation of tone (*svara-kāku*) [conveys musical pitch].
It is an indicator of mental activity;

it concerns subjects such as the performance of two types of action devoid of this [actual] engagement, the recitation of stage costumes (*nepathya*), the recitation of *vaitālīya* meters, and the speaking from a distance; its purpose is the production of beauty and the hearing from afar.
"It is that modulation of voice which will be described by him. First, he should be asked this:

regarding this object of the modulation of voice that has been mentioned, if there is some intended meaning (*artharūpa*) to be expressed therein, then there must necessarily be a modulation of meaning (*arthakāku*) distinct from the modulation of voice. For instance, even in the case of a recitation performed behind the scenes (*nepathyapāṭha*).

The chamberlain recites; "This hero Aṅgada recites," "Yaugandharāyaṇa recites"—the recitation must be of such a nature as to convey specific details regarding the conduct, mental states, and so forth [of the characters].
Even in the Vaitālīya style of recitation, which primarily aims at announcing the appropriate occasion, the meaning must necessarily be grasped.

And this has been stated: "What is the point of mimetic representation (*abhinaya*) if it is independent of the meaning? For the recitation of a book-reader, when being imitated, assumes the status of mimetic representation;
otherwise, in the absence of the nature of mimetic representation—and given its distinctness from the instruments, the actor's qualities, and the resulting aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth—"

Furthermore, what is the purpose of considering the distinction from vocal intonation (*svarātodya*), singing (*gāna*), and so forth? Others argue that by this [definition], the general characteristic of *kāku* would not be established; for even if it were so, the point "it also occurs thus" would remain unproven, since that [general characteristic] is employed by way of supporting the matter previously introduced.
This is the style of the Sage. Therefore, this verse is intended to support the three aforementioned locations.
Thus, the meaning is as follows: in the bodily lute (*vīṇā*), [the sound] arises from only the three locations characterized by the chest, head, and throat, and not otherwise.

The activity consisting of vocalization, which is clearly articulated through the sixty-six musical notes (*svaras*) and serves as the means for song, proceeds in the form of a *kāku* (modulation) that is indicative in nature.
The word "atha" (now/then) is used here in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*). For [this occurs] in the external lute (*vīṇā*) which has been reflected [therein].

There is no attainment of *kāku* apart from the essential nature of the resonant tone (*khara-svara*) characterized by passion; the mention of the lute is for the purpose of illustrating the open middle register (*vivṛta-madhya*) residing within the body.
And when standing at a distance, one should employ the head;
when not too far away, the throat; and when at the side, the chest. 107.
A wise person should illuminate with the head the speech brought forth from the chest;
in all applications of recitation, one should always effect its softening through the throat. 108.

The production of sound does not occur in the mere body for the sake of encompassing the region of the *kāka* (crow), but rather in that very [larynx]. This series of ascending positions, which corresponds to the handle of an external lute (*vīṇādaṇḍa*), is the row of steps of the positions; it is the locus for the production of sound. For this very reason, even the *kāku* intonation is characterized—[the term] *kāka* [referring to the crow-like sound].

In the case of longing, there is a longing that desires further; just as a variety of tones is perceived, that from which even a slight ground for expression arises is *kāku*. Here, the word *ku* undergoes the substitution of *kā* in the sense of "slight. Alternatively, *kāku* refers to the tongue, because it is produced through its operation.

Having thus analyzed the nature of the *sthāna* (places of articulation), he says "and addressing from afar," etc., in order to demonstrate its distinction of objects (*viṣayabheda*). "With the head" means with the *tāra* (high-pitched) sound produced by the head;
"not very far, with the throat" means with the middle [register] from the throat, which amounts to saying "nearby, with the low-pitched (*mandra*) [sound]."
Having thus explained the distinct utility of the three registers, he demonstrates them simultaneously with the verse beginning "A sentence uttered from the chest," and so forth.

The meaning of the verse is that one should begin the recitation with a low tone (*mandrasvara*), gradually ascend to a high pitch (*tāra*), and conclude with the middle register (*madhya*). For when [the speech] is neither accompanied by intensity such as anger, nor...

When one’s heart is possessed by grief and the like through a low-pitched tone (*mandra-rūpa*), then, by gradually expanding the enthusiasm toward the subject matter to be expressed, it reaches the high pitch (*tāra*) and finally comes to rest at the middle pitch (*madhya*) during the conclusion;
this is the general rule for recitation when nothing remains [unexpressed]. For this very reason, in the case of the *śānta* (peaceful) rasa:

This very rule for recitation applies when there is an absence of the influence of deviant vowels (*vyabhicāri-vala*). Let this also be a general rule regarding the *vaitālīya* recitation: in that context, there is no modulation of tone (*svarakāku*). What, then, is its scope?
It is said: it concerns cases where there is sometimes the imposition of another quality upon a collection of qualities denoted by the meaning.
A *kāku* is said to be that which sometimes conveys the mental state of the person producing the sound. In this regard,
there are the *udātta*, *anudātta*, *svarita*, and likewise the *kampita* accents of the *rasa* (flavor).
O ascetics rich in austerity, there are exactly four vocal registers (varṇas) to be employed in the practice of recitation.

In that regard, for the comic (*hāsya*) and erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiments, the recitation (*pāṭhya*) should be performed with syllables having the *svarita* and *udātta* accents; for the heroic (*vīra*), furious (*raudra*), and marvelous (*adbhuta*), with *udātta* and tremulous (*kampita*) tones; and for the pathetic (*karuṇa*), loathsome (*bībhatsa*), and terrifying (*bhayānaka*), there should be no modulation of voice (*akākuvyavahāra*), or alternatively, it may be performed according to the nature of the sound when well-composed within its own structural framework.

In this context, it functions regarding the mass of phonemes—which constitute one's own knots—as being heard from afar, heard slightly, or not heard at all; even there, it is called the modulation of tone (*svarakāku*). That which was stated as "addressing one who is situated at a distance," and so forth, is thus [understood] through the distinction between the insentient and the sentient that arises from activity distinct from one's own service.
Due to the distinction of its meaning, rasa, and tone, *kāku* is indeed threefold.
Having thus described the distinction of place (*sthāna*), he states the nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*) as they follow in sequence, beginning with "the acute" (*udātta*).
There are four [qualities]: height, lowness, mediocrity, and the suspension between both high and low.

The *svaras* (accents) are the *varṇas* (phonemes), or rather the *guṇas* (qualities); or they are so called because they reveal (*vivṛṇvate*) or manifest (*prakaṭayanti*) the specific meaning of their own object.
In the application of recitation (*pāṭhyayoga*) within poetry, one should speak of the *varṇas* alone, setting aside the affective element (*raktibhāga*) of the accent.
Regarding the absorption in the emotional state (*raktibhāga*), they have declared that there should be an application of singing (*gānayoga*) and not an application of recitation (*pāṭhyayoga*).

In this regard, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), it is said by [the author] that within the emotional state, there are the components of vowels such as the unaccented (*anudātta*) and so forth, and the components of consonants such as *ka* and so forth; and he explains their clarity or lack of clarity.

When a singer with an untrained throat begins to sing in some manner upon a stringed instrument where resonance is predominant, the *huḍukkā* and *muraja* drums and so forth are indeed perceived separately;
likewise, even there, other attributes exist as submerged due to their predominance. For this very reason, the ascetics (*tapodhanas*) have said:

The intention is that you, who perceive the subtle, are authorized here to deliberate. He states the scope of these syllables with the words "of the comic (hāsya) and the erotic (śṛṅgāra)," and so forth. In this context, such as "the middle [note] and the fifth," the correspondence of order (yathāsaṃkhyam) is not intended; thus, in the comic sentiment, [it may be] either of the middle [note] or the fifth.
Having grasped the fixed pitch (*sthāyisvara*) of the *jāti*, one should recite it by touching the high and middle registers right there.

Likewise, in the three [rasas] such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the heroic (*vīra*), one should recite the *ṣāḍjī* or *ārṣabhī* after grasping its own tonic note (*svāṃśa*) with acute accents (*udātta*) and tremolo (*kampita*). In the pathetic (*karuṇa*), one should use the *niṣāvatī* or the *gāndhārī*.
In the *sthāyin* [rasa], the recitation is performed with an *anudātta* accent; in the *vībhatsa*, based on the *dhaivata* and *aṃśa* notes, the recitation is characterized by the *svarita*;
in the *bhayānaka*, by relying on those same notes (*dhaivata* as the *aṃśa*), the recitation is primarily characterized by trembling—thus it shall be. (A-29)

By restating the accents according to their application to the *jāti*s among the phonemes (*varṇa*s), there are the acute (*udātta*), the grave (*anudātta*), the circumflex (*svarita*), and the tremulous (*kampita*). *Kāku* is of two kinds: expectant (*sākāṅkṣā*) and non-expectant (*nirākāṅkṣā*).

This is because a sentence may be either expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) or non-expectant (*nirākāṅkṣa*). A sentence whose meaning is not fully established is designated as "expectant," whereas a sentence whose meaning is fully established is called "non-expectant. (111)

In that context, "with expectancy" (*sākāṃkṣa*) refers to [a melody] beginning with *tārā* and ending with *mandrā*, whose meaning is not fixed, whose phonetic ornaments (*varṇālaṅkāra*) have not been finalized, and which resides in the registers of the throat and chest. "Without expectancy" (*nirākāṃkṣa*)...

The emphasis lies in these [syllables], but not in the vowels; however, the purpose for their separate enumeration is shown in the sixth [chapter] as being for the inclusion of the intermediate utterances (*antarālāpa*).
Having thus established the production of the nature of *kāku*, [the author now describes] its operation regarding the object of meaning.
Demonstrating the sequence of the enumeration, he says: "The *kāku* is of two kinds. Regarding the phrase "of a sentence":

where a sentence is expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), there is *kāku*; likewise, the expectancy residing in the speaker is metaphorically attributed to the sentence. And that [expectancy] is determined by the force of context and other such factors. Its specific objectivity—

And that [expectancy] is understood from that very [sentence]. Thus he says: "A sentence whose meaning is not yet complete. A sentence is *nirākāṅkṣa* (complete/without expectancy) when the very meaning that is cognized from it by the force of convention is such that it can be determined—either as deficient or as excessive—by the force of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); the opposite of that is [a sentence with expectancy].
[The sentence] is expectant.

Having thus established the nature of a sentence, he says "therein, that which is expectant," etc., in order to express the *kāku* (intonation) residing therein. That which is stated as expectant, having its meaning not yet fully determined, begins with a *manda* [tone].

It should be recited with the *tāra* [intonation] completed. Regarding how many qualifiers of action there are therein, he says "situated in the throat and chest" (*kaṇṭhoraḥsthānagata*). Likewise, the vowels such as the acute (*udātta*) and so forth, and the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) such as high, low, and bright (*dīpta*), remain incomplete, being merely half-touched.

"Where [something] has been abandoned" (*tyaktā yatra*) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Thus, that particular quality of sound which is recited as an adverbial modifier within the sentence is *kāku*. Alternatively, it may be explained through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); for a property (*dharma*) does not appear independently, but rather as residing solely in its substratum (*dharmin*).
In that case, it refers either to a specific quality that is distinct from the object itself, or to a quality residing in something other than that object, or to the absence of that object;
and so it is stated on page 392:
The name is the assigned meaning, adorned with the colors of the vowels placed upon the head,
beginning with the low (*mandra*) and ending with the high (*tāra*).
Now, as for the six ornaments (*alaṅkāra*):
High, bright, deep, low, rapid, and slow—these are indeed the ornaments of recitation; now learn their defining characteristics. (113)

*Ucca* (high) refers to a sound located in the head region that is loud; it occurs in cases of speaking from a distance, astonishment, successive conversation, calling from afar, frightening, or causing distress. *Dīpta* (intense) refers to a sound located in the head region that is even louder than the high tone; it occurs in cases of [sudden] interruption—

"Whatever was done by Rāma, that very same thing the wrathful son of Droṇa does"—here there is *kāku* (intonation). Because the syllables of the word "done" (*kṛta*) are uttered with a rising, trembling tone, and because the ornament of high intensity (*uccadīpta*) is not yet concluded, there arises through the power of *kāku* a shift to another meaning: "He does even more than this. This is that Ten-necked one (*daśakandhara*).

In the verse beginning with "miti," the interrogative intonation (*kāku*) associated with the phrase "then his son here, Aṅgada" conveys specific qualities appropriate to Vālin’s son that reside within [the speaker]. In the phrase "they will be at ease while I live," the interrogative intonation expresses a state of mental conviction (*bhāvanābhāva*), whereas the utterance of the words itself conveys a sense of possibility regarding the matter.
While performing [the action], it presents its object by means of a necessary negation.
Thus, this *arthakāku*, which consists of a gesture (*abhinaya*) that conveys the intended meaning of the matter, is expectant (*sākāṅkṣā*).
Its opposite is non-expectant (*nirākāṅkṣā*); in the case of the latter, the low tone (*mandra*) resides precisely at the head.
For we shall explain the establishment of high pitch (*tāra*) as being progressively higher and low pitch (*mandra*) as being progressively lower.
An *alaṅkāra* (ornament) is that by which the essential nature of the *kāku* (intonation) is accomplished;
and its essential nature consists of each of the three registers—upper, lower, and middle—individually.
In cases such as quarreling, disputing, resentment, shouting, assault, anger, heroism, pride, harsh and rough speech,
reviling, and wailing, the tone situated in the chest region is called *mandra*.

In cases of despondency, exhaustion, anxiety, longing, dejection, illness, play, deep wounds from weapons, fainting, intoxication, and the speaking of secret matters, that which is called the "low" (*nīca*) register resides in the chest; it is very low-pitched and is used for natural, informal speech.

In cases such as those afflicted by disease, exhaustion, fatigue, fear, falling, or fainting, the *druta* (quick) mode occurs when the breath is located in the throat. Furthermore, in cases of hurried speech, stammering, incoherent talk, fear, cold fever, terror, distress, or the reporting of urgent matters, the *vilambita* (slow/delayed) mode occurs when the breath is situated in the region of the throat.

This is because the acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), tremulous (*kampita*), and sustained (*nirvāha*) notes are produced through mental construction (*kalpanā*). Among these, the middle tone (*bhāma*) remains present everywhere even when there is no entry [into a specific state]. Thus, by means of this entry, each of the three places is taken up either upward or downward, resulting in six ornaments (*alaṅkāra*). In that regard:

The *tāra* (high pitch) is said to occur in the lower part of the head; its scope includes speaking from a distance and so forth, and it is described here as the *svarakāku*. However, when it occurs in the perception of wonder, that same [pitch] is the *rasakāku*; when intended to terrify another, that same [pitch] is the *vibhāvakāku*; and the *śrutikāku* is indeed a type of *svarakāku*.
By way of distinction, in the head (*śiras*) itself, the highest pitch (*tāra*) occurs in [actions such as] throwing upwards (*ūrdhvākṣepa*); here, the word *tāra* is an illustration for excellence.
For in this context, in [actions such as] throwing upwards, one must distinguish the three varieties—pitch (*śruti*), register (*vibhāva*), and tone (*kāku*)—according to their respective states.

In the upper part of the chest (*uras*), it is the low pitch (*mandra*); in the lower part of the chest itself, it is the lowest pitch (*mandratama*), which is "low" (*nīca*). In cases of dejection (*dainya*), [it is likewise].

Kākū attains a twofold nature: it is *rasakāku* through the offering of one's own mental state (*svacittavṛttyarpaṇāt*), and it is *vibhāvakāku* through the production of [aesthetic] form in another (*parasya rūpotpādanāt*). Both— (p.
And that [melody] is slow-paced (*stanumandra*),

and it is employed in [situations involving] love (*śṛṅgāra*), pathos (*karuṇa*), deliberation (*vitarkita*), reflection (*vicāra*), indignation (*amarṣa*), envy (*asūyitā*), discourse of indistinct meaning (*avyaktārthapravāda*), shame (*lajjā*), anxiety (*cintā*), threatening (*tarjana*), wonder (*vismaya*), the recitation of faults (*doṣānukīrtana*), and the affliction of chronic illness (*dīrgharoganipīḍanādi*).
In this regard, there are the following genealogical verses: || 114 ||
And in successive verbal disputes, harsh reproaches, the display of sharp and cruel gestures, as well as in agitation and weeping; || 115 ||
In the case of summoning someone who is out of sight, as well as in threatening, terrifying, speaking from a distance, and likewise in censuring; || 116 ||

Indeed, regarding these emotional states, the performers should always employ a modulated tone (*kāku*) that is elevated, brilliant, and swift, as it serves as the basis for various aesthetic sentiments.
In one who is diseased, afflicted by fever, tormented by fear, overwhelmed by cold, established in a religious vow, possessed of discursive thought, or severely wounded by weapons; || 118 ||

Because that [element] is emphasized there as the primary factor, whereas elsewhere both are disregarded, the designation is made solely according to the predominant part. "Speaking in one's natural state" (*svabhāvābhāṣaṇam*) refers to a case where the speaker has a hoarse or choked voice, being one who speaks while trembling with fear; such a person is called *trastapatita* (fallen into terror).

But on the occasion of fear, the *kākubhāva* (intonation) becomes indeed *dīptā* (bright/intense). The term *kaṇṭhagata* means produced in the upper part of the location of the throat; therefore, the very difference in location (*sthānabheda*) is the determining factor for its status as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). For this very reason, the laying down of the tempo (*laya*) is repeated by the word *tvarita*. [The word] *lallam* [is derived from] *laḍa*, meaning "to take delight" (*vilāsa*); thus, it is formed with the *kvip* suffix after the root *laḍ*.

Regarding the rule *karmālyupapade laḍayraikyaṃ* (when a word denoting an object is used as an upapada, the suffixes *laṭ* and *liṅ* are identical): "I think... [text missing] ...from me, the thinker, [he] thinks," by this—(p.
When speaking of secret matters, during reflection, or when established in ascetic practice,
the modulations of voice (kāku) should be made soft and low by those who employ dramatic performance.
When [the characters] Lallā and Manmanā are afflicted by fear or overwhelmed by cold,
the performers of drama should employ both slow and rapid modulations of the voice (kākubhāṣā).
In the pursuit of what has been seen and lost, likewise upon hearing what is desirable or undesirable, in the manifestation of desired objects, and similarly in thought and meditation; || 121 ||
In cases of insanity, in envy, and likewise in reproach;
in the proclamation of matters of obscure meaning, and similarly in the context of storytelling (122).
In successive discourse, in an action endowed with excellence, in a transformation, in illness, in anger, and likewise in suffering and grief; || 123 ||
In expressions of wonder and indignation, as well as in joy and lamentation,
the *kāku* (variation of tone) should indeed be slow, brilliant, and deep.

Others maintain that it is characterized by being heard with a nasal resonance (*anunāsika*). The teachers (*upādhyāya*) state that *lalla* and *manmana* occur when applied to female characters in contexts such as the playful teasing or consoling of children, and in situations such as refusing the advances of others with words like "let go" (*muñca*). Furthermore, it will be stated in the summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*) that a low-pitched intonation (*mandrā*) also occurs here.

*Ātyayika* refers to a task that must be accomplished quickly. *Āyasta* refers to agitation. *Vilambita* is produced in the lower part of the throat region. *Lalla* is simply a state of indistinctness. *Pravāda* is an expression of unclear meaning—where it is well known in the world as "internal" (*antaraṅga*), such that others may or may not understand it.

The intention of the speaker is that [the sound] here belongs neither to itself nor to another. The meaning is that among the ornaments, the three locations—high (*ucca*), brilliant (*dīpta*), and rapid (*druta*)—are accepted here as appropriate.
Whether composed primarily of short syllables or likewise composed of long syllables, the *kāku* should be raised and brilliant; it must be employed there by the performers. (125)
In those cases where the meaning is gentle and associated with pleasant states,
a tone that is low-pitched and slow is prescribed.
Even among those [passages] which may be sharp, harsh, brilliant, or elevated, performers should apply the recitation in such a way that it is endowed with various bases. 127.
In the sentiments of humor, the erotic, and the pathetic, a slow and modulated intonation (kāku) is desired;
whereas in the heroic, the furious, and the marvelous, a high and brilliant pitch is praised.

In the terrifying and the loathsome, the *drutā* and *nicā* [tones] are prescribed; thus should the *kāku* (modulation of voice) imbued with these emotional states (*bhāva*) and aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) be employed by performers. 129.

Now, there are six ancillaries (aṅgas): interruption (viccheda), offering (arpaṇa), emission (visarga), connection (anubandha), illumination (dīpana), and pacification (prasamana). Among these, "interruption" refers to that which is produced by a pause.
Then, for the purpose of summarizing everything, he says: "those which are joined with gentle objects. Like the moon (soma), they are refreshing.

The term *saumya* is derived from the class beginning with *śākhādi*. The phrase "the causes of happiness" and "that which is to be produced as happiness" are subsumed under the compound *sukhabhāvakṛta* through various types of compounding (*samāsabheda*). The expression "endowed with various substrata" means having established [the notes] in various locations; this refers to the difference in positions (*sthānabheda*) of the modulations (*kākubhiḥ*).

It has been stated that [the *kākustha*] is that which effects completion (*paryāptatākārī*). Therefore, because the *kākustha* alone is predominant, he concludes with it by saying "Now, the members" (*athāṅgāni*), and so forth.
He indicates another topic by saying: "In that regard, during the utterance of phonemes (*varṇa*), that which is devoid of the sound of the phoneme..."
"The elders say that time is the basis for the conventional usage of the limbs [of the year]. For that time is sixfold;
and from that, there is 'more,' then again 'beginning and middle,' then again 'more,' for this is indeed the division.
At the beginning it is middling and small, and at the end of the middle, there is the *ārṣaṇa*."

(397) *Arpaṇa* is that which is recited with a playful, sweet, and charming voice, as if filling the entire theater; it is called *arpaṇa*. *Visarga* is the placement of a sentence. *Anubandha* is... [text continues]

In other places as well, there may be a pause or a lack of breath. *Dīpana* (illumination) is that which is beautiful in three places and possesses an increasing tone. *Praśamana* (pacification) is the descent of high-pitched notes into a state of tranquility through the absence of irregularity in tone (*avaisvarya*).

Among these, that which occurs within the *rasa* (melodic flow) in a *vākya* (phrase)—being fast at the beginning, slow in the middle, and the reverse [slow at the beginning and fast in the middle]—is called *visarga*. When there are many [notes], it is fast; when moderate, it is medium; and when slightly fast at the end, it is an *anubandha*. This applies to the three places (*tristhāna*).

The author of the *Saṃgraha* states: "The three tempos—quick, medium, and slow—are respectively *dīpana* (exciting) when they are always ascending, and *praśamana* (soothing) when the reverse is the case; furthermore, they constitute a single form through their consistent execution.
It is according to this very opinion that [others] explain the definitions. However, this is incorrect.

There is no restrictive cause for this meaning [to be determined] by tempos such as fast (*druta*), medium (*madhya*), and so forth, nor by the reality of the tempo itself; for when the usage of tempo is equal, there is no reason for time [itself] to be unequal. Furthermore, the distinctions regarding the disparity of tempo have not been stated merely through the conceptualization of three parts in relation to the consciousness of the sentence.

In the case of verses such as the *bhujaṅgavijṛmbhitā*, because there is the possibility of an infinite number of parts, and because within three parts there is an infinity resulting from the two-fold and three-fold divisions of the fast (*druta*), medium (*madhya*), and slow (*vilambita*) tempos, the restriction to a fixed number of six [syllables] would be violated. This is evident in the first sections of the verse beginning with "kvākāryam."

A middle tempo (*madhyalaya*) is also observed; in the western regions such as Sindh and others, which provide a resting place for the bliss born of recollection, there is a practice characterized by a slow tempo (*vilambita*), thus constituting a distinction between the two tempos.
Furthermore, even when calculating the three divisions [of time], there arise infinite varieties through both equality and inequality.
How could this be? Why is all of this not subsumed under the very term "dissolution" (*laya*)?

Therefore, at the time of reciting the jewel-like words that serve as the basis for the sūtras, the sixfold set of limbs consisting of those six dharmas mentioned at the beginning is stated; and likewise in the middle.

Interruption or non-interruption, for their part, are disjunction and continuity; intensity or lack of intensity are these two, emission and release; ascent or descent are illumination and quiescence. Thus, through existence and non-existence, increase and decrease, and ascent and descent, sound possesses six varieties.
The application of the statement— therein.

In the case of *hāsya* (the comic) and *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic), the recitation (*pāṭhya*) should be characterized by expectation, offering, interruption, intensification (*dīpana*), and pacification (*praśamana*). In *karuṇa* (the pathetic), it should be characterized by intensification and pacification.
In *vīra* (the heroic), *raudra* (the furious), and *adbhuta* (the marvelous), it should abound in interruption, pacification, intensification, and continuity.

In the *bībhatsa* (disgust) and *bhayānaka* (terror) rasas, [the recitation] is characterized by the release and interruption of breath. For all of these, there is an application based on low (*mandra*), middle (*madhya*), and high (*tāra*) registers, occurring across three places of articulation. Among these, for speaking from a distance, one uses the high register with the head; for those not too far, the middle register with the throat; and for those nearby, the low register with the chest.

"One should employ the recitation" means that one should not go from low (*mandra*) to high (*tāra*), nor from high to low. This refers to the "abandonment" (*nyāsa*), which is to say, the relinquishing or disregard of the *tanana* (the continuous extension).

It should be understood in all cases that this arises from a discordance in sound (*dhvani*) regarding the specific intermediate pitches (*antarāla-śruti-viśeṣa*) prescribed by their respective tones (*svara*).

The words *hāsya* (the comic) and others are accepted as including their respective transitory states (*vyabhicārin*). Consequently, it should be understood that when there is another rasa within a different rasa, or when there is a change in voice (*kāku*) within the locus of those transitory states, [this occurs]. By the phrase "of all," etc., [the author] indicates the fundamental distinction of the bases (*sthāna*) of the subordinate elements (*aṅga*).

He reminds [the reader]. Therein, by the words "situated at a distance" (*dūrastha*) and so forth, he indicates the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of the injunctive statements (*viniyoga-vākya*) within the object of indication (*lakṣya*).

For instance, in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment, that collection of elements such as the high-pitched (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*) accents, the delivery (*arpaṇa*), and the pauses (*viccheda*), as well as the slow tempo (*vilambita*), constitute the ornament (*alaṅkāra*).

When speaking to someone situated at a distance, this should be explained with the following intent: one should perform the speech by relying on either the fifth note (*pañcama*) or another note residing in the head-register (*śirasthāna*), mixed with fourfold divisions of the tonic notes (*aṃśasvara*). Otherwise, it would be improper speech.
Otherwise, there would be redundancy with the passage beginning "When [the object] is distant, [one should place] the head," and so forth.

Now, he states the remainder of what is to be said regarding the intensification (*dīpana*) and pacification (*praśamana*): "One should not go from the low (*mandra*) to the high (*tāra*)," and so on.
This means that one should not proceed from the very low (*mandratara*) to the high (*tāra*), nor from the highest (*tāratama*) to the low (*mandra*).
In the *Uddeśagrantha* itself, certain tempos (*laya*) and pauses (*virāma*) are mentioned.
Among these, the three tempos—fast (*druta*), medium (*madhya*), and slow (*vilambita*)—are to be applied according to the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*). Therein:

In the *hāsya* (comic) and *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasas, the tempo is medium; in the *karuṇa* (pathetic), it is slow; and in the *vīra* (heroic), *raudra* (furious), *adbhuta* (marvelous), *bībhatsa* (disgusting), and *bhayānaka* (terrifying), it is fast. || 131 ||

You must not perform for me that which is enjoyed by all people;

Others, however, say: since time as a whole cannot be deliberated upon, there is no purpose in specifying it; rather, the wise consider that this dissolution (*laya*) is accepted precisely through interruption (*viccheda*). Interruption is cessation (*virāma*), and as for how long that [cessation] lasts, by that very duration dissolution is also accepted. Therefore, this examination of interruption has been described.
In this context, "there" (*tatra*) means at a point of interruption; a pause (*virāma*) should be made by him [the reciter] for the purpose of completing the sense.

"Sense" (*artha*) refers to the meaning of an intermediate sentence. The performer (*prayoktṛ*) likewise [must do so].

It has been stated here as well that one should not be dependent on the poet; rather, for the sake of the meaning, a pause (virāma) must be made. Here, "number" is an illustration of a restrictive rule, referring to one, two, or three.

Anticipating the objection that "in this way, the absence of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is a flaw," he states—demonstrating instead that this is actually an ornament: "For in sūtras, in [treatises on] sprouts, and likewise in figurative expressions (*upacāra*), words consist of few syllables in poetry. This is in many ways.

Where both hands are separated, there the gaze should be directed accordingly;
the vocal acting (vācikābhinaya) should be performed with pauses that reveal the meaning.

If there are words consisting of very few syllables that are uncompounded, as in "bahvakṣarapade daridrāśca kiṃ yaste" and so forth, there is no occurrence of the *sūcā* or *aṅkura* figures in the middle. [For example:

and for the heroine who remains hidden while observing him himself and listening likewise, there arises a seed of cessation— a sense of wonder— preceded by the indication of a desire to kiss him once again.

Because, in cases such as the circumambulation of what has been recited (*ucitaparikramaṇa*), there is an absence of variety due to the connection of words that occur earlier and consist of few syllables.
Now, he demonstrates the predominance of this member (*aṅga*) of the pause (*viccheda*) with the words "Thus, the pause" (*evaṃ virāma*), and so forth.

The phrase "in this" (*asmin*) means that when there is a pause (*virāma*), the gesture (*abhinaya*) can be employed according to its proper scope; and that [scope] is understood from the pause. In these and other such movements, as well as in the examination of the hands, the determination of the meaning is indeed accomplished through ornamentation and its cessation. || 137 ||

Thus, the vowels, their sequence, the limits, the three places of articulation, the basis, and the nature [of sound]—such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth—[are established].

One should recite the text to be chanted according to the prescribed rules— free from poetic defects, rich in defining characteristics, endowed with aesthetic qualities, and joined with appropriate vowels and ornaments.
All those ornaments and pauses that are prescribed for recitation in Sanskrit should likewise be employed in the recitation of women in Prakrit.
In this way, this [performance] is produced by the voice itself, endowed with the artistic divisions (kalās), time-measures (kāla), and rhythmic pauses (laya);
it should be employed as the recitation (pāṭhya) by performers in the enactment of the ten forms (daśarūpa).
The various types of intonation have been explained correctly and in due order;
hereafter, I shall expound the classification of the ten dramatic forms (daśarūpa). || 150 ||

The distinction [of *svara-bheda*] consists in a change of tone within that very same utterance, such as the emergence of another quality like a cawing sound (*kāku*) when there is no intention to express a different meaning; for a difference in pitch caused by the parts of the body and so forth is not an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). This chapter’s connection with the subject matter of the preceding chapter is established by the statement beginning with "free from poetic defects" (*varjitaṃ kāvyadoṣaiḥ*).
He demonstrates this:

by stating "ornaments, pauses, and so forth," he extends the application of the rules for *kāku* (intonation) formulated for *saṃskṛta* to *prākṛta* as well, which constitutes the subject matter of the chapter on *prākṛta*. Thus, he concludes the meaning of the chapter.

He outlines the subject matter of the forthcoming chapter with the words "daśarūpa" (the ten forms): the conclusion is that whatever is to be recited in the composition of the ten dramatic forms (*daśarūpa*) should be applied according to these three modes. The Eighteenth Chapter of the Nāṭyaśāstra:
O Brahmins, I shall now expound the classification of the ten types of dramatic compositions (daśarūpa).
By name, by action, and likewise by application. || 1 ||
I bow to that eye of the Lord, whose abode is the essence of radiant light, by which this form— which shines forth in manifold ways— is never truly brought into being.

The connection [of this work] has already been stated as follows: "The nature of the composition of the *kārikās* and so forth, which assist the ten types of dramatic forms (*daśarūpa*), must be explained.
To the question, "Since that [nature] will be set forth, what is the purpose of stating this [connection]?"—the purpose of this is now demonstrated.
Someone might raise this doubt regarding the summary of the essence of the Sūtras, beginning with the verse: "Rasa, bhāva... (A-6.10).

Since even the name "ten forms" (*daśarūpa*) has not been heard [before], how can it be said that there is a recitation regarding the prescription of the ten forms? To him, he replies: "I shall explain. That object which is "formed" (*rūpyate*), meaning perceived directly, is called a "form" (*rūpa*) because poetry expresses it; thus, the classification of the ten forms is conceived.

The phrase "from this" (*asmāt*) refers to the aphorism concerning the classification of the ten forms (*daśarūpa-vikalpana*). Therefore, this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), meaning "the ten forms" (*daśarūpam*).

Anticipating the objection that if it were a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the expression "poetry consisting of ten forms" (*daśarūpaṃ kāvyam*) would exclude other varieties, [the author] employs a *dvigu* compound and the inclusion of the term "pātra" and so forth.

That [explanation] was merely an effort to explain that very point. This is the meaning: since the division between the meanings of the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) in the vocal word is conceived based on the Sūtra, this portion concerning speech is described in detail; thus, that very Sūtra becomes described and expanded through the Vivaraṇa.
"Nothing is defined that has not been previously mentioned. Thus, by way of enumeration (*uddeśa*) according to name, and by way of definition (*lakṣaṇa*) according to function:
"The *nāṭaka*, the *saṃpraharaṇa*, the *aṅka*, and the *vyāyoga*... (p. 407).
The Bhāṇa, the Samavakāra, the Vīthī, the Prahasana, and the Ḍima. || 2 ||
And the *īhāmṛga* is to be known as the tenth in the characteristics of drama (*nāṭyalakṣaṇa*).
I shall explain the characteristics of these [ten types] in their proper sequence. (3)

The *vṛttis* are considered the mother of all poetic compositions (*kāvyas*). By means of this [definition], there is an exclusion of heterogeneous things; thus, the definition of action (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) is an excellent and appropriate application (*yoga*), namely a mutual relationship, as in the case of the application of the definitions of *prakaraṇa* and *nāṭaka*.

The division of the *nāṭikā* into its constituent plot elements (*itivṛtta*) is already included within the definition itself; therefore, this is not a [separate] performance (*prayoga*). The phrase "and likewise" (*tathā ca*) means that by that very mode of performance, another distinction arising from the variety of mutual relationships should be imagined. In the interpretation of "for the sake of performance" (*prayogāya*) as "from performance" (*prayogataḥ*), the term "from performance" would be entirely redundant.

In the aforementioned explanation, however, the inclusion of the *ṭotaka*, *saṭṭaka*, *rāsaka*, and so forth—defined by Kohala and others—is for the purpose of illustrating the *nāṭikā*. Regarding that, he first states the enumeration, beginning with "the *nāṭaka*," and so on.

By the word "with" (*saha*) in the phrase "together with the *prakaraṇa*," the similarity between the *nāṭaka* and the *prakaraṇa* in terms of acts (*aṅka*), interludes (*praveśaka*), junctures (*sandhi*), and other such elements is indicated.

The author states the purpose of the treatise: "The meaning of the names shall be explained precisely according to their definitions. Furthermore, although works such as the Purāṇas exist which provide instruction and demonstrate the connection between actions and their fruits, those consist for the most part of various high and low, undetermined verses from different authors; here, however, some things are to be employed and some are to be indicated.

Some things are to be inferred and some are to be disregarded; such is the application of variety. The arrangement of the junctures (*sandhi*) and so forth, as well as the ten dramatic forms (*daśarūpa*) with their purposes—this, however, is for the most part trivial fruit, as that has already been stated previously.

For this [work], such as the *itihāsa* and so forth, the distinction lies in its essence being the bliss produced by the immersion into aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) awakened through direct contemplation (*pratyakṣabhāvanā*).

Thus it should be inferred. Furthermore, since the classification of the needle and so forth exists even in the *Itihāsas* and other such works, it has already been stated that the fruit of this recitation is not merely the *Daśarūpaka*, but rather its culmination in actual performance (*prayoga*). In that regard, the nature of poetry as a "great generality" (*mahāsāmānya*) is treated in the chapter on the definition of poetry.
He shows that the intermediate general definition (avāntarasāmānyalakṣaṇa), namely "the produced" (kṛta), must be stated immediately after the enumeration (uddeśa).
Furthermore, the meaning of the sequence is that the general definitions come first, followed by the specific definitions (viśeṣalakṣaṇa) according to the order of enumeration.
In this regard, he states the general definition: "It is the matrix (mātṛkā) of all poetic works.

On this point, some say: "The general definition of the ten forms (daśarūpaka) is their origin from dramatic modes (vṛtti), because the modes and their constituent elements consist of performance (abhinaya), which is impossible within [pure] poetic works. This is incorrect. Let it be...
The meaning of the poem: For it has been stated by us in the very first chapter that the entire cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) is pervaded by the four modes of conduct.
For it is from these that this tenfold form [of drama] has issued forth through its application.

Furthermore, if the term *vṛtti* were used exclusively in reference to the subject matter of dramatic performance (*abhineya*), then the entire discussion in the chapter on *vṛtti* regarding the origin of the *vṛttis*— beginning with the verse "That which rests upon each of the *vṛttis*" (20.15)— would be irrelevant; for the Blessed One is not a performer (*abhinetṛ*), but rather...

It is merely an obsession with one's own activity. Furthermore, when the word "all" (*sarva*) refers to the subject matter at hand—namely, drama and so forth—the first half of the verse would be redundant. As for the statements: "by the Bharatas who bear their own names" (20.15), "in which there is much singing, dancing, and instrumental music" (20.47), and "possessing the representation of speech and gesture" (20.39).

The claim that the *Bhārata-vyavahāra* and the application of *Gītābhinaya* constitute various types of dramatic representation (*nāṭya*) is likewise insignificant; for the definition of the *Vṛttis* is simply this: "that which is primarily speech" (A-20). This alone is the definition of *Bhāratī*.
Everything else is merely an illustration of its application, as we shall explain in that very context.

The constituent elements of *vṛtti* (dramatic style) are indeed present in all poetic compositions. Now, one might ask: "In that case, how can being born from *vṛtti* be defined as the characteristic of the ten types of drama (*daśarūpaka*)? It is said [in the definition] "by way of performance" (*prayogataḥ*), which has precisely this meaning. Thus, the sense is this: although [these elements] exist in all [works], whether they are dramatic performances (*abhineya*) or non-dramatic compositions (*anabhineya*),...

The *vṛttis* (styles) are held to be the mothers of poems; from them—though they abide in the poet’s heart as the very form of the expressed meaning (*vācya*)—the poem is produced. Nevertheless, because it is being employed in practice, [the author] intends to show its fitness for application, and thus [derives it] from the *vṛttis*.

The meaning is that you are the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the ten forms (*daśarūpa*), which expresses the four modes of action (*vṛtti*) suitable for direct aesthetic realization (*pratyakṣabhāvanā*) within the dramatic poetry (*abhineyakāvya*) that has flowed forth. It is the "form" (*rūpa*) of the ten [types of works], beginning with the *nāṭaka*.
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Others, however, say: ten forms are possible for each single form;
thus, the constituent elements of the *vīthī* occur everywhere.

And there is the application of *bhāṇa*, which consists of speaking in accordance with the words of another, as in the case of "speaking to the air" (*ākāśabhāṣita*), such as "What do you say? and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that it is a poetic composition (*kāvyam*) of such a form, possessing these ten characteristics. For this very reason, it is not an entire dramatic work (*prabandha*) like a *nāṭaka*, but rather—
A drama possesses a certain form [of the ten types], yet it is designated as such because of its abundance of constituent parts of those characteristics.

For this very reason, the number ten is not intended as a restrictive division, which would necessitate the exclusion of genres such as the *saṭṭaka* and others; for even in those cases, there is indeed the application of the characteristics of the ten forms. We shall elaborate upon this at the appropriate occasion.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the general definition [of verbal testimony] is 'that which conveys activity suitable for performance,' then, since nothing other than activity is conceivable [in this context], these [words] would have no specific definition at all. To dispel this doubt, the following is stated as the specific [definition]:
Just as notes attain the state of scales through their birth-classes (*jāti*) and auditory intervals (*śruti*),
so indeed do poetic compositions arise through the various distinctions of *vṛtti*.
Just as the two musical scales, Ṣaḍja and Madhyama,
possess full tones and are perfected through all their modes, so too are these two poetic compositions.

In order to demonstrate the scope for [the application of] a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*), he says: "by means of *jātis* and *śrutis*, etc. By employing an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) to illustrate the subject at hand, he also elucidates that which is yet to be explained; thus, he presented an example established within the very same system (*samānatantra*). Among the notes (*svaras*), there is a *jāti* determined by the division into the ten [categories] beginning with *graha*. [For instance, a note may be] red or not red.

Or rather, *dhvani* (sound) is the location, and the interval between them is *śruti* (interval), based on the etymological derivation as object (*adhikaraṇa*), locus (*karma*), or instrument (*karaṇa*). For indeed, the rule "for a feminine [noun], the suffixes *khalan* and *āP*" is not observed in actual usage (*lakṣya*).
Among those, there are seven *jātis*, beginning with *ṣāḍjī*; of these, there are four *śrutis* for *pañcama* and three for *dhaivata*.
"Three"—this refers to the Ṣaḍja-grāma. The eleven *jātis* beginning with Gāndhārī, along with Pañcama having three *śrutis* and Dhaivata having four *śrutis*, constitute the Madhyama-grāma.
In reality, however, a *grāma* is a collection of the notes beginning with Ṣaḍja. In that context, the plural "notes" (*svarāḥ*) is used in the sense of *śrutis*.

Those who know the target [of musical theory] maintain that there is no authoritative evidence for the claim that in the Madhyama-grāma, the śruti abandoned by Pañcama is enjoyed only by Dhaivata; rather,
all [the notes] having two or three śrutis are made to possess an equal number of additional śrutis through the elevation of the śrutis.

And because there are thirty-four *śrutis* for the *kākali* and *antara* [intervals], there is a variety among all notes (*svaras*) produced by *śrutis*. This we shall explain in its proper place, so let it suffice here. However, by this illustration, the following is stated: even though there is no difference in their being a collection of notes (*svara-samudāya-rūpa*), among the notes—
By way of synonyms,
through distinctions such as being first, primary, small, large, complete, incomplete, ascending, final, and middle,
just as one scale-type (ṣaḍjagrāma) is different from another, namely the Madhyamagrāma, so it is exactly thus.

A *rūpaka* is distinguished from other *rūpakas* by a set of ten factors, such as primacy and predominance, which correspond to the *svaras*. Just as the *pañcama* note, being either four-semitone (*catuḥśruti*) or three-semitone (*triśruti*),
brings about a difference between *grāmas*, so too that very *vṛtti*— which corresponds to the *śrutis*— is sometimes complete through its constituent parts.
In some cases, there is even a deficiency [of notes]; thus, this classification of *rūpaka* has been shown by the two [verses] beginning with "by the *jātis* and *śrutis*.
Now, he briefly states the classification of *vṛtti*: "the two *grāmas* consist of complete scales.

Since the two [melodic types], which are based on the *jātis*, possess six or seven notes (*ṣāḍava* and *auḍuvika*) through their connection with partial notes (*aṃśaka*), there is indeed a deficiency of notes [in them] by way of the *jātis*.
The Ṣaḍajagrāmarāga (p. 410), as well as the Prakaraṇa and the Nāṭaka, should be known [in this manner].
It is completely perfected in all its functions and serves as the support for various bonds. || 7 ||
The Vīthī, the Samavakāra, as well as the Ihamṛga, the Utsṛṣṭikāṅka, the Vyāyoga, the Bhāṇa, the Prahasana, and the Ḍima. (8)
