Some maintain that here the term *grāma* refers to the *madhyamagrāmarāga*; however, that is incorrect, for in this context the word *grāma* denotes a collection of *jātis*. Even if there is a deficiency of notes (*nyūnasvaratā*) regarding the partial scale (*aṃśaka*), what loss is there to the completeness of the collection as a whole? Therefore, this is the meaning here:

Just as there is the production of various musical notes— possessing full or incomplete distinctions of pitch— through the conceptualization of two villages or mountain regions from a collection of sounds that is most beautiful due to its diverse arrangement and objects of perception, so it is with the *nāṭaka* and *prakaraṇa*.

The classification of varieties of *rūpaka* that are deficient in *vṛtti* is established by means of the *pūrṇavṛtti* and *vṛttyaṅga*. Thereafter, he states the *rūpaka*s deficient in *vṛtti*, beginning with "vīthī" and so forth. While it would have been sufficient to say "the remaining *rūpaka*s," the fact that he mentions each name individually indicates that there are other *rūpaka*s not mentioned here as well.

For this very reason, the enumeration of specific varieties of *rūpaka* has emerged from these [definitions], and thus it serves merely as an illustration of the definition. Consequently, through the application, option, or combination of the modes (*vṛtti*) and the constituent parts of those modes (*vṛttyaṅga*), many varieties of *rūpaka* arise. Of these, further—

By Kohala and others, only the names were set forth; however, it is precisely by means of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) that they are here subsumed. Therefore, the rule is that only the *nāṭaka* and *prakaraṇa* possess all the dramatic styles (*vṛtti*), and not the reverse;
for this is evident from the observation of the *mudrārākṣasa*, which lacks the *kaiśikī* style, and the *kṛtyārāvaṇa* drama.
Regarding the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, some maintain that only the *Sāttvatī* and *Ārabhaṭī* modes of dramatic style (*vṛtti*) are observed there.

Others, however, argue that even in that case, there must necessarily be an entry of other styles; for if it were perceived as being restricted solely to limited styles, then even if it were incomplete in its stylistic range, it would result in a discordant composition.

Precisely because it possesses the complete perfection of all its constituent parts, the *nāṭaka* (drama) and the *prakaraṇa* (play) are superior. For instance, some [teachers], following the well-known tradition, observe that the student is instructed through a *nāṭaka* whose plot is based on established history. However, others [observe] that regarding a subject matter already well-known, the student wonders, "What is this unprecedented thing? and thus [is instructed] through another form of dramatic representation (*rūpakāntara*).

All that appears as such [the world] is dependent upon the curiosity for new objects and events; thus, the disciple is disciplined by means of a *prakaraṇa* (dramatic work) whose subject matter is something to be produced. And his discipline regarding all human goals—namely dharma, artha, kāma, and even apavarga (liberation)—occurs in that manner, provided that the entire operation conducive to those ends is present.
One should have these forms fashioned without the Kaiśikī style. Hereafter, I shall explain the various types of poetic compositions.
It has as its subject matter a well-known story and features a well-known and noble protagonist;
it is supported by all dramatic activities and possesses fullness of style.
A work with only two or three styles and so forth does not constitute a *nāṭaka*; rather, it is merely a different form that bears its semblance.
In that case, even though the Kaiśikī style is absent, we shall describe the characteristics of the *samavakāra* just as there is a presence of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment;
for, if there is no difference between the *nāṭaka* and the *prakaraṇa* in terms of their possessing all the dramatic styles (*vṛtti*), what then is the distinction when the Kaiśikī is absent?

Anticipating the objection—"If [the components] are indistinguishable, what is the mutual distinction between the *vīthī* and the others?"—he demonstrates the definition of the specific distinctions implied by the word "action" (*karman*) with the words beginning "henceforth" (*ata ūrdhvam*). That [distinction] is the connection that constitutes a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) through a relationship of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*). It is the bond of composition (*bandhana*) of the poem.

"I shall explain that specific characteristic by which it is conceptualized. The *nāṭaka* (drama) is even more preeminent than the *prakaraṇa* (play), for the imaginative construction of a plot relies upon what is well-known; this is because its foundation is experience.
Even poetic conceits (*utprekṣā*) consist merely in the independent joining together of things that have already been established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

[They] act [as if] "a six-tusked elephant is running in the sky. Therefore, he first provides the definition of drama (*nāṭaka*), which demonstrates objects established by means of proof such as history (*itihāsa*) and so forth, by saying "having as its subject a well-known matter" (*prakhyātavastuviṣaya*), and so on. That matter (*vastu*) which exists in [works] such as the *Mahābhārata* is its subject (*viṣaya*).

Even in that case, if something remains somewhat unfamiliar, Śrī Śaṅkuka says that the term "renowned and noble" (*prakhyātodātta*) is used to exclude it. However, the Teachers (*upādhyāyāḥ*) have stated as follows: "The meaning is already covered by the phrase 'having a renowned subject matter' (*prakhyātavastuviṣaya*);
for in this context, renown occurs through a threefold kind of fame: that such-and-such a person is a doer of such-and-such a deed."

Regarding the phrase "another country": therein, an object renowned for its excellence is likewise a region such as Mālava or Pāñcāla; for even for a universal monarch like Vatsarāja, in a territory other than Kauśāmbī, there is that which is constant [in its depiction] unless there is the introduction of another matter.

Detailed description leads to a distaste for that [subject], because the destruction of its established reputation obstructs comprehension; what then can be said of the savoring of aesthetic flavor (*rasacarvaṇā*)? Thus, two kinds of renown have been stated;
by the phrase "famous and noble" (*prakhyātodātta*), a third kind of renown is expressed. By "noble" (*udātta*), one who is fit for the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is meant. Therefore—
The four types of heroes— *dhīralalita*, *dhīrapraśānta*, *dhīroddhata*, and *dhīrodātta*—
as well as the life stories of royal sages (*rājarṣi*) and those involving divine beings, [should be depicted]. || 10 ||

That which is endowed with various manifestations, such as the play of supernatural powers and other qualities, and is enriched by *aṅkas*, *praveśakas*, and so forth, is indeed called a *nāṭaka*. || 11 ||

Even [the lives of] kings are included. By the phrase "of the lineage of royal sages" (*rājarṣivaṃśya*), it is meant that even if a subject is famous, if it is something appropriate for the virtuous belonging to the lineage of kings equal to sages, then—despite its fame—it is not [to be used], because the conduct of gods, being full of the power of boons and the like, is unfit for instruction in means; thus, neither of these two [categories] [is to be used].

The phrase "to be bound by necessity" indicates a prohibition in terms of its result. The expression "kings like sages" is a *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison). The term "in which there is conduct befitting that lineage" is a *bahuvrīhi*. Furthermore, the conduct of the gods is not to be described in such a manner in every respect; rather, it is [described] by virtue of being the locus of the divine.

"Upagama" refers to the acceptance [of the deity] in the form of manifest banners, leaders, and so forth. Likewise, in the *Nāgānanda*, through the direct realization of the Blessed Lady who is overflowing with perfect compassion, proficiency is born. Indeed, for those whose minds are permeated by uninterrupted devotion, deities such as these become gracious.
Therefore, the practice of means should be performed preceded by the propitiation of the deity. However, if the conduct of the gods is described as the primary subject,
it must nevertheless be composed in accordance with the sentiments (rasas) of deception, pathos, wonder, or terror.

That would result merely in human behavior; on the contrary, the imposition of [human] intellect upon the gods would undermine their established majesty. Furthermore, the fault already mentioned applies there: in the absence of deception and the like, what variety could there be in such delight, since this [delight] is the very criterion [of poetry]? For this very reason, even "resonance with the heart" (hṛdayasaṃvāda) is difficult to find in the case of the deeds of the gods.

And for them there is no suffering such that it would require instruction on the means of remediation. Furthermore, the heroine, though divine, is not contradictory [to the rules], as in the case of Urvaśī, since her conduct is implied by the conduct of the hero alone. As for cases like the *ḍima* and others where divine beings serve as heroes, we shall explain our intention later. Thus, even a subject matter endowed with the three types of renown [is permissible].

Since it does not become fruitless for the sake of instruction, he says: "Endowed with various manifestations," meaning endowed with the diverse forms of the manifestations of *dharma*, *artha*, *kāma*, and *mokṣa* which constitute the fruits. Furthermore, since *artha* and *kāma* are desired by all people, their abundance is to be shown therein.

"He speaks by means of the display of supernatural powers (*ṛddhivilāsa*) and so forth" means: *ṛddhi* is the prosperity of wealth, such as sovereignty and the like; *vilāsa* indicates desire; and the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) denotes the primary [element]. Thus, the meaning is that it is endowed with the attainment of fruits characterized primarily by those [qualities]. Having given his entire kingdom to the Brahmins, that king—

One should not attach such results as "the stage of forest-dwelling (vānaprastha) must be undertaken" [to the hero's actions]. For the world is generally intent upon visible and immediate benefits; thus, the audience's appreciation for those [results] would become dull. By the word "qualities" (guṇaiḥ), the secondary activities belonging to the antagonist (pratināyaka)—which are to be discarded—are indicated. These are the misfortunes (apāya)—
That which consists of the various deeds of kings, featuring manifold sentiments, emotional states, and gestures produced by the arising of pleasure and pain, is indeed called a *nāṭaka*. (12)

The primary elements are those with which it is endowed. By refuting those positions that stand as prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*), the narrative of the hero—functioning as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—is brought to fulfillment; this results in the prosperity and abundance of the kingdom’s territories, treasury, and so forth.
The explanation is that festivals such as the *Kaumudī-mahotsava* constitute the "graces" (*vilāsa*), while matters such as peace and war constitute the "qualities" (*guṇa*).

The mere fruit of acquainting oneself with the *Cāṇakya-śāstra* is achieved through the inclusion of the entire mass of meaningful matters by means of the term "subject matter" (*vastu*) and the term "the life-story of one belonging to the lineage of royal sages. Furthermore, there are the acts (*aṅkas*) which serve as divisions for the sake of rest at the conclusion of intermediate subjects, and those [divisions] which arise by the force of specific circumstances.

The *praveśakas* are those who report the actions of persons whose deeds are not witnessed by the audience; the drama (*rūpaka*) named *Nāṭaka* is enriched by these. Therefore, he states its name: "that which is the conduct of kings. This means that because it concerns the conduct of kings—who are the subjects to be instructed—it belongs specifically to kings.

That which is called a *nāṭaka* (drama) brings about a state of submission; for it causes both the heart and the body to dance through its activity—which consists of entering the heart, producing delight, and causing exaltation—and through an activity refined by the cultivation of the means [of aesthetic realization], in both ways: as "the dancing of the actor" (*naṭanṛtta*) and as "the dance" (*nṛtta*).
They remember it; therefore, for that reason, this drama is called by that name.
Now, one might ask: why is it that this meaning, though also composed in the Purāṇas and other texts, causes only this [work] to be enacted by actors?
To this he says: "various" (nānā). It is because they enact—that is, they bring about—the various kinds of actions found herein.

It has been stated repeatedly that dramatic representations consist of the actor’s activities; through these, the thread of the plot— which brings about this state of submission and is introduced by way of the needle-hole of the most heart-stirring savoring of aesthetic flavor— becomes the weaver of the jewels of virtues such as heroism, which have taken root in the heart's Mount Rohaṇa.

Now, one might ask: why is this aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) found only in the life of a king and not in the life of a god? To this he says: "in many ways" (*bahudhā*). This refers to the accomplishment (*saṃpādana*) of the various types of arising of pleasure and pain resulting from the diversity of means and so forth; however, it is stated that such [diversity] does not exist in the life of a god. For this very reason, there is no obstruction to the aesthetic experience (*pratīti-vighāta*).
That which gives rise to a sense of distaste should not be composed in that drama. For this reason,
the conduct of a reigning king must certainly not be described therein,
because any superimposition [of such conduct] would be ineffective due to the contradiction posed by contrary public renown.

It is like the superimposition of the life-stories of characters such as Rāvaṇa, who was devoted to *yoga* and bliss. For this very reason, the term "renowned" (*prakhyāta*)—which indicates excellence—is employed repeatedly. Therefore, the Veda and the Śāstras are not drama;
for in those cases, a person is impelled by mandatory injunction (*niyoga*), and not by the production of a fruit. Even in the view where the fruit is predominant, in those [scriptures]...

There is doubt. This is likewise the case in the Purāṇas and other such texts. However, in this context [of the present treatise], pleasure and pain are established through a cognition that, though appearing as direct perception (*pratyakṣāyamāṇā*), is capable of withstanding the arising of sublation and is proven by a long-delayed realization.
"Having observed that the action is endowed with these states [of emotion] by means of the expansion of the *bindu* (the seed-syllable), there is its production (*tatpatti*).
By this statement, the following is meant: although the meaning of all dramatic forms has entered the heart and disciplines those to be trained, it is for that very reason called "drama" (*nāṭaka*).

The term "general statement" (*sāmānyavacana*) has been demonstrated in such places as [the definition of] *kārya* (plot) and *utpanna* (incident) in the treatises on drama (*nāṭaka*). Nevertheless, kings must necessarily be instructed; for by means of their instruction, the entire world becomes instructed.
Therefore, by demonstrating the conduct of kings—which is suitable to resonate with their hearts—that [instruction] is presented as the primary element within the principal subject matter.

Ministers and others are instructed as being merely auxiliary to that [instruction], because there exists a relationship between the instruction and the practice such that it appropriately brings about the attainment of the sky-like state; thus, by means of that, for the sake of the primary human goal,
this instruction for the primary disciples bestows an understanding that surpasses others, and from that very source, it grants mastery.
It is called a *nāṭaka*.

Śrī Śaṅkuka, however, explains it as follows: "The one seeking victory, the enemy, the middle one, the neutral one, the friend, and the friend of a friend"—the deeds (*carita*) of these are understood through the use of the plural number. Others, however, say: "First..."
By this noble verse, it is stated that the leaders originating from the lineage of royal sages (*rājarṣi*) are included;
thus, even Candragupta, Bindusāra, and others are subsumed.
These two meanings have been explained as being thus condensed by the preceding noble verse itself.
The meaning explained first alone is the correct one;
as for what is stated by some— "Gods are to be known as *dhīrodātta* (majestic and noble), while kings are *dhīralalita* (noble and playful)"— [that is not so].
The general and the minister are proclaimed to be *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled);
the Brahmins and merchants are to be known as *dhīrapraśānta* (calm and composed).

When this statement is examined, it follows that since gods and others cannot logically serve as the heroes of a drama, there is only one type of hero, namely the *dhīralalita* (the calm and playful). This is incorrect; for Janaka and others, or even Rāma and his kin, do not possess the quality of being *dhīralalita*. As it has been said: "The life-story of Viṣṇu, named Rāma, is victorious—sublime and noble (*dhīrodātta*)."
As for what has been recited there, the quality of *dhīralalita* (the noble-lovely) is to be described as belonging only to a king, not to anyone else;
the quality of *dhīrodātta* (the noble-magnanimous) belongs only to a commander-in-chief or a minister; the quality of *dhīroddhata* (the noble-arrogant) belongs only to gods;
and the quality of *dhīrapraśānta* (the noble-peaceful) belongs only to the twice-born (*dvijāti*). Thus it should be understood. For this very reason—
In the phrase "famous and noble" (*prakhyātodātta*), it should be explained that all four types of heroes are included.

Thus, by this verse, the etymological definition is shown; while matters such as "famous subject matter" (*prakhyātavastu*) and so forth are well-known elsewhere, the act (*aṅka*) and the interlude (*praveśaka*) are not. Therefore, first, the nature of the act shall be explained in detail.
He says: "It is endowed with this state.
415) Furthermore, that mark (aṅka) must be composed by those who know the principles of drama, accompanied by a group [of actors]. || 13 ||
The term *aṅka* (act) is a conventional designation; it causes the meanings to grow through both the *bhāvas* (emotional states) and the *rasas* (aesthetic flavors).

Whatever is the function of this drama, it must be accomplished through the principal plot (*ādhikārika-itivṛtta*) corresponding to a single stage, by means of expanding and extending the action through the formation of *bindus* (plot-seeds), and by the power of generating a continuous connection.
Having observed that the complete connection, endowed with the stages beginning with the "commencement" (ārambha), has reached its fulfillment, an act (aṅka) should be concluded.

This is what is meant: when the stage of commencement reaches completion for the plot (itivṛtta), which is woven through the "points" (bindu) and "threads" (sūtra) and moves through the five stages beginning with commencement.
Then, the "cutting of the mark" (aṅkaccheda) must be performed in the form of a second mark being connected through the door of a dot (bindu).
This should be stated likewise for each of the four stages beginning with effort (prayatna); thus, there are five marks—this is the primary rule.
Now, one might ask: "If there is such deficiency or excess in the number of acts (*aṅkas*), how can there be such insistence [on a fixed number]?

To this he says: "By those who know the essence of drama (*nāṭyatattvajña*), that act should be composed in this very manner; by the word 'also' (*api*), it is implied that it may otherwise be done. The particle *tu* indicates a distinction. When the beginning and the conclusion are primary, then—of that [act]— [The sentence continues: ...in that case, its... [text fragment].
Thus, with respect to the two states of the beginning and the conclusion, there are two *aṅkas*;

for the others, it means one *aṅka* each. That is to say, by joining all [the acts] with the two states, they are brought together; thus, because of the six *aṅkas*, starting from that point until the attainment of the seven births, there is the state of ten *aṅkas*. [This applies to] a certain state...

When one binds [the plot] by mixing it with another state after having made [that state] primary, then there is a deficiency of acts (*aṅka*) in the *nāṭikā*. This is indicated by the word "tu" and by the term "tattvajña. In that regard, the states (*avasthās*)—beginning with "commencement" (*prārambha*), "effort" (*prayatna*), and so forth—will be explained in verse 1.19. [This occurs] upon the interruption of the purposes (*prayojana*).

That which is the cause of non-interruption is called the *bindu*; that which is the subject matter (*adhikārika-vastu*) is called the *samyak-kārya* (the complete action), as will be stated [in Chapter 19].
Now, why is it called an *aṅka*? He says: "The word *aṅka* is a conventional term" [referring to] the *bhāvas* and *rasas*.

Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa and others explain the reading *gūḍha* as follows: "The word *aṅka* denotes that which is hidden (*gūḍha*), concealed (*channa*), and pervasive (*vyāpta*) in its meaning. Others read *rūḍha* and explain it thus: "It causes meanings to grow (*rohayati arthān*); by 'growth' (*rohaṇa*) is meant that part of the drama which is called the 'lap' (*utsaṅga*)."

Through the sentiments (rasas) such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and others, the objects consisting of the determinants (vibhāva), consequents (anubhāva), and transitory states (vyabhicārin)— as well as through the emotions (bhāvas) along with their determinants and so forth— it causes the objects such as the emotions themselves to ascend into the heart; it carries these objects by means of the various types of characters that will be described hereafter, beginning with the words "those heroes who have been declared."
Because it is endowed with specific formal requirements (*vidhāna*), it is called an *aṅka* due to its connection with the act of mounting, like a lap (*utsaṅga*).
This [term] is not used here in its conventional sense (*rūḍha*) as seen in other contexts—for instance, in the case of "deer-skin" (*ajājina*)—because no such function (*vṛtti*) is observed here.
Therefore, the meaning here is this: the word *aṅka* is a term conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of a "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*), and not from any other source.

The defining characteristic is that which distinguishes. This also establishes the diversity and differentiation of the dramatic form from other non-dramatic forms; for in the drama, that specific element causes even those meanings characterized by rasa and bhāva to flourish.
Since it is endowed with various kinds of rules, it shall therefore be called *aṅka*. (14)

The conclusion of the act (aṅka) should be performed by means of the interruption of the poetic narrative; the withdrawal of the seed (bīja) [of the plot] and the thread (bindu) that pervades the entire subject matter must always arise from the poem itself.

Through the process of making the commonality of heart-to-heart resonance manifest—as described in the chapter on Rasa—the ascent occurs; like a seed taking the form of a sprout, there is the growth of the emergence of the form of Rasa.
And since that [growth] is accomplished solely by those elements of the drama that are not intended for performance, it is called "the non-performable" (*anabhineya*).
By establishing a distinction, it indeed becomes the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the dramatic form (*rūpaka*) to be performed.
Thus, the etymological meaning of the word *aṅka* has been explained. Its essential nature (*svarūpa*), however, must be stated; [the author] does not show it directly, but says:
"where the matter is completed. This means that where the matter, characterized by stages such as the beginning and so forth, reaches its conclusion.

This is the conclusion [of the act]. Furthermore, even when an act has reached its completion, if the withdrawal of the seed (bīja) occurs at a point appropriate to the specific juncture (saṃdhi), then there too is a division of the act.

Thus, in the introductory acts (mukha) and the others, there are: origin (utpatti), disclosure (udghāṭana), manifestation (udbheda), the breaking open of the embryo (garbhanirbheda), and the bringing forth of the fruit (phalasamānayana).
The ten specific stages of the seed (*bīja*) are designated by the term "withdrawal" (*saṃhāra*).

Furthermore, so that there may be no interruption of the meaning upon the conclusion of an act (*aṅka*), an act should be composed such that it possesses a *bindu*—a connection that is not disjointed.
As, for example, at the conclusion of the third act in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*:
At first, by the heavy embrace of pride, she was raised high; later, by the weight of remorse, she was brought to extreme emaciation and lightness.
Now, through constant following, her limbs have become compressed as she rests within the fold of his lap.
"The tree clings to its shade as if it were a beloved who offers affection with her whole body.

(3.17) By this speech of the King, [the author] connects the acceptance of Padmāvatī’s marriage; thus, the *bindu* (linking element) that demonstrates the third stage, known as "Possibility of Attainment," is joined for the sake of the fourth act yet to come.
The ancient authorities maintain that the nature of the *aṅka* (act) has been defined by this [verse].

However, this is redundant, for what is expressed by this definition is already stated by the phrase "having observed the action endowed with its various states" (*asyāvasthopetaṃ kāryaṃ prasamīkṣya*). Therefore, the true meaning here is as follows: the nature of the *aṅka*.

By the phrase "endowed with such a state," its etymological definition (*nirvacana*) is stated; and by the phrase "the term *aṅka* is a conventional word (*rūḍhiśabda*)," its established usage is shown. By this verse, however, the threefold nature of the *aṅka* is expressed. And so it has been stated by Kohala and others:
p.
417) That in which the completion of the plot occurs and wherein the withdrawal of the seed takes place,
yet with some lingering thread of the plot remaining— that is always to be understood as an *aṅka* (act).
The enjoyment of the direct activities of those leaders who have been described should be enacted in an act (aṅka) that is not too long and is endowed with various situations. || 17 ||
The *Aṅka* (Act) is threefold, either by means of an *Aṅkāvatāra* (interlude between acts) or by means of a *Cūḍāṅka* (prologue);
the *Cūḍā* serves to introduce the subject matter through bards (*sūta*) and panegyrists (*vandī*) with many significant words.
The transition from one act to another is proclaimed as the *avatāra* (descent);
it consists of the separation of the opening of an act by means of a woman or a man.
That which is introduced at the beginning is intended as the "face" (mukha) of the act (aṅka).

In this context, the *cūḍā* (the "crest") has demonstrated that the attainment (*prāpti*) of some object is its acquisition through a means other than one's own prior intention. For example, in the *Ratnāvalī*, from the recitation of the bard, Udayana’s vision [of the queen] was attained;
thus, the correct meaning was acquired because it was rooted in the recognition of her.

Thus he speaks regarding Sāgarikā’s passion: "Ah! This is King Udayana" (1-23), and so forth. It is for that very purpose that everything, such as the spring pastimes and other events, has been introduced.
And since that alone is the root of the king's passion—manifested through actions such as [preparing] the bed and the wooden plank—it is called a *cūlikā*. Therefore, this is the first...

The *cūlikāṅka* (interlude scene): that act in which there occurs the convergence—that is, the attainment through combination—of the meaning of all the seed-words (*bīja*) present in the various acts, is the *avatārāṅka*. For example, the second act of the *Ratnāvalī*. For therein [it is said]: "For such a person as this daughter of a noble family, there is such a desire for such a bridegroom..."

"It must be so: for a maiden of such a kind, there should be a longing for a bridegroom of just such a kind"—in this way, everything belonging to the main plot (*prakṛta*) is described. However, where an event is related because it serves as a means to that [plot], its life-force consisting solely in its connection [to the main action], that is the "face of the act" (*aṅkamukha*), which is what is intended here.

By the phrase "a slight attachment of a drop," the third variety is stated. For example, in the third act of the *Ratnāvalī*, the description of the magical illusion (*aindrajāla*) constitutes a *cūlikā*; yet it is a distinct variety because there is no intention (*abhisandhāna*) regarding that [act] on the part of the characters within the act itself. In this case, however, such an intention certainly exists on the part of Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others.
Therefore, this is the summary: that which is to be described in the *aṅka*—namely, the hero, the queen, elders, the family priest, the minister, and the caravan leader. (p. 418)
For it should be understood that an act (aṅka) is indeed composed of various internal sentiments (rasas). || 18 ||
(Indeed, there should be five or ten acts in a drama and a *prakaraṇa*; that act in which all characters exit is to be known as an *aṅka*. || 19 ||)

That [plot] is first of all twofold: primary and subsidiary. Furthermore, the subsidiary is of various kinds: some achieves its utility by the power of destiny, while some does so through the force of intention. This may sometimes be composed even in a mixed manner within a single act.
In the cases of the *cūlikā* and the *aṅkamukha*, as well as in the various types of *aṅka*, there is no contact whatsoever with the primary subject matter.
Likewise, by means of the introductory scene (*praveśaka*), he says "those who are the heroes" in order to dispel doubt even regarding the principal plot:

those who are the heroes— whether *dhīrodātta* and the like, or those such as the seeker of victory (*vijigīṣu*) and his friends— as well as the antagonists (*pratināyaka*), their conduct consists of the execution of the appropriate means, and likewise, their enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) is directly perceived and present.

Wherein the mark (*aṅka*) is such that it is directly seen rather than merely indicated, it leads to—or causes one to attain—the plot or the fruit; thus, through the direct perception of the protagonist’s conduct, there arises an instructive understanding for the spectators.
Furthermore, when the enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) is not directly perceived, there occurs a sense of distaste due to witnessing only the suffering inherent therein.
It might occur for the spectator; thinking, "What is the use of this great hardship?", it was therefore stated that [the hero] should not be devoid of happiness.

The meaning of the word *tu* (but) is as follows: the conduct and enjoyment pertaining to the antagonist (*pratināyaka*), existing in various adverse states, are not to be adopted because they concern an improper object and are thus states to be rejected; however, those pertaining to the hero (*nāyaka*) are, by contrast, states to be adopted.
"Not distant" means not too long; for a long [performance] would lead to exhaustion for both the performers and the spectators.

Having thus described the conduct of the primary subject of description, he says "the hero, the goddess," and so forth, in order to show the direction of the conduct that is useful for that [subject]: "The heroes" are the principal ones; "the heroines" are the goddesses, such as Mahādevī, Bhoginī, and others; "the elders" are the mother, father, brother, teacher, and so forth.

The caravan leader (*sārthavāha*) here is the commander-in-chief (*senāpati*). Alternatively, by virtue of the narrative context, he may simply be a merchant; that is to say, this *aṅka* (act) is related to them and expresses this very meaning. For this reason, it is not endowed with a single, diverse specific sentiment (*rasa*); for instance, there is the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) in connection with the queen, and the heroic (*vīra*) in the hero, and so forth—other cases should be inferred accordingly. Regarding the heroes...

Others say [the term] refers to the Goddess and so forth. Regarding "act" (*aṅka*): the meaning is that it is called an "act" because it is marked by multiple aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), and not merely because the deeds and amorous enjoyments are directly perceived.
Anger, favor, and grief; the utterance of a curse, as well as flight and marriage;
and the witnessing of the occurrence of a marvel—these may take place within the *aṅka* (interlude) as events witnessed directly. (20)
An act (*aṅka*) should be commenced on a single day, dealing with the seed of the plot (*arthabīja*), provided it does not conflict with the performance of necessary duties. (21)
Sometimes a wise person may undertake many tasks with a single effort;
in such cases, those duties should be performed provided they do not conflict with what is essential.
However, showing that there is yet another [element] where there is an excess of coloring (*rañjana*), he says: "Anger, favor, and sorrow," and so forth.

"The casting of a curse" (*śāpotsarga*) is the destruction of the misfortune caused by a curse; the "flight" (*vidrava*) caused by the fear and terror of the apprehension of such misfortune as has been described will be discussed in the *garbhasandhi*. "Wedding" (*udvāha*) is marriage.

The production, acceptance, commencement, manifestation, and conclusion of the marvelous—this also serves as an illustration for other categories of the aesthetically pleasing (*rañjaka*). Because they have proceeded toward sensory cognition (*akṣaja-jñāna*), they are "born of perception" (*pratyakṣaja*). By the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), a portion thereof is expressed therein.
"Born"—this refers to the perceptibility of the other group of faculties; at times, there is even direct perception of reality (*tattva*).
Now, he shows that the duration of the application of the goad is this much: "proceeding for a single day.
Such a seed, endowed with an intermediate purpose or objective, is the practice of the means (*upāyānuṣṭhāna*).

An act (*aṅka*) should be composed with reference to what is worthy of description; and that which is its excellent performance in the form of a production should take place in a single day—that is, within fifteen *muhūrtas*—because during such a period, necessary activities such as eating and so forth cannot be avoided, and therefore [the performance] must follow thereafter. If, however, it is the time for the performance...

This is because it must not conflict with the necessary duties of the spectators and the performers, such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) or meals; thus, the multiplicity of actions in a single act (*aṅka*) is prohibited. However, in some cases, it is even permitted. Others, however, [hold that] the entire *āryā*...

They say [the verse] is intent on prohibition. Others, however, considering the word "ekāṅkena" as being in the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*), say that this entire Āryā is intent on injunction (*vidhi*). Those activities such as eating which must necessarily be performed—(p.
For all those who have entered the stage, there must be an exit;
having performed the action according to its purpose and aesthetic flavor, it should be endowed with the proper application of the seed-meaning. (23)
One should not employ many tasks in a single act;
for in that way, there would be a conflict among necessary duties. (24)
Having understood the state of the day as it wanes, characterized by its specific muhūrtas,
one should divide every single task in its entirety, assigning each individually to its respective numerical positions.

If all the business of the day's end were not to fit within the lap [of the performance], he addresses one who might doubt whether everything must necessarily be shown through direct observation, saying "the stage" (*raṅga*). In that context, it refers to what must necessarily be done; nor does it refer to an intermediate action introduced before completion.

He demonstrates what is called "the exit from the stage" (*pātraniṣkramaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the seed" (*bījārtha*): having established the action—which serves as the means—connected with the purpose of the "seed" (*bīja*) consisting of the initial proposal (*upakṣepa*), and which follows that purpose and is endowed with a specific excellence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), [the playwright] effects its conclusion by means of the curtain (*yavanikā*) in the form of a disappearance.
The departure [of the hero] is to be made beautiful to behold.

Others maintain that it consists of the sowing of the seed, its application, its arising, its disclosure, its manifestation, its internal development, its bursting forth, and the attainment of the fruit.
Having thus demonstrated the rule for the plot within the act (*aṅka*), he now demonstrates the rule for the duration of that plot.

Having understood the state of the day— endowed with the characteristics of the *kṣaṇas* and *muhūrtas*, such as "at this moment the twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā*) should be performed" and so forth— one should divide every task individually, in its entirely complete form, and thus in its fullness.

One should show it by means of division; that is, having divided the day and night into eight parts by means of the *nāḍikās* or by the measurement of shadow. The essential meaning is that one should record in figures the useful activity performed during a single day.

[Objection: But how can that which occurs in the midst of it—such as the midday bath, eating, and so forth—or whatever has happened on that very day, even if distant, such as the death of Daśaratha, be described? To this he says:
"the duties at the close of day. [The word] *diva-*...
Having made a mark on the body, it should be destroyed by means of incisions. || 26 ||
"But for one who must go to a distant place due to the exigencies of business, he should briefly indicate that [journey] by means of *praveśakas* following the cutting of the mark. (27)
In a drama (*nāṭaka*) or a play (*prakaraṇa*), an act (*aṅka*) should be composed with a protagonist present;
that which consists of a continuous dialogue among the attendants is to be known as an interlude (*praveśaka*). || 28 ||

Regarding the *prakaraṇa* and *nāṭaka*, there should be from five to ten acts (*aṅkas*). Whatever action constitutes the conclusion or completion [of the plot] that is not suitable to be presented directly within an act, one should effect a division of the act by means of *praveśakas*.
The *cūlikā*, *aṅka*, *avatāra*, *aṅkamukha*, *praveśaka*, and *viṣkambhaka* are intended here. Thus has Kohala stated the fivefold introduction of the plot (*arthopakṣepa*).
Such is the definition of the *aṅka*.

Having expanded upon what was stated [previously], he concludes with the second half-verse; then, showing the general definition of the *praveśaka*—which consists of the joining of scenes (*aṅka-sandhāna*)—he recites the *āryā* beginning with "sannihita-nāyaka," etc.
By the word "nāyaka" (hero), both his deeds and his amorous enjoyment are meant; these two are "present" (*sannihita*), meaning they are directly perceived.

It has been stated that even in a drama consisting of a single act, an act should be made devoid of the direct observation of the hero's actions, let alone in other types [of dramas] such as the *prakaraṇa* or the *nāṭaka*.
Others, however, connect this with the second half [of the verse], asserting that other types of drama are devoid of the *praveśaka*.
They say that these [characters] exist. Regarding the "connection with the talk of attendants" (*parajanakathānubandha*), this is the characteristic of four types:
(1) the *sūta*, *māgadha*, and so forth, who serve as the *cūlikā* or *aṅka*; (2) the male and female attendants and others who serve as the equipment for the *aṅkamukha*;
and (3) the retinue consisting of maidservants, chamberlains, and others, who are employed in the *praveśaka* and *viṣkambhaka*. This is stated without further elaboration.
The *aṅkāvatāra* is that which is connected and linked with one another. As it has been said:
"That in which one act (*aṅka*) falls into another act upon reaching its performance, due to the connection with the narrative of the dramatic purpose—that is to be known as the *aṅkāvatāra*."

In this regard, since the *praveśaka* (interlude) serves to connect the meaning of the acts (*aṅka*), he shows that the act previously introduced— pertaining to the subject matter of the *prakaraṇa* or *nāṭaka*— is presented by way of a reference to its number.
Only those acts (*aṅka*) which are composed with the complete arrangement of the junctures (*sandhi*) and the constituent elements (*vastu*) [are valid].
And at the junctions between the different acts, there are likewise as many *praveśakas*. (29)
(An *praveśaka* inserted between these two [acts], intended for brevity, should be arranged within the junctures of the plot after considering the necessary action. 30.
Having made a mark on the body, whether it be performed monthly or accumulated annually, all of that must be done; however, never after the year has passed.

The meaning is that it is improper for there to be a discrepancy— either fewer or more— in some cases ten [acts] due to gradual transition and expansion, or six due to brevity; however, in order to achieve the six diverse junctures (*sandhāna*) within the acts,
a fivefold *praveśaka* (interlude) should be employed at the junctures between acts, as indicated by the phrase "at the junctures of other acts."

The locative case is used here in the sense of connection with an action (*karmasaṃyoga*). By the word "api" (also/even), the recurrence of the term "praveśaka" (entrance) is indicated. The particle "ca" (and) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore, while the term "praveśaka" refers to the highest general category (*mahāsāmānya*) and occurs in five [types of scenes], here it applies to the middle general category, namely the two types: the *praveśaka* and the *viṣkambhaka*.

This is the meaning: because there is that which was performed within a month or accumulated over a year, and whatever business is intended for the hearts of the members of the assembly, for that reason the *praveśaka* and *viṣkambhaka* should be employed. However, when the matter to be connected is limited, the *aṅkamukha* is used; when it is slightly less, the *cūlikā*; and when it is very slight, [the *aṅkāvatāra*].

The *Aṅkāvatāra*. Regarding this, some explain it with the intention that the search for Rāma should not be undertaken immediately after the entry into Ayodhyā following the forest exile and so forth, saying: "after one month, two months, many months, a year, two years, or many years. However, at times...

However, for those of great power who can recollect even events long past, such as those of Rāma and others, a period of many years must indeed be described by means of *praveśakas*. But for those who are primarily human beings, there is no recollection whatsoever beyond a single year; and thus:
They assert that between the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Taiṣī, the long-term cycle of the year lasts for eight months until the end of the rainy season; however,
this is incorrect, because months, years, and so forth have accepted fixed measurements.
For it has been shown that a [compound] formation is impossible when [the first member] ends in the dual or plural numbers; however,
in the case of *sauryaka* and *māsajāta*, the measure exists by its very nature and functions through a distinction of number by relying on an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*).
Even if a determination such as "it is old" is made, it is not perceived;
since that [determination] is desired without any distinction [in the object], size (parimāṇa) is useless there.
If any person travels a great distance for the sake of some business,
those who know [the procedure] should likewise mark the boundary-stones there as before. (32)
Otherwise, prohibitions such as "and for more than many years" would result in a fruitless outcome.

Therefore, the compound must be formed with a word ending in the singular number alone; nor does this entail the abandonment of the narratives of the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Mahābhārata*, and so forth, for the inclusion of the term "action" (*kārya*) is precisely for this purpose.
For in whatever task has been undertaken by a sage, only that which was intended to be accomplished and accumulated is counted as the year;

other years, even if present there, are as if non-existent. Indeed, in the account of Rāma’s life, although the dwelling in the forest was to last for fourteen years, only three or four years actually passed.
In this context, since intermediate events such as the killing of Mārīca and the granting of the kingdom to Sugrīva occur,
the phrase "after that year" serves to exclude a duration of two years; thus,
even for one whose lifespan is a thousand years, there is no contradiction even when explaining deeds occurring within the interval of a hundred years.

Nothing is wrong with this. Therefore, the summary is that there are five working days in a play with five acts (*pañcāṅka*), while the detailed version is that there are ten in one with ten acts (*daśāṅka*).
He also states another reason for the division of acts: "whichever [act] occurs by virtue of the requirements of the plot."

Due to the requirements of the plot, because the action extends over such a distance that the hero— who is the protagonist— must travel a path separated by many *yojanas* every day, with stages such as his journey, rest, and sleep, how can this be demonstrated on the stage? Therefore, at the conclusion of that [section], the act (*aṅka*) must be brought to a close.

For a divine hero, such as the leader of a *ḍima* and other plays, everything is appropriate, including traveling through the sky by means of celestial vehicles and the like. However, a non-divine hero exits the *aṅka* without interruption. [Objection: But how can the necessary duties at the end of the day be accomplished?
[Response: It is as stated by the phrase "by not contradicting what is necessary," and so forth.
Therefore, not even a word more than the size of a sesame seed can be added to this statement; for this very reason, it was not recited at all by Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa and others.

The teachers, however, say: "This is not another reason; rather, it was previously stated that 'if it does not fit in the context'—an example of this very point has been shown by this noble verse. Just as the hero's journey on a long road [is understood], so too, according to the previous rule, it becomes 'suitable for that' (*tadarham*)."

This refers to the "cutting of the act" (*aṅkaccheda*), which is worthy of the aforementioned characteristics. The word *api* (also/even) indicates that there are other examples as well. The location of the *praveśaka* (interlude), whose purpose is to connect the meaning of the acts, must be stated.
He states its scope with the phrase "following after another act," meaning it occurs within an act. [The term] *aṅkāntara*...

The meaning is that it follows the interval of the preceding act; it occurs after that. Regarding the statement in the treatise on drama (*nāṭaka*) concerning the *pratyakṣānta* (the end of the subsequent act), it should be understood as referring to the expansion—that is, the making more extensive—of the concise statement of purpose known as the *anusandhāna* (linking). This is what is expressed in the context of the *vācya* (the subject matter).

Furthermore, the *praveśaka* (interlude) necessarily involves one who is engaged in providing instruction regarding the highest class of characters (*uttamaprakṛti*) through immeasurable means for the sake of numerous intermediate tasks arising from the circumstances.
A *praveśaka* (interlude) should be employed in the context of a *prakaraṇa* or a *nāṭaka*, following the sequence of acts and concerning the summarized meaning of the *bindus*. || 33 ||
It should not be practiced by superior or middling persons, nor should it be composed in an elevated style;
rather, the conduct of the Prākṛta language should be employed according to its conventional usage. || 34 ||

This *praveśaka*, occurring at the appropriate time and dealing with the subjects of exposition, preparation, and action, is joined with both meaning and expression and possesses manifold significance. (35)

The *praveśaka* (interlude) is also for the purpose of delineating the duties of ministers and others; however, because other types of drama (*rūpaka*) provide instruction on limited matters, the utility of the *praveśaka* is not as extensive there, as we shall explain later.
Now, demonstrating its distinction from the *viṣkambhaka* (prelude), the term *praveśaka*, though denoting a very specific [technical] word, [is used here].

He shows that [the command] is not [issued] by superior or middling persons; this is for the purpose of excluding those who, though superior and so forth, are merely attendants. "Udātta" refers to refined Sanskrit speech, and its negation is intended. Others, however, say: "Udātta" refers to speech that rests upon one's own personal affairs, and it is such speech that is prohibited in the phrase *āṇattaṃmi*.
For by the words "O Princess" (*bhaṭṭidārie*) and so forth, one's own action is seen as being useful only for the primary purpose, not as independent.

In that regard, the Prakrit language and the conduct and practice are indeed Prakrit. However, the phrase "resorting to usage" (*prayogam āśritya*) indicates that in some cases, due to the requirements of the performance (*prayoga*), the practice of the Sanskrit language must also be employed even in the *viṣkambhaka* (interlude).
He analyzes that which was stated as "with reference to the concise meaning" by saying, "this is the course of the rising of time.

This refers to the understanding (*gati*) of the emergence of time (*kāla-udaya*), because a certain introductory scene (*praveśaka*) indicates the emergence of time. For example: "Today, on the occasion of the spring festival, having been summoned with great honor... and so forth (*Ratnāvalī* 1). Regarding the "expression of the matter" (*artha-abhidhāna*):

Each term is connected individually; therefore, that which is appropriate for expressing the meaning of the four [categories] beginning with "exegesis" (*vyākhyā*) and ending with "subject matter" (*viṣaya*), and which proceeds with that as its objective, is what is meant by the fivefold "introduction" (*praveśaka*).
It is called "exegesis" (*vyākhyā*) because it is explained (*vyākhyāyate*). For instance, by means of a certain introduction, [the subject] is made hidden...
The meaning is that it is explained. As in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*, the minister’s spy (*māmiñja*) says:
"One should condense even a matter involving many dependencies by means of *praveśakas* or at the junctures (*sandhi*) [of the acts]. (p. 425)
Combined with many powdered words, it produces weariness for the practitioner. || 36 ||
"By those who fear negligence, [the place] is being avoided due to the presence of *hālāhala* poison.

(The attendants wander about, apprehensive of negligence. "O ascetic... (and so forth). For by this, there is no great distance mentioned; and as for the secret purpose behind placing Vāsavadattā in Padmāvatī’s house—

This has been explained. *Saṃrambha* refers to an intention directed toward a specific task; its purpose consists of seeking out means and so forth. A *praveśaka* (interlude) is that which is joined with the expression of such [intent], as in the passage from the *Nṛttapāra*: "The goal has arrived," and so on. By this...

Śālaṅkāyana has described the agitation of the ministers who, having been commissioned by the King of Vatsa— who desired to carry off Vāsavadattā and lead her to Ujjayinī— concerning the matter of their official duty,
beginning with the words "But when the task is one pertaining to authority" (19.3). Its meaning is the execution of the five constituent parts [of statecraft].

Namely: the means for initiating actions, the excellence of personnel and materials, the distinction between place and time, the remedy for setbacks, and the accomplishment of the objective. Furthermore, the *praveśaka* (interlude) is frequently characterized by such descriptions, as found in works such as the *Tāpasavatsarāja*, *Pratibhā*, *Cāṇakya*, and *Mudrārākṣasa*. As for the subject matter:
The *itivṛtta* (plot) of a future act (*aṅka*) is its specific subject matter; a *praveśaka* (interlude) is that which is joined with the expression of such [matter].

For example, in the second act of the *Nāgānanda*, the detailed description of the state of love (*madanāvasthā*) and the depiction of the sandalwood vine-cottage and other settings are shown by two female attendants. There are other [examples] of the *praveśaka* as well.
The purposes do exist; however, he says "having many meanings" (anekārtha) to indicate that this is not an exhaustive enumeration.

Anticipating the objection—"But what about such a matter as is shown in the *praveśaka*, whether in brief or in detail?"—he says "even though it rests upon many [elements]. "[Those] desiring to effect a *saṃdhi*... [is the phrase].

The five types of introductory scenes (*praveśaka*) mentioned, such as the *cūlikā* and others, serve as the means for establishing the meaning of the dramatic junctures (*aṅka*). By means of these, one should condense the extensive matter that must be related—which rests upon speech—into as much as is necessary for the connection of the plot; for [otherwise], it would be rendered fragmented by many prose passages.

Fatigue arises from words that are mostly unrefined (or unpolished). By this, he also demonstrates that at the beginning of a *praveśaka* (interlude) and similar sections, one should not employ a style characterized by *utkalikā* (excessive excitement), which is heavily interspersed with compounds; for such a style causes the breaking off of the branches of dramatic performance and, due to the ambiguity of the compounds, fails to determine the intended meaning.
If any business of the day's conclusion cannot be accomplished within the act,
it should all be arranged by means of interludes (*praveśakas*), after making a break in the act (*aṅkaccheda*).
(426) Where the completion of the plot does not occur within an act due to the abundance of the performance,
that [remainder] should be conveyed through *praveśakas* containing brief accounts of events. || 37 ||
War, loss of kingdom, death, and the siege of a city—these are manifest realities that must not be undertaken by those who seek counsel. (38)

Regarding what was stated there—that the inconsistency is of many kinds—he says, "when the purpose of the matter is completed," in order to demonstrate this. That which, although intended for direct performance (*pratyakṣaprayojya*), remains incomplete within the act due to the requirements of the performance, must be carried out by means of a *praveśaka*. The "extensiveness" (*bahutaratva*) of the performance refers to its being a locus of great importance.

Therefore, this is the meaning here: since there are many daily activities, among them that which is useful for the instruction on beautiful dramatic techniques must be shown directly [on stage]. All else—namely, the remainder of the narrative intended for the *praveśaka* (interlude) and the fulfillment of the plot through the remaining events—is minor, concise, and [treated] briefly.
This refers to the introductory scene (*praveśaka*) of which the narrative belongs. Thus, the utility of the *praveśaka* for directly enacted action has been shown;

he now demonstrates its application elsewhere as well, stating "battle," "loss of kingdom," and so forth. In battle, there is an abundance of the clashing of weapons; in the loss of a kingdom, there is falling, death, and the like; and in the siege of a city—

Regarding the giving of mechanical devices, subterranean passages, and so forth for the sake of strength: here some say that death is of two kinds—some is to be accomplished by an action belonging to another, such as the cutting off of a Daitya’s head by means of a discus; and some occurs entirely without dependence on an action belonging to another.

[The offense] arises from disease, assault, and so forth. Among these, the prohibition applies only to the first. It is for this very purpose that the term "intentionally" (*kṛta*) is included, for it denotes other actions; moreover, that [other action] is not subsumed under "fighting. This is because, even in the case of non-fighting, the [offense] was shown to apply even to one who has not suspected decapitation. They should be asked this: "This..."

We do not perceive any basis for this distinction of subject matter, namely that "death is to be enacted" while "this [other] is not to be enacted. For how could there be an exit for one who is dead, or how could there be a continued stay?
Consequently, there would be the total collapse of the entire procedure of the *dhruvā* songs and other elements essential for drama, as well as for the audience.
As for the realization of despondency (*vīrasatā*), death is common to all [situations];
therefore, death should certainly not be employed on the stage. Now, what is the purpose of describing the external manifestations (*anubhāva*) of death at this time?
Furthermore, what would be the point of describing these same manifestations even in the context of the heroic or the furious sentiments (*vīra* and *raudra*) associated with battle?

If it is asked, "How can there be a description even by those who enter [the state] without knowing its experiential power? the answer is that the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is the same even at the time of death.
In the *Aṅka*, the *Praveśaka*, or the *Prakaraṇa*, as well as in the *Nāṭaka*,
no killing should be performed involving a protagonist who is renowned and destined for prosperity.
Either retreat alone should be undertaken, or capture, or peace should be established.
Furthermore, that in which death occurs without the possibility of recovery should not be employed, as it results in the total destruction of the undertaking.
However, where there is a possibility of recovery from that [death], as in the case of Jimutavahana, that very [course of action] should be followed.
Since it consists of actions that are not determined for even a single moment, it must indeed be employed;

thus, it too is an object of the direct realization of the experience of death. Or rather, this—consisting of the commencement of the description of weapons and so forth, as well as the haughty marching even of armies—is also to be employed.

Its resolution should not be demonstrated. This very point has been clarified in the *Kāraṇa*: "That which ends only with the battle, that which lasts until death, and that which does not result in immediate recovery—such should not be presented directly [on stage], but through *praveśakas*."
The meaning is: by means of one or another of the five types of introductory devices (*upakṣepa*). Others, however, say:
death caused by disease or caused by injury may be employed on the stage; the nature of the exit should be such that it is not a departure from which there is no rebirth.

Now, he shows that in every respect, the death of which the subject matter is such that it must not be mentioned, [is expressed] by the words "in the act" (*aṅke*) and "in the introductory scene" (*praveśake*). In either a *prakaraṇa* or a *nāṭaka*, the death of the protagonist is not to be described either through direct representation or through description. "In the act" refers to direct representation, while "in the introductory scene" refers to description.

Now, one might ask: for those who maintain that no one's death can be brought about by perception (*pratyakṣa*), what is the purpose of "marking" (*aṅkagrahaṇa*) in that system? To this they reply: by the word "killing" (*vadha*), death itself is not meant;
rather, it refers to the infliction of injury or blows by another. In that context, even the infliction of injury or blows by another is demonstrated on the stage through perception.

When [the hero] has recently returned to his composure, one should not display acts such as killing for that famous protagonist (*nāyaka*). Others, however, maintain that the "famous" refers to the *patākā-nāyaka* (the secondary hero) and so forth.
"Withdrawal" means fleeing, as it is said: "When [resistance] is impossible, one should abandon everything and depart; this is seen."

(Section 9.7) For there is indeed a return for one who lives; or rather, the "taking" (*grahaṇa*) should be performed as a binding accompanied by its basis, as in the case of the Vatsarāja at the conclusion of Vāsavadattā’s dance.
As for what was stated—that *sandhāna* is simply *sandhi*:
(428) By those who know the principles of drama, [the performance] should be rendered with many poetic puns according to the aesthetic flavor (rasa). || 40 ||
One should not perform a drama or a play with a large retinue;
there should be only four or five men who serve as the characters therein. (41)
Having encountered a binding situation, one should fashion the "cow-tail-tip" treaty.
When a weak king is attacked by a powerful king who has set his wheel in motion, he should submit through a treaty.
(Arthaśāstra, Chapter 7.3)
He speaks in order to indicate the specific application of the divisions of *apasaraṇa* (departure), *bandhana* (binding), and *sandhi* (union):

whatever the primary sentiment (*rasa*) of a poem may be, and whatever its poetic meaning (*kāvyārtha*) may be, the *śleṣas* (puns) and the logical justifications for binding and so forth— characterized by these— are what constitute the actions such as departure and the rest.
The reading "kāryaviśeṣaiḥ" (by specific effects) belongs to some [authorities].

Now, in order to demonstrate the inclusion, by way of universals, of those things that cannot be employed as objects of perception, he says: "na mahājanaparivāram" (not surrounded by a great multitude). By "mahājana" (a great multitude), he means [a multitude] by way of number.
An entourage (*parivāra*) is a surrounding; whatever subject matter possesses such an entourage is a *nāṭaka*, and that is a *prakaraṇa*.

Because of the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), other [types of drama] are not to be performed either. This is what is meant: whatever requires many people to accomplish, such as the building of a bridge across the ocean and so forth—all that cannot be [accomplished] through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Likewise, it should be demonstrated before a great multitude— such as father, son, mother-in-law, daughter-in-law, teacher, and disciple—
in such a way that, due to the presence of shame, fear, and so forth, a distaste arises; or wherever there is a surrounding by the great public or the assembly,
and a contraction of the mind occurs, all of that— even including kissing— is not to be done in their direct presence.
It is to be employed. And if it is to be employed as a direct presentation (*pratyakṣa*), there are five acting persons (*kāryapuruṣa*) therein;

if there are four, such as the *prakaraṇa*, the *pataka*, and so forth, their retinue (*parivāra*) is of the same nature and likewise consists of that many. If it is a *prakarsa*, then there are ten or eight on the stage.

They have entered. However, if there were more than that, the fourfold representation (abhinaya) would not be properly discernible, like a crowd of people seen during a divine procession. Having thus explained in detail the nature of the *praveśaka* within an act (*aṅka*), he now shows the form of the drama (*nāṭaka*) as a whole collection thereof.

"Poetry is like the tip of a cow's tail," some say, meaning its parts become progressively finer. Others, however, maintain that just as in a cow's tail some hairs are short and some are long, so too are some poetic effects.
And whatever states are elevated, all of those should be made subordinate. || 42 ||

In the conclusion of all poems, which are endowed with the application of various sentiments (rasas) and emotional states (bhāvas), those who know the art must always employ the marvelous sentiment (adbhuta-rasa). 43.
I have thus duly proclaimed the characteristics of the drama (nāṭaka) in brief;
hereafter, I shall describe the characteristics of the play of intrigue (prakaraṇa) according to the rules.
In this [drama], the poet, by his own power, [depicts] the subject matter, the plot-structure, and the hero;

some [of these elements] are completed at the Opening juncture (*mukha-sandhi*), some extend as far as the Development (*pratimukha*), others conclude at the Crisis (*avamarśa*), and still others culminate in the Conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*). For example:

In the *Ratnāvalī*, the festival of joy (*pramodotsava*) is concluded within the *mukhasandhi* itself; thus, the narrative of Bābhravya, introduced in the *mukha*, reaches its conclusion in the *nirvahaṇa*. Furthermore, the essential elements (*sārarūpa-padartha*) should be placed at the end.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "Of all poetic compositions. In dramas and other such works, the marvelous rasa (*adbhuta-rasa*) must be employed in the *nirvahaṇa* (concluding) juncture. For it is in this way that those poetic compositions become properly connected to one another through the skillful arrangement of rasas and bhāvas; otherwise, they would not be so. And without a unified syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), what would be the purpose of the composition? Thus it is said:

Through the sentiments of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the heroic (*vīra*), and the furious (*raudra*), there arise the attainment of a jewel among women, the acquisition of the earth, and the destruction of enemies;

through the pathetic (*karuṇa*) and other sentiments, their cessation occurs. By this sequence, when supramundane and inconceivable desires are attained, there must be the sentiment of the marvelous (*adbhuta*). For if an extraordinary gain is conceived as the fruit [of the action], it necessarily [elicits wonder].
Since there is indeed some slight fruit of action, why would one depend on the instruction of means therein? Thus, the conclusion that [action] is not to be performed is a wonder.
How could such a thought arise in the minds of those being instructed: "Aha! Even what is difficult to achieve is accomplished through the sequence of means"?

"One must proceed by means of skillful methods. This summarizes what was stated previously and introduces another point to be discussed: "This is the definition of a drama," and so forth. While in some cases the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) is already well-known, here he shows that it is to be established with effort precisely through the power of its definition (*lakṣaṇa*). "By means of the logic of the definition" (*lakṣaṇayuktyā*) means by way of the definition.

The meaning is: "by means of" refers to the method of entering the heart, which serves as the cause and is that which is to be accomplished. In this regard, he states the name and etymology of this section along with its divisions and characteristics, beginning with the words "wherein the poet, by his own power... Here, "subject matter" (*vastu*) refers to the goal or fruit (*sādhya-phala*), and "body" (*śarīra*) refers to the means for attaining that subject matter and so forth.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: that which one composes by means of poetry, through one's own power, concerning the subject matter of poetry, should be known by the wise as a *prakaraṇa* (dramatic monologue). Where...
It should be understood by the wise that this is a treatise composed from the very beginning. || 45 ||

That which is not based on the words of a seer (anārṣa), which is not borrowed from others, and which composes poetry endowed with non-existent qualities, having a subject matter whose seed has already arisen—that too should be known as a *prakaraṇa* (drama). || 46 ||
Whatever has been stated by me regarding the subject matter, the body [of the plot], and the varieties of dramatic styles (vṛtti) in the case of the *nāṭaka*,
that should also be applied to the *prakaraṇa*, along with its defining characteristics, across all the junctures (*saṃdhi*).

In order to show that there is no part therein which is unproduced—and thus not situated anywhere as something to be grasped—he says, "that which is non-Vedic," and so forth. "Non-Vedic" refers to works such as the life story of Mūladeva, composed in the *Bṛhatkathā* and other texts distinct from the Purāṇas and similar scriptures. "Fabricated" (āhārya) means...
[The plot] such as the exploits of Samudradatta and so forth is to be extracted from the poetry of previous poets.
Now, one might object: "Since there is an absence of the author's own creative agency (*kavitva*) regarding that portion, how can the term 'play' (*prakaraṇa*) be applied? To this he replies:

"That [work] in which the seed and the subject matter are already established and pre-existent—even though it is of such a nature—it is [called a play] because of its *vastu* (subject matter) consisting of real entities."

Because it is composed as something endowed with qualities well-known from other poetic works such as the *Bṛhatkathā*, for that reason this too is a *prakaraṇa*. Thus, when the poet’s creative power provides an expansion (*adhikāvāpa*) of characters established in the *Bṛhatkathā* and so forth—such as Mūladeva and others—it is then a *prakaraṇa*. In this way...

The intended meaning is that even when describing the actions of Samudradatta and others as imagined by previous poets, the poet should compose the *prakaraṇa* by adding further details. Now, having raised the doubt as to how this [present] narrative (*vṛtta*) is to be applied, he says "that which is in the *nāṭaka*" in order to remind us of what was previously stated by means of an extension (*atideśa*).
As for my statement "thus it has been said":

by the phrase "endowed with various manifestations" (*nānāvibhūtiyukta*) and so forth, the possession of the fruit of the hero (*nāyakaphalavatva*) has been stated; that is the "body of the matter" (*vastuśarīra*). Furthermore, [the drama] is rich in acts (*aṅka*) and interludes (*praveśaka*), and possesses the various dramatic modes (*vṛtti*).

"By means of various tastes, dispositions, and gestures in many ways, it is characterized by the production of pleasure and pain"— this is the definition provided for the *aṅka* (act) and the *praveśaka* (interlude).
However, some maintain that this meaning is already established by the mention of the "body" (*śarīra*).

Therefore, "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the measurement of the act (*aṅka-parimāṇa*), as well as the requirements to be employed in the *praveśakas* that serve as the cause for connecting one act to another—
such as the statement [on page 431]: "If the business at the close of day can be accomplished by means of an act," and so forth.
That which consists of the manifold life-stories of Brahmins, merchants, ministers, priests, counselors, and caravan leaders is to be known as the *Prakaraṇa* (the genre of the play). 48.
That which does not feature a noble hero, nor celestial deeds, nor royal enjoyment, and which involves common people—that should be known as a *prakaraṇa* by those who know it. (49)

In a *prakaraṇa*, however, a play should be composed featuring servants, rogues, and merchants, involving the services of courtesans and women from low-born families, and depicting the conduct of women of humble status. (50)

All such [examples] are to be applied to this context as well. With the two verses beginning with *vipravaṇijam*, he wards off the excessive extension (*atiprasaṅga*) resulting from the principle of analogy (*atideśa*). A *saciva* is a counselor; an *amātya* is an official;
a *sārthavāha* is one who brings goods [for trade], whereas merchants (*vaṇijaḥ*) are others who engage in buying and selling in that region.

"Of many kinds" (*naikavidham*) means "joined with many sentiments" (*anekarasa-yuktam*). By saying "not prescribed by another sentiment" (*naikarasāntara-vihitaḥ*), it is indicated that this is merely an extension of that [rule]. With the phrase "renowned and noble" (*prakhyātodātta*), what was applicable is negated by the words "not noble" (*nodātta*).
And by that negation, by implication, the opposite applies to the *nāṭaka*. Furthermore, in the *nāṭaka*, a deity [is not the hero]; rather, the hero is...

He states "not a divine deed" (*na divyacaritam*) because [the rule] "it is forbidden" (*niṣiddha*) implies that [such a thing] would otherwise be introduced as something to be performed within the context. Likewise, by saying "not based on the divine" (*na divyāśrayam*), he prohibits even that which might follow from the lack of instruction regarding the employment of deities; for just as in a drama, one might suspect the entry of deities here as well, he refutes this.

Regarding the phrase "royal enjoyment": even though [the drama] is innate [in nature], this teaches that one should not imagine royal enjoyments for Brahmins and others; for this very reason, there is a restriction concerning the king. The "appropriate attendants" refer to those such as chamberlains and the like belonging to the inner apartments;
distinct from them, "external people" such as servants, slaves, and so forth, are to be employed in the *praveśaka* (interlude) and similar sections.
This is the meaning.

He demonstrates this very point by saying "accompanied by a servant, a *viṭa*, and a merchant"; that is to say, a servant (*dāsa*) takes the place of the chamberlain (*kañcukin*), a *viṭa* takes the place of the *vidūṣaka*, and a merchant (*śreṣṭhin*) takes the place of the minister (*amātya*). A *veśa* is a brothel; [the phrase refers to] a woman who is there.

The conduct regarding women of good family (*kulastrī*) is that which is endowed with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) for which the practice (*upacāra*) described in the *Vaiśika* (A-23) serves as the cause; it is that in which [the behavior] is slow. However, the teachers [hold that] it is the conduct of women from modest families.
(432) Where there is talk of the houses of the best ministers, merchants, Brahmins, priests, counselors, and caravan leaders, a courtesan should not be employed there. || 51 ||
If it is associated with a courtesan, there would be no union even with a woman of noble family; likewise, if it is associated with a woman of noble family, there would be no courtesan therein. (52)
By saying "where [this occurs]," it is shown that even a woman of noble family becomes as if of low birth there.

It is with this very intention that the doubt raised by Samudradatta upon hearing the words "Aśokadatta" and so forth in the *Puṣpadūṣitaka* is not a fault, for it serves a purpose up until the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*).

The banishment of Nandayantī and her subsequent residence within the house constitute the very root of the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture), because it is rooted in the suspicion regarding another man. For if this were not accepted, there would have been no cause for the banishment of the daughter-in-law by her father-in-law while the son was absent.

It is simply inconsistent for those of the highest rank to reside in the house of a Śabara chieftain. Therefore, this status of "highest rank" was attributed to the merchants—who are currently the highest-ranking persons suitable for a king—only with respect to their own class; as for the reproach made on that basis, it does not affect the reputation of Brahmayaśas or Svāmiyaśas.

Even if it is broken, it is indeed one's own fame. For those who strive to falsely stain [him] with infamy, it is only their own fame that is diminished; thus, he remains as one whose only remaining possession is his reputation. Indeed, suspicion and the like are not improper merely because of the title "Nāyaka" (hero), as in the case of Duryodhana. For in this context...
The hero is indeed of that same nature; let him simply be superior to other merchants and worthy of instruction in that very field—enough of this digression.
Now, for each of these seven types of *prakaraṇa*, there are three subdivisions.

To demonstrate this, he recites three Āryā verses beginning with "saciva" and so forth: In a work where the subject matter (*vārtā*) appropriate for householders—namely, the narrative (*itivṛtta*) that accomplishes the aims of man—is connected to ministers and the like, a courtesan should not be composed as the heroine (*nāyikā*); however, she may be so composed when the characters are rogues (*viṭa*) and the like who have been made the heroes (*nāyaka*).

It is thus stated that she, too, must be connected within the contemplation of the householder's life. If there were no description of the householder’s life, it would follow by implication that, just as for merchants, caravan leaders, and others, union with a courtesan is not contradictory for Brahmins and the like, and therefore she too should be presented. However, in that regard, it is not...
One should engage in union with a woman of noble family (*kulastrī*). Thus it is said: "If [the woman] is a courtesan's young girl," and "if she is employed by a man of noble family.

In this way, two pure types of [union] have been described regarding merchants, ministers, and so forth; however, that which concerns actors (*viṭha*) and the like is exclusively mixed (*saṃkīrṇa*), as it occurs with both courtesans and women born of noble families.
Alternatively, if there should be an act of service performed by a woman of a particular house or family according to the logic of the cause,
then the recitation (*pāṭhya*) should be employed there with unaltered speech and conduct. (53)
In this context, the *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) should always be employed by persons of middle status;
it follows the Sanskrit language, is concise in meaning, and is like a *praveśaka* (entrance scene).
The Viṣkambhaka should also be performed in two ways: pure (śuddha) or mixed (saṃkīrṇa).
The pure type involves a middle-class character, while the mixed type is composed of low and middle-class characters. || 55 ||
Thus it is said: "Or else, by the reasoning of the cause (*kāraṇayukti*). Because the courtesan (*veśastrī*) is the primary character in the *viṭa* (the parasite), she was mentioned first;
