however, the noblewoman (*kulastri*) is mentioned even there [in that context] due to her deference toward her father, grandfather, and so forth—this is what is expressed by the word "cause. The unaltered speech of the noblewoman is *Śaurasenī*, while that of the courtesan is *Sanskrit*. As for conduct (*ācāra*), it belongs to the noblewoman.
One who is preeminent in discipline is the opposite in another case. And so, in the *Devīcandragupta*,
there is the speech of Mādhava directed toward Vasantasenā (or rather, the speech of Candragupta directed toward Mādhavasenā):
O fair-faced one, he—who bound tears of joy to his eyes that possessed the luster of white and dark-blue lotuses; who spread perspiration over his bristling limbs;
and who brought about an increase in the fullness of his hips—[was thus transformed].
"Even by one who did not touch you, the knot of your lower garment has been loosened by your very sighs.

For here, the person to be instructed is indeed of such a kind, and the conduct [described] is likewise; thus it stands. There are twenty-one varieties in the *prakaraṇa* (drama). These are generally useful in the *prakaraṇa* with respect to the hero.

Since they occur only in the middle [of the play], the intention here is that the *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) is predominantly associated with them; with this in mind, he defines the *viṣkambhaka* in the treatise as "by persons of middle status.
It is called a *viṣkambhaka* because it "stretches across" (*viṣkambhayati*) or supports [the plot]. And it is accompanied by speech in the refined (*saṃskṛta*) language.

Since the mixed [form] also exists, the *viṣkambhaka* should be employed by means of the *praveśaka*, intending that very performance of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) as what is to be done. He clarifies that very purposeful action on page 434:

A *praveśaka* (interlude), established between acts (*aṅka*), should be performed in brief after observing the requirements of the action, as well as the purposes of the junctures (*sandhi*) and the plot elements (*artha*). || 56 ||
Furthermore, due to the connection with these two [types of heroes], practitioners must effect a distinction between them;
however, the other [type] is well-known in the application of either a *nāṭaka* or a *prakaraṇa*. (57)

"In brief, [this concerns] the junctures (*sandhi*) and the matters (*artha*). This means that the *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) should be employed between one act (*aṅka*) and another— or within an act— keeping in mind the summary of the junctures and the summary of the matters such as war, the loss of a kingdom, and so forth.

But surely this intermediate movement, which is to be employed by a character of middle status and serves to connect the *mukha* (opening) and *saṃdhi* (joint) of the drama, has been prescribed by Kohala at intervals within the *mukhāṅka*.
For it is said: "In the composition of a drama, a *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) should be performed just like a *praveśaka* (entrance scene)."
How then can it be said that [the Viṣkambhaka] follows another act? There is no fault here, for this is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). To explain:

first, the seed (*bīja*) and the drop (*bindu*) are introduced; and since ordinary people have not yet gained entry into them, and because they fall within the domain of ministers and the like, it is said that when these are introduced, the opportunity belongs exclusively to the Viṣkambhaka.

Since the concealment of counsel is equally required within the intervals of those [acts] as well, the introduction of a *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) there is likewise unrestricted. Furthermore, it is logical that where even an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is made to participate in deliberations on counsel, the *praveśaka* (entrance-scene) is not suitable for the initial presentation of the plot.

In general, because it "follows the intervals" (*aṅkāntarānusārī*), the phrase "in the middle of an interval" (*aṅkasya madhye*) already implies that it occurs within the middle of a *prastāvanā* (prologue) interval. Regarding the *praveśaka* (interlude) and *viṣkambhaka* (transition),
since gender and number are not restrictive, there may also be the entrance of women and an excess in the number [of characters].

Thus, through the *nāṭaka*, instruction regarding all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) is provided for the principal [audience], who are like kings; and through the *prakaraṇa*, it is provided for those of middle standing. Furthermore, because even therein a single act (*viśaka*) is mentioned for one possessed of unprecedented curiosity, there is a manifold instruction. In that regard, due to the overlapping nature of the definitions of the dramatic forms (*rūpaka*), [the distinction is established].

It was stated in the general definition that there are many varieties. In this regard, since the confusion of definitions for the *nāṭaka* and *prakaraṇa*— which are the primary forms that cause the proliferation of all dramatic genres (*rūpaka*)— has been demonstrated, it is with the intention that by means of them, the vision of all dramatic genres is achieved, that [the author] states the following.
(435) Based on the distinction between the *prakaraṇa* and the *nāṭaka*, the plot should be invented, the hero a king,
and it should be composed concerning a maiden from the harem or a concert hall. || 58 ||

It consists mostly of women, possesses four musical beats (*caturaṅka*), is characterized by graceful acting (*lalitābhinaya*), has well-arranged limbs, abounds in dance, song, and recitation, and is essentially devoted to the enjoyment of love (*ratisambhoga*). || 59 ||

The *nāṭikā* should be known as one characterized by royal etiquette, involving conciliation, anger, and deceit; it features a heroine who is a queen, includes female messengers, and possesses a retinue. (60)

It is worthy of being seen. However, following the order of the enumeration, he recites three verses beginning with "due to the distinction from the *prakaraṇa* and the *nāṭaka*," with the intention that there would otherwise be prolixity in detailing their characteristics and heaviness in the subsequent examination of those characteristics.
[The phrase] "due to the distinction from the *prakaraṇa* and the *nāṭaka*" means because of its difference from the *prakaraṇa* and the *nāṭaka*.

The connection with the distant [concluding statement] is: "A *nāṭikā* is to be known as such because of its difference in characteristics. It should be composed concerning an invented subject matter (*vastu*), an invented plot (*carita*), and a king as the hero, taking as the object to be attained a maiden from the inner apartments, a maiden from the music hall, or a courtesan. It is that in which women generally, or for the most part, predominate.

The meaning is that it should consist of four acts (*aṅka*), wherein the essence of any given state is to be fully incorporated into the representation of that state. "Consisting of graceful acting" (*lalitābhinayātmikā*) means that this *Kaiśikī* style is composed [of its elements].
It is that in which all four *Kaiśikī* limbs (*aṅga*) are excellently and completely established. [This applies] to the limbs (*aṅga*), the body (*gātra*), and the neck (*kaṇṭha*).

In this case, because there is no qualification of its own limbs (*svāṅga*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is employed. Others, however, maintain that even this is not the opinion of the three sages (*munitraya*) and thus should be disregarded. In this [work], the enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) preceded by sexual union, characterized by the attainment of sovereignty and so forth, is the "self" (*ātman*), meaning the primary fruit; for this very reason, he says:

This shows that if a woman engaged in the customary practices and transactions of royal conduct should direct those transactions toward another, then anger, favor, and deception arising from her previous lover must necessarily occur; thus it says "by conciliation," where the mention of "anger" follows [favor] due to the requirements of the Āryā meter.

Anticipating the objection that "she who is angry is not mentioned as anyone at all," he says "nāyaka" (the hero). The meaning is: this [work] consists entirely of both—the heroine who belongs to the hero, such as Devī and others, and the female messenger (dūtī) employed regarding another heroine who is desired by him, along with her retinue—that is, she in whom there is an abundance of attendants; thus, everything therein is dominated by these two.
Furthermore,
this [non-existence] is indeed included within both of the two entities (bhāva), because it exists in relation to them.
For this very reason, these ten forms have indeed been declared. (61)
O Brahmins, I have thus briefly stated the characteristics of the *prakaraṇa* and the *nāṭaka*;
hereafter, I shall describe the *samavakāra* according to its defining features.
All [the requirements], such as the *nāndī* verses and so forth, are exactly as before. In that regard, one heroine has already been explained.
Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa and others, following the *Saṃgraha*, maintain that this *nāṭikā* consists of six acts.
However, the venerable Śaṅkuka, declaring that this is incorrect, explains it as having eight acts; for instance, there is the queen and the maiden...

Furthermore, [the hero] is fourfold according to the distinction between the famous (*khyāta*) and the unknown (*akhyāta*), while the maidens are twofold according to the distinction between those belonging to the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*) and those from the musical troupes (*saṅgītaka*).
Ghaṇṭaka and others say: "In works such as the *nāṭaka*, it is only this much—that the hero is a king—which is adopted; however, his being famous is not required.
Other than these two types, there are eight more, making sixteen varieties. Thus, the hero—

Those who read "nṛpatiḥ" as the first [word] supply "yatra" (wherein) and thus establish a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), whereby both [the king and the place] constitute the subject matter. Others, however, join the first half-verse of the *āryā* as a separate sentence altogether,
because of the distinction between contexts (*prakaraṇabheda*) and because of the characteristic of the context (*prakaraṇalakṣaṇāṃśa*), [stating that] the object to be produced is [the king].
Since the king is established as the hero according to the characteristics of drama (*nāṭaka*), the intention is that the *nāṭikā* is of such a nature.
Others, however, maintain that the *nāṭikā* differs from the *prakaraṇa* and the *nāṭaka*; for by the word *nāṭaka*, that which is to be performed (*abhineya*) is meant.
They say that in this [Nāṭikā], the designation as "female" (strītvena) is merely figurative (rūpakamātra) for the purpose of demonstrating delicacy;
thus, even though it is a *prakaraṇikā*, it is characterized by the *kaiśikī* style due to its association with heroes such as merchants (*sārthavāha*) and others.
And although the *nāṭikā* has been described in this way, nevertheless, the definitions of the *prakaraṇa* and the *nāṭaka* remain established in that manner.
With this intention, he concludes by stating, "The definition of the *prakaraṇa* and *nāṭaka*," and then introduces another topic with the words, "Henceforth I shall explain.
Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of abandoning the order of enumeration? It has already been stated that the enumeration here is not for the sake of mere counting.

Because of its preeminence, this sequence of topics is interrupted by the discussion of the *nāṭikā* and the *prakaraṇa*. Just as there is an abundance of material to be produced in the *nāṭaka* and the *prakaraṇa*, so too is there in the *samavakāra*, because it demonstrates the means for attaining the three aims of human life (*trivarga*). It is intended solely for those devoted to various deities.
With the intention that a particular means becomes worthy of respect through the recollection of its previous practice, the divine being is here excluded from the role of the hero; and his conduct,
in its most extensive form, is demonstrated through imitation.

For those elements that fall within its scope, such as *nirveda* (world-weariness) and the like, if they are absent, the performance lacks attractiveness, just like a single portion of an act (*aṅka*) within a drama; however, this is even more pronounced at the beginning of a drama.

The *Prakarana* is composed with gods and asuras as its seeds, features a renowned and noble hero, consists of three acts, possesses three types of deception (*kapaṭa*), three types of calamity (*vidrava*), and three types of erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). (63)
It consists mostly of twelve leaders and measures eighteen channels;
I shall explain the method of its numerical arrangement according to how many channels exist therein.
The *Aṅka*, however, should be composed with laughter, with flight, with deceit, and with the *vīthī*;
it should consist of twelve *nāḍīs* and be endowed with dramatic action. (65)
It has been stated in works such as the *Nāṭaka* that conduct is not truly "pleasing" (*rañjaka*) unless it is accompanied by a group of various "pleasing factors" (*aṅgarañjaka*);

for this reason, the prohibition against a divine hero is mentioned there. For in those [dramatic works], kings and others are instructed regarding great fruits that entail abundant results and must be achieved through great effort; but it is not so here.
However, [this applies] only to those whose means consist of the three aims of life (*trivarga*).

As for other types of dramas, they do not have the three aims as their means because they consist of a single act (*ekāṅka*). Furthermore, although the *ḍima* consists of four acts, it is mentioned later;
we shall explain the reason for this in its definition. Therefore:

Because it elucidates the three aims of human life (trivarga) and possesses numerous constituent parts, its mention immediately following that [type of] metaphor is appropriate; enough of this prolixity.
That which is the seed of the conflict between gods and asuras, and the means for the attainment of its fruit, was made—that is, composed—by him. The gods and asuras, too...

The word "renowned" (*prakhyāta*) is used for the purpose of excluding those [beings] who are not well-known— such as those in the *Bṛhatkathā* and other works— who are either heard of [only in such texts] or are merely inferred by someone on their own. Although gods are more exalted than human beings, they are nevertheless called "exalted" (*udātta*) because they are primarily characterized by profundity relative to themselves.
The Blessed One, the enemy of Tripura (Śiva), and others are peaceful; Brahmā and others are haughty;

Nṛsiṃha and others are fierce. In this regard, it is stated that when [these three] are fully present, it is called a "three-act" play (*tryaṅka*). Furthermore, the three subjects—deceit, flight, and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*)—are each of three kinds therein, in every act.

The three [elements], beginning with flight (*vidrava*), are as follows: deceit (*kapaṭa*) pertains to the portion concerning the means; the apprehension of misfortune (*vyāpatti-sambhāvanā*) pertains to the portion concerning the obstacle;

and the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) pertains to the portion concerning the fruit. This applies likewise to the second and third acts. Some maintain that each act should abound in twelve principal characters (*nāyaka*). Others, however, hold that in each act there should be a hero (*nāyaka*), an antagonist (*pratināyaka*), and their respective assistants (*sahāya*).

For [the duration of] twelve [hours] is in consideration of the four-day cycle as a whole. By the statement "accompanied by laughter," he indicates that the erotic sentiment of love (*kāma-śṛṅgāra*) should be employed in the first act, because laughter (*hāsya*) enters therein.
"Endowed with action" means [it is characterized by] the erotic sentiment of love consisting of those things to be accomplished within the span of twelve *ghaṭikās*.
The second [type of] deceptive flight should be performed by relying on four *nāḍikās*.
That which is prescribed for the entry into the object (vastu-samāpanna) consists of two nāḍīs; however, the third [consists of three]. || 66 ||
The term "nāḍī" should be understood as the measure of time known as half a muhūrta;
that is the standard for a nāḍikā, which is to be added to the numerical figures as previously stated.
That which is designated by the term "nāḍikā" is established through action within the division of time;
it must be performed with effort according to the sequence prescribed in the scriptures. (68)
In a poetic composition, one act should be followed by another act with a different subject matter;
for in a *samavakāra*, they desire the plot to be unconnected [to the preceding]. (69)
The intended meaning is that one should compose the first act by means of expedients (*upāya*) characterized by *sānala* (with fire).

In the second act, [the plot] proceeds by means of expedients such as deception (*kapaṭa*) lasting for four *ghaṭikās*; however, in the third act, the entire matter is concluded by means of expedients accomplished within two *ghaṭikās*, even though this applies to each individual act.

Although there is a completion of the subject matter (*vastu*), nevertheless, by the mention of "completion of the subject matter" in the third [section], this is what is stated: first, the meaning of the three factors (*aṅga*) must be introduced regarding the seed (*bīja*);
immediately thereafter, the fulfillment of the intermediate sentence-meanings (*avāntaravākyārtha*) in the two [remaining] factors must be established as mutually qualified.

In the third act, however, there is the meaning of the intermediate sentences; that third [act] is connected with those two. In this way, everything becomes connected precisely as the cause for the accomplishment of the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*). For thus, even the vision of one who possesses continuity of thought becomes graced by the proficiency in the means for accomplishing the three aims of human life (*trivarga*).

"Even without a continuous sequence, it is completed by that much through the power of resonance within one's own heart regarding that much of the means. For this very reason, where the subject matter is thus bound and scattered, it is a *samavakāra*; he says 'act after act' (*aṅko'ṅkaḥ*) to indicate the contrast, for there is no connection of three acts."

"Mark against mark" means one after another. Regarding "the composition of a poem": the meaning is that every element is closely integrated into the poetic structure; otherwise, how could there be this boastful claim that "in a *samavakāra*, there is but a single action"?

He states this very point through an etymological explanation: "For *artha* [is] *samavakāra*. Regarding the word *samavakāra*, they maintain that the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is something unrelated—that is, not too closely connected—and yet somewhat related to a real entity (*vastu*).
Fleeing should be understood as being of three kinds: that arising from battle or water, that caused by the agitation of wind, fire, or great elephants, or that born from the siege of a city. (70)

In this context, deceit should be understood as being threefold: that which is determined by the sequence of actual circumstances, that which arises through the power of fate, or that which is instigated by another, resulting in the production of pleasure or pain. || 71 ||
In this regard, those who know the rules should separately apply the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) according to its specific requirements for the sake of dharma, artha, and kāma. (72)

By the force of the prefix *sam-* and the force of the prefix *ava-*, excellence (*atiśaya*) expressed by the prefix *prati-* is negated. It has been stated that there is "threefold flight" (*trividrava*);

that triad must now be explained. Whether caused by the insentient, caused by another, or caused by both, whatever object is of the nature of misfortune from which people flee—that is "flight," and it is of three kinds.

In that context, the mention of water, wind, and so forth is intended to illustrate what is produced by non-sentient beings; the lordly elephant serves as the illustration for what is produced by sentient beings;
and the siege of a city illustrates what is produced by both, because it is accomplished through means such as the setting of battle-fires and the like.
Deceit (*kapaṭa*) is fraud; its "resort" (*āśrayaṇa*) is its adoption. In that regard, fraud is threefold, consisting solely of the intellect.
Sometimes deception occurs through mere artifice; for that [deception] is established by the sequence inherent in the object.
The "object" is the result; the "agent" is one who brings about that result upon its attainment; and the "sequence" is the method, such as the planning of means, by which it is established.
This refers to a case where a person is deceived by a deceiver even though they have committed no offense. However, in a case where even the one being deceived...

If it is argued that there is no distinction between one who is at fault and one who is deceived by another because the deceiver lacks the intention to deceive regarding that offense— this is not possible, since in the absence of the desire to deceive, the accomplishment of deception is impossible. However, in cases where neither of the two parties possesses any fault of intentional design, [the occurrence happens] by chance (*kākatālīyena*).

Even for two who intend the same result, one may be joined with increase while the other is joined with decrease; in that case, the deception is brought about by fate (*daiva*). Nor does the happiness of one produce the suffering of another.
In the phrase "in dharma, in artha, and in kāma," the locative case expresses both the state of being an effect and the state of being a cause. Therefore, dharma...
Where there is either a cause or a virtuous means for the attainment of a heroine, that is *dharmasṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment of duty).
The same should be stated regarding *artha* (wealth) and *kāma* (pleasure). Where it is called *sṛṅgāra*, the young woman who is its object is designated as such;
where she is to be obtained through the practice of vows and other disciplines—[that is *dharmasṛṅgāra*].
That in which there is a manifold means for attaining Dharma that is beneficial to oneself,
and which is joined with vows, observances, and asceticism— this should be known as *dharma-śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment of Dharma). || 73 ||

The erotic sentiment of wealth (*arthāśṛṅgāra*) arises from the connection with desire for wealth in its many forms, or where there is pleasure (*rati*) directed toward women and objects of enjoyment for the sake of wealth. (74)

Whether it be caused by the plucking of a maiden's hair, or whether it be delightful for a man and woman who have come together, that erotic passion (kāma-śṛṅgāra) may be either secret or full of excitement. || 75 ||

And when [the goal] is attained, the connection is that self-benefit in the form of a longing for Dharma—such as sacrifices and so forth performed through union with a wife—is accomplished. "In many ways" means by way of distinctions such as kingdom, land, cattle, gold, and so on. "Great regard for pleasure for the sake of wealth" refers to both women and men.

Now, some say: "How can there be a desire for wealth among the gods? It is indeed possible among Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and others. Others say: "Whatever is to be sought after, that object exists even among the gods; therefore, this [desire] is possible there as well. But the Teachers (Upādhyāyas) say:
"In that case, the attainment of the two protagonists occurs only through another [intermediary], just as in the case of the Blessed Lord, the husband of Bhavānī."
The union with the daughter of the Mountain King (Pārvatī) by Śiva and the others serves to liberate them from their own kingdoms occupied by Tāraka.

"Lust for the maiden" means the hero's desire for her and her desire for him, brought about by mutual passion. "Secretly" refers to the attainment of garden settings and other locations by the woman and man.

If, preceded by concealment, one openly declares "I am indeed he," that erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is motivated solely by desire (*kāma*). Furthermore, in this context, the woman intended is another's wife (*parastrī*), such as Ahalyā in the case of Śakra. [Objection: But if there is a connection with the erotic sentiment in poetry, would there not be a deficiency in the *kaiśikī* style? For it is said that there is a lack [of certain elements] in the *kaiśikī* mode (*vṛtti*).
In that regard, the summary is as follows:
because of the absence of the four elements such as *narma* (jesting), as well as the embellishing factors of song, dance, instrumental music, and so forth, [the style] is *kaiśikī*.
In the *samavakāra*, poets should employ the *uṣṇih*, *gāyatrī*, and other such meters, as well as those with complex and intricate structures. (76)
Thus should the *samavakāra*, which relies upon various sentiments (*rasa*), be composed by those who know it.
Hereafter, I shall also describe the characteristics of the *īhāmṛga*.

It is brought about by the intervention of divine beings, involves a battle instigated for the sake of a celestial woman, is composed of well-arranged matters, and indeed produces a sense of wonder. || 78 ||

It consists mostly of haughty men and is composed of poetic works bound by the anger of women; thus it is deficient here. However, the teachers say that the *Kaiśikī* style does not arise merely from the presence of desire, because it is absent in those of a fierce (*raudra*) nature. That form which is characterized primarily by grace (*vilāsa*)— [The text continues: ...is the *Kaiśikī*. It is said to be the source of all [styles], for it is the most beautiful among them. It is also called *Sāttvatī*, because it arises from the essence (*sattva*). Furthermore, it is called *Kaiśikī* because it originates from the city of Kaiśika. It is also known as *Vaidarbhī*, because it is the most excellent (*vidarbha*) among all [styles]. It is also called *Lalitā*, because it is full of charm (*lalita*). It is also called *Madhurā*, because it is sweet (*madhura*). It is also called *Mṛdvī*, because it is soft (*mṛdu*). It is also called *Saumyā*, because it is gentle (*saumya*). It is also called *Prauḍhā*, because it is mature (*prauḍha*). It is also called *Vinītā*, because it is disciplined (*vinīta*). It is also called *Udārā*, because it is noble (*udāra*). It is also called *Vibhramavatī*, because it possesses graceful movements (*vibhrama*). It is also called *Hāvavatī*, because it possesses amorous gestures (*hāva*). It is also called *Bhāvavatī*, because it possesses emotional states (*bhāva*). It is also called *Rasavatī*, because it possesses aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). It is also called *Alaṃkāravatī*, because it possesses ornaments (*alaṃkāra*). It is also called *Śobhāvatī*, because it possesses beauty (*śobhā*). It is also called *Kāntimatī*, because it possesses loveliness (*kānti*). It is also called *Prasādavatī*, because it possesses clarity (*prasāda*). It is also called *Mādhuryavatī*, because it possesses sweetness (*mādhurya*). It is also called *Audāryavatī*, because it possesses nobility (*audārya*). It is also called *Gāmbhīryavatī*, because it possesses depth (*gāmbhīrya*). It is also called *Lāvaṇyavatī*, because it possesses charm (*lāvaṇya*). It is also called *Vilāsavatī*, because it possesses grace (*vilāsa*). It is also called *Hāsavatī*, because it possesses laughter (*hāsa*). It is also called *Rativatī*, because it possesses love (*rati*). It is also called *Harṣavatī*, because it possesses joy (*harṣa*). It is also called *Āhlādavatī*, because it possesses delight (*āhlāda*). It is also called *Anandavatī*, because it possesses bliss (*ānanda*). It is also called *Mohavatī*, because it possesses infatuation (*moha*). It is also called *Vismayavatī*, because it possesses wonder (*vismaya*). It is also called *Adbhutavatī*, because it possesses the marvelous (*adbhuta*). It is also called *Camatkāravatī*, because it possesses aesthetic astonishment (*camatkāra*). It is also called *Cittavatī*, because it possesses the mind (*citta*). It is also called *Manovatī*, because it possesses the mental faculty (*manas*). It is also called *Buddhivatī*, because it possesses intelligence (*buddhi*). It is also called *Jñānavatī*, because it possesses knowledge (*jñāna*). It is also called *Pratyayavatī*, because it possesses cognition (*pratyaya*). It is also called *Vikalpavatī*, because it possesses conceptualization (*vikalpa*). It is also called *Nirvikalpavatī*, because it is free from conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*). It is also called *Śūnyavatī*, because it is empty (*śūnya*). It is also called *Anātmavatī*, because it is selfless (*anātman*). It is also called *Dharmavatī*, because it possesses the Dharma (*dharma*). It is also called *Adharmavatī*, because it possesses non-Dharma (*adharma*). It is also called *Karmavatī*, because it possesses action (*karman*). It is also called *Akarmavatī*, because it is free from action (*akarma*). It is also called *Phalavatī*, because it possesses fruit (*phala*). It is also called *Aphalavatī*, because it is free from fruit (*aphala*). It is also called *Upāyavatī*, because it possesses means (*upāya*). It is also called *Anupāyavatī*, because it is free from means (*anupāya*). It is also called *Sādhanavatī*, because it possesses the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). It is also called *Asādhanavatī*, because it is free from the means of accomplishment (*asādhana*). It is also called *Siddhivatī*, because it possesses perfection (*siddhi*). It is also called *Asiddhivatī*, because it is free from perfection (*asiddhi*). It is also called *Yogavatī*, because it possesses yoga (*yoga*). It is also called *Ayogavatī*, because it is free from yoga (*ayoga*). It is also called *Samādhivatī*, because it possesses meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It is also called *Asamādhivatī*, because it is free from meditative concentration (*asamādhi*). It is also called *Jñānavatī*, because it possesses wisdom (*jñāna*). It is also called *Ajñānavatī*, because it is free from wisdom (*ajñāna*). It is also called *Bodhivatī*, because it possesses awakening (*bodhi*). It is also called *Abodhivatī*, because it is free from awakening (*abodhi*). It is also called *Mokṣavatī*, because it possesses liberation (*mokṣa*). Thus, while the subject matter concerning human goals is, in the ultimate sense, restricted to the scope of the dramatic forms (*rūpaka*) and their constituent sentiments (*rasa*), nevertheless, due to the diversity of poetic styles (*vṛtti*), the employment of other sentiments also occurs therein as subordinate elements. In this way...
Because of the connection with activities dominated by that [sentiment], a variety of dramatic modes (*vṛtti*) is entirely appropriate here.

However, the *utsṛṣṭikāṅka*, the *prahasana*, and the *bhāṇa* are dominated by the sentiments of pathos (*karuṇa*), humor (*hāsya*), and wonder (*vismaya*), and thus they are primarily characterized by the *rañjaka-rasa* (the sentiment that delights). For this very reason, women, children, fools, and the like are the intended audience (*adhikārī*) here. And it is not the case that...

In this [play], the plot is expanded; yet even the variety of the plot is not present there. For instance, in the *Utsṛṣṭikāṅka*, the three [other] modes (*vṛtti*) are indeed prohibited by the words [of the text]; how then can the *Bhāratī* mode be the mode here?
For in the *karuṇa* (pathos), physical action (*ceṣṭā*) is not predominant, and the *Bhāratī* mode, consisting of lamentation, is merely its accessory. Therefore—

The function known as *phalasaṃvitti* (the perception of the fruit) must be admitted, its definition being the experience of the fruit of speech and action. This is necessary; otherwise, in states such as fainting or death, where speech and action are absent, there would be a total absence of function (*nirvṛttikatā*). Furthermore, if [it were argued that it occurs] with a view toward the desire for the goals of human life...
Regarding the Kaiśikī style, it is stated that two modes of conduct (*vṛtti*) should be discussed with reference to both dharma and artha.

Therefore, Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa maintains that only three modes of conduct are appropriate: conduct consisting of action (which may be either righteous or unrighteous), speech as its form, and the experience of the fruit resulting from those.
As it has been said:

"In the first [type of drama], there is a sixteenfold manifestation of the fruit through speech and gesture, and by means of the four aims of human life; however, from those two, it becomes manifold due to the distinctions of aesthetic flavor (rasa)."

Regarding this, some say: although the *kaiśikī* style can be included within the *sāttvatī*, it is nevertheless mentioned separately because of its superior power to delight; furthermore, it is distinct from the *mukhaja* (facial) acting, and it does not constitute an improper mode of conduct (*anyāyavṛtti*), since there is no contradiction in its being consistent with the attainment of the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*) when it functions as a fruit-bearing activity.

If the general characteristic of *vṛtti*—namely, its nature as an activity (*vyāpāra*)—does not exist, then how can there be the status of being a *vṛtti*? And if it does exist, since no mental activity distinct from vocal and physical gestures is established in common worldly experience, one must accept that it is merely a subtle form of vocal and physical gesture. Consequently, this [definition] applies even in cases such as death and fainting.

It can be said that the occurrence of the bodily activity consisting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself is what gives rise to the recollection [of objects], as well as to the movement of the *laya* and *tāla* rhythms and singing;
furthermore, it can be asserted that even conscious awareness (*saṃvedana*) does not exist during states such as fainting.
For it is richly endowed with all the characteristics of rasa and possessed of thirteen constituent parts (*aṅgas*).

How then [could it be otherwise]? Therefore, in that case, the *sāttvatī* style alone is the mode (*vṛtti*). If, however, the designation "this poem consists of style" is based on its predominance, it is like the designation of a collection of dramatic forms (*rūpaka*) as a whole.
Even though the individual parts (*khaṇḍa*) do not possess the function, the composite form (*rūpaka*) as a whole consists of functions;
for those who follow the view that [the self] is like a fragment, there is a fifth function characterized by self-awareness during states such as fainting,
which is inferred from the cessation of all activity and through the experience of the action of fainting.

Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa and others, who establish that external objects are by nature apprehended by mental states, consider that [the function of cognition] consists of an operation of the self delimited by its result, and do not regard mere physical movement as the sole form of operation.
[The opponent argues: "Since [the *parākṛta*] has been refuted, there is no such thing as a 'fruit-function' (*phalavṛtti*); thus, there are only four functions (*vṛttis*).

But we say: why this misplaced alarm? If whatever exists here in drama must be included within the [four] functions, then let it be so—but it is not thus. For what indeed is the stage (*raṅga*)? Is it a function?

Whether it be the drum, the small kettle-drum, the flute, or whatever else the mode of expression (*vṛtti*) may be, it is activity (*vyāpāra*) that accomplishes the human goal; and since that [activity] is described as existing everywhere, the modes of expression are the "matrix" (*mātṛkā*) of poetry.
Indeed, there is nothing that can be described devoid of activity.
Even in the description of intoxication, fainting, and so forth, because the mental operation known as *sāttvatī* is possible,

and even in the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa and others where both mental and physical operations are possible, the *bhāratī* style (*vṛtti*) is said to apply because verbal operation predominates. As for the exclusion of other styles:

Because its constituent parts are not fully developed; and it has been stated more than once that no other activity is possible apart from the activities of body, speech, and mind, or their various manifestations. Therefore, the *bhāratī* style of composition is characterized by compassion as its primary element due to the abundance of lamentation.

As for what Kohala stated—that the Kaiśikī style should be employed here with the erotic, comic, and pathetic sentiments—that must indeed be disregarded because it contradicts the opinion of the Sage (Bharata). His intention, however, was that wherever the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) is not coarse or intense, that is Kaiśikī. Likewise, in the case of the *prahasana* and *bhāṇa* genres as well, [the Kaiśikī applies] precisely because of the predominance of verbal activity.

Regarding the *bhāratī* style (*vṛtti*), in states such as fainting and the like, where there is an absence of activity, there is indeed an absence of the *vṛtti*. For it is not the case that every dramatic performance must be established as being identical with the Brahman of the *vṛttis*; enough, then, of this digression. Now, at the conclusion of all [the styles], because it consists of all aesthetic flavors (*rasas*) and because its nature is inferred [from them], [it is described] in brief:
Because it is primary insofar as it bestows the capacity for linguistic proficiency, and because its constituent parts range from the *nāṭikā* down to the *bhāṇa*,
The *vīthī* may consist of a single act (*ekāṅkā*), and likewise it may be performed by one actor (*ekahāryā*) or by two (*dvihāryā*). || 112 ||
It should be endowed with the three natures—low, high, and middle—and [the following elements]:
*udghātyaka*, *avalagita*, *avaspaṇḍita*, *nālikā*, and *satpralāpa*.
Vāk-keli, prapañca, mṛdava, ādhibala, chala, trigata,
vyāhāra, and gaṇḍa— these thirteen components of this [art of debate] have been declared.
Now the *vīthī* has been fully described; I shall explain their characteristics.
As for the words whose meaning is not yet understood, those men who [study them] again with devotion— (115)
When they employ other words [to express the same], that is called *uddhātyaka*.
Because it subsists upon *mastarūpaka*, he defines *vīthī*:
"by means of those to be carried by one" (*ekahāryaiḥ*) means "spoken by an imaginary person" (*ākāśapuruṣa*); "to be carried by two" (*dvihārya*)... [and so forth].

The meaning is: "by means of the variety of utterances and responses. He enumerates the constituent parts (aṅgas): the *udghātyaka*, *avalagita*, *aspandita*, *nālikā*, *satpralāpa*, *vākkelī*, *prapañca*, *mṛdava*, *adhivala*, and *chala*—these are the *trigata*.

"Discourse (vyāhāra) and the 'swelling' (gaṇḍa)—these thirteen members have been declared. This means that this is merely an illustration. He defines these in sequence with the words "but the words whose meaning is not understood."
(454) Where, having superimposed one thing upon another, a different task is accomplished. || 116 ||
And that should be known by the practitioners of drama as *āvalagita* (the "clinging" or "adherence").
Now, if its nature consists in the variety of their speech, what is its distinction from figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) and the like?

If, however, its nature consists in being an instrument for the plot (*itivṛtta*), how is it distinct from the structural components of the junctures (*sandhyaṅga*)? [In response: Its status as an instrument for rasa [is established] through other means.
They are included within the members of the *vṛtti*. Nor is there any general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) for them apart from these.

Regarding this, some have accepted that these [members] are indeed of the specific nature of the aforementioned definitions and so forth; however, the discerning ones say that these are distinct from those.

For instance, the variety produced by the connection of questions and answers through the form of another's intention is a constituent of the *vīthī* (the dramatic path). For this very reason, [examples] have been cited; this is their general definition.
The meaning is that these are the cited answers. And all of them [are necessary], because there is no poetry devoid of answers.

Therefore, they are understood as "variegated" (*vicitra*). For this very reason, a *vīthī* (a series) is so called because it consists of a row [of speeches] that cannot tolerate any other [response], being filled with variegated utterances and replies.

However, the distinction is that for figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) such as *lakṣaṇā*, there is no form restricted solely to utterance. In that regard, when one is capable of giving the intended reply—that which is mine...

When a questioner asks with the intention of eliciting a variety of answers— based on such motives as whether what is in the mind is exactly what is being said or not— and the respondent provides a fitting reply,
that answer is called *udghātyaka*. Since it consists of an "unveiling" (*udghāta*) in the form of a question, the suffix *kan* is applied there in the sense of something unknown.
Wise men skillfully join together words that have reached their intended meaning in the form of questions, using respectful synonyms as other words in the form of answers;
this collection of answer-words constitutes the *udghātyaka*. As in the *Pāṇḍavānanda*: [Example follows]

What is the ornament of the powerful? Forgiveness. What is this humiliation inflicted by one's own kinsmen? Dependence on others. What is suffering? Being sought after by others. Who is praiseworthy? He who is relied upon. What is death? Misfortune. By whom are sorrows abandoned? By those who have conquered their enemies.
By whom was this recognized by the Pāṇḍavas while they were living in disguise in the city of Virāṭa?

Regarding the term *yatrānyasmin*: when, while a subsequent [word] is being given—even though it is preceded by a connection to another [meaning]—another effect is accomplished, that is called *avalagitam* because of its clinging (*avalaganāt*) to another effect. For example, when the Vidūṣaka asks, "Does it delight the eyes? (*avi suhāadi de loaṇāṇām*), [the King], with difficulty, [answers] regarding his pair of thighs: "It delights" (*sukhayati*). What is this called? [It is *avalagitam*.]
Although the reply beginning with "mityādi" was uttered for the purpose of informing Vasantaka, it was directed toward Sāgarikā.
But when some object has been projected, whether arising from the auspicious or the inauspicious,
When another meaning is expressed through skillful artifice, that is its "vibration" (avaspandita).
A riddle (*prahelikā*) whose meaning is approached through humor should be known as *nālikā*. (118)

When a wise person speaks even what is beneficial in the company of foolish people, [it is as if] he accomplishes the primary task called *śṛṅgāra*, which is like the life-breath of a blind man. Regarding the phrase "but when [it is] rejected": fate, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [acts] non-intentionally toward some object.

When, even though something has been indicated, another subsequent meaning is expressed out of skill and a desire to conceal that [indicated] thing—this is *avaspandita*, because, like the twitching of an eye and so forth, it makes possible the suggestion of what lies within. For example:
"Those with excellent wings, sweet voices, who have adorned the quarters, and whose undertakings are arrogant with pride..."
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra fall upon the surface of the earth, subject to the power of time.

In this matter, by the force of fate, the following meaning has emerged: "Those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—who, though possessing sweet voices, have been excessively established in their own faction and have made the quarters of the sky full of legal claims (or, possessed of pledges)—are falling.
In that regard, the response is an inauspicious obstacle. Again, the Sūtradhāra says: "Indeed..."
By describing the autumn season, [the statement] "I designate the swans as the Dhārtarāṣṭras in the expanse of the sky" and so forth,
indicates nothing other than a lack of movement; for it is not that I do not know, but rather my heart is apprehensive because of its inauspicious nature.

A *prahelikā* (riddle) is that which has its meaning approached through humor; it is an answer that brings about the disclosure of another [hidden] meaning. For this very reason, it is called a *nālikā*, *praṇālikā*, or *vyāja*—meaning a deceptive device. It is a *prahelikā* because it consists primarily of playful jesting (*helikā*) and the like. For example: "For whose sake have you come here? He is right here."

[He] stands there. Sāgarikā: Friend, for whose sake? Susaṅgatā (with a laugh): Oh, do not be suspicious! This is merely a painted panel; thus, by this artifice, both its concealment and its hidden contents [are explained].
As for the reply "in the company of foolish people," which is actually beneficial to the fool—
As with verbal deception and the like, such things are dear to fools by virtue of their pleasant aspect, but not by virtue of their beneficial aspect; thus it becomes a form of artifice.
And his word is not accepted; he should be known as one whose speech is mere idle prattle.
In this application, *vākkelī* (verbal play) consists of one or two replies;
it is that speech between two people which is unreal yet accompanied by mutual praise.
And for the sake of a single purpose, that elaborate display of his would provoke laughter;

moreover, he resorts to duality because it is established. For in this way, even a temporary anger is preserved by speaking what is pleasing, while [the truth] is realized at a later time through speaking what is factual.
Just as when a prince addicted to vice asks, "What is happiness?", he is given this reply: "In every respect, for one who is victorious at dice and devoted to the consumption of wine,
the abundance of wealth and pleasures comes into his very hands."

"Idle chatter" (*asat-pralāpa*) refers to the prattling about things that are non-existent or improper; thus it is called "idle chatter. Regarding the phrase "giving one answer to two [questions]": this is a case where there is a single response for two [inquiries].
The mention of "two" is an illustration for "many. By this, the entire category of answers to questions is encompassed. For example:
When the clouds have vanished, what beauty do rivers display?
Who indeed are the external and internal enemies that must be conquered by the wise?

Regarding that which is "unreal" (*asadbhūta*): for example, in the *Ratnāvalī*, when the King asks Susaṅgatā, "How was I, being here, known by you?", Susaṅgatā replies with an elaborate narrative (*prapañca*) beginning with, "Not only by the fluttering of my heart, O Lord, but the Queen herself will inform you," and continuing until the bestowal of ornaments. To illustrate this further—of these two...
It was said that, based on the mutual relationship between Sāgarikā and Susaṅgatā and between the King and the Vidūṣaka, one should report to the Queen something marvelous and untrue;
and therein there is both praise— “By the favor of my lord, what is this to me?”— and even humor.

There is a form of jesting; furthermore, for the sake of a certain king’s purpose, it indeed serves as the cause for union with Sāgarikā—thus, because it is stated otherwise, there is elaboration (prapañca).
For the reason that the faulting of virtues would result from the act of dispute.
Alternatively, that which consists of transforming faults into virtues should be known as "gentleness" (tanmṛdutva).
It is that wherein the speech of another and one's own [speech] arise in successive succession for both parties.
The wise should understand that *adhibala* (relative strength) is that which qualifies the specific meaning of one another.
*Chala* (quibble) is a statement intended for another purpose, which causes deception, laughter, or anger;
it is so called because it is therein that the qualities of things are treated as defects, or the defects as qualities.

That is mildness. By the phrase "caused by a dispute," he states a distinction from the [previous] definition; the meaning is that this is another mode of operation (*vṛttyantara*), namely its inherent nature (*svabhāva*). For example, in the passage from the *Veṇīsaṃhāra* (Act 3): "Whether a dog, a crow, or the son of Drupada should touch my head"—here, the subordination of the fault (*doṣa*) to the quality (*guṇa*) occurs together with the hearing of the dispute.

In the passage from the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, "Weapons have been laid down by those whose hands are no longer armed with weapons," the very virtue of fulfilling one's vow is treated as a fault by Karna; this is indeed caused by the dispute. The word *mṛdava* means crushing (*mardana*);
he protects his own side by crushing the opposing side.

"Paravacanamātmanaśca" means the speech of another and one's own speech; that in which there is a mutual attainment of specific meanings through such exchange—wherein there arises a progressively superior meaning—is "adhibala. This is what is meant: in a sequence of statement and counter-statement...
When [the plot] is being enacted,
the "superior force" (*adhibala*) arises from the connection with a superior force that is well-constructed for one's own side, by virtue of the power of mutual reliance on intelligence.
For example, in the *Nāgānanda*, starting from the words "I understand it to be the seat of passion," and so forth, by the Vidūṣaka...
Having strengthened his own position through the sequence of *sahokti* (simultaneous mention), he says: "Indeed, everything beginning from my very body is maintained by me for the sake of others"—
this is a statement intended for another purpose, being a sentence uttered with a different objective in mind.
*Chala* (quibble) is that speech which, when uttered, produces laughter in one person, anger in another, or [other reactions] in yet another. For example:
"Who would not feel anger upon seeing the face of this woman with its bitten lip?"
O you who destroy all the bees and lotuses, endure this now with an unswerving mind.
p.
458) That in which many meanings are joined by means of logical arguments due to their similarity to the sacred scriptures (śruti)—
whether it be humorous or very humorous— that should be known as the *trigata*.
Direct speech is said to be a conversation intended for a slight joke;
it may be accompanied by agitation or excitement, involve a dispute, or be characterized by censure.
Those who know the truth call this a "gaṇḍa" (a swelling) produced by the implication of the plural number.

This statement, though addressed to the husband with reference to his connection to the female friend, is intended for the purpose of convincing him; it serves as a pretext regarding his wife's own relatives, resulting in mockery from clever people and laughter from the co-wife.

The statement generates anger. Because of the similarity of hearing—that is, the similarity of sound—the nature of the question and its answer is that many [implications] are applied through logical arguments; thus, it is by means of such justifications for interrogative intonation (*kāku*) and so forth.

The word *tri* (three) is an indicator for "many"; thus, *trigata* means that which has reached many objects. In ordinary discourse, the answer is primarily the last one, being common to many questions; however, here the distinction is that the question itself is the very same as the response. For example: [Example omitted per instructions]
"O Lord of all kings, this woman, beautiful in every limb, was seen by me in this lovely forest edge while she was separated from you, O Rāma. (In the *Vikramorvaśīya*,
this very statement serves as the answer, even when employed with an expectant intonation, in the case of a reflected image.)

Since the *kāku* (intonation) has become free of expectation, like the reversal of left and right, this results in laughter; in this way, "laughter" (*hāsya*) is to be illustrated. Regarding the phrase "functioning with respect to the perceptible" (*pratyakṣavṛtti*), by the word "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*), that which is about to become perceptible is meant.
Thus, the meaning is: he whose function [occurs] toward an object that is about to become perceptible due to the power of fate.

*Vyāhāra* is that by which various meanings are represented through performance; for example, [the verse] beginning with *uddāmotkalikām* (*Ratnāvalī* 2.1), which is "endowed with agitation and flurry. Here, "agitation" refers to a specific physical manifestation, and "flurry" is the resulting excitement; thus, whatever contradictory matter is performed by this [acting] constitutes precisely the sublation of the previously stated matter.

And that statement, because it contains a perceived meaning, is like a "gaṇḍa" (a swelling or protrusion); it is a "bahuvacana" (plural) statement that is slightly incomplete. By means of the challenge (ākṣepa) created by that, it has itself attained the status of a reply to the previous statement; this is the meaning. And so says Kohala:
(459) Thus, indeed, the entire prescription of the ten dramatic forms has been declared by me according to their defining characteristics. || 226 ||
Furthermore, I shall describe the characteristics pertaining to his body regarding the arrangement of the joints.
When there is a connection of words at the end, yet a lack of connection within the sentence itself,
such that it appears as if connected— this is the *gaṇḍa*, a constituent element (*vīthyaṅga*) of the dramatic structure.
By this, incompleteness alone is indicated. For example, Duryodhana says to Bhānumatī:
"O lady with thighs like a young elephant's trunk, my pair of thighs is quite sufficient to occupy your hips for a long time" (*Veṇīsaṃhāra*).
Having entered there, the chamberlain says: "The banner of your chariot has been broken by Bhīma’s violent wind.
In this context, although the phrase "the pair of thighs" was previously understood as being at rest, it now becomes fit to be connected with the word "broken."

The *vīthī* is endowed with these thirteen components (*aṅga*). Since it is designated as containing all aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), a hero—whether superior, middling, or inferior—necessarily appears therein according to the predominance of a particular sentiment in turn.
And thus says Kohala:
"Endowed with characters that are superior, inferior, or middling, and whether it is to be carried by one person or two, that is designated as a *vīthī*. Thus [it is said].
However, since it is certain that a character of inferior nature cannot be the hero (*nāyaka*), what could one say regarding the *prahasana*, *ka*, *bhāṇa*, and so forth?

For when the predominant sentiment is the comic (*hāsya*) and so forth, the hero is indeed considered inferior. One who is connected as the primary figure through the fruit of the plot's body is called the hero. Even in the absence of a [formal] hero, his status as inferior would not be something that should not be accepted; for his inclusion as a member of the retinue is certainly unrestricted everywhere.
Concluding the subject matter of the chapter, he connects it with what is to come, stating: "Thus is the prescription of the ten forms (daśarūpa).

By the phrase "by way of definition" (*lakṣaṇataḥ*), he means this: there are exactly ten such definitions; as for the examples, what need is there to count them? This has already been demonstrated previously. In that regard, their utility for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) is as follows:
Since it has already been demonstrated during the occasion for defining each respective characteristic, no tautology is admitted; may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the "Description of the Ten Types of Drama" in the *Bhāratīya Nāṭyaśāstra*. (p. 460)
The eighteenth chapter, titled "On Names," is completed.
Thus Abhinavagupta, who is intent on the service of the feet that serve as the crest-jewel adorned by the stainless and cool-rayed moon [Śiva],
has revealed the tenfold nature [of the Tantras] along with their true essence in a concealed manner.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Formulation of the Ten Types of Drama," in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on the *Nāṭya-veda* composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Abhinavagupta.
